p.h: Out hawking: Seydyak, a Kazakh tsarevich and Karacha
p.g: A year after the Russians founded Tobolsk on the hill opposite the Tobol mouth, the Tatar prince Seydyak, a Kazakh tsarevich named Saltan and Kuchum's counsellor Karacha rode out from the old Tatar capital Sibir 'for bird sport' (falconry) with five hundred Tatars. The voevoda invited them to a feast as if for peace talks; when the guests choked on the wine he had offered, he took it as a sign of treachery, had their men cut down and sent the princes to Moscow.
p.q: По поставленіи града Тоболска во второе лето, из града Сибири, от Чувашъ вышли для птичной потехи Татара князь Седякъ да царевичь Казачьей орды Салтанъ да царя Кучума думной Татаринъ Карача, с нимъ Татаръ пятьсотъ человекъ.
p.s: Esipov Chronicle (short redaction), in Sibirskie letopisi (1907)
p.pe: Prince Seydyak, Tsarevich Saltan of the 'Kazakh horde', Karacha (Kuchum's counsellor); voevoda Danila Chulkov
p.t: In the second year after the building of the town of Tobolsk, from the town of Sibir, from Chuvash, there came out for bird sport the Tatars Prince Sedyak and the tsarevich of the Kazakh horde Saltan and Tsar Kuchum's counsellor, the Tatar Karacha, and with them five hundred Tatars.
p.c: Told from the Russian side, which presents the massacre as a justified precaution.
p.tg: falconry hunting seydyak kazakh horde tobolsk feast

p.h: A Tartar prince's widow commands the frontier
p.g: At Gartok on the western frontier Desideri found a permanent force of Tartar and Tibetan soldiers guarding the fortress of Tashigang and watching everyone who entered Tibet. Its commander, a Tartar prince, had died, and his widow had taken over the command until a new governor arrived. Desideri and his companion travelled to Lhasa under her protection; later in the book he says this 'Tartar princess' retired to a nunnery near Shigatse.
p.q: in a large plain called Cartoà a strong, permanent force of Tartar and Tibetan soldiers was stationed not only for the defence of the frontier-fortress of Treéscy-Khang and the surrounding settlements, but more especially to watch all those who from that side entered the country. The commander, a Tartar prince, had died and his widow had taken over the command
p.s: C. Wessels (1924), closely paraphrasing Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
p.c: Wessels's paraphrase rather than Desideri's exact words; the Tartars here are the Mongol garrison serving the Mongol-descended ruler of Lhasa.

p.h: Women in helmets: how Timur beat the Emperor of Tartary
p.g: Clavijo tells how Tokhtamysh, 'emperor of Tartary', raided Tabriz and was chased home by Timur. Finding the ford guarded, Timur marched upstream for three days, then had the camp women put on helmets to look like soldiers while the men doubled back, crossed at night and routed the Tartar camp. The next page tells how Tokhtamysh's servant Edigu then became the new lord of Tartary with a horde of 200,000 horsemen.
p.q: on the third night Timour Beg ordered the women to put helmets on their heads, that they might look like men ; and all the men rode on, with two horses a piece, leaving the royal encampment, the women who looked like men, the servants, and the prisoners.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.pe: Tokhtamysh and the Tartars of the Golden Horde
p.c: A campaign story told at Timur's court, not witnessed by Clavijo.
p.tg: tokhtamysh golden horde war ruse women

p.h: A Kazakh feast: mutton, broth and thumbs for napkins
p.g: At a Kazakh host's tent, the guests ate boiled mutton with no bread or vegetables, the men first and the women afterwards. Abbott is squeamish and scornful, but he records exactly how the meal was served and cleaned up.
p.q: It consisted of boiled mutton, soused in its own soup. Bread and vegetables are things quite unknown in these parts. Kuzzauks are exclusively carnivorous. … The bowls were handed to the women, who scraped them clean with their thumbs … The thumb and tongue are the only napkins in Khaurism … The Tartars are right not to eat with their women.
p.s: James Abbott
p.pl: Ustyurt plateau, between Khiva and the Caspian
p.c: Abbott's sneering tone is his own; the facts of the meal are what he saw.

p.h: Everyone who enters churns the kumiss
p.g: In a corner of the Yakut house hung a leather bag of mare's milk. Everyone who came in, above all the women, stirred it with a plunger for a few minutes before doing anything else, which produced the sour but pleasant drink Lesseps calls koumouiss. Left to ferment longer, it became strongly intoxicating.
p.q: Dans un coin de la yourte est à demeure un paquet de cuir; chaque jour on y verse du lait de jument qu'on agite avec un bâton pareil à celui qui sert à battre le beurre. Tous ceux qui entrent, les femmes sur-tout, ne manquent jamais, avant de vaquer à d'autres travaux, de battre ce lait pendant quelques minutes; de-là provient cette boisson aigrelette & cependant agréable, qu'on nomme koumouiss.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: In a corner of the yurt a leather bag is kept permanently; every day mare's milk is poured into it and stirred with a stick like the one used to churn butter. Everyone who comes in, the women above all, never fails to churn this milk for a few minutes before turning to other work; from this comes the sourish yet pleasant drink called kumiss.

p.h: Ten minutes, a pipe and a spoonful of coffee
p.g: At a khan in Pharsalus Clarke watched 'Tartar' couriers change horses. Each squatted against the wall for about ten minutes, smoked hard, gulped a spoonful of muddy coffee, said 'God be praised' and rode on, travelling night and day. Clarke says no couriers in the world could match their endurance, and that Europeans travelling alone in Turkey disguised themselves in their dress.
p.q: the Tartar squats (for it cannot be called sitting) with his back against the wall, supporting himself upon the soles of his feet, and inhaling rapidly the fumes of his pipe upon his lungs; sending it back in curling volumes through his nostrils. Then, if he can procure about as much muddy coffee as would fill the bowl of a table-spoon, he utters his Alhandilla! (God be praised !)
p.s: Edward Daniel Clarke (1816)

p.h: No true Muslims until they settle in towns
p.g: At the start of Yunus Khan's reign, the Moghuls still lived in the old way, shunning towns and farmland, and were Muslims in name only; neighbours even sold them as slaves like unbelievers. Yunus decided that they would never be good Muslims until they settled, and led them to Tashkent, though some rebelled and stayed on the steppe. Elsewhere (p. 58) Mirza Haidar records that an earlier khan had a horseshoe nail driven into the head of any Moghul who refused to wear a turban.
p.q: At the beginning of the reign of Yunus Khan, all the Moghuls dwelt, according to their old custom, in Moghulistan ; they avoided all towns and cultivated countries [and regarded them] with great repugnance. They were Musulmans in nothing but the name
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)

p.h: Tea with salt and butter
p.g: The Kalmyk princess offered Cook a dish of tea. The tea was good, he says, but the Kalmyks put salt and butter into it; he drank it out of politeness and then hurried off to get rid of it, while the Russian major laughed at him. It is an early Western description of Mongolian salted milk tea.
p.q: Accordingly a cup of tea was brought, but such as I never had tasted before this time. The tea, I dare say, was good, but the Kalmucks put salt and butter into it ; nevertheless I drank it, though extremely disagreeable
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.tg: tea butter tea food hospitality kalmyks

p.h: Shop songs about Khans and the fall of Kazan
p.g: Hearing singing from a grocer's shop in Yalta, Kohl went in and sat on an apple chest until late at night while two Tatars, an Armenian and a Circassian sang and explained their songs. Besides love songs, some were historical: about Khan Krym Giray, Khan Devlet Giray, the Russian conquest of Crimea and the taking of Kazan. Tatar history lived on in popular song.
p.q: Love formed, as usual, the principal theme, but some, to my surprise, were on historical subjects. One treated of Krim-Gerei, the last distinguished Khan of the Crimea, the friend of the well known French ambassador, Baron de Tott, another of Khan Devlet-Gerei, a third of the conquest of the Crimea by the Russians, a fourth of the taking of Kasan
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.c: Kohl relied on the singers' own explanations of the words.
p.n: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma.

p.h: Mare's milk for the gods at the great tent
p.g: The prince's summer camp stood on the sunny side of a ridge beyond the Tamir. Twice a year, on the ninth day of the ninth month and of the fourth month, his followers gathered at the great ordo-tent and sprinkled the milk of white mares as a seasonal sacrifice, using plain birchwood vessels rather than gold and silver.
p.q: 其陽帳殿在焉乃避夏之所也…至重九日王師麾下㑹于大矛帳灑白馬湩脩時祀也其什噐皆用禾樺不以金銀為飾尚質也
p.s: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: On its sunny side stands the tent-palace; this is the summer retreat... On the Double Ninth the prince's following assembles at the great ordo-tent and sprinkles white mares' milk, performing the seasonal sacrifice. The vessels used are all of birch, not decorated with gold or silver: they value plainness.
p.c: 大矛帳 is a copyist's slip for 大牙帳 ('great tooth-banner tent', the ordo), as the Siku copy reads.
p.tg: kumiss mare's milk sacrifice ordo tent-palace

p.h: The emperor serves kumis in a gold cup
p.g: At his audience in Peking, after questions translated by the Jesuit Gerbillon, Ides was handed a gold cup of 'Tartarian Liquor called Kumis' by the Kangxi Emperor himself, through the viceroy. The attendants told him it was a spirit made from mare's milk. His whole retinue was then served the same drink. The steppe drink had a place of honour at the Manchu court.
p.q: Upon which he gave the Viceroy a Gold Cup of Tartarian Liquor called Kumis, in order to hand it to me; which with due respect I accepted, and having tasted, returned it. This Kumis according to the report of the Attendants is a sort of Brandy distilled from Mares Milk.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.pe: The Manchu court of the Kangxi Emperor

p.h: Natigay, the felt household god with a wife and children
p.g: In the Latin Marco Polo of the Society's first volume, the chapter on Tartar customs describes their god Natigay (here 'Naagay'), lord of the earth who guards children, herds and crops. Every household made him of felt and cloth, with a felt wife and children beside him. At meals they smeared fat on the idols' mouths and threw broth out of the door for them before eating. The same page describes kumiss, called 'chenus'.
p.q: Lex autem eorum talis est; quia ipsi habent suum deum qui vocatur Naagay, et dicunt quod ille est deus terrenus vel deus terræ qui custodit eorum filios et eorum bestias et blada … Et faciunt istum deum de feltro et panno, et credunt quod iste deus eorum habeat uxorem et filios … Quando comedunt ipsi accipiunt carnes pingues et ungunt illi suo idolo os, et uxori et filiis idoli
p.s: Marco Polo (Latin version printed by the Societe de Geographie, 1824)
p.t: Their law is this: they have their god called Naagay, and they say he is an earthly god, or god of the earth, who guards their children, their beasts and their crops … They make this god of felt and cloth, and believe this god of theirs has a wife and children … When they eat, they take fat meat and smear the mouth of their idol with it, and of the idol's wife and children
p.c: From volume 1 of the same series (1824), not the 1839 volume.
p.tg: natigay felt idols religion household gods kumiss

p.h: A Jewish king ruling Muslims, Christians and pagans
p.g: The author describes Atil's four gates and a king who is Jewish, with judges from each faith: Muslim, Jewish, Christian and pagan. Most inhabitants were Muslims and Christians, and the leading citizens were Muslim merchants. On the same page he notes that their language resembles that of the Turks, glossed by the translator as 'Tartars'.
p.q: The king of this country is a Jew : he has in his train four thousand Mussulmans, and Khozrians (Christians), and Idolaters ; but his principal people are Jews … The principal persons of Atel are Mussulmans and merchants: their language is like that of the Turks (or Tartars), and is not understood by any other nation.
p.s: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800; bracketed words are Ouseley's)
p.c: '(or Tartars)' is the translator's gloss for 'Turks'.

p.h: Bow to the fire and the idols
p.g: When Mikhail of Chernigov came to Batu's camp, Batu ordered him to bow to fire and to 'their idols'. Mikhail refused, mocked the idols as deaf, and was killed. The episode matches western reports that visitors had to pass between fires and honour Mongol felt images, and it made Mikhail a Russian saint.
p.q: посла Батый къ Михаилу князю, веля ему поклонитися огневи и болваномъ ихъ; Михайло же князь не повинуся велѣнью ихъ, но укори й и глухыя его кумиры, и тако безъ милости отъ нечестивыхъ заколенъ бысть
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.t: Batu sent to Prince Mikhail, ordering him to bow down to fire and to their idols; but Prince Mikhail did not submit to their command, but reproached him and his deaf idols, and so he was stabbed to death without mercy by the impious ones
p.c: Told as a martyr story; the fuller hagiographic version is in later chronicles.
p.tg: religion fire idols martyrdom mikhail of chernigov

p.h: 'Swift to battle and swift to flee'
p.g: Closing its Kalka story, the Nikon compiler sums up the newcomers: nobody knew where these Tatars came from or where they went. They were quick to fight and quick to run, light and not weighed down by baggage; they fled and then turned back again, the feigned retreat that western writers also noticed. The last phrase, 'like demons', shows the chronicler's fear.
p.q: Се же первое прихоженіе Татарское на Русь; бѣ же скори на бой, такоже и на бѣганіе, легци же суща, не обременяющеся ничимъ же тяготнѣе, бѣгаеть же и паки возвращается, и злодѣиствени суть аки дѣмони.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
p.t: This was the first coming of the Tatars on Rus; they were swift to battle and likewise to flight, being light and not burdened with anything heavy; they flee and then return again, and they are evildoers like demons.
p.c: A 16th-century summary, not a 1223 eyewitness.
p.tg: warfare light cavalry feigned retreat kalka

p.h: Conquered men made to fight, and the rest 'called Tartars'
p.g: Julian explains how the Tartar army grows: they kill the rulers of conquered lands at once, drive the strong men into battle in front of them, leave the weaker men to farm, give each of them ten or more women of the dead, and order that 'from now on they be called Tartars'. Soldiers who retreat are killed by the Tartars, so they prefer to die fighting. Instead of storming strong castles they strip the land and force the local people to attack the castle.
p.q: cuilibet decem vel plures assignantes et imponunt eisdem, ut de cetero Tartari nuncupentur. … Castra munita non expugnant, sed prius devastant terram et populum depredantur et ejusdem terre populum congregatum compellunt ad pugnam ad expugnandum ipsum castrum.
p.s: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
p.t: assigning ten or more to each, and they order them that from now on they be called Tartars. … They do not storm fortified castles, but first lay waste the land and plunder the people, and compel the gathered people of that same land to fight to take the castle.
p.c: Reported by refugees and the duke of Suzdal, not seen by Julian himself.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: How kumiss is made
p.g: Rubruck gives a step-by-step account of kumiss, fermented mare's milk: foals tied to a rope, mares milked, the milk churned in a skin with a club until it bubbles like new wine and turns pungent. He found it tasted of almond milk and 'intoxicates weak heads'. On the next page he says Batu received the milk of three thousand mares every day.
p.q: When they have got together a great quantity of milk, which is as sweet as cow's as long as it is fresh, they pour it into a big skin or bottle, and they set to churning it with a stick prepared for that purpose
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.tg: kumiss cosmos mare's milk food drink

p.h: A bride's dowry measured in a pyramid of millet
p.g: In a footnote de Tott describes an old Tartar wedding custom: a dish was set on the veiled bride's head and millet poured over it until the heap reached the dish. Small brides fared badly, so by his day families simply counted measures of millet. He then speculates that European nuptial crowns and sugar-plums come from this rite.
p.q: they placed a flat dish… on the head of the new married woman; they stretched a veil over her head… after this they poured millet on the trencher, which, spreading all around her, formed a cone… her dowry was not complete until the pyramid of millet reached up to the trencher, the veil still allowing her to breath. This custom was not favourable to little persons
p.s: Baron de Tott (his own footnote, English translation, 1785)
p.c: Told in the past tense; the link to European wedding customs is de Tott's own guess.

p.h: Kumiss in the tent of a Kazakh chief
p.g: Travelling in Tartar dress with Kazakh guides, the factors reached the horde of the chief Jean Beek (Janibek Batyr). He sat on a carpet in his tent, rose to welcome them, drank a large dish of kumiss and made them drink too. The next page describes Kazakh felt tents, horse meat, drunkenness on fermented mare's milk, the dried cheese called 'crute', and their rule of never harming a guest while he is under protection.
p.q: This Tartar-chief was sitting on a carpet in his tent; he rose, and bid us welcome, and making us sit down with him, he took a large dish of kumees, which he drank, and made us do the same. We gave him some small presents, which he immediately divided amongst the company.
p.s: British factors Reynold Hogg and George Thompson, their 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.pl: Kazakh steppe, about 800 versts east of the Ural (Yaik) river
p.pe: Kazakh ('Kirgeese') Tartars of the Lesser Horde

p.h: Furs, milk and the tall bark headdress
p.g: West of the Kerulun bend the country was crowded with carts and tents, and the people raised cattle, hunted, wore furs and skins and lived on milk and meat. Married women wore a two-foot headdress of tree bark covered in wool or, among the rich, red silk, with a long 'tail' called yu-yu that looked like a goose or duck, and they entered tents backwards with heads bent so as not to knock it (next page). Bretschneider matches it with the tall headdress described by Carpini and by Rubruck, who calls it bocca. On the same page, Mongols who had waited a year for the sage brought him millet and were amazed by the jujubes he gave them, a fruit they had never seen.
p.q: They dress in furs and skins, and live upon milk and flesh-meat. The men and unmarried young women plait their hair so that it hangs down over their ears. The married women put on their heads a thing made of the bark of trees, two feet high, which they sometimes cover with woollen cloth, or, as the rich used to do, with red silk stuff.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.pl: Central Mongolia (upper Kerulun to the Tuul)

p.h: Tartar bailiffs, markets and justice under occupation
p.g: After the massacres the Tartars lured people back from the woods and set up a working occupation. Each village chose a Tartar 'king'; the invaders appointed about a hundred 'canesii' (Roger glosses them as bailiffs) who kept justice and collected horses, animals, arms and gifts. Roger's own master was one of them and ruled almost a thousand villages. 'We had peace and markets,' he writes. A few lines later the same officials summon villagers with gifts and massacre them.
p.q: et quaelibet villa elegit sibi regem de Tartaris quem optauit. … Constituerunt Canesios id est Baliuos, qui iustitiam facerent, et eis equos animalia arma exenia et vestimenta utilia procurarent. Et sic procurator meus de istis dominis erat unus, et pene mille villas regebat. Et erant Canesii fere centum. Pacem habebamus et fora, iustaque unicuique iusticia seruabatur.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.pe: Mongol occupiers and their appointed officials
p.t: and each village chose for itself a king from among the Tartars, whomever it wished. … They appointed Canesii, that is bailiffs, to do justice and to procure for them horses, animals, weapons, gifts and useful clothing. My master was one of these lords, and ruled almost a thousand villages. And there were about a hundred Canesii. We had peace and markets, and justice was kept for each person.
p.c: 'Canesii' probably reflects a local title (compare Slavic knez, 'prince, headman'); the peace was brief and ended in treachery, as Roger goes on to tell.

p.h: Muslim farmers of the Volga Bulghars
p.g: The Bulghars (written Bulkar) lived on the Itil (Volga), between the Khazars and the Slavs; their king was a Muslim. Ibn Rusta says the Khazars and the Rus came to trade with them in sable, ermine and squirrel, and that they farmed wheat, barley and millet, and that most of them were Muslims with mosques and schools. Their land around Bolgar later became part of the Golden Horde and then the Kazan khanate.
p.q: وهم قوم لهم زرع وحراثة يزرعون كل الحبوب من الحنطة والشعير والدخن وغير ذلك واكثرهم ينتحلون دين الاسلام وفى محالهم مساجد وكتاتيب ولهم مؤذنون وائمة
p.s: Ibn Rusta (Arabic text ed. M. J. de Goeje, 1892)
p.t: They are a people who have crops and ploughing; they sow every kind of grain, wheat, barley, millet and so on. Most of them profess the religion of Islam; in their settlements there are mosques and Quran schools, and they have muezzins and imams.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of the Arabic is garbled); vowel marks omitted.
p.tg: volga bulghars farming islam fur trade

p.h: Meat cured under the saddle
p.g: Here Schiltberger insists he saw it himself: on long journeys Tartars bleed their horses and cook and drink the blood, and they slice meat, salt it and ride on it under the saddle until it dries and softens. Every morning the khan drinks mare's milk from a golden cup on an empty stomach.
p.q: I myself have seen them bleed [their horses] and drink the blood after they have cooked it. … I have also seen when they are long on a journey, that they take a piece of flesh, cut it into slices, place it under the saddle, and ride on it, and eat it when they were hungry ; but they salt it first
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879; bracketed words are the translator's)
p.tg: food horse blood saddle meat travel

p.h: One god, many idols, and the sin of a knife in the fire
p.g: Sanudo's chapter on 'the customs of the Tartars' says they believe in one God, maker of all, but do not pray to him; they worship idols that give them answers. They are 'too superstitious': it is a sin to stick a knife in the fire, touch fire with a knife, take meat from the cauldron with it, or chop with an axe near the fire, 'for they think the head is thus cut off the fire'. Killing and invading other lands, he adds, they do not count as sin.
p.q: Tartari, vnum Deum colunt, factorem omnium; bonorum, & pœnarum in hoc mundo datorem: eum tamen orationibus vel laudibus aut aliter non colunt; sed idola à quibus habent responsa. … Superstitiosi sunt nimis: peccatū enim putant cultellum in igne figere, vel quomodocunq; cultello tangere, vel cum eo carnes de caldaria extrahere, vel cū securi incidere iuxta ignē: putant enim sic caput igni auferri.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: The Tartars worship one God, maker of all things, giver of good and of punishments in this world; yet they do not worship him with prayers or praises or in any other way, but idols from which they get answers. ... They are too superstitious: for they think it a sin to stick a knife in the fire, or touch it in any way with a knife, or take meat out of the cauldron with it, or chop with an axe beside the fire: for they think that in this way the head is taken off the fire.
p.c: Condensed from Carpini's report; Sanudo presents it as general knowledge.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: religion fire taboo idols superstition carpini

p.h: A Tatar curse: 'may you stay in one place like a Christian'
p.g: In his chapter on Tatar customs Guagnini says they never stay long in one place and think doing so a great misfortune. When angry they curse their children with it: may you be stuck in one place forever like a Christian and smell your own stink. He adds that they measure the growth of their realm by how many provinces they have laid waste, since they live in the open fields.
p.q: morari, iratique liberis suis sic grave malum imprecantur, dicentes: O utinam eodem in loco perinde ut Christianus perpetuo haereres, propriumque foetorem olfaceres. … Quo vero plures provincias desolaverint, hoc se regna sua (in campis enim sub dio vivere solent) ampliora reddidisse dicunt.
p.s: Alessandro Guagnini, Sarmatiae Europeae descriptio (Speyer, 1581)
p.t: (to) stay, and when angry they call down on their children this grievous evil, saying: 'O may you cling forever to one place, like a Christian, and smell your own stink.' … The more provinces they have laid waste, the larger, they say, they have made their realms (for they are used to living in the fields under the open sky).
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page ('they think it a great misfortune to stay long in one place'). The curse also appears in Herberstein, so Guagnini may be copying.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Mongol pilgrims bow nine times before the Lama
p.g: Turner watched a party of 'Kilmauks' (Kalmyk or Oirat Mongols) waiting outside the palace for a sight of the infant Lama. When he appeared they prostrated themselves nine times and then handed over bullion and goods. Turner learned that such offerings were one of the main sources of the Lamas' wealth.
p.q: There came this day, a party of Kilmauks, (Calmuc Tartars) for the purposes of devotion, and to make their offerings to the Lama … they dropped upon their knees, and struck their heads against the ground. This, with the same motions, was repeated nine times.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: Tent people who sow melons by the rivers
p.g: Among the Zagatay tents of Khorasan, Clavijo notes that these people have no other homes. In summer they camp by rivers and sow corn, cotton and melons, in winter they move to warm districts, and Timur and his army wander the same way. On the next page he describes their food of sour milk boiled with bits of dough, cooked over dung fires.
p.q: The people of these tents have no other dwelling place, and they wander over the plains, during both winter and summer. In summer they go to the banks of the rivers, and sow their corn, cotton, and melons … The lord, with all his host, wanders in the same way over the plains, winter and summer.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)

p.h: Nose rings of gold and pearls
p.g: Gmelin describes how Astrakhan Tatar women braided their hair down the back, ending for girls in a long black silk tassel threaded with silver and for married women in a ribbon. Their finery included earrings and gold or silver rings, sometimes set with pearls or gems, worn in the nostrils. With a touch of irony he argues that if Europeans find it natural to pierce ears, Tatar women may fairly do the same to their noses. On the same page he describes the Sunni Tatars praying together in the open field at the end of Ramadan, kneeling and rising in step 'like a company of soldiers at drill'.
p.q: Endlich gehören zu dem tatarischen Weiber-Putz die Ohrgehänge und die silberne und goldene manchmalen mit Perlen oder Edelgesteinen ausgezierte Ringe, welche in den Nasen-Löchern getragen werden. Wann es in Europa nicht unnatürlich läßt, durch die Ohr-Gehänge die Ohren zu verstümmeln, so kann man dem tatarischen Frauenzimmer das Vergnügen mit Recht gönnen eine ähnliche Operation mit den Nasen vorzunehmen.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin
p.t: Finally, Tatar women's finery includes earrings and silver and gold rings, sometimes adorned with pearls or precious stones, which are worn in the nostrils. If in Europe it does not seem unnatural to mutilate the ears for earrings, one may fairly grant Tatar ladies the pleasure of performing a similar operation on their noses.
p.tg: dress jewellery nose rings women hair

p.h: Khalkha princes spellbound by puppets at the emperor's feast
p.g: An editor's note describes the great assembly at which the Khalkha khans submitted to the Kangxi emperor. At the feast, rope-dancers and puppets played 'much as in Europe', and the Khalkhas, who had never seen such a show, forgot to eat; only the Grand Lama stayed grave. The emperor then dressed the princes in Manchu robes, which they wore from then on before him.
p.q: Ce festin fut entremêlé de divertissemens exécutés par des danseurs de corde, qui firent divers tours de souplesse. Il y eut aussi des marionnettes, qui jouèrent à-peu-près comme en Europe. Les Kalkas, qui n'avoient jamais vu ce spectacle, oublioient de manger, par l'admiration qu'il leur causoit. Le grand Lama parut insensible à ces frivolités
p.s: Editor's note (signed 'Editeur') in Mailla's Histoire générale de la Chine, drawing on the Jesuit Gerbillon's journal
p.pe: Khalkha Mongols (Kalkas), their Grand Lama, and Manchu court
p.t: The feast was interspersed with entertainments by rope-dancers, who performed various feats of agility. There were also puppets, which played much as in Europe. The Khalkhas, who had never seen this spectacle, forgot to eat, so much did it amaze them. The Grand Lama appeared untouched by these frivolities
p.c: The place and year are not printed on this page; they are those of the Khalkha submission that the note describes. Gerbillon was an eyewitness, but the Paris editor paraphrases him.
p.tg: khalkha kangxi puppets feast manchu dress

p.h: Forced to wear the Tartar queue
p.g: The general description explains that since the conquest the Chinese must shave their heads in the Tartar manner and keep only one lock hanging behind. Thousands, it says, chose death rather than lose their long hair. This is the Qing head-shaving order, told from the Chinese side.
p.q: since this Famous Empire fell under the Tyrannous yoke of the Tartars, and became subject to them, they have also submitted to the Tartarian mode of cutting and wearing the Hair: for now the Chineses do cut off all their Hair after the manner of their Conquerour, and reserve only one Lock, which hangs down behind
p.s: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini

p.h: Crimean Tatars deny ever eating horse
p.g: A striking correction to older European books: Holderness says the Crimean Tatars of her day did not eat horse meat and denied that they ever had. Seventeenth century writers such as Chevalier had made horse-flesh the signature Tartar food.
p.q: The custom of eating horse-flesh is not in use among the Crim Tatars of the present day, and they indeed deny that it was ever their practice.
p.s: Mary Holderness

p.h: Kumis in golden bowls at the emperor's feast
p.g: At the Kangxi emperor's banquet for the Russian envoy, after a meal of nearly three hours, two great golden bowls of kumis, which Brand says is a Tartar drink made from mare's milk, were brought to the emperor. The envoy was called up to the throne and ordered to drain one bowl completely; the embassy staff were then served kumis too, followed by tea boiled in milk.
p.q: wurden dem Bogdegan zwey grosse güldene Schalen mit einem Tranck, (welcher auf tartarisch Kumis genannt wird, und der von Pferde-Milch abgezogen seyn solle,) überreichet, welcher gleich darauf den Herrn Envoye vor sich auf seinen Thron entbiethen ließ
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.t: two great golden bowls with a drink (which in Tartar is called kumis, and is said to be made from mare's milk) were handed to the Bogdikhan, who immediately afterwards had the envoy summoned before him on his throne
p.tg: kumis mare's milk kangxi court banquet

p.h: Horses never harnessed to a cart, even for the khan
p.g: Tatars train to ride from the cradle and keep riding into old age, despising carriages even when ill. Michalo says even a leading woman going to the khan's court rides in a closed cart drawn by one or two oxen, glittering with gold and jewels inside, because it is forbidden to harness even the worst horse to a vehicle, though a man may own a thousand horses. He sets this against Lithuanian ladies driven in carriages drawn by six or eight horses.
p.q: Et mulier apud illos etiam primaria, & vel Caesaris necessaria regiam accessura, non verecundatur caveae suae obturatae reclusa, auro vel gemmis intro nitens, bove vehi uno; aut propter plaustri grossitiem duobus. Equum autem vel deterrimum iungi vehiculo, nefas est & religio cuilibet eorum
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: And among them even a woman of the first rank, even one close to the khan, going to the palace, is not ashamed to ride shut in her closed cage, gleaming inside with gold and jewels, drawn by one ox, or by two if the cart is heavy. But to yoke even the worst horse to a vehicle is sacrilege and forbidden to every one of them

p.h: Left on the steppe for the dogs
p.g: Zwick found the body of a Kalmyk woman laid out in furs under a felt, with wooden cups and utensils beside her. This, he says, was the normal way of disposing of commoners, whose bodies were eaten by dogs and vultures; the dogs that fed on them were then driven off as unclean. Princes and Lamas, by contrast, were cremated with ceremony, and their ashes mixed with mortar for a chapel or tomb.
p.q: At some distance from our tent, we found the corpse of a Calmuc woman, laid out in a fur dress, and covered with coarse felt. Wooden drinking vessels, and other unimportant utensils, were laid by her side. This is the common way of disposing of the dead, amongst the Calmucs of inferior rank, so that the bodies are usually devoured by dogs and vultures.
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: A Tartar grandee eats half-raw pork at the council table
p.g: At their first reception in Beijing the envoys sat with the council, whose Tartar members wore plain clothes and sat on a bench covered with old linen. The presiding lord grew hungry and ate half-raw pork 'more like a Butcher, then a Prince'. The Jesuit Adam Schall, dressed in Tartar fashion, interpreted. The Dutch were shocked by the lack of ceremony.
p.q: his Highness found himself hungry, and sent for a piece of Pork to satisfie his Appetite, which was half-raw, whereof he did eat most heartily, in a slovenly manner, that he looked more like a Butcher, then a Prince … When Dinner was brought up, his Highness and the rest of the Tartar Lords fell on again as greedily, as if they had eat nothing all that day
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
p.pe: Tartars (Manchu lords of the Qing council)
p.c: Written with obvious Dutch disdain; a contrast with Chinese court manners rather than neutral description.

p.h: The queue: 'the most open and degrading mark of conquest'
p.g: After the Manchus took Peking, Davis writes, the Chinese were forced to shave their long hair and adopt 'the Tartar fashion of a long plaited tress, or tail', and Tartar dress, on pain of death. He reflects that changing the whole nation's costume touches every single person and is the plainest possible sign of conquest. The old Chinese costume, he notes, now survives only on the stage.
p.q: In other respects, too, they were commanded to adopt the Tartar habit on pain of death; and many are said to have died in preference to submission… an entire alteration in the national costume affects every individual equally, from the highest to the lowest, and is perhaps, of all others, the most open and degrading mark of conquest.
p.s: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page ('The conquered Chinese were now compelled to shave the thick hair...'), n199.

p.h: The khan strikes the red-hot iron
p.g: To remember the escape from Irgana-kon, Abu'l Ghazi says, the Mongols held a yearly ceremony: a piece of iron was heated red-hot, the khan struck it first with a hammer, then the tribal chiefs and officers in order of rank, then the common people. It ties Mongol kingship to smithing and iron.
p.q: They kindle upon that Day a great Fire, wherein they put a Piece of Iron to make it red-hot; after which the Chan gives the first Stroke with a Hammer upon the Piece of Iron, and then all the Heads of the Tribes and other Officers of Distinction, each according to his Rank, give it a Stroke with a Hammer
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.c: He says the Mongols 'still' observe it, but gives no date or place for the rite.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.

p.h: Kumiss: drunk all summer, never sold
p.g: Elphinstone describes how the Uzbeks make kimmiz (kumiss) by leaving mare's milk overnight in a skin and then beating and rolling it until morning. He notes that it can only be had in the last two months of summer, that people who can afford it stay drunk for much of that time, and that it is never sold. Nearby he adds that Uzbeks love horse-flesh but usually have to make do with beef.
p.q: The liquor thus made is of a whitish colour and a sourish taste: it is only to be had in plenty during the two last months of summer, and those who can afford it are generally drunk for the greater part of that period; but kimmiz is not sold, and those only can enjoy it who have mares enough to make it in the house.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)

p.h: A goat's blood on the bride's toe
p.g: At the same wedding Vigne is allowed to watch a rite he says belongs only to the Timurid family. The bride pushes her bare, henna-dyed foot out of her palanquin and the groom, still in his wedding clothes, kills a goat and touches her great toe with its blood. Vigne presents this as something he saw with his own eyes and believes no European had seen before.
p.q: I was admitted, as a great favour, to see a custom peculiar, I believe, to the Timurians, and which, perhaps, no European ever saw before … she thrust her bared foot … through the sliding doors, and the bridegroom touched her great toe with the blood of a goat, which I saw him kill with his own hands
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)
p.c: Vigne's claim that the custom is peculiar to the Timurids is his belief, not something he checked.

p.h: Drinking their horses' blood, prizing mare's milk
p.g: On long rides, Herberstein was told, Tartars open a vein in their horse and drink the blood, believing it does the animal good. They steer by the Pole Star, which they call the 'iron nail'. On the same page he describes their love of mare's milk and how chiefs share out the entrails of a slaughtered animal and lick the knife clean.
p.q: Moreover, if during a long ride they are troubled with hunger or thirst, it is a practice to lance the veins of the horses on which they sit, and relieve their craving by drawing their blood ; and they think that this is an advantage to the animals. As they nearly all wander on uncertain tracks, they are accustomed to direct their course by the observation of the stars
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.c: Reported from Russian and Lithuanian informants, not seen by Herberstein.
p.tg: horses blood mare's milk navigation food

p.h: The salt-lake fair where Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars sold horses and captives
p.g: At the Yamysh salt lakes, where the 'Siberian kingdom' ended, 30 or 40 river boats came every year from Tobolsk, Tomsk and other towns to load natural salt. While the Russians gathered it, a fair sprang up: many thousands of Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars came to sell horses, captives and Chinese goods. After two or three weeks everyone left and the place stood empty again, and Spafarii suggests a fort should be built there.
p.q: А въ то время, какъ Рускіе люди собираютъ соль изъ озера, учинится ярмарокъ. И приходятъ многіе тысящи людей Калмыки и Бухарцы и Татары и торгуютъ съ Рускими людьми. И они продаютъ лошади, и ясырь, и иные китайскіе товары. И держатъ тотъ ярмарокъ недѣли по 2 и по 3
p.s: Nikolai Spafarii (ed. Yu. V. Arsenyev, 1882)
p.pe: Kalmyks, Bukharans and Tatars trading with Russians
p.t: And at the time when the Russian people gather salt from the lake, a fair takes place. And many thousands of people come, Kalmyks and Bukharans and Tatars, and trade with the Russian people. And they sell horses, and captives, and other Chinese goods. And they hold that fair for 2 or 3 weeks
p.c: 'Yasyr' means captives taken in raids and sold as slaves.

p.h: Graves dug for pilgrims to Mecca
p.g: In Alushta Webster watched villagers dig two holes near the mosque for the two oldest men, about to leave on pilgrimage to Mecca. If they did not return, their upright gravestones topped with turbans would be set up there. The whole village was to share a feast paid for by voluntary gifts.
p.q: The two oldest, and for whom this ceremony was acting, were to set out, in two days, on a pilgrimage to Mecca, and, should they not return, their monuments, upright stones, surmounted by turbans, would be placed on the spot where the holes were dug.
p.s: James Webster

p.h: Nomads beyond the Wall who ate only meat
p.g: Between Cialis and the Chinese frontier, the account says, the country was notorious for Tartar raids: merchants scouted from the hills by day and travelled silently by night, and passed Muslim travellers who had been murdered for going alone. The Tartars rarely killed the settled locals, calling them their slaves and shepherds whose flocks they could seize. They refused grain and rice as fodder for animals, lived on meat including horse, mule and camel, and were said to live past a hundred.
p.q: quanquam raro Tartari indigenas ipsos mactent, asserentes eos esse servos suos ac pastores, quibus arietum greges, & boum armenta eripiunt; sed neque frumento, neque oriza aliove legumine ipsi vescuntur, dicentes hoc iumentorum esse non hominum pabulum: sola igitur carne vesci solent, nec ab equis, mulis, aut Camelis abhorrent, & tamen fama est eos diutissime vivere, & fere annorum centum excedere senectutem.
p.s: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries, reporting Goes's journey (1615)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongol nomads north and west of the Great Wall)
p.t: although the Tartars rarely kill the local people themselves, saying that they are their slaves and shepherds, from whom they carry off flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. They themselves eat neither grain nor rice nor any other pulse, saying that this is fodder for beasts, not food for men; so they live on meat alone, and do not shrink from horses, mules or camels. And yet it is said that they live very long, often past a hundred years.
p.c: Travellers' report passed through Isaac the Armenian and Ricci; the hundred-year lifespan is explicitly rumour ('fama est').

p.h: Milk at court, in memory of Tartar origins
p.g: Asking about the 'milk-tea' that was to have been served at the cancelled audience, Ellis learns it is simply milk, served to recall the Manchu dynasty's Tartar origins; likewise the emperor carves meat with a knife rather than chopsticks at state meals. Ellis adds that the conquerors profess to value their ancestors' simple ways but have lost their energy.
p.q: This milk-tea, it appears, is simply milk; chaya, or tea, being affixed to the names of many beverages besides that made from the tea plant. The milk is given as a record of the Tartar origin of the reigning family. Another instance of the anxiety to preserve these recollections is, that the Emperor, on state occasions, uses a knife to divide his meat, instead of chop-sticks.
p.s: Henry Ellis

p.h: An oath sworn on drawn daggers
p.g: When envoys of Khan Sachmat (Sheikh Ahmed of the Great Horde) concluded an alliance against Moscow with Polish and Lithuanian lords at Kraków, the Tatars sealed it their own way. They poured cold water over drawn daggers and, one after another, sipped it as it dripped from the points, cursing whoever first broke the treaty to vanish like that water. In a footnote Schlözer remarks drily that this Christian alliance with Tatars came decades before the French scandalised Europe by allying with the Ottomans.
p.q: wobey die Tataren, nach ihrer Landessitte, auf gezückte Dolche kaltes Wasser gossen, und solches, so wie es von der Spitze herabträufelte, einer nach dem andern schlürften, mit dem Fluche, daß wer den Bund zuerst bräche, wie dieses Wasser vergehen solle.
p.s: August Ludwig Schlözer (1785), following Polish-Lithuanian chroniclers
p.pe: Kipchak (Great Horde) Tatars of Khan Sheikh Ahmed (Sachmat)
p.t: whereby the Tatars, after the custom of their country, poured cold water on drawn daggers and, as it dripped from the point, sipped it one after another, with the curse that whoever first broke the alliance should pass away like this water.
p.tg: oath daggers alliance great horde diplomacy

p.h: An oath sworn over the shaman's drum
p.g: A Yakut accused of stealing cattle could clear himself by oath. He stood before the fire facing the sun, called down the loss of family, cattle, sunlight and life if he were guilty, stepped over the shaman's drum and robe, and breathed smoke from butter thrown on the coals. Some tribes also made him bite a bear's head, believing a bear would kill the perjurer. Many innocent men preferred to pay rather than swear.
p.q: A magician places his tambour and dress before the fire, the embers of which are burning. The accused stands before it, facing the sun, and says: "May I lose during my life all that man holds dear and desirable, father, mother, wives, children, relations; all my possessions and cattle; the light of the sun, and then my own life
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)

p.h: 'This is how Abraham lived'
p.g: While he sketched, the Tatars crowded round him, as surprised by his clothes as he was by theirs. The women spun and carded wool for the tent felts and burned dried cow dung for fuel. He found their way of life close to that of the Arabs, and thought this must be how Abraham and the patriarchs lived, content in tents as Europeans are in palaces.
p.q: Leur manière de vivre approche assez de celle des Arabes, & ils paroissent aussi contens de leurs demeures, qu'on l'est parmi nous des Palais, & des plus belles maisons. Cela me remet dans l'esprit l'ancienne manière des Orientaux, & je m'imagine que c'est ainsi que vivoient Abraham & les autres Patriarches
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: Their way of life is quite close to that of the Arabs, and they seem as content with their dwellings as we are with palaces and the finest houses. This brings to my mind the ancient way of the Orientals, and I imagine that this is how Abraham and the other patriarchs lived

p.h: Tartar law: the victim's family carries out the sentence
p.g: A Jew's slave murdered his master and then converted to Islam hoping for pardon. De Tott explains that under Tartar law the injured family must execute the criminal themselves. Khan Maksud Giray refused to spare the convert, saying he would hand over his own brother if guilty; in the end the Jews were allowed to stone the murderer according to the law of Moses.
p.q: by the Tartar law the criminal must perish by the hand of the injured person, or by his heirs. It was objected then, but in vain, that a Turk could not be delivered up to the Jews. “I would deliver up my brother to them,” replied the Kam, “if he was guilty; I leave Providence to reward his conversion, if it be sincere; it is my duty to do justice.”
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.tg: law justice khan jews blood revenge

p.h: Winter dead hung in trees until spring
p.g: Levshin reports that in some clans of the Middle and Great Hordes, rich people who died in winter were not buried at once but hung in trees wrapped in felt or linen, and in spring carried to Turkestan to be buried near the shrine of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi, the Kazakhs' revered saint. He then explains how graves were dug with a side niche so the earth would not press on the body.
p.q: Богатыхъ людей, умирающихъ зимою, въ нѣкоторыхъ поколѣніяхъ Средней и Большой Орды, вмѣсто погребенія, вѣшаютъ на деревьяхъ, обвернувъ въ войлокъ или въ полотно; весною-же отвозятъ ихъ въ Туркестанъ
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.pe: Kazakhs of the Middle and Great Hordes
p.t: Rich people who die in winter, in some clans of the Middle and Great Horde, instead of being buried are hung in trees, wrapped in felt or linen; and in spring they are carried to Turkestan
p.tg: burial khoja ahmed yasawi turkestan felt winter

p.h: White furs for the New Year
p.g: At each year's end the whole camp moved its tents to a fresh site to celebrate the New Year. There was a great feast in front of the tents at which everyone from the prince down wore pure white furs, and three days later they went to the great tent to offer New Year greetings. White was the lucky colour of the Mongol New Year (the White Month).
p.q: 比歳除日輙迁帳易地以為賀正之所日大晏所部於帳前自王以下皆衣純白裘三日後方詣大牙帳致賀礼也
p.s: Zhang Dehui, Record of a Journey (Qiujian ji juan 100 = Yutang jiahua juan 8; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: On the last day of the year they always move the tents to a new site, as the place for celebrating the New Year. That day there is a great banquet for all his people in front of the tents, and everyone from the prince down wears pure white furs. Only after three days do they go to the great ordo-tent to offer their New Year greetings.
p.tg: new year white furs feast ordo

p.h: The 'genuine Tartars' are going native
p.g: After praising Tartar warfare, Polo adds a striking remark: in his day the Mongols were changing. Those settled in China had taken up the religion and ways of the Chinese, and those in the Middle East had adopted Muslim customs. It is an eyewitness observation that the conquerors were being absorbed by the settled peoples they ruled.
p.q: But I must add also that in these days they are greatly degenerated ; for those who are settled in Cathay have taken up the practices of the Idolaters of the country, and have abandoned their own institutions ; whilst those who have settled in the Levant have adopted the customs of the Saracens.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.pe: Mongols settled in China and in the Ilkhanate
p.c: 'Idolaters' means Buddhists and followers of Chinese religion; 'Saracens' means Muslims.

p.h: Welcomed at the Tatar village of Birna
p.g: After a near-fatal sledge accident, Chappe reached Birna, a Tatar village. Villagers came out a verst to meet him with signs of friendship, led him to their headman (chosen, he says, for his merit without any election) and gave him a meal of honey, butter and vegetables. Their houses were as clean as Siberian ones were dirty; they lived much like their neighbours except that they were Muslims.
p.q: J'arrivai enfin à Birna; ce Village est habité par des Tartares. Plusieurs étoient venus au-devant de moi à un werst de leur Village … Ils m'avoient fait préparer une espece de dîner qui consistoit dans du miel, du beurre & quelques légumes. Leurs maisons sont aussi propres que celles des Sibériens le sont peu. Au reste, ils vivent à-peu-près de la même façon, excepté qu'ils sont Mahométans.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.t: At last I reached Birna; this village is inhabited by Tartars. Several had come out a verst from their village to meet me … They had prepared a kind of dinner for me consisting of honey, butter and a few vegetables. Their houses are as clean as those of the Siberians are not. For the rest, they live in much the same way, except that they are Mahometans.
p.tg: hospitality village islam clean houses food

p.h: Horse meat at the butcher's, kumiss only on the steppe
p.g: In Yarkand horse meat was sold openly in butchers' shops, cost the same as mutton and was not thought unlawful. Kumiss (fermented mare's milk), the classic 'Tartar' drink of older books, was drunk not by the townspeople but by the Kalmuks and other nomadic tribes. The informants also said Islam was not kept very strictly there, and that people were more tolerant than in Kokand.
p.q: Horse-flesh is sold in the butcher's shops, and generally eaten: it is not considered unlawful food by the people of the country, and generally sells for the same price as mutton. Kimmiz is not used by the inhabitants of the towns, but by the Kalmuks, and other roving tribes.
p.s: W. H. Wathen, reporting his informants
p.pe: Townspeople of Chinese Tartary; Kalmuks and other nomads

p.h: Raiders with two horses each
p.g: Perry explains why the rich land west of the lower Volga lay empty: raids by the Kuban Tartars, who plundered and burned villages and carried off cattle and people. They came in summer, each man with two horses to change as he rode, with sentries all round, and were gone before the Russians could react. A page later he tells how three to four thousand of them reached his own camp at dawn and drove off about 1400 horses.
p.q: The said Tartars when they make their Incursions, it is usually in the Summer time, when there is Grass enough on the Ground; and each Man for Expedition sake takes two Horses, which they change as they ride, sometimes sitting upon one, and sometimes upon another. They always travel with Centinels at a convenient Distance from all Sides of their main Body,
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.pl: Steppe between Saratov and the Caspian

p.h: The nomad Horde sows its grain
p.g: From the Venetian Josafa Barbaro, who lived at Tana, Hammer reports that Ulu Muhammad kept his camp moving for eleven years without letting the Horde sow in March and wait for the harvest, so it suffered grain shortage and lived on meat and milk alone. Normally, in February the camp announced the sowing day; those who wanted to grow grain drove out with wagons and seed to fields a day or two from the camp. The harvest was rich: fifty-fold for grain and a hundred-fold for millet. Nomads, in other words, also farmed.
p.q: Sonst war es der Gebrauch, dass im Monathe Februar im Lager der Tag, an welchem im März gesäet werden sollte, ausgerufen ward. An diesem Tage fuhren die, so Getreide bauen wollten, mit ihren Wagen und Samen auf die gewöhnlich vom Hoflager Eine oder zwey Tagreisen entlegenen Felder und bestellten dieselben. Die Ernte war ergiebig, denn der Boden gab das Fünfzigfache des Kornes
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), following Josafa Barbaro's Viaggio alla Tana
p.pl: Golden Horde steppe near Tana (Azov), Russia
p.pe: The Horde of Ulu Muhammad and Küchük Muhammad (Golden Horde Tatars)
p.t: Otherwise it was the custom that in the month of February the day on which sowing should take place in March was proclaimed in the camp. On that day those who wished to grow grain drove with their wagons and seed to the fields, usually one or two days' journey from the court camp, and tilled them. The harvest was plentiful, for the soil gave fifty-fold of the grain
p.tg: farming grain millet nomads barbaro tana

p.h: A camp of two hundred tents on the Yegorlyk
p.g: Güldenstädt camped beside a Nogai aul of about 200 kibitkas (felt tents). He admired their horses, broad in croup and chest with short thick necks, and their big greyish-white cattle, but noted that most sheep had died in the war's many marches. The herders had nothing to offer but butter and sour milk, which they eagerly traded for millet, since grain was short until the harvest.
p.q: Wir standen hier neben einem an 200 Kibitken starken Aaul, der ein Theil vom Onokusch Aul ist und zu Jedissan gehört. … Man sahe hier bey diesen Nagaijern ein große Heerde von Pferden und Rindvieh. … Außer Butter und saurer Milch konnte man bey diesen Hirten Volke nichts haben, das sie uns begierig zubrachten
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1791)
p.pe: Yedisan Nogais (Onokush aul, chief Islam Murza)
p.t: We stood here beside an aul (camp) some 200 kibitkas (tents) strong, which is part of the Onokush aul and belongs to Yedisan. … One saw here among these Nogais a great herd of horses and cattle. … Apart from butter and sour milk nothing could be had from this herding people, which they eagerly brought to us
p.c: His remark on the same page that the Nogais thanked God and blessed the Russian empress for their new prosperity was written in an official report, just after Russia had brought these hordes under its control.

p.h: A Swedish prisoner casts cannon for the Dzungar ruler
p.g: A Russian soldier freed from Dzungar captivity told Unkovsky that a foreign sub-lieutenant, Renat, captured with the Russians in 1716, had cast seven bronze cannon and three mortars for the ruler, and that other captive officers had taught the Dzungars to make cloth and needles; one was said to be making velvet in Yarkand. It shows a steppe state importing skills through its prisoners.
p.q: слышалъ, что иноземецъ штыкъ-юнкеръ Ренотъ, которой взятъ съ ними въ полонъ съ Корякова, вылилъ Контайшѣ семь пушекъ мѣдныхъ, три мортиры. Да у него жъ Контайши въ Ургѣ поручикъ Дебешъ и другіе офицеры научили дѣлать суконъ, иголъ. А нынѣ слышно, что оной Дебешъ дѣлаетъ въ Эркени бархатъ.
p.s: Ilya Lychagin, freed Russian captive, as recorded in Unkovsky's interrogation records (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: he heard that the foreigner, sub-lieutenant of artillery Renat, who was taken prisoner with them at Koryakov, cast for the Kontaisha seven bronze cannon and three mortars. And at the same Kontaisha's Urga, Lieutenant Debesh and other officers taught them to make cloth and needles. And now it is said that this Debesh is making velvet in Erken (Yarkand).
p.c: Hearsay from a former captive. Renat is the Swedish officer Johan Gustaf Renat, later known for his maps of Dzungaria (a modern identification).

p.h: A Tatar lament for five slain Cossacks
p.g: After a hand-to-hand fight at the mouth of the Ishim in which five of Yermak's Cossacks died, the chronicle says the Tatars still sang about it at their gatherings, weeping, with a Tatar refrain that it translates. The song was known as 'the Tsaritsa's lament'. It is a rare glimpse of Tatar oral memory of the war.
p.q: и о тѣхъ пяти человѣкахъ Татара поютъ съ плачемъ при бесѣдахъ въ пѣсняхъ припѣваючи: янымъ, янымъ, битъ казакъ, битъ казакъ, сирѣчь: воины, воины, пять пять человѣкъ побѣдиша и разориша. И сія пѣсня и словетъ царицынъ плачь.
p.s: Kungur (Remezov) chronicle, article 100 (1880 printed text)
p.t: and about those five men the Tatars sing with weeping at their gatherings, with the refrain: 'yanym, yanym, bit kazak, bit kazak', that is: 'warriors, warriors, five, five men we defeated and destroyed.' And this song is called the Tsaritsa's Lament.
p.c: The refrain is Tatar in Russian letters; the other scan of this edition (T0442 n95) reads 'бишь', closer to Tatar 'bish' (five), which fits the chronicler's own gloss. The translation of the Tatar words is the chronicler's.
p.tg: song lament oral tradition cossacks ishim

p.h: The 'Tartar ceremony': nine knocks of the head
p.g: The embassy's quarrel was over the 'Tartar ceremony' demanded before the emperor. Ellis notes that the English word kowtow is loose: the court rite is properly 'thrice kneeling and nine times bowing the head', a Manchu court protocol.
p.q: The Tartar ceremonial has perhaps improperly been rendered by the Chinese word ko-tou, which more strictly signifies three simple genuflexions, a mode of salutation practised even in private life. The court ceremony has a different name, implying thrice kneeling and nine times bowing the head, San-kwei-keu-kou.
p.s: Henry Ellis (footnote)

p.h: Natigay, the felt god of the household
p.g: Polo says the Tartars worship a high god of heaven and an earth god, Natigay, who guards children, cattle and crops. Every household had felt figures of him, his wife and children, and at meals they greased the idols' mouths with fat and sprinkled broth outside the door. Yule links Natigay to the Mongol 'ongon' spirit figures that Pallas later saw among the Buryats.
p.q: They show him great worship and honour, and every man hath a figure of him in his house, made of felt and cloth ; and they also make in the same manner images of his wife and children. … And when they eat, they take the fat of the meat and grease the god's mouth withal, as well as the mouths of his wife and children.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.tg: religion idols felt natigay shamanism kumiss

p.h: Two horses each: one to ride, one to eat
p.g: Tartar soldiers, says Fletcher, bring two horses, one to ride and one to eat, and horseflesh is their main food. He adds something he saw himself: when the Crimean prince Kiriach Murza came to Moscow with 300 Tartars, he was welcomed with two fat horses, ready skinned, for supper.
p.q: every man with his two horse at the least, the one to ride on, the other to kill, when it commeth to his turne to have his horse eate. For their chiefe vittaile is horse flesh, which they eate without bread or any other thing with it.
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: The general claim is hearsay; the Moscow banquet for Kiriach Murza is what Fletcher himself witnessed.

p.h: Portrait of a Tatar noblewoman in a headdress of gold ducats
p.g: De Bruyn painted a young Tatar woman of high rank in the governor's house. Under her veils she wore a pointed, mitre-shaped headdress covered in gold ducats and embroidered with pearls, silver chains with little boxes for prayer books, and hair bound with black ribbon. She came with three women attendants and a Tatar escort known to the governor.
p.q: Cette coifure étoit toute couverte de ducats d'or, comme il a déjà été dit, & pointue en forme de mitre, brodée d'un grand nombre de perles … Cette demoiselle étoit une des plus considerables d'entre les Tartares; & étoit accompagnée de trois femmes de sa suite, & conduite par un Tartare, connu du Gouverneur.
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: This headdress was entirely covered with gold ducats, as has already been said, and pointed like a mitre, embroidered with a great number of pearls … This young lady was one of the most considerable among the Tartars, and was accompanied by three women of her suite and escorted by a Tartar known to the governor.
p.c: The portrait was engraved for the book.

p.h: Horned masked dancers and stones thrown at China
p.g: Before the New Year the lamas performed a masked dance (the Buddhist tsam) before a great tent. Unkovsky describes masked dancers wearing caps with horns, one like a cow's, one like a wild goat's, cymbals, drums and long brass trumpets, and an offering blown up in a fire. At the end the whole crowd, the ruler among them, marched east and hurled stones, sticks and earth toward the east with a great shout, 'as if for victory over the Chinese', their enemy at the time.
p.q: Вышли два человѣка, закрытыя лица, на шапкахъ по два рога было; у одного коровей, у другого яко у дикой козы … и весь народъ, ухватя что попало въ руки (камень или палку или земли), съ великимъ крикомъ бросали на востокъ, будто бы въ побѣду на Китайцевъ; притомъ и самъ Контайша шелъ.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: Two men came out with covered faces, with two horns each on their caps; one had cow's horns, the other horns like a wild goat's … and all the people, seizing whatever came to hand (a stone or a stick or earth), threw it toward the east with a great shout, as if for victory over the Chinese; and the Kontaisha himself walked with them.
p.c: The meaning of the stone-throwing ('as if for victory over the Chinese') is Unkovsky's reading.
p.tg: tsam lamas masks buddhism new year

p.h: Queens on the throne, faces uncovered
p.g: After Friday prayer Uzbek Khan sat in a 'golden alcove' on a gilded, jewelled throne, with his four wives seated on the throne beside him in full view. When each wife came in, the khan rose and led her by the hand to her seat. Ibn Battuta, used to royal women being hidden, was struck by this, and a page earlier he notes that Turkish noblewomen here went unveiled and were highly respected. He was given sheep, a horse and a leather bag of kumiss.
p.q: Whenever one of these wives enters, he arises, and taking her by the hand, puts her into her place upon the throne. Thus they are exposed to the sight of all, without so much as a veil.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.tg: women khatuns throne court ceremony kumiss

p.h: Tartar raiders on the road to the Great Wall
p.g: The Portuguese lay brother Bento de Goes travelled overland from India towards China in 1603 to 1605. On the last stretch he found the country between Cialis and the Chinese wall 'notorious for its Tartar raids': merchants crossed it by night in silence, and the bodies of lone Muslim travellers lay by the road. Goes adds a telling detail (in the sentence that follows this excerpt): the Tartars did not usually kill the local people, whom they treated as their servants and herdsmen and occasionally robbed of their flocks.
p.q: "The country between Cialis and the Chinese wall," Goes writes, "is notorious for its Tartar raids, so that traders always cross it in the greatest fear, sometimes even under cover of night and in the strictest silence. One often comes across the dead bodies of Mohammedans who have attempted the journey unaccompanied, though on the other hand the Tartars are not wont to kill the native population
p.s: Bento de Goes, as recorded in Matteo Ricci's Commentari and translated by C. Wessels (1924)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongol and Turkic nomads of the steppe)
p.c: Goes died in China in 1607; his account survives through Ricci's reworking of his notes, so the wording is Ricci's.
p.tg: raids caravans great wall nomads trade

p.h: Herdsmen give kumis, milk, wool and cheese
p.g: The poem's chapter on how a ruler should treat the keepers of the horse herds lists what they provide: food, drink and horses to ride, and kumis (fermented mare's milk), milk, wool, butter, sour milk and cheese, food and clothing and coarse wool for ropes. The poet calls them useful and honest but 'without knowledge', people from whom a prince should not expect law or manners. It is a courtier's view of the herding life that fed the court.
p.q: 3 Zu essen, zu trinken, Pferd zu reiten . . . . . Hengste Stammt von diesen her, so auch . . . . 4 Kimis, Milch, Wolle, Schmalz, saure Milch und Käse, Speise und Kleider, sowohl als grobe Wolle für Stricke.
p.s: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), in Vambery's German translation (1870)
p.pe: Turkic herders of the Qarakhanid realm
p.t: 3 Food, drink, horses to ride … stallions come from these (people), and also … 4 Kumis, milk, wool, butter, sour milk and cheese, food and clothing, as well as coarse wool for ropes.
p.c: Vambery's translation leaves gaps where he could not read the manuscript.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: kumis mares milk herders horses food

p.h: 'Our conquerors, Sir, have left us very poor'
p.g: In the morning Jesse's Tatar host was surprised to be paid, explaining that most of his guests were Russians travelling on duty, who did not pay. His short reply about the conquerors is a rare recorded Tatar voice on life under Russian rule, a generation after annexation.
p.q: Our host appeared rather astonished at being remunerated, in the morning, and said that the generality of his visitors were always on duty; adding, “Our conquerors, Sir, have left us very poor.”
p.s: Captain William Jesse, quoting his Tatar host (through an interpreter)
p.c: Heard through an interpreter by a strongly anti-Russian author.

p.h: Koumis, chess and music in a Tartar coffee-house
p.g: Drawn in by music, Alexander entered a Tatar coffee-house in Akmetshet. Greeks and Tatars sat cross-legged on carpets, smoking long pipes and drinking coffee; an old man urged a youth to drink koumis, which Alexander calls a spirit distilled from mare's milk; two men played chess; and three musicians played a stringed instrument and a drum and sang.
p.q: on entering it, I found it divided into compartments by railings, and Greeks and Tartars were sitting cross-legged on carpets, and smoking cherry-stick chebouks and drinking coffee. A gray-beard, in a corner, was encouraging a youth to drink koumis or spirits, distilled from mare's milk. A grave-looking pair were engaged at chess ; and in the window-seat were three musicians
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: Koumis is fermented mare's milk; the distilled spirit made from it is a different drink, and Alexander may be running the two together.

p.h: How kumiss is made, and what it tastes like
p.g: Rubruck explains the Mongols' summer drink, fermented mare's milk. Foals are tethered on a line so the mares let themselves be milked; the milk is churned in a skin with a club until it bubbles like new wine and turns sour. He found it prickled the tongue, left a taste of almonds and could make a weak head drunk; a clear black kind, cara-cosmos, was kept for the great.
p.q: ils le versent dans vn outre, ou autre vaisseau, là où ils le battent & remuent tres-bien … cela commence à boüillir comme du vin nouueau, puis à s'aigrir, comme du leuain … cela pique la langue comme feroit du vin raspé quand on le boit. Lors que l'on a acheué de boire, cela laisse sur la langue vn goust d'amande, & resioüit grandement le cœur
p.s: William of Rubruck (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: they pour it into a skin or other vessel, where they beat and stir it very well … it begins to bubble like new wine, then to turn sour like leaven … it stings the tongue like rough wine when you drink it. When you have finished drinking, it leaves a taste of almonds on the tongue and greatly cheers the heart

p.h: A goose and a loaf on the table: 'the fearsome name of the Tatars'
p.g: Gmelin admits the travellers had feared the very name of the Tatars. After a few days among them it sounded quite different: everywhere a gift was waiting, usually a plucked goose and a baked loaf, and at Ulga also honey and hazelnuts. He is honest that the courtesy had limits: one host hid rather than hand over his horses, and the soldiers found him and took them anyway.
p.q: Wir haben sie überhaupt als leutseelige Leute befunden, und der uns ehemahls fürchterliche Name der Tataren kam uns nun ganz anders vor. An allen Orten, wo wir hinkamen, fanden wir auf dem Tische schon ein Geschenke vor uns, welches gemeiniglich in einer abgefederten Gans und einem gebackenen Brodte bestund
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pl: Tatar villages east of Kazan (Kursa to Ulga)
p.t: On the whole we found them friendly people, and the name of the Tatars, once so frightful to us, now sounded quite different. Everywhere we came we found a gift already waiting for us on the table, usually a plucked goose and a baked loaf

p.h: Crimean guides who led a Turkish army to starve
p.g: Asked how the Muscovites had inflicted a great defeat on the Turks when a river diversion was attempted, Possevino's informant said it was not the Muscovites but the Crimean Tatars who did it. Though allies of the Turks, they feared a heavier yoke if the scheme succeeded, so they offered themselves as guides and led the Turkish troops through vast forests and foodless country until nearly all died of hunger and toil.
p.q: cladem Moscus intulisset, cùm Tanaim deriuari iussisset in Boristhenem: respondit, hoc non à Moscis, sed à Tartaris Præcopensibus, licèt Turcarum fœderatis, accidisse, ægrè ferentibus id fieri, vnde grauius sibi iugum pendere prospicerent. Quamobrem cùm sese duces itineris Copijs Turcicis exhibuissent, per ingentes syluas, & loca commeatus egena, eas circumduxisse, vt fame, ac labore pleræq; omnes fermè interierint.
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586), reporting an unnamed informant 'N.'
p.t: ... the Muscovite had inflicted [so great a defeat on the Turks], when he had ordered the Don to be diverted into the Borysthenes: he answered that this was done not by the Muscovites but by the Precop Tartars, though allies of the Turks, who resented the scheme because they foresaw a heavier yoke hanging over them. So, offering themselves as guides to the Turkish forces, they led them round through huge forests and places without supplies, so that almost all of them perished of hunger and toil.
p.c: Hearsay. The river named is garbled: the real 1569 Ottoman plan was a Don to Volga canal to reach Astrakhan (a reader of this copy wrote 'Volgam' in the margin).
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.
p.tg: crimean tatars ottomans 1569 don-volga canal guides

p.h: A Yakut prince buried with his favourite horses
p.g: Lesseps had been shown old Yakut coffins hung in trees, but says the Yakuts now buried their dead like Christians. At a prince's funeral his favourite horse and the best of his herd, richly harnessed, were tied to two carved or painted posts by the grave and killed over his body. Their hides and heads were then hung in nearby trees as a 'mausoleum', and the mourners roasted and ate the two horses on the spot.
p.q: Si c'est un prince, on le revêt de ses plus riches habits & de ses plus belles armes. … Le cheval favori du prince & le meilleur du haras, tous deux richement harnachés … marchent à côté du convoi. Arrivés au lieu de la sépulture, ils sont attachés à deux poteaux plantés auprès de la fosse. Pendant qu'on inhume leur maître, on les égorge sur son corps,
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.t: If it is a prince, he is dressed in his richest clothes and finest weapons. … The prince's favourite horse and the best of his herd, both richly harnessed … walk beside the procession. On reaching the burial place they are tied to two posts planted by the grave. While their master is buried, they are slaughtered over his body,
p.c: Lesseps describes the rite from what his Yakut host and others told him, not from a funeral he attended.

p.h: Killing a man is no sin, but leaving the bridle on is
p.g: In his chapter on Tartar customs Hayton says they name God simply and immortal but honour him with no prayers, fasts or penances. A Tartar would not think it a sin to kill a man, yet would think he had sinned mortally if he left the bit in his horse's mouth while it grazed. When they cross lands short of food they drive cows and mares with them, living on the milk and eating horse meat, which they think good.
p.q: Le Tartar ne reputaroit avoir fait pechié d'oucivre I home; e se il laissoit le frein en la bouche de son cheval, quant il deüst paistre, il quideroit pechier mortelment. … e vivent du lait, e la char des chevaus mangent, e lur pert bone char.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: A Tartar would not reckon it a sin to kill a man; but if he left the bridle in his horse's mouth when it should graze, he would think he had sinned mortally. … and they live on the milk, and eat the flesh of horses, and it seems good meat to them.
p.c: The editor notes this chapter overlaps with John of Plano Carpini's earlier description, so parts may be borrowed rather than observed.
p.tg: religion sin horses mare's milk horse meat

p.h: Dried fish for bread, and mare's milk from a leather bag
p.g: The Nogais near Astrakhan lived on their herds, hunting and fishing. Sun-dried fish served them as bread, they ate camel and horse meat, and they prized mare's milk, which they offered the ambassadors from a leather bag. On the same page he describes their fat-tailed sheep, two-humped camels and small tough horses, and the white linen coifs hung with Russian coins worn by the women.
p.q: Their ordinary food is fish dry'd in the Sun, which serves them instead of bread. … They eat Camels and Horse-flesh, and drink water and milk. Mares milk they much esteem; with this they treated our Ambassadors, when we gave them a Visit, taking it out of a … Leather-bag, to present it to us.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.tg: food mare's milk kumiss fish herds

p.h: The feigned flight, which they call a dance
p.g: Herberstein explains the classic steppe tactic: attack from a distance, pretend to flee, shoot backwards at the pursuers, then wheel round and charge. The Tartars fight in a wheeling circle rather than a battle line and, he says, call this manoeuvre 'a dance'. Without shield, lance or helmet they avoid close combat in narrow places.
p.q: they do not, however, continue this mode of warfare long, but pretending flight, take an opportunity while their enemies are pursuing them to discharge their arrows backwards, and then, when the ranks of the enemy are broken, turn their horses suddenly round and attack them.
p.s: Sigismund von Herberstein (translated by R. H. Major, 1851-52)
p.pl: Steppe frontier of Muscovy and Lithuania

p.h: A Tatar camp near Astrakhan, 'as Abraham must have lived'
p.g: Visiting the Tatar camp a short mile from Astrakhan, the traveller found families camped apart in tents shaped like parrot cages, very clean and well furnished. They lived from their herds, burned dried cow dung stacked around the tents like peat, and, he thought, lived as contentedly in their tents as Europeans in palaces. He sketched a finely dressed young woman and compared their life to the Arabs and the biblical patriarchs.
p.q: Ihre Zelte sind wie die Papageyen Bauer, nur nach Proportion nicht so hoch, sehr reinlich und mit guten Meublen versehen… Ihre Wärme schaffen sie sich von Küh-Mist, den sie trucknen und zu recht machen, wie wir unsern Torff, und in Hauffens um ihre Zelte legen. Ihre Lebens-Art kommt mit der Arabischen ziemlich überein
p.s: Journal of an unnamed painter-traveller (evidently Cornelis de Bruyn, 1703) printed in Weber, Das veränderte Russland
p.t: Their tents are like parrot cages, only not so high in proportion, very clean and provided with good furniture… They get their warmth from cow dung, which they dry and prepare as we do our peat, and lay in heaps around their tents. Their way of life agrees fairly well with the Arabs'
p.tg: tents dung fuel nomads astrakhan women

p.h: Passports for the dead
