p.g: At an old woman's burial in Karagoss, Holderness watched the body laid in a side niche of the grave with papers written by the mulla: one on the breast describing the dead woman's character, one in the hand as a passport at the gates of Heaven, and one above the head warning the Evil One away. Stakes, hay, earth and stones then sealed the grave.
p.q: some papers written by the Mulla were disposed about it; one being placed on the breast, expressive of the character of the deceased; another in the hand, intended likewise as a sort of passport at the gates of Heaven; and a third above the head, which is said to be an intimation to the Evil One to refrain from disturbing the bones of a true believer.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: The meaning of each paper is what she was told; the Arabic texts were never translated for her.

p.h: A Chinese portrait of the Tatars: wool tents, hot stones, tree burials
p.g: Rémusat translates a Chinese geography, the Kouang-iu-ki, on the Tha-tche (Tatars): they follow rivers and pastures with their herds, dress in hides, make tents of coarse wool, cure illness by burning the sick part with a heated stone, sing and dance at funerals, and some place the corpse in a tree and burn the bones three years later. Rémusat judges such Chinese portraits 'not lacking in accuracy and fidelity'.
p.q: Les Tha-tche suivent les rivières et les lieux fertiles en pâturages … Ils font leurs tentes avec de grosses étoffes de laine. … Lorsqu'ils sont malades, ils font chauffer une pierre, et se brûlent eux-mêmes (la partie malade). Aux funérailles, ils accompagnent le mort en chantant et en dansant. Quelques-uns placent le cadavre sur un arbre, et, trois ans après, ils recueillent les os et les brûlent.
p.s: The Chinese geography Kouang-iu-ki, translated by Abel-Rémusat
p.pe: Tha-tche (Tatars, as Chinese writers used the name)
p.t: The Tha-tche follow the rivers and the places rich in pasture … They make their tents of coarse woollen cloth. … When they are ill, they heat a stone and burn themselves (on the sick part). At funerals they accompany the dead singing and dancing. Some place the corpse in a tree, and three years later they gather the bones and burn them.
p.c: A Chinese outsider's summary that lumps northern peoples together; Rémusat warns that Chinese writers confuse nations with similar ways of life.
p.tg: tents wool funerals medicine tree burial

p.h: A khan's grave hidden in a sacred mountain
p.g: Mustawfi records that the Ilkhan Arghun was buried on the mountain of Sujas and that, following Mongol custom, the grave was concealed and the whole mountain made a forbidden sanctuary (qurugh). His daughter later revealed the grave and founded a dervish lodge there, a Muslim practice laid over a steppe one.
p.q: The sepulchre of Arghun Khan was made in the mountain of Sujas, and according to Mongol custom, they concealed the place, making the whole mountain an inviolable Sanctuary (Qurugh), so that people could not without difficulty pass that way. Arghun's daughter, Uljay Khatun, however, made manifest her father's grave, founding a Darvish-house, and settling a community here.
p.s: Hamdallah Mustawfi (translated by G. Le Strange, 1919)

p.h: 'No Chinese may punish me on the Tartar side of the wall'
p.g: Although Chinese and Tartars had one master, Staunton found the Great Wall still treated as the boundary between two peoples. Just past it, a Tartar attendant facing punishment by Chinese mandarins loudly refused, claiming they had no authority over him on the Tartar side. On the next page a Chinese mandarin dares not sit before a Tartar officer of equal rank.
p.q: The line it has traced, continues still to be considered as a demarkation between the respective nations of Chinese and Tartars. … one of the Tartar attendants was about to be punished for some misdemeanour, by order of the Chinese mandarines; but he resisted with much vehemence, loudly exclaiming, that no Chinese had a right of exercising authority over him on the Tartar side of the great wall.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton

p.h: Tartar captives hauling brick and lime in Poland
p.g: Slavery ran both ways. Chevalier says the Poles kept most Tartar prisoners as chained slaves, used 'as Beasts' to carry building materials, firewood and other loads, living on bread and water. He saw two or three hundred of them in Warsaw, earning a little by making and selling whips.
p.q: the rest are kept as Slaves, having always Irons upon their feet, and are made use of as Beasts to carry all manner of burthens, Lime, Brick, and all other materials for building … when I was at Warsaw, I had opportunity to take notice of two or three hundred of them
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

p.h: Mongke Khan: one God, many ways, like fingers on a hand
p.g: After a debate between Christians, Muslims and Buddhists at his court, Mongke Khan explained the Mongol faith to Rubruck. The Moal believe in one God, he said, but God gives different peoples different ways, as he gives the hand different fingers. It is a vivid statement of the Mongol court's religious tolerance, spoken through an interpreter.
p.q: "We Moal," he said, "believe that there is only one God, by whom we live and by whom we die, and for whom we have an upright heart." … "But as God gives us the different fingers of the hand, so he gives to men divers ways.
p.s: Mongke Khan, as reported by William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)
p.c: Mongke's words reached Rubruck through an interpreter, William Boucher's son.
p.tg: religion tolerance mongke tengri one god

p.h: An ironworks inside a family yurt
p.g: Gmelin rode to see a Tatar ironworks and at first could not find it: no building looked any different. The furnace was simply the cooking hollow found in every yurt, topped with a clay cone about a foot high and blown by two bellows, and the family went on living around it. Two men did all the work; from three pounds of ore they got about two pounds of iron, impure-looking but, he thought, very good.
p.q: Wir konnten auch gleich sehen, daß man wegen des Schmelzofens nicht nöthig habe, eine besondere Jurte zu bauen, sondern daß eine jede Jurte darzu tüchtig sey. Ja es hinderte auch die Leute nicht in eben dieser Jurte zu wohnen, welches alles schon ein großer Vortheil vor den Europäischen Eisenhütten ist, die man mit großen Kosten aufführen muß.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.pl: Gadöwa, on the Kondoma river, Kemerovo region
p.pe: Tatars of the Kondoma valley (the people now called Shors)
p.t: We could see at once that no special yurt needs to be built for the furnace, but that any yurt will serve. Indeed it did not even stop people living in that same yurt, which is already a great advantage over European ironworks, which have to be built at great expense.

p.h: Manchu grandees carry their ancestors' bones home to Tartary
p.g: Hüttner reports that viceroys and the highest ministers were mostly chosen from Tartar grandees, a measure he thought 'probably very necessary': according to a Chinese popular rumour, the emperor so feared losing the Chinese throne that he was having metal cast and heaped up in wide vaults under a riverbed near Mukden in Tartary (the scan is damaged at this point). And he calls it certain that Tartar nobles often moved the long-buried bodies of their forefathers from China to Tartary, fearing they would one day have to leave the country and unable to bear abandoning their ancestors' ashes to the enemy.
p.q: Es ist auch zuverlässig, dass die vornehmen Tartaren die längst beerdigten Leichname ihrer Voreltern häufig aus China nach der Tartarei führen; weil sie fürchten, über kurz oder lang dieses schöne Land verlassen zu müssen
p.s: Johann Christian Hüttner (1797)
p.pe: Manchu ('Tartar') nobility of the Qing empire
p.t: It is also certain that the Tartar nobles often carry the long-buried bodies of their forefathers from China to Tartary, because they fear that sooner or later they will have to leave this beautiful country
p.c: The treasure-vault story is explicitly a popular rumour, and the OCR of that sentence is badly damaged; the reburial claim is stated as fact but is also hearsay.
p.tg: manchus reburial ancestors mukden rumour qing

p.h: Ten thousand Tartars sent to hunt ginseng
p.g: Jartoux writes that the emperor, wanting Tartars rather than Chinese to profit from ginseng, ordered ten thousand Tartars in 1709 to gather it, each owing him two ounces of the best, with the rest bought at its weight in fine silver. His survey party met these herb-hunters in the wilderness; on the same page he describes their troops of a hundred men advancing in a line through the forest. The letter opens with a Tartar villager near the Korean border bringing him four whole plants in a basket.
p.q: L'Empereur souhaitant que les Tartares profitassent de ce gain, préférablement aux Chinois, avait donné ordre, cette même année 1709, à dix mille Tartares, d'aller ramasser eux-mêmes tout ce qu'ils pourraient de gin-seng, à condition que chacun d'eux en donnerait à Sa Majesté deux onces du meilleur, et que le reste serait payé au poids d'argent fin.
p.s: Pierre Jartoux, letter from Peking, 12 April 1711
p.t: The Emperor, wishing the Tartars rather than the Chinese to profit from this trade, had ordered ten thousand Tartars that same year, 1709, to go and gather for themselves all the ginseng they could, on condition that each of them would give His Majesty two ounces of the best, and that the rest would be paid for at the weight of fine silver.

p.h: Women whose headdresses look like helmets and lances
p.g: Married Mongol women wore the bocca (bogtak), a tall bark frame covered with silk and topped with a tuft of quills and peacock feathers. Rubruck says a group of ladies riding in the distance looked like soldiers in helmets with lances raised, and that women rode astride like men. He adds, less kindly, that the fattest women with the smallest noses were thought the most beautiful.
p.q: and one sees them from afar, they look like soldiers, helmets on head and lances erect. For this bocca looks like a helmet, and the tuft above it is like a lance. And all the women sit their horses astraddle like men.
p.s: William of Rubruck (translated by W. W. Rockhill, 1900)

p.h: Tatar women's sugar-loaf caps, and equal marriages
p.g: Chappe describes the dress of the Tatars of Birna: the men in wool tunics, long robes and boots with shaved heads, the women in shorter robes and tall sugar-loaf caps sewn with copper coins and glass beads. Wives shared most of their husbands' work and were treated gently, with 'perfect equality' between them, which he contrasts with the seclusion of Siberian Russian wives.
p.q: L'habillement des femmes Tartares differe peu de celui des hommes : il est plus court, & la ceinture est par-dessus la robe. Leur coeffure est un bonnet, souvent fait en pain de sucre; il est couvert de copecks & de grains de verre … Elles partagent la plupart des travaux de leurs maris : ceux-ci les traitent avec douceur : une parfaite égalité regne entre eux.
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.t: The dress of Tartar women differs little from that of the men: it is shorter, and the belt is worn over the robe. Their headdress is a cap, often shaped like a sugar loaf, covered with kopecks and glass beads … They share most of their husbands' work; the husbands treat them gently; a perfect equality reigns between them.
p.c: A one-day visit; the plate 'Tartares des environs de Kazan' in the same volume illustrates the dress.

p.h: Nomads who sowed and reaped
p.g: Barbaro answers the obvious question of where so many people got their grain. Each February the horde announced where sowing would happen; volunteers went with seed, carts and families, ploughed and sowed, and later returned to harvest while the khan's camp circled nearby. He says the yields were huge.
p.q: About the mooneth of Februarie they make proclamacons throughout the Lordo, that he which woll sowe shall prepare his things necessarie against the mooneth of Marche, to sowe in such a place. … And there do they eare, sowe, and tarie, till they haue furnisshed that they came for, which doon they retorne to their Lordo.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

p.h: Spices come by the Tartar road through Baghdad and Tabriz
p.g: Sanudo, a Venetian with merchant experience, argues that the Pope should ban trade with Mamluk Egypt because goods can come instead through the lands of the Tartars. Christian merchants, he says, can travel from the Tartar dominions all the way to India, and many have gone and come back, whereas the Sultan lets no Christian pass; light, precious spices such as cloves, nutmeg and mace already reach the Mediterranean via Baghdad and Tabriz.
p.q: ab hac parte scilicet dominii Tartarorum, vsque in Indiam ipsi mercatores Christiani poterunt dirigere gressus suos, cùm multi sint, qui iam iuerunt & redierunt. … sciendum est quod à partibus Tartarorum, scilicet à Baldach & à Thorisio, à magno tempore citra conducta sunt & cōducuntur ad præsens ad Mare Mediterraneum, quasi omnia mercimonia modici ponderis, & magni prætii
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.pe: Mongols of the Ilkhanate (Persia and Iraq)
p.t: from this side, namely the dominion of the Tartars, Christian merchants will be able to direct their steps as far as India, since there are many who have already gone and come back. ... it should be known that from the parts of the Tartars, namely from Baghdad and from Tabriz, for a long time past and at present almost all goods of small weight and great price are carried to the Mediterranean Sea
p.c: A policy argument for a trade embargo; his trade information came from Venetian and other merchants.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: trade spices tabriz baghdad india ilkhanate

p.h: Shaved heads, queues and horse-hoof sleeves
p.g: When the Tartars took a city in Liaodong, they proclaimed that no one would be killed who cut his hair and wore Tartar dress. Martini then breaks off to describe their manners: head and beard shaved except the moustache, a long braided tuft at the back, a low round cap trimmed with beaver or sable. The next pages add long robes with sleeves cut like a horse's hoof, a sabre hung point forward, silk or horse-skin boots, broad saddles, and the remark that they are like 'our Tartars of Europe' but not so barbarous.
p.q: For the Tartars (that I may say something of their Manners, as my subject gives me occasion) doe shave both the Head and Beards reserving only the Mustachoes, which they extend to a great length, and in the hinder part of their heads they leave a Tuft, which being curiously woven and plated, they let hang down carelesly below their shoulders;
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)

p.h: Tax farmers driven out by the town assemblies
p.g: The Horde's tribute had been farmed out to Muslim merchants, who bought the right to collect it and charged interest. In 1262 the towns called their assemblies (veche) and drove them out of Rostov, Vladimir, Suzdal and Iaroslavl. The same entry tells of a renegade monk, Zosima, who became a Muslim under a Tatar official named Kutlubii and was killed in Iaroslavl.
p.q: вложи ярость въ сердца крестьяномъ, не терпяще насилья поганыхъ, изволиша вѣчь, и выгнаша изъ городовъ, изъ Ростова, изъ Володимеря, изъ Суждаля, изъ Ярославля; окупахуть бо ти оканьніи бесурмене дани, и отъ того велику пагубу людемъ творяхуть
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Muslim ('besermen') tax farmers working for the Horde; townspeople of Rostov, Vladimir, Suzdal, Iaroslavl
p.t: [God] put fury into the hearts of the Christians, who, not bearing the violence of the pagans, summoned the veche and drove them out of the towns, out of Rostov, out of Vladimir, out of Suzdal, out of Iaroslavl; for those accursed besermen had bought up the tribute, and from that they worked great ruin on the people
p.tg: tribute tax farming besermen veche uprising

p.h: God called Tagri and sacrifices to the prophet Elijah
p.g: Klaproth says the ordinary Bassian Tartars had no fixed religion: they called God 'Tagri' rather than Allah, offered lambs, dairy and beer to the prophet Elijah on mountain tops with song and dance, ate pork and kept sacred springs. Like other Tartars they foretold the future from sheep's shoulder-blades cracking in the fire. Only their chiefs had been made Muslim by the Circassians.
p.q: The common people have, strictly speaking, no established religion, but worship God, whom they call Tagri and not Allah, as the giver of all good, and the prophet Elijah… who, according to them, frequently appears on the summits of the highest mountains, and to whom they offer sacrifices of lambs, milk, butter, cheese, and beer (ssra), accompanied with singing and dancing.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
p.c: Based on informants' reports rather than long residence.

p.h: Muslim Tatars and the sultan as caliph
p.g: Although the Tatars were declared independent of the Ottomans, the memoir keeps a religious tie. Because 'the Tatar nation is of the religion of Islam', and two caliphs cannot coexist under Islamic law, Russia agrees that the Tatars acknowledge the Ottoman sultan, 'caliph and head of all Muslim rulers and protector of the Two Holy Cities', as holding supreme spiritual authority over them. It shows the Crimean Tatars as a Muslim people whose faith linked them to Istanbul.
p.q: ولکن تاتار ملتی دین اسلامدن اولمغيله … روسيه دولتی رضاداده اولورکه شفقتلو قدرتلو پادشاه آل عثمان حضرتلری خليفه ورئيس جمله حکمداران مسلمين وحرمين شريفين حاميسی اولمغيله ذات شريفه‌لرنده رخصت علياء روحانيه مرکوز بولنديغی تاتارلر قبول واعتراف ايده‌لر
p.s: Ottoman chancery memoir on the Tatars and their khans (item IV in the library catalogue, put into Turkish by the reis ul-kuttab Abd al-Razzaq Efendi), undated copy c.1775 to 1780
p.t: But since the Tatar nation is of the religion of Islam … the Russian state consents that the Tatars accept and acknowledge that supreme spiritual authority is vested in the noble person of His Majesty the compassionate and mighty Padishah of the House of Osman, as caliph and head of all Muslim rulers and protector of the Two Holy Cities.
p.c: Treaty-style wording agreed between two empires; it states a legal position, not what ordinary Tatars believed.
p.n: Transcribed from the manuscript image (corpus OCR of this manuscript is garbled).

p.h: Tatar archers who never miss
p.g: The account of the 1382 siege describes Tatar archery: their arrows fell on the walls like rain, some shot standing, others ran back and forth, others galloped and shot to both sides, forward and back, 'without a miss'. The defenders answered with crossbows, stone-throwers, boiling water and even the first cannon mentioned in Moscow.
p.q: Бѣ же приступъ ихъ ко граду яръ зѣло и ови отъ нихъ стояще стрѣляху, а друзіи скоро рищуще сѣмо и овамо, тако изучени быша, и стрѣляху безъ погрѣха; а иніи на конѣхъ борзо велми гоняюще, и на обѣ руцѣ и паки напреди и назадъ скорополучно стрѣляху безъ погрѣха.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 11 (1897)
p.t: Their assault on the city was very fierce; some of them shot standing, and others ran swiftly here and there, so well were they trained, and shot without a miss; and others, galloping very fast on horses, shot swiftly to both hands, and again forward and backward, without a miss.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: 'Worse than evil is Tatar honour'
p.g: The chronicler breaks off to lament what homage meant: a great prince who ruled Kiev, Vladimir and Galich now knelt and was called a slave, and paid tribute in fear for his life. He adds that the Tatars had poisoned Grand Prince Iaroslav of Suzdal and knifed Mikhail of Chernigov for not bowing to the bush. Daniil stayed 25 days before he was sent home with his lands confirmed.
p.q: О злѣе зла честь Татарьская! Данилови Романовичю князю бывшу велику, обладавшу Рускою землею, Кыевомъ и Володимеромъ и Галичемъ, со братомъ си инѣми странами: нынѣ сѣдить на колѣну и холопомъ называеться, и дани хотять, живота не чаеть и грозы приходять.
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pe: Batu's Horde; Prince Daniil of Galicia
p.t: O, worse than evil is Tatar honour! Daniil Romanovich was a great prince, who ruled the Russian land, Kiev and Vladimir and Galich, with his brother, and other lands: now he sits on his knees and is called a slave, and they want tribute, he does not expect to live, and threats come.
p.c: The poisoning of Iaroslav is the chronicler's claim (Carpini reports a similar suspicion); it is not proven.

p.h: A Tatar lament: 'five Cossacks'
p.g: At the mouth of the Ishim there was a fierce hand-to-hand fight in which five of Yermak's Cossacks died. The chronicle says the Tatars still sang about it at their gatherings, weeping, with the refrain 'yanym, yanym, bish kazak', which it translates as 'warriors, warriors, five men defeated and ruined'; the song was called 'the tsaritsa's lament'. The Tatar words more likely mean 'my soul, my soul, five Cossacks'.
p.q: и о тѣхъ пяти человѣкахъ Татара поютъ съ плачемъ при бесѣдахъ въ пѣсняхъ припѣваючи: янымъ, янымъ, бишь казакъ, бишь казакъ, сирѣчь: воины, воины, пять пять человѣкъ побѣдиша и разориша. И ся пѣсня и словетъ царицынъ плачь.
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
p.t: and about those five men the Tatars sing with weeping at their gatherings, in songs with the refrain: 'yanym, yanym, bish kazak, bish kazak', that is: 'warriors, warriors, five, five men defeated and destroyed'. And this song is called the tsaritsa's lament.
p.c: The chronicler's translation of the Tatar refrain is loose; the song itself is reported, not transcribed in full.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.
p.tg: song lament music oral tradition ishim

p.h: Dummies on spare horses to fake an army
p.g: Bishop Benedict of Várad chased a small Tartar band that had sacked Eger. Knowing they were few but had many horses, the Tartars made dummies and figures, set them on the empty horses like riders and hid them behind a low hill. When they pretended to retreat and the 'army' of dummies came out in battle order, the Hungarians thought they had fallen into an ambush and fled, and were cut down.
p.q: Fecerunt autem laruas et monstra quamplurima; ea super equos vacuos tamquam si essent milites ordinando. Et equos illos sub quodam monticulo, paucis cum eis relictis seruientibus dimiserunt … Et dum ipsi cum laruis exierunt sub monte, et ut condictum erat acie ordinata; Hungari hoc videntes, et opinantes eis insidias factas terga dederunt, et fugam velociter inierunt.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: They made a great many masks and figures, setting them on the empty horses as if they were soldiers. And they left those horses below a little hill, with a few servants left with them … And when these came out from under the hill with the masks, in battle order as had been agreed, the Hungarians, seeing this and thinking an ambush had been laid for them, turned their backs and quickly took to flight.
p.c: Roger was not at this skirmish; he reports it from those who were.

p.h: A whole horde on the move
p.g: The missionaries travelled with Erdeni's horde as it moved camp. The column was more than a verst wide: strings of camels carrying the tents, goods and children in baskets, then the herds. No one walked; even mothers with babies rode. Zwick describes the migration as a festive show at which families displayed their best clothes and carpets.
p.q: The main body of this moving multitude extended more than a verst in breadth, and consisted of single columns of camels, bearing tents, household goods, and children, who were stowed in baskets; next followed troops of horses, cattle and sheep … Nobody performs a migration on foot … we even saw mothers on horseback with infants, who were hardly out of the cradle
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: A sorceress envoy demands a tenth of everything
p.g: The Tatars came to Ryazan land 'without number, like locusts'. From their camp they sent envoys to the Ryazan princes, a woman sorceress and two men, demanding a tenth of everything: of people, of princes and of horses. The editor's footnote on this page adds that another copy lists the horses by colour, ten of each. The princes answered that when none of them were left, all would be theirs.
p.q: придоша иноплеменьници, глаголеми Татарове, на землю Рязаньскую, множьство безъ числа, акы прузи … и оттолѣ послаша послы своя, жену чародѣицю и два мужа съ нею, къ княземъ Рязаньскымъ, просяче у нихъ десятины во всемъ, и въ людьхъ, и въ князьхъ, и въ конихъ, во всякомъ десятое.
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.t: foreigners called Tatars came upon the Ryazan land, a multitude without number, like locusts … and from there they sent their envoys, a woman sorceress and two men with her, to the Ryazan princes, asking of them a tenth of everything: of people, and of princes, and of horses, a tenth of everything.

p.h: A minstrel's song: 'Return, O Timour!'
p.g: At a feast for the Moon festival a Mongol bard (toolholos) played a three-stringed fiddle and, at the priests' request, sang the 'Invocation to Timour', a lament for lost greatness that begs a hero to return and make the Mongols warriors again. Huc reproduces it in translation. It shows nineteenth-century Mongols remembering their imperial past in song.
p.q: "When the divine Timour dwelt within our tents, the Mongol nation was redoubtable and warlike; its least movements made the earth bend; its mere look froze with fear the ten thousand peoples upon whom the sun shines.
p.s: A Mongol minstrel, as rendered by Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)
p.c: Huc gives a free French rendering of an oral song; the 'Timour' of the song may not be the historical Tamerlane.

p.h: 'I'll make you a real Tartar': travelling on sheep
p.g: When Gerard could not find porters for his grain on the empty high plateau, his friend Putee Ram brought a flock of sheep. The trick was to load the grain on the sheep, eat the grain first, and then eat the sheep. It is a neat picture of how people actually crossed the high Tibetan uplands.
p.q: I'll make you a real Tartar: you have grain for ten or twelve days, and now you have no use for porters; load the sheep with the grain, finish it first, and then kill and eat the sheep : this is the way we travel on the uninhabitable tracts ; we never think of grain as long as we have plenty of sheep.
p.s: Putee Ram of Soongnum, quoted by Alexander Gerard (footnote)

p.h: Tartars learned letters, and idols, from the Uighurs
p.g: Hayton says that before their expansion the Tartars had no letters at all, which is why he cannot give dates for their early history. When their armies reached the kingdom of 'Tarse' (the Uighurs), they learned writing there, and because the people were idolaters they also began to worship idols, while always confessing one immortal God above the others.
p.q: En celes [parties] les Tartars apristrent letres, car avant ne avoient letres nules. E por ce que les habiteors de celes contrées estoient touz ydolatres, les Tartars comencierent aorer les ydoles; mès tout adès confessoient le Deu inmortel, plus grant que les autres.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: In those parts the Tartars learned letters, for before they had no letters at all. And because the inhabitants of those lands were all idolaters, the Tartars began to worship idols; but they always confessed the immortal God, greater than the others.

p.h: A Russian archbishop's report: food, prayer and women archers
p.g: Peter, an archbishop who had fled Russia before the Tartars, was questioned in the West, and Matthew records his answers. The Tartars, he said, eat horse and dog meat and in need even human flesh, but cooked, not raw; they drink blood, water and milk. Each morning they raise their hands to heaven to worship the Creator, toss the first morsel into the air and pour the first drink on the ground, and claim John the Baptist as their leader. Their women fight, and are excellent archers.
p.q: Carnes comedunt jumentinas, caninas, et alias abominabiles, etiam in necessitate humanas, non tamen crudas, sed coctas. Sanguinem, aquam, et lac bibunt. … Quolibet mane manus ad caelum levant, Creatorem adorantes. Comedentes vero, primum morsellum in aera jaciunt; bibentes, prius partem in terram fundunt, in veneratione Creatoris. Et dicunt se habere sanctum Johannem Baptistam pro duce. … Mulieres bellatrices, praecipue sagittatrices optimae sunt.
p.s: Peter, a Russian archbishop, as recorded by Matthew Paris under 1244 (Luard, vol. 4)
p.pe: Mongols (Tartars) as described by a refugee
p.t: They eat the flesh of horses and dogs and other abominable things, even human flesh in necessity, yet not raw but cooked. They drink blood, water and milk. … Every morning they raise their hands to heaven, worshipping the Creator. When eating, they throw the first morsel into the air; when drinking, they first pour part onto the ground, in veneration of the Creator. And they say they have Saint John the Baptist as their leader. … The women are warriors, and especially excellent archers.
p.c: Peter had fled the Tartars and his account mixes real observation (libations, sky worship) with rumour; the John the Baptist claim is unexplained. Luard notes the same account appears in the Burton Annals, given at the Council of Lyons.

p.h: 'They made a rampart of their saddles'
p.g: Reinaud quotes Abu'l-Fida's own chronicle of a skirmish before the battle of Marj al-Suffar in 1303, in which Abu'l-Fida fought. A group of Tartars who had dismounted were surrounded and offered their lives; they answered with arrows, made a barricade of their horses' saddles, and fought until every one was killed. It is an eyewitness picture of Mongol soldiers from the other side.
p.q: Une partie des Tartares ayant mis pied à terre, nous les entourâmes et nous leur offrîmes la vie; mais ils reçurent nos propositions à coups de flèches, et, se faisant un rempart des selles de leurs chevaux, ils soutinrent un nouveau combat. Ils furent tous massacrés jusqu'au dernier.
p.s: Abu'l-Fida's Chronicle, quoted in Reinaud's introduction (1848)
p.t: Some of the Tartars had dismounted; we surrounded them and offered them their lives, but they answered our offer with arrows, and, making a rampart of their horses' saddles, fought a fresh battle. They were all killed to the last man.
p.c: Written by a victorious enemy commander.

p.h: Slave caravans on the road to Khiva
p.g: Abbott travelled alongside caravans that had carried grain south and were returning to Khiva with captives, many from Herat. He describes the women riding with their captors and the men walking the whole way, chained by the neck at night.
p.q: They had brought grain from Khiva, and are returning thither laden with slaves, many of whom are natives of Heraut. … But the men are chained together by the throats at night, so that rest is scarcely possible, whilst the contact of the frozen iron with their skin must be torturous. For them also no carriage is found, they walk the whole way
p.s: James Abbott
p.pe: Turkmen traders and their captives from Herat

p.h: Ibn Battuta at Özbeg Khan's court: unveiled, honoured wives
p.g: Hammer retells Ibn Battuta's visit. Every Friday Özbeg sat under a golden vault called the golden alcove, on a silver-plated, jewelled throne, with his sons on either side and his daughter before him. Whenever one of his wives came in he rose, took her by the hand and led her to her seat; all were unveiled. Each wife had her own house and household, and Ibn Battuta marvelled at the freedom and standing of women among the Tatars, so unlike Arab and Persian harem seclusion.
p.q: So oft eine seiner Gemahlinnen hereinkam, stand er auf, nahm sie bey der Hand, und führte sie auf ihren Platz; sie waren alle unverschleyert. … Die Frauen Usbeg's waren hochgeehrt. Jede hatte besonderes Haus und besonderen Hofstaat; überhaupt verwundert sich Ibn Batuta über die Freyheit und das Ansehen, welches die Frauen (ganz im Gegensatze arabischen und persischen Haremszwanges) bey den Tataren genossen.
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), summarising Ibn Battuta (from Lee's English translation, 1829)
p.pl: Özbeg Khan's camp, North Caucasus steppe; Sarai
p.pe: Golden Horde court of Özbeg (Uzbek) Khan
p.t: Whenever one of his wives came in, he stood up, took her by the hand and led her to her place; they were all unveiled. … Özbeg's wives were highly honoured. Each had her own house and her own household; in general Ibn Battuta wonders at the freedom and esteem which women enjoyed among the Tatars (quite unlike the compulsion of the Arab and Persian harem).
p.c: Hammer paraphrases; Ibn Battuta's own words are in his Rihla.
p.tg: ibn battuta court women ozbeg khan throne

p.h: A white tent for a daughter who may marry
p.g: When a daughter of these settled Tatar farmers was ready to marry, her family covered her tent with white linen tied with red strings and set a painted cloth on top, with a painted wagon beside it as her dowry. Suitors took the hint, and the girl generally went to the man who offered her father the best present.
p.q: When any of their daughters become marriageable, they cover her tent with white linen, and put a painted cloth on the top, which is usually tied with red strings: they have also a painted waggon on the side of the tent; and this is to be her marriage portion. Those who design to marry observe this signal,
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
p.pe: Tatars of Crimean descent settled around Astrakhan

p.h: The Xiongnu: no cities, no fields, no writing
p.g: Sima Qian's classic description of the Xiongnu, north of China: herders of horses, cattle and sheep who move with the grass and water, with no cities, no settled life and no farming, though each had his own allotted land. No writing: laws are proclaimed orally. Boys ride sheep and shoot birds; all fighting men are mounted archers. It is the oldest template for Chinese and later European pictures of the steppe nomad.
p.q: Перекочевываютъ съ мѣста на мѣсто, смотря по приволью въ травѣ и водѣ. Не имѣютъ ни городовъ, ни осѣдлости, ни земледѣлія; но у каждаго есть отдѣленный участокъ земли. Письма нѣтъ, а законы словесно объявляются. Мальчикъ, какъ скоро можетъ верхомъ сидѣть на баранѣ, стрѣляетъ изъ лука пташекъ и звѣрковъ
p.s: Sima Qian, Shiji (c. 100 BCE), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
p.pe: Xiongnu (Huns), in Bichurin's view ancestors of the Mongols
p.t: They move from place to place according to the abundance of grass and water. They have neither cities, nor settled dwelling, nor farming; but each has his allotted piece of land. There is no writing, and laws are proclaimed orally. A boy, as soon as he can sit astride a sheep, shoots little birds and small animals with a bow
p.c: A Chinese court historian writing about an enemy; Bichurin's footnote equates the Xiongnu with the Mongols of his day, a view historians no longer accept.
p.tg: xiongnu nomads no cities archery shiji

p.h: Kimiz: mare's milk that makes you drunk
p.g: Wood explains how the Kirghiz and Uzbeks make kimiz (kumiss) from mare's milk, churned overnight and ready by sunrise. A spoonful, he was told, makes a man drunk, but their spoons are huge. He also passes on, while flagging it as hostile gossip, a claim that kimiz season brought drunken excess.
p.q: The Kirghiz, as well as the Uzbeks, keep brood mares, according to their means, and the acidulated milk of these animals yields them in spring the intoxicating liquor called kimiz. … A spoonful will produce inebriety, but their kashuk or spoon is much more capacious than the largest upon our tables.
p.s: John Wood
p.tg: kumiss mare's milk drink horses kirghiz

p.h: Clean houses and full granaries: Tatar farmers
p.g: In a short 'Note on the Tartars' written as he crossed from Yekaterinburg towards Kazan, Lesseps says the cleanliness inside Tatar houses astonished him after a year among Kamchadals and Koryaks. These Tatars, he stresses, were settled farmers, rich in grain and cattle, and Muslims.
p.q: Je dirai seulement de ces derniers, que la propreté de l'intérieur de leurs habitations m'a étonné, sans doute parce que je m'étois un peu trop familiarisé avec le défaut contraire parmi les Kamtschadales, Koriaques, &c. Ces Tartares sont sédentaires, agriculteurs & riches en blés & en bestiaux; ils professent la religion Mahométane.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps
p.pe: Muslim Tatars of the Urals and Volga region
p.t: I will only say of the latter that the cleanliness of the inside of their dwellings astonished me, no doubt because I had grown rather too used to the opposite fault among the Kamchadals, Koryaks and so on. These Tartars are settled, farmers, and rich in grain and cattle; they profess the Mahometan religion.

p.h: A bride carried home unseen
p.g: Holderness, often invited to village weddings, describes how the bride travelled in a curtained cart and was kept from every eye: she was given sherbet and a lamb at her new door, then, behind screens of blanketing, wrapped in a sheet and carried into the house by her brother.
p.q: When she reaches the door of her new prison, sherbet is brought her to drink, and some kind of sweetmeat is given with it. She is next presented with a lamb, which is actually put into the carriage with her … wrapped in a sheet, she is carried by her brother into the house.
p.s: Mary Holderness
p.c: 'New prison' is Holderness's own judgement.

p.h: Prince Michael refuses to bow to Chinggis Khan's image
p.g: Carpini tells how Michael of Chernigov, a great Russian prince, came to submit to Batu. He was first made to pass between two fires, then told to bow southwards to the image of Chinggis Khan. He answered that he would gladly bow to Batu and his servants, but not to the image of a dead man, since Christians may not; after repeated refusals he was kicked in the chest until he died.
p.q: undè nuper contigit quod Michael, qui fuit unus de magnis ducibus Rusciæ, cùm ivisset ad reddendum se Bati, fecerunt eum priùs inter duos ignes transire; post hoc dixerunt ei quod ad meridiem Chingis-can inclinaret: qui respondit quòd Bati et servis suis etiàm inclinaret libenter, sed imagini hominis mortui non inclinaret, quià non licet hoc facere christianis
p.s: John of Plano Carpini
p.pe: Mongols of the Golden Horde; Russian princes
p.t: So it recently happened that Michael, one of the great dukes of Russia, when he went to submit to Batu, was first made to pass between two fires; after this they told him to bow to the south to Chinggis Khan. He answered that he would willingly bow to Batu and even to his servants, but he would not bow to the image of a dead man, because Christians may not do so
p.c: Carpini reports this as recent news, not as something he witnessed; Michael was later venerated as a martyr, so the story also served Christian purposes.
p.tg: purification by fire chinggis khan image martyrdom russia

p.h: Raising a khan on white felt
p.g: Schiltberger says the Great Tartars sow only millet, eat no bread and drink no wine, but drink mare's and camel's milk and eat horse and camel meat. The khan and his people live in the open fields winter and summer. A new khan is set on a white felt and lifted up three times, carried round the tent, and given a golden sword.
p.q: It is also to be noted, that when they choose a king, they take him and seat him on white felt, and raise him in it three times. Then they lift him up and carry him round the tent, and seat him on a throne, and put a golden sword in his hand.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.c: He witnessed several quick changes of khan while with Chekre, but does not say which enthronement he saw.

p.h: Turkmens: no chiefs, no nobles
p.g: Fraser says Turkmen camps of 30 to 200 families followed an elder but had no rulers or nobles, and anyone who tried to seize power would be destroyed. Only a rare figure like Genghis Khan or Timur, he adds, could force such people into a single powerful union.
p.q: But they have no governors, chiefs, or nobles among them : and if any one should attempt to arrogate superior consideration to himself, or openly aim at power or authority, it would be the signal for his destruction. … Such an event can only occur, when some individual supereminently endowed with talents and courage, like a Chengiz, or a Timour, arises to force into union substances naturally repellent
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.tg: turkmen government elders equality genghis khan

p.h: 'If their religion be right, why do they not do right?'
p.g: Half the labourers on Perry's canal were Mordva and Cheremis 'Tartars', long under Russian rule. Asked why they would not be baptized, they told him that images terrified them, because God is one and cannot be pictured, and he lives in heaven. They taunted Russians with the question, 'if their Religion be right, why do they not do right?' Perry adds that he found them more honest than the Russians.
p.q: …they say, that the Ruses using of Images, is a Terror to them to think of embracing their Religion; for that there is but one God, and that he cannot be pictured or described by Men; they look up towards the Heavens, and say, that he resides there, and of whom they are afraid to do Evil;
p.s: Captain John Perry (The State of Russia, 1716)
p.pe: Mordva, 'Morsie' and Cheremis (Mari), whom Perry calls Tartars
p.c: Perry's 'Tartars' here are mainly Finnic peoples (Mordvins, Mari), not Turkic Tatars.

p.h: A note hidden in a gun barrel
p.g: Preparing to leave, Muraviev found a slip of paper secretly pushed into his gun barrel by Russian captives, begging him to tell the Tsar of more than 3,000 Russian slaves suffering in Khiva. Elsewhere he says most were kidnapped on the Orenburg frontier by Kazakhs and sold at Khiva, and that Russian slaves were the khanate's only smiths.
p.q: As I was preparing to clean this gun, I discovered a slip of paper in one of the barrels, on which the following was written in Russian : "We venture to inform your Honor that there are over 3,000 Russian slaves in this place, who have to suffer unheard-of misery from labour, cold, hunger, &c. Have pity on our unhappy situation and reveal it to the Emperor.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev, quoting a note from Russian slaves (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: Better than a dog? A khan's conversion to Islam
p.g: The young Moghul khan, feeding his dogs pork during a hunt, asks a captured Persian-speaking holy man whether he is better than the dog. The shaikh answers that with faith he is better, without it the dog is. Moved, the khan promises to become a Muslim when he rules, and years later the shaikh's son holds him to it. Mirza Haidar heard it from the holy man's descendants.
p.q: He was, at that time, feeding some dogs with swine's flesh, and he asked the Shaikh angrily : "Are you better than this dog, or is the dog better than you ?" The Shaikh replied : "If I have faith I am better than this dog ; but if I have no faith, this dog is better than I am."
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)
p.pe: Tughluk Timur Khan of the Moghuls
p.c: Family and religious tradition, told about two centuries after the event.
p.tg: islam conversion tughluk timur dogs hunt

p.h: A khan buried under a hill with slaves and impaled horses
p.g: Ibn Battuta reports that a Mongol khan was killed by rebel kinsmen and buried with about a hundred relatives. The khan was laid on a couch in an underground chamber with his weapons, gold and silver vessels, four slave women and six favourite servants, and earth was heaped over it into a hill. Four horses were impaled on stakes on the mound. Everyone wore white hoods for mourning.
p.q: a large sepulchre was dug for him under the earth, in which a most beautiful couch was spread, and the Khan was with his weapons laid upon it. With him they placed all the gold and silver vessels he had in his house, together with four female slaves, and six of his favourite Mamluks … and the earth heaped upon them to the height of a large hill.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: He says the khan was killed before he reached the capital, so the burial is almost certainly reported, not seen; the translator notes he could find no record of such a khan's death, and no Yuan emperor died this way at that date.
p.tg: burial kurgan human sacrifice horses yuan

p.h: Measured against the linchpin of a cart
p.g: After defeating the Tatar tribes at Dalan Nemurges, Chinggis and his kinsmen met in a single tent and decided the fate of the prisoners. Every Tatar male taller than the linchpin of a cart was to be killed and the rest enslaved and shared out, as revenge for Tatar killings of Chinggis's forefathers (including, in the chronicle's story, the poisoning of his father Yesugei). The chronicle goes on to say the plan leaked, the Tatars barricaded themselves in and fought with knives hidden in their sleeves.
p.q: From olden days the Tatar people Have destroyed our fathers and forefathers; To avenge our fathers and forefathers, And requite the wrong, for them We shall measure the Tatars against the linchpin of a cart, And kill them to the last one, We shall utterly slay them. The rest we shall enslave: Some here, some there, dividing them among ourselves!
p.s: Anonymous author of the Secret History (translated by Igor de Rachewiltz, 2015)
p.c: The editor's footnote explains that only those taller than the linchpin were to be killed; the scene is told from the victors' side.
p.tg: tatar tribe revenge war execution carts

p.h: 'Houses mean slavery'
p.g: Meyendorff explains why well-off Kazakhs refused to farm: they feared becoming serfs tied to the soil and liked to say they were as free as the birds. An old saying warned that they would lose their freedom once they began living in houses and farming, and the fate of the Bashkirs under Russia seemed to prove it.
p.q: It is therefore easy to imagine why Kirghiz in easy circumstances never cultivate the ground … they have an ancient tradition which says "The Kirghiz shall lose their liberty whenever they begin to live in houses
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)
p.c: The OCR garbles the end of the saying on this page; the quote stops at 'houses' (the saying continues 'and to follow agricultural pursuits').

p.h: A Turkmen singer like an Aeolian harp
p.g: After dinner in a Goklen chief's tent, two musicians played until past midnight. Fraser found the singing far sweeter than Persian music: the singer's voice imitated the vibrating string of the tar, and the audience rocked and shouted with delight.
p.q: the measure was always closed by a single line or chorus that died away in a very sweet and singular cadence, infinitely more agreeable than any music I ever heard in Persia, for the singer did not strain his voice in the way usual in that country, but taught it most curiously to follow the inflections of the tarr, imitating the sound and undulations of the wire
p.s: James Baillie Fraser
p.pe: Goklen Turkmens at the camp of Khallee Khan

p.h: 'We get drunk every day': a mare's-milk spirit party
p.g: At a drinking bout with Kalmyk clergy, Bergmann watched a boy of ten or twelve drain five bowls and a sixty-year-old gelung twelve. He noticed for the first time that fermented mare's milk (tschigan, which the Tatars call kumiss) was intoxicating even before distilling: the drinkers began to speak Tatar and Russian and even scraps of German. When he asked whether such parties were frequent, the old monk answered flatly that they got drunk every day, and the others said it was a kind of medicine. Bergmann doubted it and blamed the drink for the eye troubles common among Kalmyks.
p.q: Die kalmükischen Trinker waren alle so voll von den Dünsten dieses Getränks, daß sie Tatarisch und Russisch zu sprechen, und einige sogar deutsche Brocken um sich zu werfen anfingen. … Ich fragte, ob man hier öfters dergleichen Tschigangelage anzustellen pflegte. Der Alte antwortete mir ganz kathegorisch: „Wir besaufen uns alle Tage.”
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann
p.t: The Kalmyk drinkers were all so full of the fumes of this drink that they began to speak Tatar and Russian, and some even to throw about scraps of German. … I asked whether such tschigan parties were often held here. The old man answered me quite categorically: 'We get drunk every day.'
p.tg: kumiss milk spirit drinking clergy languages

p.h: A riddle: 'like a white tent, with no door'
p.g: The Codex preserves Cuman riddles, the oldest recorded Turkic riddles. This one runs: 'Like a white tent, it has no mouth. That is the egg.' Kuun reads 'akkoy' as 'ak ev', literally 'white house', and renders it 'the tent of a new bride'. The riddle draws on the everyday sight of a tent, the home of the people who told it.
p.q: [6,] akkoy mania avzu joh. ol jumurtka.
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, German part (riddle 6), ed. Geza Kuun 1880
p.t: Like a white tent (ak ev), it has no mouth. That is the egg.
p.c: Kuun's footnote on the page explains 'akkoy' as 'ak ev', 'tentorium novae nuptae' (the tent of a new bride); the gloss depends on his reading.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: riddle felt tent white tent bride folklore

p.h: Unwashed lamb and mare's milk that 'stank most horribly'
p.g: Hiding from the khan's search on a Volga island, the starving Contarini was fed by his Tatar guide's people. They killed a lamb for him and cooked it without washing it, saying washing spoils the flavour. They pressed mare's milk on him as a strengthening drink, and were offended when he refused it.
p.q: a lamb was killed in my honour, which was partly roasted and partly boiled, but no trouble whatever was taken to wash the flesh, as they say that washing takes all the flavour away … Mare's milk was also brought, which they hold in great esteem … as they say it gives great strength to man; but, as it stank most horribly, I refused to taste it
p.s: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)
p.tg: kumiss mare's milk food hospitality meat

p.h: Wishing an enemy a house and a job
p.g: Bell describes the Volga Kalmyks as herders who despise settled work. They have no craftsmen except armourers, and their worst curse is that a man should live in one place and labour like a Russian. On the same page he praises their language for lacking oaths and quotes their proverb 'Though a knife be sharp it cannot cut its own handle'.
p.q: They have no mechanics, except those who make arms. They avoid all labour as the greatest slavery; their only employment is tending their flocks, managing horses, and hunting. If they are angry with a person, they wish he may live in one place, and work like a Russian.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: The kadi's wife examines an English arm
p.g: Only the interpreter and a twelve-year-old boy were allowed into the women's room. The kadi's wife wore a turban with diamonds and pearls, scarlet-dyed nails and a face painted white and red with the veins drawn in blue. Craven's gloves seemed to trouble her, and once they were off the lady took her hand and felt her arm up to the shoulder, nodding approval, before coffee and rose-petal sweetmeats signalled the end of the visit.
p.q: She made me a sign to sit down; and my gloves seeming to excite much uneasiness in her I took them off … upon which she drew near, smiled, took one of my hands between her's, and winked and nodded as a sign of approbation
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)

p.h: Gravestones of a princess and a man from Samarkand
p.g: The journal prints some fifty epitaphs from Bulgary's grave mounds, copied in 1722 on Peter the Great's orders and translated into Russian by an akhun, a local translator and an Armenian (for the Armenian stones). Each begins 'The Lord is the living and immortal God' and gives a name and a Muslim year: a man 'from the city of Samarkand', a patriarch from Shirvan, a woman 'from the kingdom of Bulgaria', and this princess Sara, daughter of Achmet, who died in the year 670 of the Hijra (1271 or 1272). A translator's footnote notes that the year 623 (1226) appears most often and guesses there was an epidemic that year.
p.q: Der Herr ist der lebendige und unsterbliche Gott. Dies ist die Grabstätte der überaus gottseligen, sehr barmherzigen, sehr schönen, hochgebornen und unbefleckten, verehrungswürdigen und vielgläubigen Fürstin Sara, Tochter Achmets. Sie starb im Jahr von Mahomed 670.
p.s: Bulgar gravestone inscription, as translated in 1722 and printed in Lepekhin's journal (German translation, 1774)
p.pe: Muslim inhabitants of medieval Bulgar (epitaphs in 'Tatar script')
p.t: The Lord is the living and immortal God. This is the resting place of the most godly, very merciful, very beautiful, high-born and spotless, venerable and most faithful princess Sara, daughter of Achmet. She died in the year of Mohammed 670.
p.c: A translation of a translation (Arabic-script original, then Russian, then German); names may be distorted.

p.h: Felt idols, the god Natagai, and a smiths' New Year
p.g: Hammer gathers the old Mongol religion from Rubruck, Marco Polo and Rashid al-Din: idols of felt and silk, offered the heart of each slaughtered animal; prayer facing south; worship of sun, stars and elements, with food and drink dedicated before meals; a chief god Natagai honoured with his whole family; libations to the four quarters outside the tent. He lists three yearly feasts: the smiths' festival recalling the exodus from Ergene Kun, the khan's birthday, and the herd festival with mare's milk poured for Khubilai's ten thousand white horses. In a footnote he quotes Rashid al-Din that on New Year's night Chinggis Khan's family hammered iron on an anvil and gave thanks.
p.q: Die Mongolen hatten Götzenbilder aus Filz und Seide. Wenn sie ein Thier schlachteten, wurde den Götzenbildern das Herz dargebracht, und sie betheten gegen Mittag gewandt, wie die Moslimen gegen die Kaaba. Sie betheten die Sonne und die Sterne sammt den Elementen an … Ihr vorzüglicher Gott hiess Natagai, und ward mit seiner ganzen Familie von allen Tataren verehrt.
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1840), compiling Rubruck, Marco Polo and Rashid al-Din
p.pe: Mongols ('all Tatars') before their conversion to Islam
p.t: The Mongols had idols of felt and silk. When they slaughtered an animal, the heart was offered to the idols, and they prayed facing south, as the Muslims face the Kaaba. They worshipped the sun and the stars together with the elements … Their principal god was called Natagai, and he was worshipped with his whole family by all Tatars.
p.c: A patchwork of travellers' reports; Schmidt objected in the margin that no trace of the smiths' feast survived among Mongols, and Hammer answered with Rashid al-Din.
p.tg: religion idols felt natagai festivals mare's milk

p.h: The census: tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands
p.g: The Horde sent census takers who counted the Suzdal, Riazan and Murom lands and set up officers over tens, hundreds, thousands and ten-thousands, the Mongol decimal system, before returning to the Horde. Clergy were not counted, in line with the Mongol practice of exempting religious men from tax.
p.q: Тое же зимы пріѣхаша численици, исчетоша всю землю Суждальскую, и Рязаньскую, и Мюромьскую, и ставиша десятники и сотники и тысящники и темники, и идоша въ ворду, толико не чтоша игуменовъ, черньцовъ, поповъ, крилошанъ, кто зрить на святую Богородицю и на владыку.
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Mongol census officials ('chislenitsy') of the Golden Horde
p.t: That winter the census takers came, and counted all the Suzdal land, and the Riazan and the Murom, and appointed chiefs of ten, of a hundred, of a thousand and of ten thousand, and went off to the Horde; only they did not count abbots, monks, priests, choir clergy, whoever looks to the holy Mother of God and to the bishop.
p.tg: census tax decimal system clergy exemption

p.h: A captive Tartar prince who galloped home from Isfahan
p.g: Chardin tells the court story of 'Abouel-Kazi', a prince of Khwarazm captured in a Persian victory over the Uzbeks. Shah Safi treated him as royalty in Isfahan for ten years, until he feigned illness, went to a spa, and rode off with twenty Uzbek horsemen sent to fetch him. He became khan and stayed a friend of Persia. This is Abu'l-Ghazi Bahadur, khan of Khiva, later author of a famous history of the Turks.
p.q: To whom the Yusbeck Prince thus briskly answer'd; I am highly oblig'd to the King of Persia, but I owe more my own Country and Relations that call me back. 'Tis my Father that sends me these Men, to facilitate my return to my Native soil
p.s: Jean Chardin, 'The Coronation of Solyman III' (appended to the 1691 English edition)
p.c: Court gossip retold decades later; details such as the role of the prince's father may not match other accounts.

p.h: The Pig Road: how the Belgorod Tatars came raiding
p.g: The book records the raiding roads the Tatars used. Along the 'Svinaia doroga' (Pig Road) the Belgorod Tatars from the Dnieper used to ride on the Rylsk, Karachev, Orel and Bolkhov districts, led by Bakai Murza, 'when there were no steppe towns yet'. They crossed the Seim 40 versts below Kursk, where there were now villages and a watch post. Muscovy's southern towns were built along these routes to block them.
p.q: А Свиною дорогою прихаживали отъ Днѣпра Бѣлогородскіе Татарове, на Рыльскіе, и на Карачевскіе, и на Орловскіе, и на Болховскіе уѣзды, хаживали Бакай Мурза, какъ не было Польскихъ городовъ, а Семь рѣку лаживали подъ Городенскимъ городищемъ, ниже Курска верстъ съ 40
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.pl: Ryl'sk, Karachev, Orel and Bolkhov districts
p.t: And by the Pig Road the Belgorod Tatars used to come from the Dnieper onto the Rylsk and Karachev and Orel and Bolkhov districts; Bakai Murza used to come, when there were not yet the steppe towns; and they used to cross the Seim river below the Gorodensk gorodishche, about 40 versts below Kursk
p.c: 'Polskie goroda' here means the new towns of the 'Pole' (steppe frontier), not Polish towns.
p.tg: raids roads fords belgorod tatars frontier

p.h: Printed scrolls from Kalmyk temples
p.g: Strahlenberg corrects another author: the idols and manuscripts sent to Europe did not come from Samarkand or the Caspian but from pagan temples and tombs in the Kalmyk lands along the upper Irtysh. The writings are in Tangut (Tibetan), Mongol and Kalmyk script, printed rather than written, in gold or silver letters on varnished cotton or silk paper. In a footnote he says he saw a wooden printing block for Kalmyk letters in the governor's house at Tobolsk in 1723.
p.q: …were brought from the Desarts of the Kalmucks, on each Side of the River Irtisch, upwards, out of the Pagan Temples and Tombs; And as to the Manuscripts, … they consist of Tanguthian, Mungalian and Kalmuckian Characters, not upon Parchment, but upon a thick Paper, made of Cotton or Silk, done over with black and blew Varnish; Upon which the Characters or Letters are not wrote, but printed,
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)

p.h: The census: Tatars ride the streets writing down houses
p.g: Novgorod split over the Mongol census. The Tatars threatened to leave ('give us the number, or we go') while the common people swore to die for St Sophia rather than be counted. In the end the boyars gave way, and the census takers 'began to ride through the streets writing down the Christian houses'. The chronicler complains that the boyars made it easy for themselves and hard for the poor.
p.q: и рѣша Татарове: даите намъ число, или бѣжимъ проче; и чернь не хотѣша дати числа, но рѣша: умремъ честно за святую Софью и за домы ангелскыя … и почаша ѣздити оканьнии по улицамъ, пишюче домы христьяньскыя
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Tatar census officials of the Golden Horde
p.t: and the Tatars said: give us the number, or we will run away; and the common people would not give the number, but said: let us die honourably for St Sophia and for the houses of the angels … and the accursed ones began to ride through the streets, writing down the Christian houses
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: The head man calls the horses from the minaret
p.g: Tatar villages had to supply post horses to travellers in turn. Jesse describes the village head man (bashi) climbing the wooden minaret in the middle of the village to shout out the names of those whose horses were due, with replies coming back from around the village.
p.q: On arriving at a station, the Bashi, or head man, was not always in the way; when found, he immediately ascended the wooden minaret in the centre of the village, and commenced calling a roster of those whose horses were next for duty, a reply was soon elicited from one corner or another
p.s: Captain William Jesse
p.tg: minaret post horses village government timber

p.h: The dead hung in trees for birds and wolves
p.g: Bunge asked his Kalmyk neighbours how they buried their dead, since the stone mounds nearby (the 'Chud graves') were far older. He was told that burial depended on the dying person's wish and the shaman (kam): a few were burned or buried, but most were wrapped in felt or a horse hide and hung in a tree in the forest, with a horse as the usual offering.
p.q: Die Todten werden entweder, jedoch selten, verbrannt, oder sie werden in die Erde verscharrt, oder endlich, was der häufigste Fall seyn soll, sie werden in einen Filz, oder ein Pferdefell eingewickelt, an einer abgelegenen Stelle eines Waldes an einen Baum aufgehängt, und den Vögeln und Wölfen preis gegeben. Gewöhnlich ist dies mit einigen Ceremonien verbunden, und ein Pferd ist das gewöhnliche Todtenopfer.
p.s: Alexander von Bunge (diary printed in Ledebour's Reise, part 2, 1830)
p.t: The dead are either burned, though rarely, or scraped into the earth, or finally, which is said to be the commonest case, they are wrapped in a felt or a horse hide, hung on a tree in a remote part of a forest, and left to the birds and wolves. Usually this is accompanied by some ceremonies, and a horse is the usual funeral offering.
p.c: Bunge says on the next page that he did not witness these rites and reports them from what he was told.
p.tg: burial tree burial shaman horse sacrifice altai

p.h: Batu's demand: a tenth of everything
p.g: Camped on the river Onuza, Batu sent envoys to the Riazan princes asking for a tenth of everything: princes, people, armour and horses. The princes answered: 'when we are gone, all will be yours.' One manuscript printed alongside says the envoys were 'a sorceress woman and two men with her', a detail that may echo Mongol shamanesses or may be later colour.
p.q: И оттолѣ послаша послы своя жену чародѣйцу и два мужа съ нею ко княземъ Рязаньскимъ, просяще у нихъ десятины во всемъ: въ князехъ, и въ людехъ, и въ доспѣсехъ, и въ конехъ.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, variant text of the Tolstoy (Golitsyn) copy printed in parallel, PSRL vol. 10 (1885)
p.pe: Batu's envoys; the princes of Riazan, Murom and Pronsk
p.t: And from there they sent their envoys, a sorceress woman and two men with her, to the Riazan princes, asking of them a tenth of everything: of princes, and of people, and of armour, and of horses.
p.c: The 'sorceress' appears only in the parallel copy; the main Nikon text simply says 'envoys'. The tithe demand matches the Novgorod First Chronicle.

p.h: Why the Kirghiz prefer daughters
p.g: Among the Kirghiz, Wood learned, a daughter was more welcome than a son: herding needs few men, and a girl brought a large bride price. He also records that a widow passed to her husband's brother, and that a stranger who married her started a blood feud.
p.q: With the Kirghiz, a daughter is more desired than a son. Their flocks and herds, though large, do not require many men to manage them … But for a daughter a large sum is obtained … often as much as £40, if she be not above fifteen years of age.
p.s: John Wood

p.h: A great man buried sitting in his tent, with a mare and foal
p.g: Carpini describes the secret burial of a Mongol noble: he is buried out on the steppe with his tent, seated before a table with a bowl of meat and a cup of mare's milk, with a mare and foal and a saddled horse. Another horse is eaten and its skin, stuffed with straw, is raised on four poles, so the dead will have a home, milk and horses in the next world. His name may not be spoken for three generations.
p.q: on l'enterre secrettement en la campagne, auec sa loge, & est assis au milieu d'icelle, auec vne table deuant luy, & vn bassin plein de chair, & vne tasse de lait de iument; On enterre aussi auec luy vne iument, & son poulain; & vn cheual sellé & bridé: & mangent vn autre cheual, dont ils remplissent la peau de paille
p.s: John of Plano Carpini (French translation by Pierre Bergeron, 1634)
p.t: they bury him secretly in the open country, with his tent, and he is seated in the middle of it, with a table in front of him and a bowl full of meat and a cup of mare's milk; they also bury with him a mare and her foal, and a horse saddled and bridled; and they eat another horse, whose skin they stuff with straw
p.c: Carpini did not witness a noble burial; he reports Mongol practice as described to him.

p.h: Units of ten, blood from a horse's vein and dried milk
p.g: Polo explains the decimal army (officers over ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, the 'toman'), scouts on every side, and how little gear a rider carried: two leather milk bottles, a small pot and a small tent. In emergencies they rode ten days without a fire, drinking blood from their horses' veins, and carried dried milk paste that churned into a meal inside the bottle as they rode.
p.q: And in case of great urgency they will ride ten days on end without lighting a fire or taking a meal. On such an occasion they will sustain themselves on the blood of their horses, opening a vein and letting the blood jet into their mouths, drinking till they have had enough, and then staunching it.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)
p.c: Blood-drinking is also reported by Herberstein, Schiltberger and others; Polo describes the practice rather than a scene he witnessed.
p.tg: warfare decimal army horse blood dried milk kurut

p.h: Horsemeat, mare's milk and 'no lies' among the Sarai Tatars
p.g: On the Tatars around old Sarai, Evliya writes that they love horseflesh above all, some boiling it and some eating it raw with the blood running, and drink boza, kumiss (mare's milk) and camel's milk. He claims they know no backbiting, slander or lies, since they fear no one. All these Tatars are desert-dwellers who move with their camel-carts, and they became Muslims (Hanafi and Shafi'i) after Chinggis Khan.
p.q: همان جمله‌سی زیاده محبت اتدکلری آت اتیدر ونیجه قبیله‌سی آت اتن بشررلر ونیجه قبیله‌سی قانی آقیده آقیده اتی چیك یرلر صو یرینه بوزا وآت سودی قمزی ودوه سودی ایچرلر ... وجمله تاتار صحرا نشینلردر دوه عربه‌لریله بنوب کوچرلر
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pe: Nogay and other Tatars of the Volga (the 'Sarai Tatars')
p.t: What all of them love most is horse meat: many tribes cook horse meat, and many tribes eat the meat raw with the blood running. Instead of water they drink boza, mare's-milk kumiss and camel's milk … and all the Tatars are desert-dwellers; they mount their camel-carts and migrate.
p.c: Mixes observation with stock claims; Evliya's Volga journey is thought partly invented or exaggerated.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.
p.tg: horsemeat kumiss boza nomads carts nogay

p.h: The fish-skin Tartars of the Ussuri
p.g: On the Ussuri, Grosier says, live the 'Yupi-tatse' (Chinese for 'fish-skin Tartars'). They live almost entirely on fish and dress in fish skins, dyed three or four colours and stitched so finely with thin thongs that the seams look like silk. On the next pages he describes their bark canoes, hair hung with little mirrors, and a lady who drove a sledge pulled by a hundred dogs.
p.q: The river Ousouri, on the banks of which these people live, must supply them with abundance of fish, since they have no other food, and scarcely any clothes but what they make of their skins. They have the art of dressing these skins, and of dying them three or four colours ;
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Grosier (English translation, 1788)
p.c: From the Jesuit map-makers who surveyed Manchuria about 1709; Grosier calls them 'stupid and clownish', a prejudice he inherits.
p.tg: fish skin hezhe nanai amur clothing

p.h: The Turkish khan's tame deer at the Thousand Springs
p.g: The meadows of the Thousand Springs were where the khan of the Western Turks came every summer to escape the heat. Herds of deer there wore bells and rings and were so tame they barely ran from people, because the khan loved them and decreed death without pardon for anyone who killed one. Xuanzang passed this way on his outward journey.
p.q: 突厥可汗每来避暑中有羣鹿多飾鈴鐶馴狎於人不甚驚走可汗愛賞下命羣屬敢加殺害有誅無赦故此羣鹿得終其夀
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji, book 1 (Chinese text, Siku quanshu copy)
p.t: The khan of the Turks comes here every year to escape the summer heat. There are herds of deer, many decorated with bells and rings, so tame with people that they hardly startle and run. The khan loves them and has ordered his followers that anyone who dares to kill one will be executed without pardon, so these deer live out their natural lives.

p.h: Tribute sworn on a bloody sabre
p.g: Yermak sent the fifty-leader Bogdan Briazga down the Irtysh to bring the Tatar and Ostyak districts under the tsar and collect yasak (fur tribute). At the first district he stormed a strong little town, hanged the best 'mergens' (warriors) by the leg and shot them, collected tribute 'by the sabre', laid the bloody sabre on the table and made the people kiss it as an oath to pay every year. The terror, says the chronicle, silenced the whole district.
p.q: И пріѣхавъ въ первую Аремзянскую волость, и городокъ крѣпкій взялъ боемъ, и многихъ лутчихъ мергеней повѣсилъ за ногу и розстрѣлялъ, и ясакъ собралъ за саблею, и положилъ на столъ кровавую, и велѣлъ вѣрно цѣловати за государя царя, чтобъ имъ служить и ясакъ платить по вся годы
p.s: Kungur (Brief Siberian) Chronicle, Remezov tradition, 1880 edition
p.pe: Cossack Bogdan Briazga and the Tatars and Ostyaks of the lower Irtysh
p.t: And coming to the first, the Aremzian district, he took the strong little town by battle, and hanged many of the best mergens by the leg and shot them, and collected the yasak by the sabre, and laid it, bloody, on the table, and ordered them to kiss it in faith to the sovereign tsar, that they would serve and pay yasak every year
p.c: The sabre oath (shert) reflects local oath customs that the Russians adopted; the details come from Cossack tradition.
