p.h: A princess with an ox-bladder at her neck
p.g: The ambassadors visited Princess Bike, mother of the Tartar prince Mussal, in a hall with earthen walls lined with vaulted niches full of silk bedding and Persian carpets, weapons hung on the pillars. She and another lady wore a blown-up ox-bladder wrapped in an embroidered scarf behind the neck: the badge of widowhood. Her servants still bore the scratches of mourning on their faces.
p.q: She wore, at her neck behind, an Ox-bladder, blown to the utmost, which was wound about towards her hair, with a rich Scarf embroider'd with Gold and Silk … Behind the Chair stood a Lady, who had also a Bladder at her neck, and we were told afterwards that it was the Badge of Widdowhood.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.pl: Terki, on the Terek river, North Caucasus

p.h: Olla Billa: the Tartar war cry
p.g: Fletcher describes Tartar raiders setting dummy riders on spare horses to look more numerous, and charging with the cry 'Olla Billa' (Allah, bi-llah), which he translates 'God help us'. He contrasts their refusal to surrender with the behaviour of Russian and Turkish soldiers.
p.q: When they make any onset their manner is to make a great shoote, crying all out together, Olla Billa, Olla Billa, God helpe us, God helpe us. They contemne death so much as that they chuse rather to die then to yeeld to their enimie, and are seene when they are slaine to bite the very weapon
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

p.h: Sorcery, Chinggis Khan's dreams and bowing to a bush
p.g: On his way to Batu, Daniil passed through the camp of the commander Kuremsa and was horrified by Tatar religion as a Christian saw it: shamans' 'kudesy' (sorcery), the 'dreams' of 'Chigizakon' (Chinggis Khan), and visiting kings and princes being led around a bush to bow to the sun, the moon, the earth and the souls of their ancestors. At Batu's camp Sangur, a man in the service of Prince Yaroslav, told him that his 'brother' Yaroslav had bowed to the bush and he must do so too.
p.q: видя бо обладаемы дьяволомъ: скверная ихъ кудешьская бляденья и Чигизаконова мечтанья, скверная его кровопитья, многыя его вольшбы; приходящія цари, и князи и велможѣ, солнцю и лунѣ и земли, дьяволу и умершимъ въ адѣ отцемъ ихъ и дѣдомъ и матеремъ, водяше около куста покланятися
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843)
p.pl: Pereiaslav and the Volga (Kuremsa's and Batu's camps)
p.pe: Tatars of Kuremsa and Batu; Prince Daniil of Galicia
p.t: for he saw them possessed by the devil: their foul sorcerers' ravings and the dreams of Chigizakon, his foul blood-drinkings, his many witchcrafts; the kings and princes and nobles who came were led around a bush to bow to the sun and moon and earth, to the devil and to their fathers and grandfathers and mothers who have died and are in hell
p.c: A hostile Christian description; the chronicler learned it from Daniil's party, not from Mongol informants.
p.tg: religion shamans chinggis khan ancestor worship bush

p.h: A wooden idol with glass eyes facing the door
p.g: In the same yurt Ledebour saw the household idol hanging opposite the entrance, a roughly carved piece of wood with a head and eyes of glass or coral, surrounded by offerings of squirrel and ground-squirrel skins and eagle claws. The woman of the house served milk from the kumiss bag to his Kalmyk guides but boiled milk to his Russians.
p.q: Dem Eingange gegenüber hängt ein Idol, möglichst roh aus einem Stücke Holz geschnitzt, an dessen oberem Ende man gewöhnlich einen Kopf darzustellen versucht hat, mit eingesetzten Glasaugen oder Korallen. Daneben hängen gewöhnlich mancherlei Opfer aufgehängt, als ein, Eichhörnchen oder ein Zieselfell, und besonders häufig eine Adlerklaue.
p.s: Carl Friedrich von Ledebour
p.t: Opposite the entrance hangs an idol, carved as crudely as possible from a piece of wood, at whose upper end a head has usually been attempted, with inset eyes of glass or coral. Beside it hang various offerings, such as a squirrel or a ground-squirrel skin, and especially often an eagle's claw.

p.h: Horse meat cooked under the saddle
p.g: Chevalier repeats the famous story that Tartars on the march softened horse meat by riding on it under the saddle and ate it with no sauce but the horse's sweat. He adds that they chose worn-out, sick or lame horses for this, not the best ones. At home they ate millet porridge and boiled horse meat.
p.q: when they goe to war and are upon their March, they make it ready, or rather mortify, or just heat it, under their Saddles, and eat it afterwards in this condition without any other sauce then the froth upon the Flesh, made by the sweating of the Horse
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.c: The saddle-meat story goes back to medieval writers and is a stock European image of steppe warriors; Chevalier does not say he saw it.

p.h: Women who ride into town with bow and arrows
p.g: Riccoldo says Tartar women are held in great honour, run the realm or the household, buy and sell, and are fierce and warlike. He adds from his own eyes that they ride like men and that he often saw them entering cities armed with bows and arrows. Elsewhere on the same page he explains their tall crowns, topped with a foot to remind them they are still under their husbands.
p.q: et ipse sunt, que gubernant regnum vel domum, et emunt et vendunt, et sunt feroces et bellicose. Equitant autem vt viri, et frequenter vidi eas intrantes ciuitates cum arcu et sagittis accinctas vt viros.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)
p.t: and it is they who govern the kingdom or the household, and they buy and sell, and they are fierce and warlike. They ride like men, and I often saw them entering cities girded with bow and arrows like men.

p.h: Bodies kept at home; lords buried with horse and slaves
p.g: Jordanus heard that in this empire the dead are neither burned nor buried, sometimes for ten years, because the family cannot yet afford the proper rites; the body is kept in the house and served food as if alive. Great lords are buried with a horse and with one or two of their favourite servants alive. The first part fits Chinese custom; the second, steppe Mongol practice.
p.q: Ibi, mortuos suos non comburunt; non etiam sepeliunt, aliquotiens per decem annos; … sed tenent eos in domibus, et ministrant sibi cibaria, sicut si esset vivus. Magni domini, cùm moriuntur, sepeliuntur cum equo uno, et cum uno vel duobus suis servitoribus vivis sibi magis dilectis.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.t: There they do not burn their dead, nor even bury them, sometimes for ten years; … but they keep them in their houses and serve them food as if they were alive. Great lords, when they die, are buried with one horse and with one or two of their best loved servants alive.
p.c: Hearsay mixing Chinese and Mongol customs.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; the editor's '(sic)' after 'vivus' omitted.
p.tg: burial funeral human sacrifice horses ancestors

p.h: A new khan lifted on white felt
p.g: At Güyük's enthronement the princes and nobles set him on a golden seat, then moved him down onto a felt on the ground and told him to look up to God in heaven and down to the felt on earth: rule justly and the earth would obey him; rule badly and not even the felt he sat on would be his. Then they raised him and his wife together on the felt and proclaimed them khan and great lady. Caps flew, belts were thrown over shoulders, the crowd knelt nine times, and for seven days meat, salt and mare's milk were handed out from the khan's tent; the women's seats in the golden throne tent were of white felt.
p.q: setzten ihn vom goldenen Stuhle auf eine Filzdecke auf die Erde und sagten: Schaue auf zu Gott im Himmel und nieder auf den Filz zur Erde; wenn du gut regierst, wenn du gerecht, freigebig, die Prinzen und Freiherren ehrst, wird dir die Erde unterthan sein nach deinem Willen; im Gegentheil wirst du arm, verachtet und elend sein und nicht einmal der Filz wird dein gehören, auf dem du sitzest.
p.s: Joseph von Hammer-Purgstall (1842), after Carpini and Mirkhwand
p.pe: Mongol princes and nobles; Güyük Khan and his wife Oghul Qaimish
p.t: they moved him from the golden seat onto a felt rug on the ground and said: Look up to God in heaven and down at the felt on the earth; if you rule well, if you are just and generous and honour the princes and lords, the earth will be subject to you at your will; otherwise you will be poor, despised and wretched, and not even the felt you sit on will be yours.
p.c: Hammer's footnotes cite Carpini, who was present in 1246, and the later Persian historian Mirkhwand; the page does not make clear which detail comes from which.
p.tg: enthronement felt guyuk kurultai mare's milk

p.h: Pigs as a border defence
p.g: Russian borderers, Fletcher says, kept almost nothing but pigs, because Muslim Tartar raiders would not touch or drive them off. He also notes that the Crimean khan was now largely picked by the Ottoman sultan and paid him a tenth of his war booty.
p.q: The Russe borders (being used to their invasions lightly every yeere in the sommer) keepe fewe other cattel on the border parts save swine onely, which the Tartar will not touch nor drive away with him ; for that he is of the Turkish religion, and will eate no swines flesh.
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

p.h: Fighting harder for their hair than for their emperor
p.g: The Manchus took the south of Zhejiang easily, Martini says, until they ordered everyone to cut their hair in Tartar fashion. Then soldiers and townspeople alike rose up, fought 'more desperately for their Hair' than for king or kingdom, and drove the Tartars back across the Qiantang river. Elsewhere (p. 108 to 109) he says the Tartars made refusing the haircut high treason, and many Chinese chose death instead.
p.q: But when they commanded all by Proclamation to cut off their Hair, then both Souldier and Citizen took up Arms, and fought more desperately for their Hair of their Heads, than they did for King or Kingdom, and beat the Tartars not only out of their City, but repulst them to the River Cienthang
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.pe: Manchu Tartars and the Chinese of Zhejiang
p.c: Martini was living in Zhejiang at the time, but he did not witness every battle he describes.

p.h: 'Sweet words and soft silks': a khan's warning about China
p.g: Bilge Qaghan tells his people that the forest of Otuken is the true centre of their realm. The Chinese give gold, silver and silk without trouble, but their words are sweet and their riches soft; with them they lure distant peoples close and many Turks who settled near China died. If the Turks stay in Otuken and send caravans, they will keep an eternal empire. It is the steppe ruler's own argument for staying nomads rather than moving into Chinese-style towns.
p.q: Habitant ce pays j'entrai en relations avec le peuple chinois. L'appel du peuple chinois, qui nous donne sans peine tant d'or, d'argent, d'isigti, de soie(?), était doux, ses richesses étaient molles. En s'insinuant par leur doux appel et leurs richesses molles, ils (les Chinois) firent approcher d'eux le peuple lointain.
p.s: Bilge Qaghan (inscription composed by Yollugh Tegin), Kul Tegin inscription, 732, in Vilhelm Thomsen's French translation (1896)
p.t: Living in this land I entered into relations with the Chinese people. The call of the Chinese people, who give us so much gold, silver, isigti and silk(?) without trouble, was sweet, and their riches were soft. Worming their way in with their sweet call and soft riches, they (the Chinese) drew distant peoples close to them.
p.c: Thomsen marks 'silk' and some verbs as uncertain; the moral is the khan's political advice, not a neutral report.
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: The Lord's Prayer in the language of the Horde
p.g: The German Franciscan part of the Codex contains Christian texts turned into Cuman for preaching. This is the start of the Lord's Prayer: 'Our father who art in heaven, blessed be thy kingdom, thy will be done as in heaven so on earth, give us this day our daily bread'. Elsewhere in the Codex the word for God is 'Tengri', the old Turkic name of the sky god, as Kuun's word index shows.
p.q: Atamis kim köctä sen. Algiszle bulsun senig hanlechin. bulsû senig tilemegin nezikkim kocta alley ierda. kundegi ötmackimisni bisga bugun bergil.
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, German (Franciscan) part, c.1330 to 1340, ed. Geza Kuun 1880
p.t: Our father who art in heaven. Blessed be thy kingdom (khanate). Thy will be done, as in heaven so on earth. Give us today our daily bread.
p.c: A missionary translation, so it shows the language, not the beliefs of the people who spoke it. 'Kingdom' is rendered with the Turkic word for a khan's realm.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: lords prayer christianity missionaries franciscans cuman

p.h: Tartar women who ride astride
p.g: Davis quotes the account of Macartney's embassy passing through Peking. Many women in the crowd were said to be Tartars. Their feet were not bound, their thick-soled broad-toed shoes looked clumsy next to Chinese women's tiny ones, they wore a patch of vermilion on the lower lip, and some rode horseback astride like men.
p.q: Among the spectators of the novel sight some women were observed; the greatest number were said to be natives of Tartary or of a Tartar race. Their feet were not cramped like those of the Chinese;… A few of the Tartar ladies were on horseback, and rode astride like men.
p.s: Account of Lord Macartney's embassy (Staunton), quoted by John Francis Davis
p.c: A quotation from the 1797 embassy account, not Davis's own observation.
p.tg: women unbound feet riding manchus beijing

p.h: Honoured by the number of dogs
p.g: Hanway reports that the Kalmyks threw their dead into open fields for dogs to eat, and that a body eaten by more than six dogs did honour to the dead. He also describes their small wooden idols dressed in rags, caressed in good seasons and beaten in bad ones. Near Astrakhan he later saw many human skulls lying on the steppe, 'for the Khalmucks always leave their dead uninterred'.
p.q: They throw their dead into open fields, to be devoured by dogs; of which many run wild, and some are kept for this purpose. If their bodies are thus devoured by any number exceeding six, they think honourably of the state of the deceased; otherwise he is a disgrace to his relations.
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)
p.c: Partly hearsay; Hanway admits he could not talk with them and judges only 'the externals of a religion'.

p.h: The Tatar envoys: 'we have not taken your towns'
p.g: Before the Kalka battle the Tatars sent envoys to the Rus princes, who had allied with the Polovtsy (Cumans). They said they had not touched Rus land, towns or villages and had come against 'our slaves and grooms, the pagan Polovtsy'. The princes killed the envoys. The chronicle records the Mongol claim that the steppe nomads were their runaway subjects.
p.q: се слышимъ, оже идете противу насъ, послушавше Половьць, а мы вашеи земли не заяхомъ, ни городъ вашихъ, ни селъ вашихъ, ни на васъ придохомъ; нъ придохомъ, Богомъ пущени, на холопы и на конюси свое, на поганыя Половчь.
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841), reporting the envoys' words
p.pe: Tatar (Mongol) envoys to the Rus princes
p.t: we hear that you are coming against us, having listened to the Polovtsy; but we have not taken your land, nor your towns, nor your villages, nor have we come against you; but we have come, sent by God, against our slaves and grooms, the pagan Polovtsy.

p.h: 'The dead are really dead': a Volga 'Tartar' on the afterlife
p.g: Olearius lodged at Kazan in the same house as a Cheremis man of about 45, and when talk turned to the resurrection the man laughed. The Cheremis, he writes, lived in poor huts, kept no churches, priests or books, sacrificed horses and hung the skins on poles, and feared spirits rather than a hell. They were Mari, a Finnic-speaking people, but to Olearius they were one more kind of Tartar.
p.q: and said to me, Those who are dead are really dead, and will never return again, no more than my Horses and Cows, which are long since rotten. I asked him whether he knew who Created this World, and made Heaven and Earth? his answer was, … The Devil may haply know.
p.s: Adam Olearius (English translation by John Davies, 1669)
p.pe: Cheremis (Mari), whom Olearius counts among the Tartars

p.h: 'Drink our black milk, mare's kumiss'
p.g: Inside Batu's tent Batu asked Daniil whether he drank 'black milk, our drink, mare's kumiss'. Daniil said he never had, but would if ordered. 'You are now one of us, a Tatar: drink our drink,' said Batu. Then Daniil went to pay respects to Batu's senior wife Barakchin, who sent him a cup of wine because, she said, he was not used to milk.
p.q: «пьеши ли черное молоко, наше питье, кобылій кумузъ?» Оному же рекшу: «доселѣ есмь не пилъ, нынѣ же ты велишь, пью.» Онъ же рче: «ты уже нашь же Татаринъ, пій наше питье.» Онъ же испивъ поклонися, по обычаю ихъ
p.s: Hypatian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 2 (1843), reporting Batu's words
p.pe: Batu; Prince Daniil of Galicia; Batu's wife Barakchin
p.t: 'Do you drink black milk, our drink, mare's kumiss?' He said: 'Until now I have not drunk it; now, since you order it, I drink.' And he said: 'You are already one of us, a Tatar; drink our drink.' And he drank and bowed, according to their custom
p.tg: kumiss mare's milk hospitality batu homage

p.h: A sorceress is a 'kam khatun', a shaman woman
p.g: Under the verb 'to divine' the glossary gives the Cuman 'kamlik etermen', literally 'I do shamaning', and a later hand added 'incantatrix' (enchantress) as 'kam katun kisi', a shaman-woman. 'Kam' is the old Turkic word for a shaman. The steppe people living around the Italian colonies still had words for shamans and women diviners.
p.q: adiuino ram mecunem kamlik etermen ranzilic etarmen … incantatrix kam katun kisi dir
p.s: Codex Cumanicus, Latin-Persian-Cuman glossary (Italian part, dated 11 July 1303), ed. Geza Kuun 1880, entry for 'enchantress' added by a third hand
p.t: I divine: (Persian) ram mikunam / (Cuman) kamlik etermen, (also) ranzilik etermen … enchantress: she is a kam khatun person (a shaman woman).
p.c: Kuun notes the 'incantatrix' line was added by a later hand.
p.n: Checked against the page image (the corpus OCR misreads 'kamlik' as 'kamhk').

p.h: Dressed like the Turks, crowned with a wooden horn
p.g: In Himatala, near Badakhshan, people behaved and dressed like the Turks, in wool, skin and felt. Married women wore a wooden horn about three feet long on the head, with two branches standing for the husband's father and mother; when one parent-in-law died a branch was removed, and when both were dead the horn was given up.
p.q: In respect of their modes of behaviour and forms of etiquette, their clothes of wool, and skin, and felt, they are like the Turks. Their wives wear upon their head-dress a wooden horn about three feet or so in length. It has two branches (a double branch) in front, which signify father and mother of the husband.
p.s: Xuanzang and Bianji (translated by Samuel Beal, 1884)
p.pe: People of Himatala, living like the Turks

p.h: The slave market at Karasu
p.g: Evliya describes a great slave market beside the walls of Shirin Bey's khan at Karasubazar, where mothers were sold away from sons and brothers from sisters amid weeping. He calls the traders a merciless people, cursed in a saying as 'sellers of men', and warns buyers about the tricks of dealers and midwives. The Crimean economy rested heavily on captives taken in raids.
p.q: وبیوك جسر باشنده بر واسع میدانده شیرین بکی خانك دیواری دبنده بر عظیم اسیر بازاری دورر بو دخی بر عبرت نما بازار نحوستدرکم حقلرنده ( بایع البشر وقاطع الشجر وخارق الحجر لعن الله فی الدنیا والآخرة ) ... دینلمش اسیرجی قوملریدر زیرا بوقوم زیاده‌سیله بی‌رحم قومدرلر
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars and captives (Russians, Circassians, Abkhaz)
p.t: At the head of the great bridge, in a wide square below the wall of Shirin Bey's khan, there is a huge slave market; this too is an ill-omened market, a lesson to behold, for of them it is said: 'The seller of men, the cutter of trees and the breaker of stone, God curse him in this world and the next' … They are slave-dealing peoples, for this people is exceedingly merciless.
p.c: Evliya was himself a slave-owner and took captives on raids; he condemns the dealers, not the institution.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.

p.h: A horse thief's punishment
p.g: A Kazakh horse thief was sentenced to death, but the elders asked for mercy as a good omen for the journey with the Russians. Instead he was blackened with soot, tied to a horse's tail and whipped by a laughing crowd, while his own horse was slaughtered and shared out among the onlookers.
p.q: The robber, half naked, having about his neck some stripes of black felt, was forced by two men on horseback who carried large whips, to run to the nearest tent, where his face was blackened with soot and marched through a group of Kirghiz; they then tied him to the tail of a horse, and forced him to hold a cord between his teeth.
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: Paying the bride price by instalments
p.g: A Tatar groom had to pay a bride price (kalym). If he could not pay at once, the bride stayed with her father until the whole sum was paid off bit by bit, but meanwhile the groom could visit her secretly, a custom called 'going to the bosom', with strict limits. Lepekhin adds that these visits let the groom get to know his bride and, if he found something amiss, cancel the match and recover part of the price. The mullah then completes the marriage by asking set questions three times, answered by the groom's helper and the matchmaker.
p.q: widrigenfalls bleibt die Braut so lange bey dem Vater, bis der Bräutigam die ganze Summe nach und nach abgezahlet hat. Indessen hat der Bräutigam das Recht, seine Braut insgeheim von Zeit zu Zeit zu besuchen, welches bey ihnen an den Busen gehen heißt … denn nur bis auf den Busen der Braut, aber weiter nicht, darf sich die Freyheit des Bräutigams erstrecken.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.t: otherwise the bride stays with her father until the groom has paid off the whole sum little by little. Meanwhile the groom has the right to visit his bride secretly from time to time, which they call 'going to the bosom' … for the groom's liberty may extend only as far as the bride's bosom, and no further.

p.h: Singing kites over Khiva
p.g: For weeks Abbott heard a strange humming music over Khiva at night. It turned out to be paper kites with a taut string stretched across a bent crosspiece, which hummed in the wind and were left flying all night. He thought the idea worth copying in England.
p.q: Seeing some children on the road with their paper kites, I approached to examine the contrivance, by which these toys emit a musical sound, whilst floating in the air. … And, as numbers of these kites are left floating in the air all night, the effect is that of aerial music ; monotonous, but full of melancholy interest.
p.s: James Abbott

p.h: Siberia asks to pay tribute: a sable per man
p.g: Envoys came to Moscow from Ediger, 'prince of Siberia', and from 'all the Siberian land'. They congratulated Ivan IV on taking Kazan and Astrakhan and asked him to take Siberia under his protection and set tribute. They agreed on one sable per 'black' (tax-paying) man, plus a squirrel skin for the collector, and said they had 30,700 such men. This is the first Moscow record of the Siberian khanate that Yermak would later conquer.
p.q: били челомъ государю ото князя Едигеря и ото всей земли, чтобы государь ихъ князя и всю землю Сибирьскую взялъ во свое имя и отъ сторонъ ото всѣхъ заступилъ и дань свою на нихъ положилъ … а черныхъ у собя людей сказали 30 тысящь семъсотъ человѣкъ.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
p.pe: Ediger, prince of Siberia, and his envoys Tiagriul and Paniady
p.t: they petitioned the sovereign on behalf of Prince Ediger and of all the land, that the sovereign take their prince and all the Siberian land in his name, and defend them from all sides, and lay his tribute on them … and they said they had 30,700 black [tax-paying] people.
p.c: Ediger was a Taibugid prince, not a Chinggisid; the head count is what the envoys stated.

p.h: Given to the khan as a present: twenty years at court
p.g: The author explains how he knew: for his sins he was captured by 'barbarians', taken to Kazan and given to the khan as a gift. The khan took him into his household to stand before him, and he stayed twenty years, until Kazan fell and he left for the Moscow tsar. He says he often questioned the wisest Kazan nobles and heard things from the khan's own mouth. Captives in service at a Tatar court were common.
p.q: Грѣхъ ради моихъ случи ми ся плененну быти варвары и сведену быти въ Казань, и даша мя царю Казанскому въ дарехъ; и взятъ мя царь съ любовію къ себѣ служити, во дворъ свои, постави мя предъ лицемъ своимъ стояти. И бывъ тамо 20 лѣтъ, по взятіи же Казанскомъ изыдохъ исъ Казани, на имя царево Московсково.
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: The anonymous author; the khan of Kazan
p.t: For my sins it befell me to be captured by barbarians and taken to Kazan, and they gave me to the tsar of Kazan as a gift; and the tsar took me with love into his service, into his court, and set me to stand before his face. And having been there 20 years, after the taking of Kazan I left Kazan, in the name of the Moscow tsar.
p.c: The author's own claim; no other source confirms his identity.

p.h: Unshod horses like wild goats; mare's blood with curdled milk
p.g: Their horses, Thomas writes, were small but strong, able to bear hunger and toil, running over rocks without iron shoes like wild goats and content with a little straw after three days of hard work. The men too cared little for food: they disliked bread, ate any meat, clean or unclean, and drank curdled milk mixed with horse blood.
p.q: equos breves, sed fortes, patientes inediae, & laboris … Per rupes vero, & lapides absque ferramentis discurrunt, ac si caprae forent silvestres: Tribus enim continuis diebus labore quassati parvo stipularum pabulo sunt contenti, homines simili modo nil pene de alimentorum perceptione curantes, sola crudelitate pascuntur, usum panis abhorrent, mundorum & immundorum carnibus indifferenter utuntur, & lac concretum cum sanguine potant equino
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: their horses short but strong, enduring hunger and toil … They run over rocks and stones without iron shoes, as if they were wild goats; after three days of continuous labour they are content with a little fodder of straw. The men likewise care almost nothing about taking food; they feed on cruelty alone, loathe the use of bread, eat the flesh of clean and unclean animals alike, and drink curdled milk with horse's blood
p.c: 'They feed on cruelty alone' is rhetoric; the horse blood detail echoes reports of Mongols bleeding their horses on campaign.

p.h: Nine animals for one stolen
p.g: Crossing the Kipchak steppe by hired cart (araba), Ibn Battuta noticed huge herds grazing with no herdsmen. He explains it by the harsh law on theft: a thief had to return the animal with nine more, and if he could not, his children were taken, or he himself killed. He also notes that the treeless steppe folk burned dung for fuel.
p.q: he is compelled to return it with nine others of equal value. But, if this is not in his power, his children are taken. If, however, he have no children, he is himself slaughtered just like a sheep.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: The sentence begins on the previous page (n102): a man 'convicted of having stolen a beast'. The law is what he was told, not a case he saw.

p.h: Beijing's Tartar women ride astride and walk the streets
p.g: In Beijing Barrow saw women in the crowds, in the lanes and on horseback riding like men, and all of them were Tartars (Manchus). Unlike Chinese women, they did not bind their feet: on the next page he describes their thick-soled shoes and painted faces, while Chinese women stayed indoors.
p.q: Women in Pekin were commonly seen among the crowd, or walking in the narrow streets, or riding on horseback, which they crossed in the same manner as the men, but they were all Tartars. They wore long silken robes, reaching down to their feet
p.s: John Barrow

p.h: Crowning a khagan by half-strangling him
p.g: When a new Khazar khagan was made, a silk cord was tied tight around his throat and he was asked how many years he would reign. If he outlived the number he named, he was put to death. The author also says the khagan had a golden throne and pavilion, and that nobles would kill themselves on his order.
p.q: they bring him forth, and tie a piece of silk about his throat, so tight that he can scarcely draw his breath. At that moment they ask him, how long he will hold the sovereignty ? He answers, " so many years." … when that space is fulfilled, they put him to death.
p.s: The 10th-century author attributed to Ibn Hawqal (translated by William Ouseley, 1800)
p.c: Reported by hearsay; similar sacred-kingship customs are described by other Arabic writers.

p.h: No writing, notched sticks and a kept word
p.g: The diarist was struck that the Mongols he met used no writing: they settled business by word of mouth and recorded contracts by cutting marks on wood. He praises them as never disobeying orders and never breaking their word, people who had 'preserved the customs of the early ages'. The first sentence finishes his description of the married women's tall headdress.
p.q: Therefore, when entering a tent, they are accustomed to go backward, inclining their heads. These people (the Mongols) have no writing. They settle their matters by verbal convention, and when they enter into contracts they cut certain marks on wood. They are never disobedient to orders, and never break their word. They have preserved the customs of the early ages.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.c: '(the Mongols)' is Bretschneider's insertion. His note (after Palladius) says the Uighur script reached the Mongols a few years later, but most modern historians date its adoption at Chinggis's court to about 1204, so the diarist is describing ordinary herders rather than the Khan's chancery.

p.h: A Tartar lady tries on the ambassador's hat
p.g: Riding past the old imperial court at Nanjing, the Dutch were invited in by a Tartar lady of about forty, 'very debonair and free'. She came out to meet the ambassador, admired how their swords bent without breaking, put his hat on her own head and unbuttoned his doublet. She then served them a strong drink made of beans. A lively picture of a Manchu noblewoman's easy manners with strangers.
p.q: we past by the Gate of the old Imperial Court, where sat a great Tartar Lady, with her servants waiting upon her, about forty years of Age: She very civilly sent to our Interpreter to invite the Embassadours into her House … She was very debonair and free, looked upon our Swords, and much admired their bending without breaking: She took the Embassadours Hat, and put it on her own Head
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)

p.h: Türk funerals: slashed faces and a stone for every man killed
p.g: From the Chinese histories Visdelou describes the Tou-kiue (Göktürks): a gold wolf's head on their standard because they believed they sprang from a she-wolf, tallies notched on wood because they had no writing, and funerals where the body lay in a tent, relatives sacrificed sheep and horses and cut their faces so blood mixed with tears, and stones were piled on the grave, one for each man the dead had killed.
p.q: Dans leurs funérailles, on plaçoit le corps du mort sous une tente. … Alors ils se déchiquetoient le visage avec des couteaux, & de cette façon leur sang se mêloit avec leurs larmes … Ils amassoient des pierres sur le lieu de la sépulture & y plaçoient des marques. On y mettoit autant de pierres que le mort avoit tué d'hommes durant sa vie.
p.s: Claude de Visdelou, translating the Chinese histories
p.pe: Tou-kiue (the ancient Turks), counted among the Tartars
p.t: At their funerals the dead man's body was laid under a tent. … Then they slashed their faces with knives, and in this way their blood mingled with their tears … They heaped stones on the burial place and set markers there. They put as many stones there as the dead man had killed men during his life.
p.tg: turks burial stones mourning wolf standard

p.h: 'You Arabs are a stupid people': why the Rus burn their dead
p.g: At the end of the famous ship funeral, in which a slave girl was killed and burned with her master, a Rus man spoke to Ibn Fadlan through the interpreter. Arabs, he said, bury their dearest in the earth to be eaten by worms, while the Rus burn theirs in an instant so they go straight to paradise. Then he laughed and said God's love had sent the wind to speed the fire.
p.q: ihr Araber, sagte er, seyd doch ein dummes Volk: ihr nehmt den, der euch der geliebteste und geehrteste unter den Menschen ist, und werft ihn in die Erde, wo ihn die kriechenden Thiere und Würmer fressen. Wir dagegen verbrennen ihn in einem Nu, so daß er unverzüglich und sonder Aufenthalt in's Paradies eingeht.
p.s: A Rus man, reported by Ibn Fadlan via an interpreter (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
p.t: 'You Arabs,' he said, 'are a stupid people: you take the one who is dearest and most honoured to you among men and throw him into the earth, where crawling creatures and worms eat him. We, on the other hand, burn him in a moment, so that he enters paradise at once and without delay.'
p.c: Words reported through an interpreter.

p.h: Graves trampled flat so no sign remains
p.g: Thomas says the Tartars did not like to throw away their lives. If one of them fell in battle, the others at once carried him off, buried him in a very hidden place, levelled the mound and trampled the spot with their horses' hooves so that no sign of a grave could be seen. Hidden burial is also reported for Mongol rulers by later writers.
p.q: Ipsi Tartari non se libenter morti exponunt, sed si quem eorum in bello mori contingat, statim rapiunt, & efferentes in occultissimo loco terra infodiunt, complanantes tumulum, & locum equorum pedibus conculcantes, ne quod sepulturae appareat signum
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: The Tartars themselves do not willingly expose themselves to death; but if one of them happens to die in battle, they carry him off at once, and taking him to a most hidden place bury him in the earth, levelling the mound and trampling the spot with the feet of their horses, so that no sign of a burial appears

p.h: 'We see so many poor Russians who believe in Christ'
p.g: When the travellers urged the Voguls to give up their 'errors' and accept Christ, they gave a sharp reply: they saw every day many poor Russians who believed in Christ and could barely earn a crust of bread, and as for salvation, they would live and die as their ancestors had. Brand adds that they neither farm nor trade and live by hunting sable and elk.
p.q: was das zeitliche Wohlseyn anlangt, sehen wir täglich vor unsern Augen so viel arme Russen, welche, ob sie wohl an Christum glauben, dennoch kaum ein Stuck Brodt erübrigen können, was aber die ewige Wohlfahrt anlangt, müsten sie fernerhin also leben und sterben, wie ihre Vor-Eltern, sie möchten gut oder übel geglaubt haben.
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.t: as for well-being in this life, we see daily before our eyes so many poor Russians who, though they believe in Christ, can scarcely spare a piece of bread; as for eternal welfare, they must go on living and dying as their forefathers did, whether they had believed well or badly.

p.h: Kalmyks who live in houses on carts
p.g: Evliya says the Kalmyks have no fleas, lice, bedbugs, snakes, scorpions or tarantulas among them, because their round houses stand on carts and they live on the open steppe. He then begins his description of their appearance: small eyes, said to come from the salt mines of the region.
p.q: وبونلرده اصلا پیره وکهله وتخته بتی ویلان وچیان وعقرب اولمز زیرا درم اولری عربه‌لر اوزره اولوب صحرا نشینلردر
p.s: Evliya Celebi (Ottoman text, Istanbul 1928, vol. 7)
p.t: Among them there are no fleas, lice, bedbugs, snakes, tarantulas or scorpions at all, because their round houses are on carts and they are desert-dwellers.
p.c: The link between cart-houses and the absence of vermin is Evliya's own explanation. 'Kalmyk' here means Oirat Mongols recently arrived on the Volga, whom he treats as a kind of Tatar.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR is partly garbled); bracketed variant markers omitted.
p.tg: kalmyks yurts carts houses on wheels vermin

p.h: Burial on a scaffold, and a horse left to starve
p.g: Shangin admits he could learn little reliable about their burials; Cossacks told him they sometimes burned their dead, which he doubted. What he was sure of is that they never bury them in the ground: he found many corpses in full dress with their riding gear in caves and on high open rocks, and they also lay the dead on a scaffold of brushwood on tall poles, wrapped in skins with saddle and harness under the head. Often a horse is tied beside it until it drops from hunger.
p.q: So viel ist gewiß, daß sie selbige nie in die Erde vergraben … Sie machen auch wohl auf hohen Stangen, von Strauchwerk, ein Gerüst, und legen die Leiche, mit Fellen bekleidet darauf, Sattel und Zeug unter den Kopf und bedeckt mit Haarfilzen. Dazu wird oft noch ein Pferd … welches endlich vor Hunger umfällt.
p.s: Peter Ivanovich Shangin, journal of an Altai journey (translated by P. S. Pallas), Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 5 (1793)
p.t: This much is certain, that they never bury them in the earth … They also make a scaffold of brushwood on high poles and lay the corpse on it, dressed in skins, with saddle and harness under the head and covered with hair felts. Often a horse is added as well … which finally drops from hunger.
p.c: Cropped margin; a few letters at line starts restored and one gap marked.

p.h: A young mare killed for an honoured guest
p.g: Reuilly says Tatar nobles still kill a horse to feast a distinguished guest. When he arrived at the house of Atai Myrza's brother, the prince told him a young mare had been slaughtered in his honour; the interpreter explained this was the greatest compliment, since a mare was the most precious thing he could offer.
p.q: They still retain the practice of killing a horse, to make a feast on the arrival of a guest of distinction. On my arrival at the house of the brother of Atai Myrza, this prince said to me, “You are very welcome. As soon as I hear that you had come, I ordered a young mare to be killed, to give you a feast.”
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)
p.pe: Crimean Tatar nobility (family of Atai Myrza)

p.h: Mare's milk and blood soup at the emperor's feast
p.g: Discussing Chinese drinks, Davis says the Tartars still show their pastoral origins in a liking for a strong spirit distilled from mutton, and that one of the soups served at the imperial banquet for Amherst's embassy at Tianjin was said to be made of mare's milk and blood. Davis was on that embassy, but he reports the soup's recipe as hearsay.
p.q: The Tartars are said still to preserve a remnant of their pastoral state, in their predilection for a strong liquor which is distilled from mutton. One of the soups, too, presented at the imperial feast conferred on the last British embassy at Tien-tsin, was said to be composed of mare's milk and blood!
p.s: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
p.c: Both claims are introduced with 'said'.
p.tg: mare's milk mutton spirit banquet pastoral

p.h: 'Very far removed from the ferocity' of the Tartar legend
p.g: Gerard spent days travelling with boys from Tibetan villages as guides and describes them with real affection. He directly rejects the reputation for ferocity that the word Tartar carried in Europe. When he fell ill with rheumatism at Peenoo in Spiti, the villagers brought medicine, sugar, spices and tea.
p.q: They are of a mild and benevolent disposition, very far removed from the ferocity commonly attached to the character of a Tartar. I have had many instances of their humanity. At Peenoo, in Speetee, where I was confined to my bed for two days with rheumatism, I never experienced more attention
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.c: Gerard himself warns that he may have taken 'too favourable a view' of them (p.109).

p.h: The viceroy's guard: 'Tartars by nation, not Chinese'
p.g: In the account of the Franciscan friars who entered China in 1579, Mendoza describes the Guangdong viceroy's guard of more than two thousand men in silk livery and shining iron helmets with great plumes, swords on the stairs and lances in the courtyards with an arquebusier between each pair. The whole guard, the friars understood, 'was of men who were Tartars by nation, and not Chinese', and they could not find out why, though they asked.
p.q: Estaua la guarda del Virey (que passauan de dos mill hombres) puesta en hylera, y todos vestidos de librea de seda, y en las cabezas, zeladas de yerro muy relucientes, con muy grandes plumages. … Toda esta guarda (segun entendieron) era de hombres Tartaros de nacion, y no de Chinos, sin poder sauer la caussa, aunque la inquirieron con diligencia.
p.s: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585), from the report of the Franciscan mission of 1579 (Pedro de Alfaro and companions)
p.t: The viceroy's guard (which was more than two thousand men) was drawn up in a line, all dressed in silk livery, and on their heads very shining iron helmets with very large plumes. ... This whole guard (as they understood) was of men who were Tartars by nation, and not Chinese, without their being able to learn the reason, though they inquired diligently.
p.c: The friars saw the guard but could not confirm who the men were; 'Tartars' may mean Mongols or other northern soldiers in Ming service.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.

p.h: Why the Torghuts left the Volga: conscription, hostages and religion
p.g: The emperor gives the Torghuts' reasons for leaving Russia: the Russians kept demanding soldiers, had taken Ubashi's son as a hostage, and had a different religion and no regard for the Lamas' faith the Torghuts followed. On the same page they set out with wives, children and baggage, crossed the Kazakh country and the deserts by Lake Balkhash, and after eight months and more than ten thousand li reached the Ili frontier. The volume's preface puts their number at 500,000.
p.q: Les Russes ne cessant point d'exiger de lui qu'il leur fournît des soldats … en dernier lieu lui ayant enlevé son propre fils pour leur servir d'otage, étant outre cela d'une religion différente de la sienne, & ne faisant aucun cas de celle des Lamas dont les Tourgouths font profession, Oubaché & les siens se sont enfin déterminés à secouer un joug
p.s: The Qianlong emperor (monument on the Torghut migration), translated by Joseph-Marie Amiot
p.t: The Russians never ceasing to demand soldiers from him … and lately having taken his own son from him as a hostage, being moreover of a different religion from his and making no account of the religion of the Lamas which the Torghuts profess, Ubashi and his people at last resolved to shake off a yoke
p.c: The emperor's version stresses a free and willing submission to himself; Amiot's own note (n438) adds that the nation reached Ili in rags, with nothing to live on.
p.tg: torghut exodus volga buddhism russia migration

p.h: The Tatars had no writing, so they learned it from the Uighurs
p.g: Explaining Chinggis Khan's laws, Juvaini says that since the Tatars had no script, Mongol children were taught to write by the Uighurs. The laws were then written on rolls called the Great Book of the Yasa, kept in the treasuries of the leading princes. This is also a clear case of Juvaini using 'Tatar' for the Mongols.
p.q: و چون … تاتاررا خطی نبوده است بفرمود تا از ایغوران کودکان مغولان خط درآموختند و آن یاساها و احکام بر طوامیر ثبت کردند و آنرا یاسا نامه بزرگ خوانند و در خزانه معتبران پادشاه زادگان باشد
p.s: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
p.t: And since the Tatars had no script, he ordered that the children of the Mongols should learn writing from the Uighurs; and those yasas and ordinances were written down on rolls, which they call the Great Book of Yasas, and it is kept in the treasury of the chief princes.
p.c: One garbled word before 'Tatars' (probably 'people') is marked with an ellipsis.

p.h: Steppe nomads who flee from smallpox
p.g: Chappe was told by several people that the nomadic 'Tartars' south of Siberia hardly knew smallpox and dreaded it so much that a sick person was left alone in a tent with food while the camp moved elsewhere. Those who came into Siberia caught it at once, and many died. Chappe says he checked the story as best he could but could only rest it on trustworthy witnesses.
p.q: Différentes personnes m'ont attesté le fait singulier, que les Tartares vagabonds situés au Midi de la Sibérie ne connoissent presque point cette cruelle maladie. Ils en ont une si grande horreur, que si quelqu'un en est attaqué, on le laisse seul dans une tente, avec des provisions de vivres, & l'on va camper ailleurs. Les Tartares qui pénetrent dans la Sibérie en sont attaqués presque aussi-tôt
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.pe: 'wandering Tartars' of the steppe south of Siberia
p.t: Various people assured me of the singular fact that the wandering Tartars south of Siberia hardly know this cruel disease at all. They have such a horror of it that if someone catches it, he is left alone in a tent with provisions, and the others go and camp elsewhere. The Tartars who come into Siberia are attacked by it almost at once
p.c: Hearsay, as Chappe admits. 'Tartares vagabonds' probably means Kazakh and other nomads of the steppe frontier.

p.h: Songs to the moon by the Syr Darya
p.g: Wintering among the reeds of the Syr Darya was the Kazakhs' great wish. Meyendorff describes men sitting half the night on a stone, gazing at the moon and singing sad improvised songs, and regrets never hearing the heroic songs that only professional bards performed.
p.q: The Kirghiz often pass half the night seated on a stone, gazing at the moon, and singing melancholy impromptu words to airs not less so. They also have historical songs, which celebrate the great actions of their heroes, but these are chaunted only by professional singers, and I greatly regret not having heard them.
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: First taste of kumiss, and a moving city of carts
p.g: Rubruck says that in two months between Soldaia and Sartaq's camp they never slept under a roof and saw no village, nor any trace of a building, except great numbers of Cuman tombs. One evening his guide gave him kumiss; he broke into a sweat from horror and novelty, but found it very tasty. Next morning the carts of the commander Scatatai, loaded with houses, looked to him like a great city coming towards him.
p.q: Illo sero dedit nobis garcio, qui ducebat nos, bibere cosmos, ad cujus haustum totus sudavi propter horrorem et novitatem, quia nunquam biberam de eo. Valde tamen sapidum videbatur michi, sicut vere est. Mane ergo obviavimus bigis Scatatay honustis domibus, et videbatur michi quod obviaret michi civitas magna.
p.s: William of Rubruck
p.t: That evening the lad who was guiding us gave us kumiss to drink, and at the first draught I sweated all over from horror and novelty, for I had never drunk it before. Yet it seemed to me very tasty, as indeed it is. In the morning we met Scatatai's carts loaded with houses, and it seemed to me that a great city was coming to meet me.
p.tg: kumiss mare's milk wagons moving city

p.h: Monasteries, choirs and red hats like cardinals
p.g: In the Great Tartar's empire, Jordanus was told, there are idol temples and monasteries of men and women just as in Europe; they chant in choir and say prayers exactly like Catholics, and the great 'pontiffs of the idols' wear red capes and red hats like cardinals. The splendour of their sacrifices is beyond belief. It is an early European comparison of Buddhist (probably Tibetan) monastic life with Catholic ritual.
p.q: In isto imperio, sunt templa idolorum, et monasteria hominum et mulierum, sicut inter nos; et ita tenent chorum, et dicunt orationes suas, rectè sicut nos; et pontifices majores idolorum portant cappas rubeas et capellos rubeos ad modum cardinalium nostrorum.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.pe: Buddhists under the Great Tartar (Yuan China)
p.t: In this empire there are temples of idols, and monasteries of men and of women, as among us; and they keep choir and say their prayers just as we do; and the great pontiffs of the idols wear red capes and red hats in the manner of our cardinals.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image.
p.tg: buddhism monasteries lamas religion red hats

p.h: Before Chinggis: clothes of dog and mouse skins
p.g: Juvaini describes the Mongols' homeland as a barren land bordered by Khitai (north China), the Uighurs, the Kirghiz and Tangut. Before Chinggis Khan, he says, they had no ruler, fought and stole from each other, and paid tribute to the Khan of Khitai. The page also says (in badly garbled OCR) that a chief was marked out only by stirrups of iron. Then comes the twist: now they wear silk and brocade and jewels pour into their tents.
p.q: و پوشش از جلود کلاب و فارات و خورش از لحوم آن و میتهای دیگر و شراب از البان بهایم و نقل از بار درختی بشکل ناژ که فسوق گویند
p.s: Ata-Malik Juvaini (Persian text, ed. Mirza Muhammad Qazvini, 1912)
p.t: Their clothing was of the skins of dogs and mice, their food the flesh of those animals and of other dead things, their wine the milk of beasts, and their dessert the fruit of a tree shaped like the pine, which they call qusuq.
p.c: A rags-to-riches set piece that flatters the dynasty's rise; Juvaini had not seen pre-Chinggis Mongolia.
p.tg: poverty furs milk pine nuts origins

p.h: Nogay herdsmen, 'inhabitants of waggons'
p.g: Crossing the sandy steppe on the way to the Crimea, Alexander passed herds of horses guarded by Nogay Tartars and their dogs. He likens them to the wagon-dwellers Herodotus described among the Scythians, notes their two- and four-wheeled carts drawn by horses, oxen or camels, and describes their sheepskin caps, grey coats and sandals of leather or linden bark.
p.q: passed several taboons of horses guarded by wild-looking Nogay Tartars and their dogs: these are the Hamaxobitii, or inhabitants of waggons, of Herodotus : their arbas are two or four-wheeled, and drawn by horses, oxen, or camels. The dress of these nomade tribes harmonises well with the Scythian deserts which they frequent ; a rough sheep-skin cap, a grayish surcoat reaching below the knees
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.c: The Herodotus comparison is Alexander's classical flourish, not evidence that the Nogays descend from Scythians.

p.h: The dead in the yurt, faces cut, stones for the slain
p.g: Heikel quotes the Chinese account of Turk funerals: the body is laid in the yurt, relatives sacrifice horses and sheep, ride six times round the tent and gash their faces so that their tears run with blood. The body is burned with the dead man's horse and belongings, and the ashes are buried in autumn or spring. A statue of the dead is placed in a small building by the grave, with a painted record of his battles, and stones are set up for every enemy he killed, 'sometimes up to 100 and even 1000'.
p.q: »Le corps du défunt est placé dans la yourte, devant laquelle les enfants et autres parents du défunt des deux sexes déposent en offrandes des chevaux et des moutons qu'on a tués. Ils font à cheval six fois le tour de la tente, en se tailladant le visage avec un couteau, de telle façon que leurs larmes se teignent de sang.
p.s: Chinese annals quoted by Axel Heikel in Inscriptions de l'Orkhon (Helsingfors 1892)
p.t: 'The body of the dead man is placed in the yurt, in front of which his children and other relatives of both sexes lay out as offerings horses and sheep that have been killed. They ride six times round the tent on horseback, gashing their faces with a knife, so that their tears are dyed with blood.'
p.c: Heikel's version says six circuits; Thomsen's version of the same Chinese text (1896) says seven.

p.h: Supper cooked by the best cook of the horde
p.g: Curious about Nogai food, de Tott watches a young cook stir roasted millet flour into boiling water, then crumble in balls of salted, dried mare's-milk cheese until the mixture turns to a dough he turns out by hand. He liked the dish better than expected, but admits he could not bring himself to enjoy the mare's milk.
p.q: he then asks for one of the white balls, which was cheese, made of mare's milk, saturated with salt, and dried… he then draws out his flat knife, empties the kettle on his hand, and presents me with a cylinder of puff-paste in a spiral form. I was anxious to taste it, and was really better pleased with the mess than I expected.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)

p.h: Why a Manchu prince could not write 'prendre'
p.g: Parrenin reports a friendly debate with a Manchu prince who praised the Manchu alphabet over European letters. Parrenin challenged him to write the French words prendre, platine, griffon and friand; he could not, because Manchu cannot put two consonants together, so he had to write perendre, pelatine, feriand. Parrenin adds that the script lacks initial B and D, writing P and T instead.
p.q: Essayez, par exemple, si vous pourrez écrire ces mots: prendre, platine, griffon, friand. Il ne le put, parce que dans la langue Tartare on ne peut joindre deux consonnes de suite; il faut placer entre deux une voyelle, & écrire perendre, pelatine, feriand, gerifon, &c.
p.s: Dominique Parrenin, letter to the Académie des Sciences
p.t: 'Try, for example, whether you can write these words: prendre, platine, griffon, friand.' He could not, because in the Tartar language two consonants cannot be joined in a row; a vowel must be placed between them, and one writes perendre, pelatine, feriand, gerifon, etc.

p.h: Bashkir summer evenings on kumys
p.g: In summer the Bashkirs lived almost entirely on soured mare's milk. The men, with little to do, went from yurt to yurt emptying the milk skins in cheerful talk, and kumys was strong enough that on warm summer evenings nearly all the men were drunk. The same page says a bride was paid for in livestock: the author saw a young wife who had cost 200 head, namely 60 horses, 40 cows and 100 sheep.
p.q: Sie leben des Sommers fast einzig von gesäuerter Pferdemilch (Kumiß), und da sie müßig sind, gehen die Mannsleute in Kosch von einer Jurte zur andern und leeren die Milchschläuche unter fröhlichen Gesprächen aus. Der Kumiß hat doch so viel Geist, daß man an den warmen Sommerabenden fast alle Mannsleute betrunken findet.
p.s: J. P. Falck, arranged and supplemented by J. G. Georgi (1786)
p.t: In summer they live almost only on soured mare's milk (kumys), and as they are idle, the men go in company from one yurt to another and empty the milk skins amid cheerful conversation. Yet kumys has so much spirit that on warm summer evenings one finds nearly all the men drunk.

p.h: A friar with a cross before the Great Khan
p.g: The Pope's gifts included big European warhorses, and the Khan was delighted with them. Marignolli entered the palace in full vestments behind a cross, with candles and incense, singing the Creed, and blessed the Khan. He adds that the court then lodged the 32 members of the mission and paid for everything, food, drink and even paper for lanterns, for three or four years.
p.q: Maximus autem Kaam visis dextrariis, & donis Pape, & literis bullatis … gavisus est gaudio magno … Ego autem solempniter indutus cum Cruce pulcherrima, que me precedebat cum luminaribus & incenso cantando: Credo in unum Deum; intravimus coram illo Kaam in glorioso pallacio residente, & cantu finito, largam dedi recipienti humiliter benediccionem.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: The Great Khan of the Tartars (Yuan emperor) and his court
p.t: The great Khan, seeing the warhorses, the Pope's gifts and the sealed letters … rejoiced with great joy … And I, solemnly vested, with a most beautiful cross carried before me with candles and incense, singing 'I believe in one God', we went in before the Khan as he sat in his glorious palace; and when the singing was over I gave him a full blessing, which he received humbly.
p.c: Marignolli's own account of his success; 'humbly' is his view of how the Khan received the blessing.

p.h: Servants and horses burned with the dead
p.g: When the Chinese ignored his complaints, the Tartar king (Nurhaci) vowed to celebrate his father's funeral with the lives of 200,000 Chinese. Martini explains that when a Tartar of rank died, servants, women and horses, with bows and arrows, were thrown into the funeral fire to serve him in the next life, a custom he says they gave up after conquering China.
p.q: For it is the custom of the Tartars when any man of quality dyeth, to cast into that fire which consumes the dead Corps, as many Servants, Women, and Horses, with Bows and Arrows, as may be fit to attend and serve them in the next life: Though now since they conquered China, they have left off this barbarous custome,
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: Reported, not witnessed; Manchu funeral sacrifice (of wives and servants) is attested, but the scale is probably exaggerated.

p.h: The Great Tartar: rich, just, and paying in paper
p.g: Jordanus opens his chapter on the Great Tartar by saying he reports only what trustworthy people told him: the Great Tartar is very rich, very just and very generous, rules four realms each as big as France, and feeds and clothes for life anyone who cannot earn a living. In his lands paper stamped with black ink passes for money and buys gold, silver, silk, gems and anything else. Paper money is the Yuan chao.
p.q: De Magno Tartaro, quod audivi à fide dignis narro: scilicet, quòd est ditissimus, justissimus, atque largus valdè. Iste habet quatuor regna sub se, æqualiter magna sicut regnum Franciæ, et benè habitata. … In dominio istius, currit, pro monetâ, papyrus signata cum encausto nigro, cum quâ habetur aurum, argentum, sericum, lapides pretiosi, et simpliciter omnia quæ vult homo.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.pe: The Great Tartar (the Yuan emperor of China)
p.t: Of the Great Tartar I relate what I have heard from trustworthy people: that he is very rich, very just and very generous. He has under him four kingdoms, each as large as the kingdom of France, and well peopled. … In his dominion paper stamped with black ink runs as money, with which one obtains gold, silver, silk, precious stones and simply everything a man wants.
p.c: Hearsay that closely echoes Marco Polo.

p.h: Marco Polo: all who meet a khan's funeral are killed
p.g: Discussing where Marco Polo's 'Altai' was, Humboldt quotes Polo's story that Chinggis Khan and all his descendants were carried back to be buried in the Altai, however far away they died, and that everyone met on the road was killed to serve the dead khan in the next life. In a note he compares this to Herodotus' account of Scythian royal funerals some 1,700 years earlier.
p.q: « Tchinghiz lui-même et tous ses descendants, dit Marco-Polo, ont leur sépulture dans l'Altai. On les porte vers ce lieu, et fussent-ils morts à quarante journées de distance. Tous ceux qui se trouvent sur la route au passage du corps des grands-khans, sont impitoyablement mis à mort pour servir leur souverain et maître dans l'autre vie. »
p.s: Marco Polo, quoted in French by Alexander von Humboldt
p.pe: Mongol grand khans (the house of Chinggis)
p.t: 'Chinggis himself and all his descendants,' says Marco Polo, 'are buried in the Altai. They are carried there even if they died forty days' journey away. All those who happen to be on the road as the body of the great khans passes are mercilessly put to death, to serve their sovereign and master in the other life.'
p.c: Polo was repeating what he was told; Humboldt uses the passage to locate Polo's 'Altai' (the mountains of northern Mongolia), not to vouch for the killings.

p.h: Wooden horses and dog carts on the snow
p.g: The gazetteer quotes the Yuan imperial geography: the people of Kaiyuan were strong, warlike and practised archers and hunters, and had 'wooden horses' (skis) tied to both feet that could keep up with a galloping horse on snow and ice, and light boat-shaped wooden 'dog carts' pulled by several dogs. The editors add that in Manchu these are called suntaha and sherhe, in Chinese pali (sledges), and that they are still used throughout Jilin and Heilongjiang.
p.q: 開元勁健善戰習射獵有狗車木馬輕㨗之便木馬形如彈弓…一左一右繫於兩足激而行之雪中冰上可及奔馬狗車以木為之其制輕簡形如船…以數狗拽之
p.s: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription), quoting the Yuan Comprehensive Geography (Yuan yitong zhi)
p.pe: Peoples of the lower Sungari and Amur
p.w: Yuan period, noted as still in use 1784
p.t: The people of Kaiyuan are strong, good fighters and practised at archery and hunting. They have the convenience of dog carts and wooden horses, which are light and quick. The wooden horse is shaped like a bow... one on the left and one on the right, tied to the two feet; pushing off, they glide along and on snow and ice can keep pace with a galloping horse. The dog cart is made of wood; it is light and simple, shaped like a boat... and pulled by several dogs.

p.h: A Jewish toll-keeper asks if anyone is left in Lithuania
p.g: At Perekop, the single gate into the Crimea, Michalo met a Jewish toll collector who watched endless columns of Lithuanian captives being brought in and asked whether there were still any people left in their lands, and where so many came from. Michalo then describes how the stronger male captives were mutilated, branded and chained to work by day and locked up by night, while young women were kept for pleasure.
p.q: Unde Iudeus quidam ibi in Taurica ad portam eius unicam illam, teloneo praesidens & innumeram semper hominum nostrorum captivorum multitudinem importari illuc cernens, quaerebat ex nobis utrum adhuc homines in regionibus nostris supersint, nec ne, & unde hic tantae mortalium copiae.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars; Lithuanian and Ruthenian captives
p.t: So a certain Jew there in Taurica, in charge of the toll at its one and only gate, and always seeing an innumerable multitude of our people brought in as captives, asked us whether there were still any people left in our lands or not, and where so great a supply of mortals came from.

p.h: Chess with the Kalmuks at Teshu Lumbo
p.g: Bogle's happiest hours at the Panchen Lama's monastery were spent playing chess with a party of Kalmuk pilgrims. He notes their rules (no castling, no stalemate) and how they played as a team: whenever a 'Siberian' sat down to play, two or three friends put their 'great bare heads together' over every move. Bogle learned to recruit his own team of Tatars and beat them.
p.q: In my first trials of skill with the Tatars, I used often to come off loser. For when a Siberian sits down to chess, he gets two or three of his countrymen to assist him; they lay all their great bare heads together canvassing and consulting about every move.
p.s: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)
p.pe: Kalmuks (Mongol pilgrims; Markham glosses them as Sokpas of north-east Tibet)

p.h: Tatar songs 'like the Scottish Highlanders''
p.g: Pallas dismisses Mongol music as wailing and inharmonious and claims the Mongols passed this 'corrupted taste' to the Crimean Tatars, outdone only by Nogai songs. By contrast, he says, the Kazan Tatars, the Bashkirs and the 'unmixed' Siberian Tatars have quite tolerable melodies, much like the songs of the Scottish Highlands. He adds that the Mongols can write down music in Tibetan letters with lines showing rising and falling notes.
p.q: eben diesen verdorbenen Geschmack haben die Mongolen den Krymischen Tataren mitgetheilt, deren elendes Geschrey, durch die Nogaischen Gesänge noch weit übertroffen wird, da doch die Kasanischen und Baschkirischen, wie auch die Sibirischen unvermischten Tataren ganz erträgliche Melodien haben, welche sehr nach den Gesängen der Schottischen Hochländer arten.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801)
p.pe: Crimean, Nogai, Kazan, Bashkir and Siberian Tatars; Mongols
p.t: the Mongols have passed on this same corrupted taste to the Crimean Tatars, whose miserable screeching is far surpassed by the Nogai songs, whereas the Kazan and Bashkir, and also the unmixed Siberian Tatars, have quite tolerable melodies, which very much resemble the songs of the Scottish Highlanders.
p.c: A personal and prejudiced judgement of taste, not a description of how the music works.

p.h: A lama general leads the Mongols against Ladakh
p.g: The chronicle tells how the Lhasa government, fearing the king of Ladakh, chose by divination a Mongol lama at Ganden monastery named Tshewang, who gave up his vows and led the Mongol tribe and a Tibetan army into Ladakh. The Ladakhis held Basgo castle for three years until the king called in the Mughal governor of Kashmir.
p.q: At that time there happened to be at Dgah-ldan lamasery a Mongol lama, called Tshe-dban. The calculations pointed out him [as the destined leader]. He, accordingly, turned layman, and, heading the Mongol tribe and a powerful army [of Tibetans], he [soon] reached [Ladakh].
p.s: Chronicles of Ladakh (La dvags rgyal rabs), translated by A. H. Francke (1926)
p.pe: Mongols (Sog po) sent from Lhasa; Ladakhis
p.c: Francke dates the war to about 1650; modern historians place the Tibet-Ladakh-Mughal war in 1679 to 1684. Square brackets are Francke's.

p.h: Raw meat, blood and a smell carried on the wind
p.g: Cruz describes the Tartars as reddish, naked from the waist up, eating raw meat and smearing their bodies with its blood, so that they stink. An old Chinese man told him that when Tartar raiders approached with the wind behind them, the Chinese could smell them coming. In war, he adds, they carry raw meat under themselves to eat. This is a Chinese stereotype passed to a Portuguese friar, not something Cruz saw.
p.q: da cinta pera cima, comẽ carne crua, e vntã os corpos com ho sangue della: pello qual comũmẽte sam fedorẽtos e tem mao cheiro. Afirmou me hũ China velho q̃ algũas vezes quãdo elles vinham cõtra as terras da China, se ho vento vinha da parte donde elles vinham, que eram sentidos pello cheiro: e quãdo vã aa guerra leuã ha carne crua debaixo de si pera comerẽ
p.s: Gaspar da Cruz, O.P. (Tractado, Évora 1569)
p.t: [they go naked] from the waist up, eat raw meat, and anoint their bodies with its blood, for which reason they commonly stink and have a bad smell. An old Chinese man assured me that sometimes, when they came against the lands of China, if the wind blew from where they were coming, they were detected by the smell; and when they go to war they carry the raw meat underneath them to eat.
p.c: Hostile Chinese hearsay. The sentence begins at the foot of the previous page, where Cruz calls these people commonly reddish ('bermelha') and says they go naked.
