p.h: The Khan takes your silver and pays in paper
p.g: All the silver merchants bring into Cathay, Pegolotti warns, is taken by the lord of Cathay into his treasury, and the merchants are given paper money in exchange: yellow paper stamped with the lord's seal. Everyone in the country must accept it, and he adds that prices are not raised because the money is paper. This is the Yuan paper currency that amazed European visitors.
p.q: Tutto l'argento, che i mercatanti portano, e che va al Gattajo, il Signore del Gattajo lo fa pigliare per se, e mettelo in suo tesoro, e mercatanti che lui portano ne dà loro moneta di pappiero, cioè di carta gialla coniata della bolla del detto Signore
p.s: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
p.pe: The lord of Cathay (the Mongol Yuan emperor)
p.t: All the silver that the merchants carry with them to Cathay, the lord of Cathay has taken for himself and put into his treasury, and to the merchants who bring it he gives paper money in exchange, that is, yellow paper stamped with the seal of the said lord

p.h: Broad chests, short legs, white skin: a Tartar portrait
p.g: Thomas describes the invaders as terrifying to look at: short legs but huge chests, broad faces, white skin, beardless cheeks, hooked noses and small eyes set far apart. Their armour was made of ox hide in overlapping plates, light but, he says, impenetrable. It is one of the earliest European portraits of the Mongols, and notably it calls their skin white.
p.q: Terrificum valde exhibent faciei aspectum, breves habent tibias, sed vasta pectora, lata est facies, & cutis alba, imberbis gena, & naris adunca, breves oculi spacio longiore disjuncti. Arma eorum sunt quaedam tegmina ex taurinis coriis laminarum more compacta, impenetrabilia tamen, & valde secura.
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: They present a very terrifying face: they have short legs but vast chests; the face is broad and the skin white, the cheeks beardless and the nose hooked, the eyes small and set wide apart. Their armour consists of coverings made of ox hides fitted together like plates, yet impenetrable and very safe.
p.c: Second hand, and 'terrifying' is Thomas's judgement; other writers of the time describe Mongol features differently.

p.h: Bait on the ice: how they crossed the frozen Danube
p.g: In a hard winter the Danube froze over, which had not happened for many years, but the Tartars did not dare ride onto the ice. They drove horses and cattle onto the bank and left them unguarded for three days. The Hungarians, thinking the enemy gone, crossed and led the animals over the ice, which showed the Tartars that it would bear horses; they then crossed in one rush (as the next page tells).
p.q: Et ecce in hieme niuis et glaciei abundantia superuenit, ita quod Danubius, quod non acciderat a multis retroactis temporibus, gelabatur. … Multos equos et animalia super ripam Danubii adduxerunt, et neminem per tres dies ad eorum custodiam dimiserunt; ita quod bestiae sine custodibus pergere videbantur, nec aliquis eorum in illis partibus apparebat.
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: And then in winter a great deal of snow and ice came, so that the Danube froze, which had not happened for many years past. … They brought many horses and animals onto the bank of the Danube and left no one to guard them for three days, so that the beasts seemed to be wandering without keepers, and none of the Tartars appeared in those parts.

p.h: 'Have you a medicine of immortality?'
p.g: At his first audience, in the Khan's camp south of the Hindu Kush, Chinggis welcomed the sage, fed him and asked outright for an elixir of immortality; Changchun answered that there were ways to preserve life but no medicine for immortality, and the Khan praised his honesty. At a later audience the sage firmly refused to drink the tung lo set before him, which Bretschneider explains as kumiss or other fermented milk (p.94). His teaching was translated into Mongol by the councillor A-hai and written down in both Chinese and Mongol (p.95).
p.q: After this he asked: "Sainted man, you have come from a great distance. Have you a medicine of immortality?" The master replied: "There are means for preserving life, but no medicines for immortality." Chinghiz lauded him for his sincerity and candour. By imperial order two tents were pitched for the master east of the emperor's tents.
p.s: Li Zhichang, disciple of Changchun, in the Si yu ki (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.tg: chinggis khan immortality audience daoism kumiss

p.h: Two kinds of Tatar marriage
p.g: Gmelin explains that at a Tatar betrothal the bride's side names a fine, from fifty to a hundred roubles, that the groom must pay if he mistreats his wife, withholds food and clothing, or is caught in adultery. In a footnote he adds that there are two ways of marrying. In one, the wife is kept for life in the women's quarters, may not even look out of the window and does no housework, sitting 'like a statue with folded hands'. In the other she may go where she likes and appear in public, but must run the household.
p.q: Die Tataren verheurathen sich mit ihren Weibern auf eine zweyfache Art. Bey der einen werden die letztern eingeschränkt, und so der Gewalt der Männer übergeben, daß sie Lebenslang in dem ihnen angewiesenen Weiber-Behältniß verbleiben müßen, nicht Erlaubniß haben aus dem Fenster zu sehen … Bey der andern Art haben die tatarische Weiber die Freyheit überall hinzugehen, wo sie wollen, und ohngescheut in dem Publiko zu erscheinen.
p.s: Samuel Gottlieb Gmelin (footnote)
p.t: The Tatars marry their wives in two ways. In the one, the wives are confined and so given over to the power of their husbands that they must stay for life in the women's quarters assigned to them and are not allowed to look out of the window … In the other, Tatar wives have the freedom to go wherever they like and to appear in public without fear.

p.h: Tatar boat-haulers flogged by Russian soldiers
p.g: Going up the Tobol river from Tobolsk to Tyumen, the embassy's boats were towed the whole way by Tatars. In Tulishen's own Chinese words, there was no towpath, the men waded through mud until their legs bled, and the Russian soldiers kept whipping them until the envoy, unable to watch, told them to stop. It is one of the few moments where the author shows personal feeling.
p.q: 途中皆搭搭拉之人挽縴岸傍林木叢宻無縴路俱行泥水之中兩足肌膚破損血水淋漓俄羅斯兵丁猶加笞楚催促余不忍視呵責方止
p.s: Tulishen (Chinese text, Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pl: Tobol river, between Tobolsk and Tyumen
p.t: All along the way the Ta-ta-la (Tatar) people hauled the towropes. The banks were thick with trees and there was no towpath, so they all walked in mud and water; the skin of their legs and feet was torn and blood ran down, yet the Russian soldiers still flogged them on. I could not bear to watch, and only when I rebuked them did they stop.
p.c: Staunton's English version of the same scene is on T0019 n156 (p.112).
p.tg: labour boat hauling russian rule tatars

p.h: Captives sold at Caffa, as far as Persia and India
p.g: Chevalier says Crimean Tartars left farming to Christians, Jews and their own slaves, and counted their wealth in horses, cattle and captives taken in raids. The captives were sold to merchants at Caffa and shipped east, and Polish women, he says, could end up in harems in Persia and India.
p.q: Their Horses and Cattel are their Riches, with the Booty and Slaves of both Sexes, which they take in their incursions and sell to the Merchants of Caffa … especially the Women and Maids of Poland, who are carried away sometimes as far as Persia and India, to furnish the Serraglios of those Countreys
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.c: Written from the Polish side of a long frontier war.

p.h: One language and one script 'in all these kingdoms'
p.g: Kuun quotes a Franciscan missionary from the order's annals: he decided first to learn the language of the land, and 'by the grace of God' learned Cuman and the Uighur script, which were used in common 'throughout all these kingdoms'. It shows the Horde as a literate world with a shared Turkic language and an old Uighur script, not a land without writing.
p.q: Ego vero, consilio habito, prius volui linguam terrae addiscere, et per gratiam Dei addidici linguam Cumanicam et literaturam Uiguricam, qua quidem lingua et literatura utuntur communiter per omnia regna ista
p.s: An anonymous Franciscan missionary, quoted by Geza Kuun (1880) from the annals of the Franciscan order
p.pe: Cumans and Tatars of the Golden Horde
p.t: But I, after taking counsel, wished first to learn the language of the land, and by the grace of God I learned the Cuman language and the Uighur script, which language and script are used in common throughout all these kingdoms.
p.c: The missionary is not named on this page; Kuun cites the annals of the Friars Minor (Rome, vol. VII).
p.n: Checked against the page image.

p.h: Water, millet beer and mare's milk
p.g: Here Chevalier speaks as an eyewitness: in Poland he saw Tartar prisoners carry dead horses out of stables to feast on. He then lists their drinks: water, snow in winter, horse broth, 'Breha' (a millet drink, the steppe boza), and for the better-off mare's milk, mead and spirits, even though Islam forbade them wine.
p.q: I have seen at my being in Poland, divers Tartar prisoners come and take away dead Horses out of the Stables to feast one another with … their drink is ordinarily clear water, and in winter snow … or else Breha, which is a drink made with boiled Millet, but those who are better accommodated, and more delicate, drink Mares milk, Mead, and Strong waters
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

p.h: A khan deposed for breaking Genghis Khan's Yasa
p.g: Ibn Battuta visited the camp of Sultan Tarmashirin, a devout Muslim khan who prayed in a mosque inside his camp. He explains that Genghis Khan's law book, the Yasa, required an annual assembly where nobles could depose a ruler who had broken its rules. Tarmashirin had abolished that assembly, so, after Ibn Battuta left, the Tartars and their nobles deposed him and he was killed.
p.q: Now, Tarmashirin had entirely abolished the observance of this day, which gave very great offence. Some time, therefore, after we had left the country, the Tartars, together with their nobles, assembled and deposed him, appointing for a successor one of his relations
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)
p.c: The deposition happened after he left, so he reports it second-hand; his account of the Yasa assembly is not confirmed by other sources.

p.h: Captured in Daghestan: dragged behind horses, shot with blunted arrows
p.g: After a shipwreck on the Caspian coast, Struys and his companions were stripped by one band and then seized by another, who took them for spies of the rebel Razin. He describes being tied to horses' tails and driven barefoot through thorns, then bound to a tree and struck with arrows whose points had been blunted to make the torment last. Russian slaves of the prince vouched that they were Dutch, which saved their lives (two pages later).
p.q: ils nous attachèrent à la queue de leurs chevaux, nous faisant suivre à reculons & les piés nus, au travers des ronces & des épines dont le chemin étoit tout couvert … me rattacher à un arbre, où ils me percèrent à coups de flèches dont ils avoient émoussé le fer
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.pe: Tartars of Daghestan (the men of 'Sultan Osmin')
p.t: they tied us to the tails of their horses, making us follow backwards and barefoot through the brambles and thorns with which the road was covered … tie me to a tree, where they pierced me with arrows whose iron they had blunted
p.c: His own ordeal, but told in a ghost-written book that heightens every drama.

p.h: A stuffed horse on four birch poles, facing east
p.g: The Teleuts, Gmelin notes, were not Muslims; each morning they turned to the rising sun and prayed 'do not strike me dead'. By the village stood their 'taülga', four birch posts in a square. Once or more a year they killed a horse, ate it in a circle, stuffed the skin and set it on the posts facing east. They now built these close to the village, he says, because they had noticed the Russians knew better uses for the hides.
p.q: Sie schlachten ein Pferd, ziehen demselben die Haut ab und verzehren das Fleisch nahe bey dem Taülga … Die Haut stopfen sie aus, und setzen das Pferd … oben auf den Taülga … Sie haben gemerckt, daß die Russen ihre Häute besser zu gebrauchen wissen, deswegen bauen sie ihre Taülga jetzo allzeit nahe bey dem Dorfe.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: They slaughter a horse, strip off its skin and eat the flesh near the taülga... They stuff the skin and set the horse... on top of the taülga... They have noticed that the Russians know how to make better use of their skins, so they now always build their taülga close to the village.

p.h: A wedding song called 'Yermak'
p.g: At the same wedding two Tatar musicians, one with a reed pipe with finger holes (its end taken wholly into the mouth) and one with an ordinary violin, played for the guests. They singled out one tune they found moving. It was called 'Yermak', after the Cossack leader who conquered Siberia in the 1580s, and they said it dated from the time he brought their forefathers under Russian rule.
p.q: Sie nennten das Lied Jermak und sagten, daß es zu der Zeit gemacht wäre, da Jermak Sibirien eingenommen, und ihre Voreltern durch seine Dienste unter die Russische Bothmäßigkeit gebracht hätte.
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: They called the song 'Yermak' and said it had been composed at the time when Yermak took Siberia and, through his services, brought their forefathers under Russian rule.

p.h: Millet porridge, mare's milk and distilled spirit
p.g: Most Tatars, Broniewski says, neither plough nor sow but live from horses, camels, cattle and sheep. The nobles have bread, meat, distilled spirit and mead; the ordinary people have no bread but eat pounded millet mixed with milk and water, called 'cassa', and drink mare's milk and eat cheese. Worn-out camels, horses and oxen are slaughtered for meat.
p.q: plurimi etiam agros non colunt, nec serunt, equis, camelis, bobus, vaccis, pecoribus & ouibus abundant, ac inde victitant. Nobiliores tamen panem, carnes, cibum, vinum crematum & mulsum potum habent, agrestiores verò pane carent, verùm milio concusso, lacte & aqua diluto, quem cassa vulgo nominant, pro cibo, pro potu lacte equino & caseo vtuntur.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.t: many do not till fields or sow, but abound in horses, camels, oxen, cows, cattle and sheep, and live from them. The nobles, however, have bread, meat, food, burnt wine and mead to drink; the rustics lack bread, but use pounded millet diluted with milk and water, which they commonly call cassa, for food, and mare's milk and cheese for drink.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.
p.tg: food millet mare's milk kumiss spirits herds

p.h: How a raider carried off his captives
p.g: Riding with the khan's army on its last great slave raid into Russian New Serbia, de Tott watches a single Tartar manage a whole captured family and flock: children in a sack at the saddle, the girl in front, the mother behind, the father and son on led horses. He admires the skill but calls the scene an image of 'avarice' and 'the most cruel injustice'. He reckons about 20,000 captives were taken.
p.q: Five or six slaves, of different ages, sixty sheep, and twenty oxen, the prize of a single man, do not embarrass him. The children, with their heads peeping out of a sack, hanging by the pummel of the saddle; a young girl sitting before, leaning on her left hand; the mother behind on the crupper, the father on a led horse, the son upon another
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.pe: Crimean and Nogai Tatars (Krim Giray's army)

p.h: How to make koumis
p.g: At a steppe village hospitable Tatars brought koumis and a brandy distilled from mare's milk. Maria took down the recipe for her husband: warm mare's milk, a sixth part warm water and a starter of old koumis, sour milk or rye leaven, churned and left to ferment a day and a night. She found it sourish-sweet and pleasant.
p.q: To any given quantity of warm Mares' Milk, the Crim Tartars add a sixth part warm water of the same temperature, with a little old Koumis, sour cows' milk, or a piece of sour leaven of their rye-bread, as a ferment; and mix all together in a species of churn… The koumis has a sourish sweet taste by no means unpleasant to my palate
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)

p.h: 'To us he has given wheels'
p.g: Describing the Nogais before their settlement in villages, Xavier says a family could pack wife, children and goods into its felt-covered wagon (araba) within an hour and roll off towards the horizon. He quotes a Nogai saying that sums up the old nomad view of the world: God gave wheels to them and houses and ploughs to others.
p.q: Such is the order established by God himself," cried the Nogai, " to us he has given wheels, to other nations fixed dwellings and the plough."
p.s: a Nogai saying, quoted by Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: A god-king for the Tartars from the Volga to Korea
p.g: Stewart explains the Dalai Lama's place in the Tartar world: he is worshipped by the 'heathen Tartars' across the whole breadth of Asia, and the more distant ones treat him as God himself. He adds that even the Manchu emperor of China honours him and keeps a lama envoy at the palace in Peking.
p.q: Every body knows that the Delai Lama is the great object of adoration for the various tribes of heathen Tartars, who roam through the vast tract of continent which stretches from the banks of the Volga to Correa on the sea of Japan, the most extensive religious dominion, perhaps, on the face of the globe.
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.pe: Buddhist Tartars (Mongols, Kalmyks and other Inner Asian peoples)
p.c: General knowledge of the day, drawn from books and Bogle's reports, not from travel among the Tartars.
p.tg: dalai lama buddhism religion mongols kalmyks

p.h: The khan's letter: 'You live in houses, how will you escape me?'
p.g: Julian carried to King Bela a letter the Tartar ruler had sent, written in 'pagan letters and the Tartar tongue', which a pagan he met in Cumania translated. The khan, calling himself the messenger of the heavenly king, demands Bela's surrender and the return of the Cumans who fled to Hungary, and draws a sharp contrast: the tent-dwelling Cumans might escape him, but a king who lives in houses, castles and cities cannot.
p.q: Facilius enim est Cumanis evadere quam tibi, quia illi sine domibus cum tentoriis ambulantes possunt forsitan evadere. Tu autem in domibus habitans habes castra et civitates, quomodo effugies manus meas?
p.s: The Tartar khan's letter to King Bela IV, as translated and reported by Friar Julian (printed by Hormayr, 1842)
p.pe: The Tartar khan ('Chayn', probably Batu) and King Bela IV
p.t: For it is easier for the Cumans to escape than for you, since they, going about without houses, with tents, may perhaps escape. But you, living in houses, have castles and cities: how will you flee my hands?
p.c: Known only through Julian's Latin rendering of an oral translation.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Tatar prisoners in Novgorod: baptism or the river
p.g: The Second Novgorod Chronicle, a terse 16th-century town record, notes that in 1552 sixty Kazan Tatars were brought from Moscow and three new prisons were built for them. On this page, under the winter of 7065 (1556 to 1557), it records that clerks handed the Tatars held in the prisons who wished to be baptised over to the monasteries, while 'those who did not wish to be baptised, they threw into the water'.
p.q: давали дьяки по монастыремъ Татаръ, которые сидѣли въ тюрмѣхъ и захотѣли креститись; которые не захотѣли креститись, ино ихъ метали въ воду.
p.s: Second Novgorod Chronicle (printed in the same PSRL volume, 1841)
p.pe: Tatar prisoners (Kazan Tatars brought to Novgorod after 1552)
p.t: the clerks gave out to the monasteries the Tatars who sat in the prisons and wished to be baptised; those who did not wish to be baptised, they threw into the water.
p.c: This is the Second Novgorod Chronicle, not the First, though it is bound in the same volume. The chronicle does not say explicitly that these were the Kazan prisoners of 1552.
p.tg: prisoners baptism kazan tatars execution religion

p.h: Huts on wagons, and guns lent only for the winter
p.g: In summer the Nogais, like the Kalmyks, move camp for food and fodder, carrying their goods on camels and setting their huts on great wagons made for the purpose. In winter they camp around Astrakhan for mutual defence against Kalmyk raids across the frozen Volga, and the Russian governor lends them weapons each winter and takes them back each summer, keeping one of their princes as hostage.
p.q: pour le transport de leurs meubles, ils ont des chameaux, & mettent leurs hutes sur de grands chariots faits exprès … Pour repousser les insultes qu'ils en reçoivent, le Gouverneur d'Astracan qui les protège, leur prête des armes tous les Hivers, & les reprend tous les Etés
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: for carrying their goods they have camels, and they put their huts on great wagons made for the purpose … To repel the attacks they suffer from them, the Governor of Astrakhan, who protects them, lends them arms every winter and takes them back every summer
p.c: How the governor handled weapons and hostages was information Struys had from others.

p.h: A horse on a pole for the dead lord
p.g: Riccoldo describes Tartar funerals: cooked meat, clothes and money buried with the dead, and for a great lord a horse ridden to exhaustion, killed, stuffed with green grass and hung up on a stake, told to be ready whenever its master rises again. He adds that they once buried up to twenty living slaves with a lord until Christians shamed them out of it, and that Tartars even paid bishops to be buried in Christian cemeteries.
p.q: et equus cadit, et ipse exenterat eum et euacuat omnia de ventre equi, et implet herba viridi, et postea infigit palum magnum per posteriora, et facit palum exire vsque ad os, et ita dimittit equum impalatum, et suspendit eum et mandat ei, quod sit paratus, quandocumque wlt dominus surgere
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.t: and the horse falls, and he guts it and empties everything from the horse's belly and fills it with green grass, and then drives a great stake in from behind and makes the stake come out at the mouth, and so leaves the horse impaled, and hangs it up and orders it to be ready whenever its lord wishes to rise
p.c: He does not say he watched a funeral; this is presented as general custom. The horse-on-a-pole rite matches steppe burial practice reported by other travellers.

p.h: Buried beside ruins they hold sacred
p.g: Meyer reports that the Kazakhs like to bury their dead near other graves or near ruins of old buildings they regard as holy, and that rich sultans were carried all the way to holy places near Tashkent. In winter the body was sewn into cloth and leather and kept in a separate yurt until it could be moved. This helps explain why the Ablaikit bricks ended up in Kazakh tombs.
p.q: Ihre Todten beerdigen sie gerne in der Nähe anderer Gräber oder Ruinen alter von ihnen für heilig gehaltenen Gebäude. Vor allen sind ihnen (wenigstens den Kirgisen der Umgebungen von Kar-Karaly) mehrere Orte in der Nähe von Taschkent heilig, und die Leichen reicher Sultane werden oft dorthin abgeführt.
p.s: Carl Anton Meyer (diary printed in Ledebour's Reise, part 2, 1830)
p.t: They like to bury their dead near other graves or ruins of old buildings which they hold to be holy. Above all (at least for the Kirghiz around Karkaraly) several places near Tashkent are holy to them, and the corpses of rich sultans are often carried there.
p.c: Partly hearsay: Meyer says he never attended a Kazakh funeral. The same page notes the Kazakh language barely differs from Tatar and uses Tatar script.

p.h: Belt wrestling at the Tatar Sabantuy
p.g: Rose and Humboldt were taken to the Saban, the Tatar festival held every year after sowing, when for a week people gathered on a meadow outside Kazan for games. He describes wrestlers who threw off their coats, looped their belts round each other's backs and tried to lift and throw the opponent. Winners were cheered and given small gifts by rich Tatars, who also served the guests kumiss in tents.
p.q: Wir hatten durch unsern längern Aufenthalt noch Gelegenheit den Saban, ein ländliches Fest der Tataren kennen zu lernen, das sie alljährlich nach beendeter Aussaat feiern. … Die Kämpfer hatten ihr gewöhnliches Oberkleid abgeworfen, ihre Gürtel um des Gegners Rücken geschlungen, und suchten nun denselben mittelst der Gürtel in die Höhe zu heben und umzuwerfen.
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.t: Through our longer stay we also had the opportunity to get to know the Saban, a rural festival of the Tatars which they celebrate every year after the sowing is finished. … The fighters had thrown off their usual outer garment, slung their belts round the opponent's back, and now tried by means of the belts to lift him up and throw him down.
p.tg: sabantuy wrestling festival kumiss kazan tatars

p.h: Raised on black felt: a khan election Hayton saw twice
p.g: Hayton says the Tartars still make their lord the way they made Genghis: the whole people gathers in a field, the chosen man is seated on a black felt, the nobles and Genghis's kin lift him high and set him on a rich throne, and all kneel to him. He adds that he himself was present at two such elections, and marvels that for all their conquests they never changed their first custom.
p.q: Quant volent eslire leur seignor, e j'ai esté II foiz à la eleccion de l'empereor des Tartars, e ai veü coment tous les Tartars s'assembloient en un grant champ, e celui qui devoit estre leur seignor faisoient seoir sur un feltre noir, e metoient un riche siege au mi d'eaus.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, La Flor des estoires de la terre d'Orient (French text, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: When they want to elect their lord (and I have been twice at the election of the emperor of the Tartars, and saw how all the Tartars gathered in a great field), they seated the one who was to be their lord on a black felt, and set a rich throne in their midst.

p.h: A Kachin shaman in ribbons and printed cotton
p.g: Pallas saw a young Kachin shaman perform at the Karysh mine. The man was said to have been mad, or to have played mad, for years before taking up the craft, and still sometimes 'witched' all night until he collapsed. As a beginner he had no drum, only a paddle-shaped rattle stick; a shaman earned the right to a drum by sacrificing a horse and stretching its hide over it.
p.q: Ich habe den Aufzug eines jungen Katschinzischen Zauberers, der viele Jahre, ehe er das Handwerk angefangen, närrisch gewesen oder sich närrisch angestellt hatte, in Karysch gesehn… Er gauckelte ohne Mütze und hatte nur bunt ausgenähte lederne Strümpfe und am Leibe einen engen, ganz beschmutzten Kittel, von bunt gedrucktem baumwollenen Zeuge (Kitaika) an
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: I saw the costume of a young Kachin sorcerer, who for many years before taking up the trade had been mad or had pretended to be mad, at Karysh… He performed his tricks without a cap and wore only brightly embroidered leather stockings and on his body a tight, very dirty smock of brightly printed cotton cloth (kitaika).

p.h: The road to Cathay is safe, day and night
p.g: According to merchants who had used it, the road from Tana to Cathay was perfectly safe by day and by night. The one risk was death: if a merchant died on the way, the lord of the land took everything he carried, unless a brother or close companion was there to claim it. On the same page Pegolotti advises hiring an interpreter and two servants who speak Cuman, the Turkic language of the steppe, and taking flour and salt fish for the journey, since meat is plentiful everywhere.
p.q: Il cammino d'andare dalla Tana al Gattajo è sicurissimo e di dì, e di notte secondo che si conta per gli mercatanti, che l'hanno usato: salvo se il mercatante, che va, o che viene, morisse in cammino, ogni cosa sarebbe del Signore del paese, ove morisse il mercatante, e tutto prenderebbono gli uficiali del Signore
p.s: Francesco Balducci Pegolotti (ed. G. F. Pagnini, 1766)
p.pe: Merchants on the Mongol roads; officials of the Tartar lords
p.t: The road from Tana to Cathay is perfectly safe, by day and by night, according to what the merchants say who have used it; except that if a merchant, going or coming, should die on the road, everything would belong to the lord of the country where he died, and the lord's officials would take it all
p.c: Reported from merchants' experience; Pegolotti himself is not known to have made the journey.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: A bride for forty mares
p.g: Among the Nogais, Pallas reports, the bride price (kalym) paid to a rich bride's father is forty mares, two horses fully harnessed, a suit of armour, a gun and a sabre. They live mainly on horse meat and mare's milk 'like the ancient Mongoles', a diet the Crimean Tatars have given up, and keep a love of wandering.
p.q: Conformably to the usage of all Asiatic nations, a Kalim or marriage portion, which, with the opulent, consists of forty mares, two horses completely caparisoned, a suit of armour, a gun, and a sabre is, on the celebration of the nuptials, delivered to the father of the bride. Their food, like that of the ancient Mongoles, consists principally of horse-flesh and mares' milk;
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pl: Molochnaya River steppe, north of the Crimea
p.tg: bride price kalym mare's milk horse meat nogais

p.h: A patent from Batu: 'be the eldest of all princes'
p.g: Five years after the conquest the grand prince rode 'to the Tatars, to Batu', and sent his son Konstantin on to the Great Khan ('Kan') in Mongolia. Batu received him with honour and named him senior over all Rus princes. The chronicle records the start of the system in which Rus princes held their thrones by the khan's word.
p.q: Великый князь Ярославъ поѣха въ Татары къ Батыеви, а сына своего Костянтина посла къ Канови; Батый же почти Ярослава великою честью, и мужи его, и отпусти й, рекъ ему: «Ярославе! буди ты старѣй всѣмъ княземъ въ Русскомъ языцѣ.»
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Batu, khan of the Golden Horde; Grand Prince Iaroslav Vsevolodich
p.t: Grand Prince Iaroslav went to the Tatars, to Batu, and sent his son Konstantin to the Kan; Batu honoured Iaroslav with great honour, and his men, and let him go, saying to him: 'Iaroslav! be thou the eldest of all princes in the Russian nation.'
p.tg: batu great khan patent horde politics

p.h: The baskak's warning: heads tied to saddle straps
p.g: After a quarrel with the local princes, the baskak Akhmat had captured boyars killed, their bodies hung on trees without heads and right hands, and told pilgrims to spread the message that anyone who disputes with his baskak will end the same way. His men then tied the heads to their saddle straps. The Laurentian text starts mid-story because leaves are missing from the manuscript.
p.q: «вы есте гости, а паломници, ходите по землямъ; тако молвите: хто иметь держати споръ съ своимъ баскакомъ, тако ему будеть;» а что изъимано людій черныхъ и съ женами и съ дѣтми, то все попровадилъ прочь. А трупья бояръ тѣхъ повелѣ по деревью извѣшати, отъимая голову и правую руку; и начаша бесурмене вязати головы боярьскыя къ торокомъ
p.s: Laurentian Chronicle, PSRL vol. 1 (1846)
p.pe: Akhmat, Muslim baskak (tax agent) of the Kursk land, and his 'besermen'
p.t: 'You are guests and pilgrims, you travel through the lands; say this: whoever will hold a dispute with his baskak, so it will be with him.' And whatever common people were seized, with wives and children, he sent all of them away. And he ordered the corpses of those boyars hung up on the trees, cutting off the head and the right hand; and the besermen began to tie the boyars' heads to their saddle straps
p.c: The opening of the story is lost in the codex; the chronicler blames Rus sins and princely feuds as much as the baskak.

p.h: Caravans on carts with no need for provisions
p.g: Ibn Arabshah says caravans used to set out from Khwarazm and travel by cart (ajal) across the steppe to Crimea, a journey of about three months, without fear. They carried no food or fodder and took no guide, because the steppe was so thick with peoples and so full of security and food that they only ever stopped at some tribe, and only halted with people who honoured their guests.
p.q: وكانت القوافل تخرج من خوارزم وتسير بالعجل وهم آمنون من غير ريب ولا وجل … فكانت القافلة لا تحمل زادا ولا عليقا ولا يصحبون معهم رفيقا وذلك لكثرة الامم ووفور الامن والماكل والمشرب من الحشم فلا يصدرون الا عن قبيله ولا ينزلون الا عند من يكرم نزيله
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.pe: Tatars and Turks of the Golden Horde steppe
p.t: Caravans used to leave Khwarazm and travel by cart, safe, without doubt or fear … The caravan carried no provisions and no fodder, and took no companion along, because of the multitude of the peoples and the abundance of security, food and drink among the retinues; they set out only from a tribe and halted only with someone who honoured his guest.
p.c: Nostalgic description of the steppe before Timur's invasions, written decades later.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.
p.tg: caravans carts hospitality trade khwarazm crimea

p.h: Chinggis Khan's law set above Islam
p.g: Ibn Arabshah says Timur spoke Persian, Turkish and Mongol but no Arabic, and held to the 'Chinggis Khan rules' (the yasa), treating them like branches of Islamic law. So, he says, did all the Chaghatay, the people of the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan, whom he calls rabble. For this reason, he adds, leading jurists declared Timur an unbeliever.
p.q: وكان معتقدا للقواعد الجنكيزخانيه وهي كفروع الفقه من الملة الاسلاميه … وكذلك كل الجغتاي واهل الدشت والخطا وتركستان اولئك الطغام كلهم يمشون قواعد الملعون جنكيزخان على قواعد الاسلام
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah (Arabic text, print catalogued 1842)
p.pl: Transoxiana, the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan
p.pe: Timur, the Chaghatay, the people of the Dasht (Golden Horde Tatars)
p.t: He held to the rules of Chinggis Khan, which are like the branches of jurisprudence in the Islamic faith … And so do all the Chaghatay and the people of the Dasht, Cathay and Turkestan, that rabble: all of them put the rules of the accursed Chinggis Khan ahead of the rules of Islam.
p.c: Religious polemic. It shows that Chinggisid law still mattered in Muslim Central Asia c.1400, but the tone is hostile.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.
p.tg: yasa chinggis khan islam law language

p.h: An old Tartar woman's welcome
p.g: At the village of Koochook Koi (Kuchuk-Koy) an old Tatar woman invited Alexander in for bread and bekmes, a thick pear syrup. He records her dress closely: a white headcloth over hair in six long plaits, a coloured petticoat under a blue knee-length coat held by a patterned belt, and silk trousers gathered at the ankle. A little girl nearby wore a red fez with silver coins sewn on the front.
p.q: a clean old Tartar woman invited me to eat some bread and bekmis with her : her head was enveloped in a white handkerchief … her hair, in six long plaits ; her coloured petticoat was covered with a blue surcoat reaching below the knees, and confined round her waist with a figured belt ; her trousers were of silk, drawn in at the ancles
p.s: James Edward Alexander (1830)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars of the south coast

p.h: Captives sacrificed before the battle of 1618
p.g: Semedo translates a memorial sent to the Wanli emperor by the President of the Council of War in 1618. It reports that the Tartars had massed to 'take this world of China', broke through the walls, seized Chinese prisoners and sacrificed them the day before the battle, acclaiming their own king as king of Beijing. Semedo says he translated it at the time and later found it printed in Europe.
p.q: En este tiempo con grã poder i multitud, entrando los muros, prendieron algunos de los nuestros para sacrificarlos; i sacrificaron el dia antes de la batalla con grãdes aclamaciones de su Rey, llamandole ya Rey de PeKim.
p.s: President of the Chinese Council of War, memorial of 1618, as translated by Álvaro Semedo (Spanish edition, Madrid 1642)
p.t: At this time, with great power and multitude, entering the walls, they seized some of our men in order to sacrifice them; and they sacrificed them the day before the battle, with great acclamations of their king, calling him already King of Peking.
p.c: A Chinese official's war report, written to alarm the emperor; Semedo only translates it.
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image; long s normalized, abbreviation marks (q̃, õ, ẽ) kept as printed.

p.h: Allies, not subjects: the Kalmyks and Russia
p.g: Explaining why Russian generals let irregular cavalry plunder freely, Cook says these troops were Cossacks, Kalmyks or other Tartars on the borders. The Kalmyks owned no subjection, only Russian protection, and could not be forced to move; even their khan could not act without the consent of his many elders, some of them lords of five or six thousand fighting men.
p.q: The Kalmucks acknowledge no subjection, but only live under the protection of Russia. They are barbarous to a great degree, but yet they must be treated with great lenity ; for, if they do not incline to leave their own country, the whole force of Russia is not able to oblige them, nor even their prince, unless with the approbation of their seniors
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.pe: Kalmyks and other Tatars serving as Russian irregulars

p.h: A Tatar convert tears his beard
p.g: A lame Tatar from the Arsk district came to Kazan to be baptized, saying his legs were healed the moment he heard that the Moscow tsar had taken Kazan and filled it with churches. Warned not to return to his old faith, he tore out some of his beard and crumbled the hairs, saying he would sooner be crumbled like them. Later his kinsmen hacked him to death. It is a story of conversion and of Kazan Tatars' resistance to it.
p.q: Татаринъ же абіе рукою напрасно исторже часть власовъ своея брады и раздроби ихъ на малыя крупицы, глаголя: «Азъ тако уразумѣхъ великую силу и милость Бога вашего, яко его ради готовъ есмь не токмо многія скорби терпѣти, но аще и сицевъ раздробленъ буду, яко же раздробихъ власы моя, никако же не отвергуся его».
p.s: Anonymous author of the History of the Kazan Tsardom, PSRL vol. 19 (1903)
p.pe: A Tatar from the Arsk side, baptized Stefan
p.t: The Tatar at once suddenly tore out with his hand part of the hair of his beard and crumbled it into small bits, saying: 'I have so understood the great power and mercy of your God that for his sake I am ready not only to suffer many sorrows, but even if I am crumbled like this, as I have crumbled my hairs, I will never renounce him.'
p.c: A pious conversion tale in the hagiographic style.

p.h: Sober Tatars who still enjoy a drink
p.g: Commenting on Ibn Fadlan's horror at Rus drinking, Frähn notes that not all Muslims keep the ban on wine. Among the Tatars of Russia, he says, 'sober as this people is', he met many who did not refuse wine and strong drink, though he never saw them drink too much. It is a small firsthand note on real Tatars by a scholar who knew them.
p.q: Und so habe ich auch unter den Tataren Russlands, so nüchtern dieses Volk auch ist, nicht wenige gefunden, die Wein und derlei starke Getränke nicht verschmähten, wenn ich sie gleich nie das Maass überschreiten sah.
p.s: C. M. Frähn, editor's note (1823)
p.t: And so among the Tatars of Russia too, sober as this people is, I have found not a few who did not scorn wine and such strong drinks, though I never saw them exceed moderation.
p.c: Editorial observation, not part of Ibn Fadlan's text.

p.h: A wooden idol dressed like a Russian woman
p.g: Baraba hunters took a small carved wooden idol called a Saltan into the forest on its own sled, dressed in bright cloth in imitation of Russian women's clothes. The first catch was offered to it. After a good season they hung the idol all over with sables and other furs, which were left to rot, because selling them was thought an unforgivable crime. Ides regrets the waste of fine skins.
p.q: When they go into the Woods in order to hunt furred Animals, they carry their Saltans along with them; which is a rough Image, as well carved in Wood as they can do it with a Knife: This they cloath in a Stuff dress of all sorts of colours, in imitation of the Habit of the Russian Women
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Ides's own route followed the Irtysh and Ob rivers north of the Baraba steppe, so this part of his closing survey is probably based on reports.

p.h: Eighty blows for a taste of wine
p.g: Attacking drunkenness in Lithuania, Michalo says more Lithuanians are executed for theft and robbery in a single month in one district than in one or two hundred years across all the Tatar and Muscovite lands where drink is forbidden. Among the Tatars, anyone who so much as tastes wine gets eighty blows with a stick and a fine of as many coins.
p.q: Certe apud Tartaros, qui modo vinum gustaverit, is & octoginta fustuarijs ictibus percutitur, & totidem nummis multatur.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 3 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: Certainly among the Tartars, whoever has merely tasted wine is struck eighty blows with the cudgel and fined as many coins.
p.c: Eighty lashes is the Islamic penalty for drinking; Michalo states the law, not a case he saw.

p.h: Tengri, sun and moon, and felt idols called ongon
p.g: In his opening survey d'Ohsson sums up the old steppe religion: a supreme being called Tangri, like the sky; worship of sun, moon, mountains, rivers and elements, with bows to the south and drink sprinkled to the heavens; and little wooden or felt figures, ongon, hung on the walls of their huts, bowed to and fed by smearing meat or milk on their mouths. The page before describes burial with a mare, a foal and a saddled horse.
p.q: Ils reconnaissaient un Etre Suprême, qu'ils désignaient ainsi que le ciel, par le nom de Tangri. … Leurs divinités étaient représentées par de petites figures de bois ou de feutre, nommées Ongon, qu'ils suspendaient aux parois de leurs huttes; ils s'inclinaient devant ces idoles, et leur offraient les prémices de leurs repas, en leur frottant la bouche avec de la viande ou du lait.
p.s: Constantin d'Ohsson
p.pe: the 'Tatar' peoples of the steppe (Mongols and neighbours)
p.t: They acknowledged a Supreme Being, whom they called, like the sky, by the name Tangri. … Their divinities were represented by small figures of wood or felt, called Ongon, which they hung on the walls of their huts; they bowed before these idols and offered them the first portions of their meals, rubbing their mouths with meat or milk.
p.c: A synthesis of Carpini, Rubruck and Persian sources, not a separate witness.

p.h: Why no empire can conquer people who move every month
p.g: Explaining why the Ottomans do not try to rule the Caucasus and the steppe directly, Chardin argues that settled people in towns can be conquered and held, but people who move all their lives cannot. It is his own reflection, but it neatly explains why steppe peoples were so hard for empires to pin down.
p.q: For if the People that inhabit those parts, were united into Cities and strong Places, there might be a way found to reduce 'em, and keep 'em in Subjection. But which way is it possible to subdue a People that change their Habitations every Month, and all their Life-time wander up and down the Country?
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.c: Chardin's own opinion, not a report of what he saw.

p.h: Nailed by the ear to his own shop door
p.g: Describing justice under the khans, she says judges ruled on the spot and punished at once: cheating shopkeepers were nailed by the ear to their doors, small offences got the bastinado and serious ones the bowstring for Muslims but a halter for Christians and Jews. She adds that Turks and Tatars rarely cheated.
p.q: A shopkeeper caught in the act of cheating with false or short weights was nailed by the ear to his own shop-door, that the whole market might know the knave, and watch him in future… Lesser offences were instantly punished with the bastinado, and greater with the bow-string, if a true believer; for a halter was the portion of an infidel
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: Describes the system before Russian rule, which she did not see.

p.h: Fighting on horseback 'the Kalmuk way'
p.g: The Panchen Lama told Bogle that the Lhasa regent did not want Gorkha envoys to enter Tibet in case they learned 'the manner of the Kalmuks fighting on horseback', which Tibetans practised too, and showed him the style with his hands. It hints at how Mongol cavalry methods were treated as a military secret.
p.q: Gesub, among other reasons, objects to their coming into Tibet lest they should learn the manner of the Kalmuks fighting on horseback, which is practised in this country (describing it at the same time by motions), and should teach it to the Gorkha Rajah's people.
p.s: The Panchen (Teshu) Lama, as reported by George Bogle (edited by Markham, 1876)

p.h: A Turkish dialect even Turks struggle with
p.g: Reuilly says the Tatars speak a Turkish dialect so mixed with Mongol and Arabic words that a Turk finds it hard to follow, and the Nogais are hardest of all to understand because they speak fast and gutturally.
p.q: Though the general language of the Tartars is only a Turkish dialect, yet it is intermixed with such a number of Mogol and Arabic words, that a Turk has a difficulty to understand it. The Nogays in particular render themselves scarcely intelligible, by the quickness with which they speak, and the guttural pronunciation.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

p.h: Tartar soldiers paid more than Chinese
p.g: Davis explains the dual army. The 'trusty Tartar troops' are ranged under eight standards, yellow, white, red and blue, plain and bordered, said to be 80,000 men; the Chinese serve under the green flag. A Tartar foot soldier gets two taels a month plus rice, a Chinese only 1.6 taels without rice. He also notes that Tartars under the law are punished with the whip instead of the bamboo.
p.q: A great difference seems to exist between the pay of Tartars and Chinese. One of the former, being a foot-soldier, is allowed two taels per month, or about five-pence a day, with an allowance of rice; one of the latter, only one tael and six-tenths, without the rice.
p.s: John Francis Davis (The Chinese, 1836)
p.pe: Manchu Tartar bannermen and Chinese Green Standard troops
p.c: Davis says 'seems to exist'; the figures come from report.

p.h: The Wuhuan: round yurts facing east, meat and kumiss
p.g: The Chinese histories describe the Wuhuan as skilled mounted archers and hunters who move with their herds, with no permanent home, living in round yurts with the door facing east, eating meat, drinking kumiss and wearing coloured woollen cloth. Bichurin's summary treats them as a branch of the 'house of the Tatar khan', the Donghu.
p.q: Ухуаньцы искусны въ конной стрѣльбѣ изъ лука; занимаются ловлею звѣрей и птицъ, Переходятъ со скотомъ съ мѣста на мѣсто, смотря по достатку въ травѣ и водѣ; постояннаго прибыванія не знаютъ. Живутъ въ круглыхъ юртахъ, изъ коихъ выходъ обращенъ къ востоку. Питаются мясомъ, пьютъ кумысъ; одежду дѣлаютъ изъ разноцвѣтныхъ шерстяныхъ тканей
p.s: Chinese dynastic history (Hou Han shu), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1851
p.t: The Wuhuan are skilled at shooting the bow from horseback; they hunt beasts and birds, move with their livestock from place to place according to the supply of grass and water, and know no permanent dwelling. They live in round yurts whose entrance faces east. They eat meat and drink kumiss, and make their clothing of many-coloured woollen fabrics
p.c: Bichurin's link of the Wuhuan to a 'house of the Tatar khan' is his own reconstruction.

p.h: Bards who sing all night
p.g: Rich Khivans kept bards who sang the deeds of ancient heroes on a lute, growing more ecstatic as the audience applauded, sometimes through the whole night while the listeners sat still and silent.
p.q: The wealthy Khivans generally keep a bard in their service, who entertains them with stories and songs, and airs played on a sorry kind of lute. Sometimes they compose ballads relating the deeds of ancient heroes. … This singing is kept up the whole night not unfrequently, during which the host and his guests sit attentively listening, motionless, and apparently buried in meditation.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: Shooting arrows at the thunder
p.g: From Chinese annals Klaproth lists the customs of the High Carts people: bride-price paid in oxen and horses, weddings feasted on curdled mare's milk and roast meat, and a terror of lightning. When a bolt struck they shrieked, shot arrows at the sky and moved camp, then came back the next year to burn a ram in a pit while their sorceresses performed.
p.q: Quand la foudre tombait, les Kao tchhe poussaient des cris affreux, tiraient des flèches contre le ciel, quittaient leur camp et le transportaient plus loin. L'année suivante, quand leurs chevaux étaient bien gras, il y revenaient en grand nombre, faisaient une fosse dans laquelle ils brûlaient un bélier : les sorcières exécutaient alors leurs prestiges.
p.s: Julius Klaproth, translating Chinese dynastic histories
p.t: When lightning struck, the Kao-tche let out terrible cries, shot arrows against the sky, left their camp and moved it further off. The next year, when their horses were well fattened, they came back in great numbers and dug a pit in which they burned a ram; the sorceresses then performed their magic.
p.c: Chinese court historians wrote about northern neighbours with open disdain ('a barbarous and cruel people'), and Klaproth passes this on.

p.h: Nomads turning farmers on the khan's orders
p.g: Unkovsky notes that thirty years earlier the Kalmyks had little grain because they did not know how to plough, but now fields were multiplying: not only their subject Bukharans (settled Turkestani farmers) but many Kalmyks had taken up farming by the ruler's order. He lists wheat, millet, barley and rice, and melons, apricots, grapes and pomegranates from Yarkand and the other towns under Dzungar rule.
p.q: Предъ симъ временемъ лѣтъ за тридцать хлѣба мало имѣли, понеже пахать не умѣли. Нынѣ пашни у нихъ отъ часу умножаются, и не токмо подданные Бухарцы хлѣбъ сѣютъ, но и Калмыки многіе за пашню пріемлются, понеже о томъ Контайши приказъ есть.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: Some thirty years before this they had little grain, because they did not know how to plough. Now their fields multiply by the hour, and not only the subject Bukharans sow grain, but many Kalmyks are taking up ploughing, because there is an order from the Kontaisha about it.
p.c: The same page opens with Unkovsky's prejudiced remark that Kalmyks learn cunning and theft from childhood.

p.h: Hire a 'Tartar' to handle your journey
p.g: In practical advice for travellers, Jaubert says that in Turkey one can make a deal with a 'Tartar' who will supply everything needed on the road, but warns never to pay him the whole sum in advance; in Persia the custom was unknown. In the Ottoman Empire a 'Tatar' was a government courier, and Jaubert himself travelled with one, Omar, who renamed himself Aly in Persia.
p.q: Dans le premier de ces pays, on peut faire marché avec un Tartare qui se charge de vous fournir tout ce qui est nécessaire; mais il faut se garder de le payer d'avance en totalité. En Perse, cet usage est inconnu.
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
p.t: In the first of these countries one can strike a bargain with a Tartar who undertakes to supply you with everything necessary; but take care not to pay him the whole in advance. In Persia this custom is unknown.
p.c: Here 'Tartar' is an Ottoman job title, not an ethnic label.

p.h: Kalmyk chiefs who wear deer antlers
p.g: From Bukhara merchants Burnes heard that Kalmyk Tartars settled around Ili and Yarkand marked their chiefs and nobles by fixing deer's horns on their skull-caps, the size of the antlers showing rank. He adds a crude rumour about their women, and says the Chinese used Kalmyks to guard the frontier.
p.q: There are Calmuk Tartars settled around Eela and Yarkund, who have a singular custom to distinguish their chiefs and grandees, by fixing deer's horns on their skull-caps.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: Hearsay; the next page adds a sexual slander Burnes 'was assured' of.

p.h: Yellow caps and red caps across all Tartary
p.g: Watching monks in yellow robes and conical yellow hats, Turner explains that Tibetan Buddhism is split into yellow-hat and red-hat sects that between them cover 'almost the whole of Tartary'. The red hats allow their priests to marry. The yellow, favoured by the Emperor of China, is the most orthodox and powerful.
p.q: I notice this peculiarity of colour in their dress, as it is a distinction adopted, to mark one of the two religious sects that divide almost the whole of Tartary, from Turkistan to the eastern limits of this continent. The other colour is red; and the tribes are known as belonging to the red, or the yellow cap.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.c: The claim that these sects cover all Tartary 'from Turkistan' is a large generalisation from what he was told.
p.tg: buddhism yellow hat red hat religion monks

p.h: Turkmen roadside grave mounds
p.g: Riding with a sayyid near the Caspian, Burnes asked about mounds of earth with a pole in the centre. They were 'yoozka', marking where someone had died or been laid out, and Turkmen said a blessing as they passed. Burnes remarks that they were not graves but barrows raised in honour of the dead, and suspects the custom was 'Tatar'.
p.q: They are not graves, but mounds or barrows raised in honour of the dead. I entertain an impression that the usage is Tatar; but I had no opportunity of further investigation.
p.s: Alexander Burnes (1834)
p.c: Burnes's 'Tatar' origin is an untested hunch, as he admits.

p.h: Tartar herdsmen and their yaks
p.g: Near his camp Turner met Dukba herders who lived only in tents. One brought him milk and butter. Their 200 to 300 yaks, owned by three families, grazed the mountains by day and at dusk were called in, tied in a double line before the tents and guarded by two big Tibetan mastiffs. They moved north to south with the seasons.
p.q: Near our encampment, was a party of Tartar herdsmen, called Dukba, whose sole occupation is tending cattle, and who always live in tents. One of them brought me a large quantity of milk, which was excellent, and some very good butter.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: The Tartar princes and their fiefs
p.g: After the birthday festivities the tributary Tartar princes went home. Staunton describes them as chiefs of large clans who owed troops in wartime under the 'grand banners of Tartary', held hereditary fiefs that needed the emperor's investiture, and usually married women of the imperial family.
p.q: They were the chiefs of numerous clans dependent on them, and could bring large bodies of troops into the field. They were often called upon in time of war, and had their respective stations, rank, and duty, assigned to them under the grand banners of Tartary. Their lands, or fiefs, were properly hereditary by primogeniture
p.s: George Leonard Staunton

p.h: Horsehair and bullets left at a holy place
p.g: At the same brick shrine birch poles were hung with tufts of horsehair and rags, and the ledges held pebbles, lead bullets, an arrow and gunpowder. Pallas explains that the Kazakhs believe leaving hair from a horse's tail at a holy place helps the horse, and that leaving some small thing is a general Tatar custom. The Tatars of his own escort added offerings after praying.
p.q: Die Kirgisen nehmlich glauben, daß es ihrem Pferde zuträglich ist, wenn etwas Haar von deßen Schweif an einem so heiligen Ort zurück gelassen wird, und überhaupt ist es eine tatarische Gewohnheit bey solchen Bethäusern, oder andern heiligen Plätzen, die sie der Andacht wegen besuchen, irgend etwas, so sie bey sich führen, zurück zu lassen.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pl: Kazakh steppe between the Ui and Tobol
p.pe: Kazakhs (Kirgis) and Tatars of Pallas's escort
p.t: For the Kirgis believe that it is good for their horse if some hair from its tail is left at so holy a place; and in general it is a Tatar custom, at such prayer-houses or other holy places they visit out of devotion, to leave behind something they carry with them.

p.h: Free men who elect their own leaders
p.g: Georgi describes the Tatars' legal position in the empire: they were free, never subject to serfdom, and kept their own customs. They chose their own headmen, usually from nobles and princes who traced their descent in a direct line from Chinggis Khan and Batu. He adds that their tribute was light and some groups served as Cossacks instead.
p.q: Die Tataren sind freye, der Leibeigenschaft gar nicht unterworfene Leute, und bleiben bey ihren väterlichen Verfassungen ungestört. Sie wählen ihre Vorgesetzte aus ihren Mitteln, und gewöhnlich aus ihren Adel, der zum Theil aus Fürsten besteht, welche ihre Abkunft von Tschingis, Bathi und andern berühmten Beherrschern in gerader Linie abzuleiten pflegen.
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: The Tatars are free people, not subject to serfdom at all, and they remain undisturbed in their ancestral constitutions. They elect their superiors from among themselves, usually from their nobility, which partly consists of princes who are accustomed to derive their descent in a straight line from Chinggis, Batu and other famous rulers.
p.c: An official Academy view of imperial policy; it describes the law as intended, not every local reality.
p.tg: law nobility chinggis khan serfdom tribute

p.h: A Muslim gravestone dated 1346
p.g: Klaproth read Arabic gravestones at Madzhar: one for 'Sina, son of Mohammed, son of Chalil' of AH 747 (1346-1347), another for a judge of AH 777 (1375-1376), which he carried away. All dated stones he saw belonged to the 8th Islamic century. He notes Pallas missed them because peasants had built them into their yards.
p.q: Here is buried the deceased, who needs the mercy of God in eternity, Sina, son of Mohhammed, the son of Chalil..... in the year of the era seven-and-forty and seven hundred.
p.s: Julius Klaproth, translating an Arabic gravestone (English translation, 1814)
p.pe: Muslim Tatars of the Golden Horde

p.h: A Tobolsk mullah's book of Tatar history
p.g: While making his map as a prisoner, Strahlenberg befriended the Bukharan and other Muslim residents of Tobolsk. Their chief priest showed him two manuscripts from the city of Turkestan, one on the Persian dynasties and one on Tartary, called 'Chingis' or 'Kitap' (book). On the next page he tells how a Tatar explained it word by word in Russian and two Swedish officers wrote it down in German: this became the German text of Abulghazi's history.
p.q: Weil ich mich aber absonderlich an ihren vornehmsten Priester, Agun Asbackewitz genannt, so ein gar freundlicher Mann war, adressirte, wurden mir … auch zweene Manuscripta von ihm hervor gezeiget, eines betreffend die Persischen Dynastien, das andere aber die Tatarey, welches letztere er nur Tzingis oder Zingis, item: Kitap oder Buch nannte; beyde aber aus der Stadt Turckestan erhalten hatte
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (Vorbericht, Stockholm 1726)
p.pe: Bukharan and Tatar Muslims of Tobolsk
p.t: But because I addressed myself especially to their chief priest, called Agun Asbackewitz, who was a very friendly man, he showed me … two manuscripts, one concerning the Persian dynasties, the other Tartary, which latter he called only Tzingis or Zingis, or Kitap, that is, book; both of which he had obtained from the city of Turkestan
p.c: The OCR of this copy is badly garbled Fraktur; the quote has been restored letter by letter from the damaged text, so check the scan.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: The best drinker is called Bahadur
p.g: At Timur's feasts, cup-bearers made guests drain full cups in one pull, and refusing was an insult to the lord. The heaviest drinker earned the title bahadur, 'valiant'. Timur even sent the envoys a jug of wine beforehand so they would arrive in a jovial mood. The food was roast horse, sheep and rice.
p.q: They call the man who drinks the most wine Bahadur, which is as much as to say "a valorous man" ; and he who does not drink, is made to do so, although he does not wish it.
p.s: Ruy González de Clavijo (translated by Clements R. Markham, 1859)
p.c: Markham's footnote on the same page adds a Victorian moral comment of his own.
p.tg: wine feast bahadur court horse meat

p.h: Gravestones in Turkish, Arabic and Armenian
p.g: Rose reports what was known of Bulghar's gravestones from copies made for Peter the Great in 1722, since most stones had been built into the church. There were 27 in Turkish, 20 in Arabic and 3 in Armenian, each with a Quran verse, the name and lineage of the dead and a date. The oldest group, of 1226, gives the year by a chronogram meaning 'the coming of oppression', which Klaproth linked to an early Mongol raid.
p.q: Unter den Inschriften befinden sich 27 in türkischer, 20 in arabischer und 3 in armenischer Sprache. Sie enthalten alle einen Spruch des Koran … Die meisten und zugleich ältesten Inschriften sind aus dem Jahre 623 der Hedschra, oder dem Jahre 1226 unserer Zeitrechnung, aber das Todesjahr ist bei diesen nur durch ein Chronogramm, welches die Ankunft der Unterdrückung bedeutet, angegeben
p.s: Gustav Rose (summarising Klaproth's edition of copies made for Peter the Great)
p.pe: Muslim inhabitants of Bulghar under the Golden Horde
p.t: Among the inscriptions are 27 in Turkish, 20 in Arabic and 3 in Armenian. They all contain a saying from the Quran … Most and at the same time the oldest inscriptions are from the year 623 of the Hijra, or 1226 of our era, but in these the year of death is given only by a chronogram meaning 'the coming of oppression'
p.c: Second-hand: based on copies of copies, and Rose notes the Armenian texts could not be deciphered.

p.h: Kalmyks who pity people tied to one place
p.g: Another footnote quotes Bell on the Dzungar Kalmyks of Tsewang Rabdan (the 'Kontaysha'), who could field 100,000 horsemen. Bell, relying on Russians who had visited, says they lived in tents all year and found it amusing to pity settled people who had to work for a living, which they considered 'the greatest slavery'.
p.q: These Tartars live in tents, all the year, removing from place to place, as called by necessity or inclination. This is the most ancient and pleasant manner of life. It is entertaining to hear them commiserate those who are confined to one place of abode, and obliged to support themselves by labour, which they reckon the greatest slavery.
p.s: John Bell of Antermony, quoted in a footnote by the translator G. T. Staunton
p.c: Bell's information came from Russian officials who had been sent to the Kontaysha.

p.h: A funeral like a wedding
p.g: He describes the funeral of a young unmarried man: the body in his best clothes on a bier under a canopy, musicians and young people in finery, feasting and merrymaking at the grave while the parents weep, so that it becomes the wedding he never had. He adds firmly: 'All this I have seen.'
p.q: It is also the custom in the country, that when a young man, who has not had a wife, dies, he is dressed in his best clothes, and players carry him, and he is laid on a bier, and a canopy is placed over him.
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.c: On the same pages he calls these people Christians who worship a nativity picture; editor Neumann suggests they were Buddhists he mistook for Christians.

p.h: The 'valiant fool'
p.g: The bravest Tatar warriors, Barbaro says, earned the title 'Tulubagator', which he translates 'valiant fool', an honour like 'the wise' or 'the handsome' in Italy. The editor explains it as tulu bahadur; bahadur is the root of the Russian bogatyr, hero. He follows it with the story of a Tatar merchant who chased forty Circassians alone.
p.q: The hablemen are verie valiaunt and hardie, in such wise that some of them for their excellencie are called Tulubagator, which signifieth a valiaunt foole : being a name of no lesse reputacon amongst them than the sernames of wisedome or beaultie with vs
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.c: 'Fool' is Barbaro's own gloss; the etymological note is the 1873 editor's.

p.h: A Buryat chief's Buddhist shrine tent
p.g: Georgi visited the Khori Buryat chief (taisha) Dorzhi, who kept a separate yurt for Lamaist (Tibetan Buddhist) worship, with a prayer wheel at the door. Inside were images of the Buddhas (burkhans), silver offering bowls and censers, long horns, cymbals and conch shells, and five chests of Mongol and Tibetan books. Among them, treated with great respect, was a Church Slavonic Psalter.
p.q: Dieser Mann hatte eine besondere Burchanjurte für den Lamaischen Götzendienst. Vor derselben stand eine Bethmühle (Kurdu). Die Jurte war voll von Burchanen, Opferschälchen, langen musikalischen Instrumenten, Lamakleidern, Rosenkränzen und Büchern. … Unter denselben befand sich auch der sauber gebundene Davidische Psalter in Sklawonischer Sprache, dem sehr ehrwürdig begegnet wurde.
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: This man had a special burkhan-yurt for Lamaist worship. In front of it stood a prayer wheel (khürdü). The yurt was full of burkhans [Buddha images], offering bowls, long musical instruments, lama robes, rosaries and books. … Among them was also a neatly bound Psalter of David in the Slavonic language, which was treated with great reverence.
p.c: Georgi calls the Buryats a Mongol people, not Tatars; they belong here as the kind of people older European maps placed in 'Tartary'.
p.tg: buryats buddhism yurt prayer wheel psalter

p.h: Turkmen slave raids on the road to Mashhad
p.g: In the appended notice on Mazandaran, Colonel Trezel explains why pilgrims to Mashhad gathered at Astarabad in caravans of seven or eight hundred. Turkmen raiders roamed the plains, plundered everything and carried off men and even children able to keep up, sending them to herd flocks around Bukhara and Samarkand; Sunni Turkmen, he says, were driven against Shia Persians by hope of plunder and by religion.
p.q: Les Turkomans rodent sur toutes ces plaines, pillent tout ce qu'ils trouvent, et emmènent en esclavage les hommes et les enfans même en état de suivre leurs courses. Ils les envoient garder leurs troupeaux dans les plaines de Bokhara et de Samarcand. Ces peuples sont animés contre les Persans par l'espoir du pillage et par la différence des opinions religieuses, parce qu'ils sont sunnys.
p.s: Colonel Camille-Alphonse Trezel (Notice sur le Ghilan et le Mazenderan, printed with Jaubert)
p.t: The Turkmen roam all these plains, plunder everything they find, and carry off into slavery the men, and even the children able to keep up with their raids. They send them to guard their flocks on the plains of Bukhara and Samarkand. These peoples are driven against the Persians by hope of plunder and by difference of religious opinion, because they are Sunnis.
p.c: Trezel reports what he learned in Persia; he did not enter Turkmen country, and he does not call the Turkmen Tartars.

p.h: Hazara wives who run the household
p.g: Elphinstone is surprised to find that among the Hazaras, a tribe he calls nearly savage, women have more standing than anywhere nearby. They manage the house and property, are consulted on everything, are never beaten and are not secluded. He also records, from hearsay, lurid claims about their morals which he admits are contradictory.
p.q: The wife manages the house, takes care of the property, does her share of the honors, and is very much consulted in all her husband's measures. Women are never beaten, and they have no concealment.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: From informants; the same page repeats gossip about Hazara women that Elphinstone himself calls inconsistent.

p.h: Bride price and wives in Tatar villages
p.g: In the village he notes that women walked about unveiled, that village men rarely had more than one wife, and that a bride price (kalym, which he writes 'halim') was paid, sometimes 500 roubles even among peasants. He adds that the Tatars kept some village arrangements secret from Russian officials.
p.q: In the Tatar villages the men have rarely more than one wife ; in the towns, particularly among the rich merchants, bigamy frequently occurs, but to have more than two wives is very rare. The women are sold, and the halim paid for them, which even in the case of peasants frequently amounts to five hundred roubles.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.c: 'The women are sold' is his gloss on the bride-price custom, based on what villagers told him.
p.tg: marriage bride price kalym women polygamy

p.h: Wooden idols with human faces
p.g: When their boats arrived, each Rus trader went to a tall wooden post carved with a human face and ringed by smaller figures, bowed to the ground and listed his slave girls and sable furs, asking for a rich buyer. If trade went well he slaughtered cattle and sheep, left the meat before the idols and hung the heads on the posts; when dogs ate it at night, he said his lord was pleased.
p.q: Er tritt zu der großen hölzernen Figur, wirft sich vor ihr zur Erde nieder und spricht: o mein Herr! ich bin aus fernem Lande gekommen, führe so und so viel Mädchen mit mir, und von Zobeln so und so viel Felle,
p.s: Ibn Fadlan as quoted by Yaqut (German translation by C. M. Frähn, 1823)
p.t: He goes up to the large wooden figure, throws himself on the ground before it and says: 'O my lord, I have come from a distant land, bringing so many girls with me, and so many sable skins.'
p.tg: idols religion sable slave trade rus

p.h: Tartars wield brush and sabre and scorn trade
p.g: An essay on money-lending in China contrasts the two ruling peoples: the Chinese are no warriors and prize learning, while the Tartars aim to handle the brush as well as the sabre and write works of every kind in Manchu, but would think it beneath them to practise a craft or trade. The same page praises their energy and toughness and says they spend freely rather than save.
p.q: Nos Chinois ne sont pas guerriers, mais ils se piquent de sagesse & d'habileté. Les Tartares visent à manier aussi-bien le pinceau que le sabre; ils composent en Tartare des ouvrages dans tous les genres … Les Tartares croiroient s'avilir de faire un métier ou commerce, & nos Chinois regardent le triste métier des armes comme la derniere ressource du défaut de mérite.
p.s: Anonymous Peking missionary (essay on interest on money in China, Mémoires vol. 4, 1779)
p.pe: Manchu banner people ('Tartares') in Qing China
p.t: Our Chinese are not warriors, but they pride themselves on wisdom and skill. The Tartars aim to handle the brush as well as the sabre; they compose works of every kind in Tartar [Manchu] … The Tartars would think it degrading to practise a craft or trade, and our Chinese regard the sad trade of arms as the last resort of those without merit.
p.c: A generalisation about national character by a writer living in Peking.

p.h: Kumis, but not the intoxicating kind
p.g: In a footnote Wrangel says the Yakuts make kumis from mare's milk 'in the same manner as in Tartary', except that they have not learned, like the Tartars, to make it intoxicating. It is so nourishing that a couple of skins of kumis hung from the saddle are often the only food carried on a hunting trip of several days.
p.q: This well known beverage, prepared from mares' milk, is made here in the same manner as in Tartary; only the Jakuti have happily not learnt, like the Tartars, to make it intoxicating. It is an agreable beverage, and so nourishing, that a couple of large skins full of kumys hung to the saddle, are often the only provisions taken for a foraging excursion of a few days.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840), footnote
p.c: Sauer (W008) reports that Yakut kumis could intoxicate if drunk in quantity, so accounts differ.

p.h: Forty thousand axemen cut the road
p.g: King Béla had blocked the mountain passes into Hungary with barricades of felled trees. Thomas says the Tartars had forty thousand men with axes marching ahead of the army, cutting down woods, laying roads and clearing obstacles, so that the great barricades of fir and oak were crossed as if they were made of straw, then broken up and burned.
p.q: habebant autem quadraginta millia securigeros, qui praeibant exercitum, sylvas caedentes, vias sternentes, & omnia offendicula ab ingressibus removentes. Quamobrem indagines, quas Rex parari fecerat, tam facile transcenderunt ac si non ex ingentium abietum, & quercuum fuissent extructae congerie, sed ex levibus essent stipulis praeparatae
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: they had forty thousand axe-bearers who went before the army, cutting down forests, laying roads and removing every obstacle from the approaches. Therefore they crossed the barricades that the king had had prepared as easily as if they had been built not of a pile of huge firs and oaks but of light straw
p.c: The number is Thomas's figure from report, not a count.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: A steppe where hardly anyone is sober in summer
p.g: Lange (as abridged by Pallas) notes that the Mongols live mainly on brick tea boiled with milk and butter, bought from the Chinese, and in the milking season distil milk brandy and drink it warm, so that apart from girls and children one rarely meets a sober person in their camps. They also make small cheeses and air-dry strips of meat for the hungry winter.
p.q: Vom Frühling bis in den Herbst, so lange das Vieh häufige Milch giebt, ziehen sie häufigen Milchbranntewein ab, und trinken ihn gleich warm auf, daher man in selbiger Zeit, ausser Mädchen und Kindern, selten einen nüchternen Menschen in den mongolischen Lägern antrifft.
p.s: Lorenz Lange (journal of 1727 to 1728, translated and abridged by P. S. Pallas, 1781)
p.pl: Khalkha Mongolia (between Selenginsk and the Tola River)
p.t: From spring until autumn, as long as the cattle give plenty of milk, they distil a great deal of milk brandy and drink it straight away while warm, so that at that time, apart from girls and children, one seldom meets a sober person in the Mongol camps.
p.c: A generalisation by a Russian caravan official, abridged by Pallas; not a measured observation.

p.h: A Mongol twelve-year calendar in the Crimea
p.g: Pallas finds that the Crimean Tatars still use the Mongol twelve-year animal cycle, though some names have lost their meaning (the 'tiger' year became a small grey insect). They use it to forecast the weather and harvests of coming years, and Pallas, who lived among them, says their forecasts were generally wrong.
p.q: This aera, which recommenced in 1792, and will terminate with the year 1803, serves chiefly for predicting the nature and fertility of future years; but, in such conjectures, the Tartars are generally mistaken, as far as I could judge during my residence among them.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.tg: calendar animal cycle divination mongol heritage

p.h: Dancing golden peacocks and ladies crowned with a 'foot'
p.g: In the palace hall are golden peacocks that flap their wings when Tartars clap their hands, which Odoric thinks is done by devilry or hidden machinery. He then describes the court seating and the tall headdress of married Mongol women, which he likens to a man's foot topped with crane feathers and pearls. Yule's note links this to the bogtak headdress also described by Rubruck and Ibn Battuta.
p.q: In the hall of the palace also are many peacocks of gold. And when any of the Tartars wish to amuse their lord, then they go one after the other and clap their hands ; upon which the peacocks flap their wings, and make as if they would dance. Now this must be done either by diabolic art, or by some engine underground.
p.s: Friar Odoric of Pordenone (translated by Henry Yule, 1866)

p.h: No bread, only meat and fermented milk; the Tatars will drink it
p.g: Instead of flour the Dzungars sent the embassy chigan, fermented milk, saying they had no grain and ate only meat and drank chigan. Unkovsky answered that some of his people would drink it and some would not, since a Christian fast was about to begin: during it nobody but the Tatars would drink chigan. The 'Tatars' here are the Muslim service Tatars of Tobolsk and Tara travelling with him.
p.q: а вмѣсто муки и крупъ привезли чигану, объявляя, что у нихъ нынѣ хлѣба нѣтъ, и люди ихъ нынѣ не ѣдятъ, токмо мясо, и пьютъ чиганы. Сказано имъ, что наши люди иные будутъ пить чиганъ, а иные не будутъ; а особливо съ завтрешнего числа начнется у насъ постъ … и никто, кромѣ Татаръ, чигану пить не будутъ
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.pe: Dzungars (Oirats); Siberian service Tatars in the Russian suite
p.t: and instead of flour and groats they brought chigan, declaring that they have no bread now, and their people are not eating now, only meat, and drink chigan. They were told that some of our people will drink chigan and some will not; and especially since from tomorrow our fast begins … and nobody except the Tatars will drink chigan
p.tg: chigan fermented milk kumiss food service tatars

p.h: A ring of 3,000 guards closes on the game
p.g: The emperor hunted almost daily. Verbiest describes the Manchu ring hunt: 3,000 guardsmen spread out in a circle at least 3,000 paces across, then walked inward in step until it was only 300 paces wide, trapping everything inside.
