He watched two or three hundred hares taken in less than a day, and elsewhere over a thousand deer, besides bears, boars and more than sixty tigers.
p.q: they Reduced this great Circle to another much less, which had about 300 paces in the Diameter : So that all the Beasts which had been stayed within the first, found themselves taken in this last as in a Net … I saw taken in this manner two or three hundred Hares in less then one day, without counting an Infinite of Wolves and Foxes.
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)

p.h: Tea that tastes like soup
p.g: Tibetan butter tea, bought at the Gartok fair, is made with butter, salt, spices and a little meal instead of milk and sugar. Gerard grew to love it. Every traveller arriving at a Tartar village was offered a dish of it, and it was kept ready most of the day.
p.q: During my stay at Soongnum, Putee Ram insisted on bringing me daily tea, prepared after the Tartar fashion, which tastes like soup, and I took a great liking to it. The Tartars drink it in large quantities ; and when they arrive at their encamping ground, their first occupation is to make the tea
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

p.h: Praying once a year is enough
p.g: Ides lodged a night with the Voguls and asked about their religion. Once a year they go into the woods, kill one animal of each kind, hang the carcass on a tree and bow to it, then feast; and they saw no reason to pray more often. On the same page he notes that a good hunting dog was laid to rest in its own little wooden hut raised on four props of earth.
p.q: Their whole Religious Worship consists in making an Offering according to their Custom once each Year: When they go in crouds into the Woods, and kill one of each Species of Beasts … they flea off the Skins, hang up the Carcass on a Tree, and fall prostrate to the Earth, and in their way, Pray to it … What need of Praying any oftner than once a Year, say they?
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)
p.c: Based on one night's conversation through interpreters.

p.h: Winning the Mongols through their lamas
p.g: Verbiest explains that the 'Tartarian Monarch that Conquered China' won over the Mongols partly by courting their Buddhist lamas, who persuaded their people to submit. The emperor still gave the lamas presents and used them to keep the Mongols obedient, though Verbiest believed he privately despised them. He adds that the land had been divided into 48 tributary units.
p.q: one of his first Cares was to engage to his Interest by his Royal Bounties, and by Demonstration of a Singular Affection, the Lamas (or Preists) these Men having a great Repute above all those of their Nation, easily perswaded them to Submit to the Government of so great a Prince
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: Court knowledge and Verbiest's own reading of the emperor's motives; as a rival missionary he was hostile to the lamas.

p.h: Inside a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
p.g: Ides, curious to see Tatar worship, visited a mosque at Tobolsk with the governor, without whom he would not have been let in. The mosques had large open windows and carpeted floors with no other ornament; worshippers left their shoes at the door. The mufti was an Arab, and the Tatars honoured anyone who could read Arabic. Many Kalmyk slaves lived in the area.
p.q: Les Tartares, qui demeurent à Tobol, & à plusieurs lieues aux environs, sont tous Mahometans. Mr. Isbrants, étant curieux de voir leurs cérémonies, se rendit dans une de leurs mosquées, accompagné du Waiwode, sans quoi il n'auroit pû y être admis. Elles sont entourées de grandes fenêtres, qu'on laisse ouvertes, & le pavé en est couvert de tapis, sans autre ornement.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides's route to China (1692-1695), summarized by the editors of the 1718 French edition of Le Brun and inserted in it
p.t: The Tartars who live at Tobolsk and for several leagues around are all Muslims. Mr Isbrants, curious to see their ceremonies, went to one of their mosques accompanied by the voevoda, without whom he could not have been admitted. They are surrounded by large windows, which are left open, and the floor is covered with carpets, with no other ornament.
p.c: Ides's eyewitness visit, reported second-hand in this book.

p.h: Muslims who learned letters and law from the Turks
p.g: The Crimean Tatars are Muslims with mullahs and mosques and write in Arabic letters, somewhat cruder than the Turks'. Broniewski believes that before they came into Crimea they were a wild steppe people without Muslim laws, letters or customs, and that the nobles learned 'civility' and the faith from the Turks.
p.q: Tartari illi Mahometani sunt, presbyteros & templa Mahometica habent, literis Chaldaicis vel Arabicis à Turcis paulò corruptioribus vel rudioribus illi vtuntur, etsi antequam in Tauricam seu Peninsulam venerant, moribus multo agrestioribus gens ea fera & campestris … fuisse videntur: nam illis Mahometicis legibus, iuribus, litteris & moribus illa tum prorsus caruit.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.t: Those Tartars are Muslims; they have priests and Muslim temples, and use Chaldaic or Arabic letters, somewhat more corrupt or rougher than the Turks', although before they came into Taurica or the peninsula that wild steppe people seems to have had much ruder manners ... for it then wholly lacked those Muslim laws, rights, letters and customs.
p.c: His view of their earlier 'wildness' is a guess, not something he could observe; the Golden Horde had adopted Islam long before.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.
p.tg: islam religion writing arabic script mosques

p.h: Decrees in Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan
p.g: After the Qing armies drove the Dzungars out in 1720, Desideri reports, Tibet's government passed to the Emperor of China, run by ministers some of whom were Chinese, some 'Chinese Tartars' and some Tibetans. Every decree had to be issued in three languages: Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan. 'Chinese Tartars' was the usual period term for the Manchus, so within one book 'Tartar' shifts from Mongols to Manchus.
p.q: Till October 1720 Tibet was a monarchy under an absolute and independent king. From that time, however, all power has passed into the hands of the Emperor of China and the actual government consists of a body of ministers appointed by him, some of whom are Chinese, some Chinese Tartars, others again Tibetans. All decrees must be promulgated in three languages Chinese, Tartar and Tibetan.
p.s: C. Wessels (1924), summarising Ippolito Desideri's manuscript
p.c: A summary by Wessels, not Desideri's own words. Which 'Tartar' language is meant (Manchu or Mongol) is not stated.

p.h: Manchu troops in long robes
p.g: From the boats Ellis sees soldiers under distinctive flags pointed out as Manchu Tartars. Their weapons look like Chinese troops', but they wear long gowns instead of jackets.
p.q: Last evening we observed some troops on the opposite bank with peculiar flags, which were described as Man-tchoo Tartars. There did not seem any difference in their arms or accoutrement, but instead of jackets they wore long dresses.
p.s: Henry Ellis

p.h: Ghost weddings for dead children
p.g: Polo reports that when a boy and a girl died unmarried, their families arranged a marriage between them, drew up a contract, burned it so the couple would know in the next world, and burned paper pictures of the dowry. Yule notes this is really a Chinese custom, though he trusts Polo that Mongols practised it too.
p.q: And marry them they do, making a regular contract ! And when the contract papers are made out they put them in the fire, in order (as they will have it) that the parties in the other world may know the fact, and so look on each other as man and wife.
p.s: Marco Polo (translated by Henry Yule, 1871)

p.h: A mosque in every village, plain inside
p.g: Every Tatar village Lepekhin saw on the Cheremshan had its own mosque (metschet) and clergyman, and larger villages two or three. The mosques were bare of ornament except for a carpet on the wall and another on the floor at the place of the akhun, the senior cleric. He goes on to explain the ranks of Tatar clergy (akhun, mullah and abyz, muezzin), how only the akhun may wear the turban, and how the clergy judge quarrels and punish offenders by the Koran.
p.q: Die Tatarn, welche am Tscheremschan wohnen, sind, so viel ich ihrer habe zu sehen bekommen, alle mohamedanischer Religion, und jedes Dorf hat seine Metschet und seinen Geistlichen … In ihren Metscheten ist nichts von Zierrathen zu sehen, außer an dem … Platz des vornehmsten Geistlichen des Achun.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.t: The Tatars who live on the Cheremshan are, as far as I have seen of them, all of the Mohammedan religion, and every village has its mosque and its clergyman … In their mosques there is nothing ornamental to be seen, except at the place of the chief clergyman, the akhun.
p.c: Marginal headings printed beside the text break into the OCR line; they are left out with ellipses.

p.h: Kalmyk monks who write from top to bottom
p.g: At the Moravian colony of Sarepta, Güldenstädt questioned two Moravian Brethren who had spent the summer living with the Kalmyk horde to learn the language. They told him the clergy had smooth-shaven heads, could read, and wrote from top to bottom on silk paper with a pointed stick; they healed only by prayer and might demand a sick man's whole property as an offering to Burchan. Kalmyks dried strips of meat for winter and preferred animals that had died on their own. Güldenstädt keeps the Kalmyks separate from the Tatars throughout.
p.q: Die Geistlichen erkennet man an dem ganz glatt abgeschornen Kopf. Diese lernen auch lesen und schreiben; sie schreiben von oben nach unten, gemeiniglich auf Seidenpapier mit einem spitzigen Stökgen. … Zur Bezahlung ihrer Cur fordern sie öfters das ganze Vermögen von den Kranken, nicht für sich, sondern zum Opfer für ihren Burchan, so nennen sie ihren Gözen.
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1787), reporting what Moravian missionaries told him
p.t: The clergy are recognised by their completely smooth-shaven heads. They also learn to read and write; they write from top to bottom, usually on silk paper with a pointed little stick. … As payment for their cure they often demand the whole property of the sick, not for themselves but as an offering to their Burchan, as they call their idol.
p.c: Secondhand from missionaries hoping to convert the Kalmyks. Pallas's footnote on the previous page corrects the ‘white’ and ‘black’ division: white meant families of princely blood, black the commoners.

p.h: Priests who dealt in slaves
p.g: Wood says the Sunni Uzbeks of Kunduz treated persecution of Shia Muslims as proof of faith, and that their religious leaders were the biggest slave dealers, buying Shia captives and justifying it as good for the soul. Elsewhere he describes chained slave tributes on the road to Kunduz.
p.q: These mullahs, or priests, are the most notorious slave dealers in the land, and encourage the odious traffic among their disciples, by readily purchasing of them whatever victims of the Shiah creed they may entrap. The good of the soul is assigned as ample extenuation
p.s: John Wood
p.pe: Uzbeks of Kunduz and their mullahs
p.c: Wood writes as a hostile Protestant observer; the slave trade itself is confirmed by many sources.

p.h: Horsemen raised to arms from the cradle
p.g: A compiled portrait of the Tartar soldier: iron helmets with dyed horse-tail plumes, bows and sabres but no muskets, nearly all cavalry. They are pale, silent, trained to arms from infancy, unmatched archers, and eat any flesh half cooked. The same page calls them 'a Nation of Plunderers' and says few have any religion beyond some lamas.
p.q: They are whitish of Complexion, not talkative, but silent, and well composed, bred up to Arms from their very Cradles, which makes them such excellent Souldiers … They eat whatsoever they can get, but chiefly flesh, and that half roasted or boiled, being not curious of what sort it is, whether of Camels, Horses, or other Creatures.
p.s: Johan Nieuhof, general description of China (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669); this part is compiled, largely from Martino Martini
p.c: Compiled, and mixes observation with hostile stereotypes about plunder and irreligion.

p.h: A child's body left in a leather sack
p.g: On the road the mission was startled to find a dead child sewn in a leather sack, with a scrap of sheepskin, millet and bread laid on top. Timkovsky says this was the usual Mongol way of disposing of the dead, and goes on to explain that lamas chose between burning, water burial, exposure on a platform or leaving the body on the steppe for animals and birds.
p.q: We were greatly surprised at seeing on the road, six wersts from Elesoutou, the dead body of a child in a leather sack. Upon the sack was a little piece of sheep-skin, some millet, and some bread. This is the usual manner of burying the dead among the Mongols.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

p.h: The price of a Nogai bride
p.g: Among the Nogais a groom never saw his bride before the wedding and bargained with her family for her price. Xavier gives the going rates: four or five hundred rubles and a couple of score cows for a handsome girl of good family, less for widows. On the same page he adds that Crimean mountain Tatar and Kalmyk wives cost less and were bought by poorer men.
p.q: A handsome girl of good family costs four or five hundred rubles, besides a couple of score of cows and a few other beasts. Young widows are cheaper, and old women are to be had for nothing. The bride's price is paid on the spot by the wooer
p.s: Xavier Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)
p.c: Written from outside and with some disdain; how widely these prices applied is not stated.

p.h: Obo: stone cairns for the spirits of the land
p.g: Bichurin explains the obo cairns he saw on hilltops: small round mounds of stones heaped on every notable height by a main road. Once a year Mongols gather there to honour the guardian spirits of the district with wrestling, horse racing and archery. Every rider passing an obo dismounts, kneels on the south side, bows three times and leaves something: a khadag scarf, an arrow, a scrap of cloth, horsehair or a pebble.
p.q: Это суть священныя мѣста, при которыхъ Монголы собираются однажды въ годъ для поклоненія духамъ покровителямъ страны. Здѣсь-то происходятъ ихъ празднества, сопровождаемыя борьбою, конскимъ ристаніемъ и стрѣляніемъ изъ луковъ. Въ прочее время каждый Монголъ, проѣзжающій мимо Обо, сходитъ съ лошади, становится предъ онымъ съ южной стороны на одно колѣно, и, поднося сложенныя ладони ко лбу, дѣлаетъ троекратное поклоненіе.
p.s: Iakinf (N. Ya. Bichurin), 1828
p.t: These are sacred places, where the Mongols gather once a year to worship the guardian spirits of the country. Here their festivals take place, accompanied by wrestling, horse racing and archery. At other times every Mongol riding past an obo gets off his horse, kneels on one knee before it on the south side and, raising his folded palms to his forehead, bows three times.
p.c: Bichurin's definition of an obo (a small round mound of heaped stones on heights by a main road) is on the preceding page, n95.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Reading the future in a mutton bone
p.g: Before helping his ally Malik Husayn retake Herat, Timur strips a leg of mutton to the bone and performs 'the usual ceremonies' to read an omen from it; the sign is good, and the city falls by surprise at dawn. The translator adds a footnote that the Tartars play with sheep bones instead of dice. Omens run all through these memoirs.
p.q: At this time there was a stewed leg of mutton before us, the bone of which was sticking out ; I took it, and having stripped it of all the meat, I resolved within myself to draw from it an omen, whether Melk Hussyn would be successful in his enterprize. I performed the usual ceremonies, and the result was favourable
p.s: Attributed to Timur (translated by Charles Stewart, 1830)
p.c: The footnote about sheep-shank games is Stewart's, not the text's.

p.h: Tatar religion: one God, Christ a prophet, prayer morning to night
p.g: Michalo summarises Tatar Islam as a Christian of his day understood it: a law shared with the Turks and other 'Saracens', professing one simple God, Christ as holy prophet and final judge born of a virgin but not crucified, and circumcision at the age Ishmael was circumcised. On the next page he praises their prayer morning, afternoon and evening, their fasting and their alms, and says they laugh at Christian fasts and churches.
p.q: Deum unicum & simplicem profitetur, Christum vero, sanctum Prophetam & iudicem mundi postremum, Virgine pura natum, sed non passum credit. Circumcisionem observat.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 10 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: It professes one simple God, and believes Christ to be a holy Prophet and the last judge of the world, born of a pure Virgin, but not to have suffered. It observes circumcision.

p.h: The Kalmyk story of Shakyamuni
p.g: In a footnote Strahlenberg records the Kalmyk account of 'Xacamuni', that is the Buddha Shakyamuni: once a prince in India, taken up to heaven alive for his holiness, whose celibate sons explain why lamas may not marry, and one of whom brought the religion to Tibet. It is a garbled but recognisable outline of Buddhist teaching as told to a Swedish captive.
p.q: They say that 4000 Years ago, he was only a Soveraign Prince, in India; But on Account of his unparallel'd Sanctity, God had taken him up to Heaven alive; But the Place whither he was translated, none of them pretend to know.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg, author's footnote (English translation, 1738)

p.h: Not savages: a defence of the Uzbeks
p.g: Elphinstone argues that the European picture of the Uzbeks as ferocious barbarians comes from confusing them with the Kalmyks (the garbled word in the scan) and 'other rude Tartar tribes' further north. He does not hide the slave trade in Bukhara, but on the word of Afghan and Tajik travellers he calls the Uzbeks 'as good a people as any in Asia'. The rest of the page, badly scanned, says that anyone who imagines the Uzbeks as savages will be surprised to learn that Bukhara rivals Peshawar in population, has numerous colleges and caravanserais, and tolerates all religions.
p.q: of the Uzbeks, appear to be unjust, and is probably owing partly to our confounding them with … other rude Tartar tribes between them and Russia … men are sold in Bokhaura like cattle; but in other respects, by all that I can learn, both from Afghaun travellers, and from Taujiks of Bulkh and Bokhaura, I have reason to think the Uzbeks as good a people as any in Asia.
p.s: Mountstuart Elphinstone (1815)
p.c: Second-hand; he names his sources as Afghan travellers and Tajiks of Balkh and Bukhara.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.

p.h: Leather masters and 'dressing-gown Tartars'
p.g: Among the street cries of St Petersburg Kohl heard 'Kazan boots' and 'Bukhara dressing-gowns'. He credits Mongols and Tatars with founding almost every branch of Russian leatherwork, from Moscow's embroidered caps and belts to Kazan's morocco boots, and says Tatar sellers of silk robes were nicknamed 'dressing-gown Tartars'.
p.q: The Mongolians and Tartars are distinguished for their skill in the preparation of leather, and almost every branch of manufacture connected with this article in Russia has had its origin from them … Dressing-gowns are almost the only things that do not come through Russian hands, but from those of the Tartar makers … where they are often called “dressing-gown Tartars.”
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.pe: Tatars (from Kazan and Central Asia) trading in the capital
p.c: The claim that Russian leatherwork originated with the Tatars is Kohl's generalisation.

p.h: Kalmuk pilgrims bring silver, furs and camels
p.g: While Bogle stayed at Teshu Lumbo a large Kalmuk caravan arrived to worship the Panchen Lama, offering silver, furs, silk and dromedaries. They stayed a month, went on to Lhasa, and then went home, about three months' journey north. Elsewhere Bogle says Kalmuk tribes came every year with camels loaded with Siberian furs and hides.
p.q: Among the rest of his votaries were a large caravan of Kalmuks, who offered up to his shrine talents of silver, furs, pieces of silk, and dromedaries. They remained about a month at Teshu Lumbo, and then proceeded to Lhasa, where, having spent about ten days, they returned to their own country, which was about three months' journey to the northward.
p.s: George Bogle (edited by Clements R. Markham, 1876)

p.h: 'No purse being necessary among these Tartars'
p.g: Walking toward Tyumen with sore feet, Cochrane stopped at a small Tartar village where he was fed for nothing. He shook hands with his host, received the Muslim blessing 'Peace be with you', and squatted on his heels with the family to eat. Hospitality to strangers comes up again and again in his account of the Siberian Tatars.
p.q: At the last station, a small Tartar village, I was regaled with pork, bread and eggs, at free cost, no purse being necessary among these Tartars. I partook of the wholesome fare a la Tartare, shaking hands first with the host, and receiving his blessing of "Peace be with you," then squatting on my hams, like the rest of the company.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: A Muslim household serving pork is surprising; Cochrane may have misidentified the meat or the village.

p.h: Justice on the spot
p.g: In the camp, Barbaro says, quarrels were settled without violence or paperwork: the parties walked off together and asked the first respectable man they met to judge, and his verdict was accepted, with bystanders as witnesses. He also describes petitioners kneeling repeatedly as they approached the lord's pavilion.
p.q: Whan a difference groweth betwene partie and partie, and wordes multiplied (not aftre the maner of our quarters, for these do vse no violence), thei both or moo (if they be moo) arise and go what waie they thinke good : and to the first man of any estimacon that they meete they saie : Master, do vs right, for we here are in controversie
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)

p.h: Washing clay for Tatar and Turkish ladies
p.g: Six versts from Inkerman a soapy clay was dug from pits and tunnels. Turkish and Tatar women used it in the bath to wash their faces, and it was shipped in quantity from Balaklava to Constantinople. The Tatars called it simply kil, while mineralogists knew it as 'keffekil', probably, Hablizl thinks, because it was once shipped from Kaffa (Feodosia).
p.q: Die Türkischen und Tatarischen Frauenzimmer bedienen sich desselben beym Baden zum Waschen des Gesichts. Er wird sehr häufig, von Baluklawa aus, nach Constantinopel geführt … Die Tataren nennen ihn Kil und nicht Keffekil, unter welchem letztern Namen er sonst unter den Mineralogen bekannt ist.
p.s: Karl Ludwig Hablizl (German translation, 1789)
p.t: Turkish and Tatar ladies use it in the bath for washing the face. It is shipped very often from Balaklava to Constantinople … The Tatars call it kil and not keffekil, the name under which it is otherwise known among mineralogists.

p.h: Horsehair for the spirit of the mountain
p.g: Crossing a mountain, Wrangel's lead Yakut driver pulled a few hairs from his horse's mane and tied them to a tree as an offering to the spirit of the mountain. Travellers on foot planted a stick instead. Even baptised Yakuts kept the custom, and the drivers sang songs praising the landscape, which his sergeant explained was meant to flatter the spirit.
p.q: Our leading postilion got off his horse, plucked a few hairs from the mane, and fastened them to the tree with much solemnity of manner. He told us that this was a customary offering to the spirit of the mountain, to obtain his protection during the journey, and that foot-passengers placed a stick in the ground with the same intention.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
p.pl: Road from Yakutsk to the Kolyma

p.h: Shooting backwards while fleeing, 'as the Tartars still do'
p.g: Telling how Cuman horsemen raided the Latin crusaders besieging Adrianople in 1205, Peyssonnel describes their tactic of fleeing while loosing arrows backwards without stopping, 'as the Tartars of today still do'. The Latins could not catch them, because the Cumans were more lightly armed and had faster, better-trained horses.
p.q: Les Comains prirent la fuite, en se contentant de faire de temps en temps quelques décharges de flèches, par derrière, sans arrêter leur marche, comme font encore les Tartares d'aujourd'hui. Les Latins ne purent atteindre ces ennemis, qui étoient armés plus légèrement qu'eux, & avoient des Chevaux plus vîtes, & mieux exercés à la course.
p.s: Charles de Peyssonnel
p.pe: Cumans; Crimean and Nogai Tatars of the 18th century
p.t: The Cumans took flight, contenting themselves with loosing a volley of arrows behind them from time to time without halting, as the Tartars of today still do. The Latins could not overtake these enemies, who were more lightly armed than they and had faster horses, better trained for running.

p.h: The Tartar haircut forced on the Chinese
p.g: Before the Tartars began to rule, Careri says, the Chinese wore their hair long, wound behind the head in a knot pinned with silver. After 'the empire of the Tartar' everyone was ordered, on pain of death, to cut it and adopt the Tartar style: shaved head with one tuft, which the Chinese wore braided, sometimes down to the legs. Loose wide-sleeved robes were also banned for Tartar dress, 'which the Chinese felt, and still feel, in their hearts'.
p.q: Prima che cominciassero a dominare i Tartari, portavano i Cinesi lunghi i capelli, avvolgendogli dietro la testa … ma dopo l'Imperio del Tartaro, fu ordinato a tutti, in pena della vita, di tagliarsegli; e di andare alla maniera Tartara, colla testa rasa, e un ciuffo
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.t: Before the Tartars began to rule, the Chinese wore their hair long, winding it behind the head ... but after the empire of the Tartar, everyone was ordered on pain of death to cut it, and to go in the Tartar manner, with the head shaved and a tuft
p.c: He saw the result; the history is from Jesuit sources. The corpus OCR reads 'miniera' for 'maniera'.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: queue hair dress manchus qing conquest

p.h: Fleeing to China: 6,000 Yakuts in one year
p.g: Sauer reports that Yakuts and Tungus unhappy under Russian rule were slipping away to the upper Amur valleys under Chinese protection, where they had reportedly built strong places. Russian officials told him more than 6,000 Yakuts moved to China in 1787 with all their goods, and his footnote remarks that such migrations reduced 'the number of Tartars tributary to Russia'. Elsewhere he blames heavy exactions by Russian officials for the Yakuts' decline.
p.q: In the year 1787, there migrated to China, from the districts of Olekma, Yakutsk, and the Vilui, more than 6000 Yakuti, with all their possessions
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802), citing Russian officials Evers and Kyshkin
p.c: The figure is second-hand, from two Russian assessors.

p.h: Kimmiz and horse flesh among the Uzbeks
p.g: Fraser's informants told him the Uzbeks were fond of kimmiz (kumiss), fermented mare's milk shaken in a skin for hours, and often got drunk on it in season. He also heard, and heard denied, that they preferred horse meat to beef.
p.q: it is said they are fond of horse flesh, which they prefer to beef : I have heard this denied ; but I do not know which statement is the true one. There is no doubt of their fondness for the national and intoxicating drink, called kimmiz, prepared from mares’ milk, by shaking it violently in a skin for several hours.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser

p.h: A Tatar funeral feast of thirty oxen for Yermak
p.g: In the same chronicle story, the Tatars repented of mistreating Yermak's body, wished they had made him their king, and buried him under a spreading pine at the Begishev burial ground, holding a memorial feast 'after the Tatar custom' at which thirty oxen and ten rams were eaten. They shared out his weapons and clothes, and one coat of mail was offered to a famous Ostyak idol.
p.q: Man habe ihn an dem Begischewischen Begräbniß-Orte unter einer krauß-astigen Fichte zur Erden bestattet, und zu seinem Gedächtnisse nach Tatarischem Gebrauche ein Todtenmahl angestellet, auf welchem 30 Ochsen und 10 Hammel verzehret worden.
p.s: Gerhard Friedrich Müller (Sammlung Russischer Geschichte, vol. 6, 1761-1762), retelling the Siberian (Remezov) chronicle
p.t: They buried him at the Begishev burial ground under a pine with crooked branches, and in his memory held a funeral feast after the Tatar custom, at which 30 oxen and 10 rams were consumed.

p.h: Hidden grain pits and a camp struck in half an hour
p.g: The same Tatars stored grain and fodder in deep pits in the ground, covered so skilfully that only the diggers could find them again, dug either inside the tents or out in the fields. When they moved on, tents came down and were loaded in less than half an hour, carried by oxen and horses. He adds they were Muslims 'intermix'd with strange superstitions' about fortune-telling.
p.q: The Tartars store up their Corn and their Forrage, as do all the Country-People in the East, in deep Pits under Ground which they call Amber, or Magazines. Which they cover so exactly, that you cannot discern where they have remov'd the Earth
p.s: Jean Chardin (English translation, London, 1691)
p.pl: Salt pits near Caffa, eastern Crimea
p.tg: storage pits grain nomads moving camp

p.h: Shamans and the household god Ongon
p.g: Passing the Ongon mountains, named for the 'king of the Shamans', Timkovsky notes that shamanism survived among the Mongols despite the Buddhist lamas. He gives the Mongol words for male and female shamans and describes Ongon, a household guardian made of scraps of red cloth that women kept in the tent and appeased with offerings when things went wrong.
p.q: Among these people a man is called beg, and a woman ouddogoun, in the Mongol language. They are distinguished by an ardent imagination in the evocation of spirits, which throws them into wild transports. Ongon is their household divinity, which watches over their families and flocks. These remnants of the Shamanic faith have still many zealous partisans among the Mongols
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)

p.h: Cutting out the illness with a knife
p.g: The Relation describes the Bukharans' cure for sickness: a mullah reads from a book, blows on the patient several times and makes passes with a sharp knife around his face, believing this cuts the root of the illness, which they hold to be the Devil's work. The dead, it adds, are buried with a Koran on the chest in a pleasant grove fenced with a hedge or palisade.
p.q: Lorsqu'un Bouchar tombe malade, voici le remede dont il se sert; Un Mula lui lit un passage de quelque livre, souffle à plusieurs reprises sur lui, & d'un couteau bien aiguisé fait plusieurs gesticulations tout autour du visage du Malade. Ils s'imaginent que par cette opération ils coupent la racine de la maladie, qu'ils disent d'ailleurs être l'ouvrage du Diable.
p.s: Anonymous author of the 'Relation de la Boucharie'
p.t: When a Bukharan falls ill, this is the remedy he uses: a mullah reads him a passage from some book, blows on him several times, and with a well-sharpened knife makes various passes all round the sick man's face. They imagine that by this operation they cut the root of the illness, which they say is the work of the Devil.
p.c: An outsider's description of a healing rite, written with some condescension.

p.h: A khan who rules by consent
p.g: A Kazakh khan held power of life and death, Meyendorff says, but his only real check was public opinion: unhappy followers simply rode off and chose another leader. A khan kept power through courage, gifts and a friendly mullah to interpret the law.
p.q: The khan has in fact the power of life and death among the Kirghiz, who have no security against his tyranny, except public opinion, and no where is it so powerful as among the pastoral tribes. The discontented party quickly desert an unjust judge, and choose another for themselves.
p.s: Georg von Meyendorff (translated by William Monteith, 1840)

p.h: Tatar women spinning thread from nettles
p.g: On the road to Tobolsk in 1786, Sauer noted Tatar farmers who also made and sold neat worsted carpets. Coming back in 1794, he saw Tatar women near Tara spinning thread from nettle fibres, making linen as good as flax. The Siberian settlers also told him that trade with the Mongols was not as open as before.
p.q: The Tartar women about Tara were preparing nettles, and spinning thread from the fibres; the linen made of which was fine and good, apparently equal to that made of flax. I have already mentioned the neat carpets then made by these industrious people.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)

p.h: A Yuan official teaches pottery, metalwork and boats
p.g: The same note says that before the Yuan official Liu Haoli arrived, the local peoples made cups from willow wood and hollowed out logs as troughs to cross rivers, and did not know how to cast farm tools. Liu reported this to the court, which sent craftsmen to teach pottery, metal-casting and boat-building. It is a Chinese state view of 'civilising' the Siberian frontier.
p.q: 先是數部民俗皆以杞栁為杯皿刳木為槽以濟水不解鑄作農器好禮聞諸朝乃遣工匠教為陶冶舟楫土人便之
p.s: Song Lian and the Ming history office, History of the Yuan (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: Before this, the custom of these several tribes was to make their cups and dishes of willow and to hollow out logs as troughs for crossing water; they did not know how to cast farm tools. Haoli reported this to the court, which then sent craftsmen to teach them pottery, metal-casting and boats, and the local people found it convenient.
p.c: Told from the point of view of the imperial administration.

p.h: Judges who are clerics, and no one carries a sword at home
p.g: Michalo contrasts Tatar order with Lithuanian lawlessness: among the Tatars no one overeats and no one starves, there are no beggars, thieves, false witnesses or corrupt judges, and it is forbidden to carry a sword while travelling inside their land. Justice is given free by religious judges (qadis), with no fee taken, and everyone from nobles to commoners lives under one law and the same dress and food.
p.q: Unde minime opus est apud eos angi quenquam sollicita rerum suarum custodia, nec se armis onerare domi ad privatam sui defensionem. Nam iter habenti intra regionem eorum ferre telum, enorme & illicitum est.
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 1 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: So there is no need among them for anyone to worry anxiously about guarding his goods, or to load himself with weapons at home for his private defence. For it is outrageous and unlawful for anyone travelling within their land to carry a weapon.
p.c: Idealised for moral contrast with Lithuania.

p.h: Nogai river raiders attack an English barge
p.g: Forty miles above Astrakhan, the English barge was attacked by about 300 Nogai Tatars in eighteen boats, armed with swords, spears and bows. After a two-hour fight the English firearms drove them off, and the English later heard from an escaped Russian prisoner that 120 raiders had died. Banister, the editors note, survived thanks to a mail shirt.
p.q: the Nagaian Tartares, being a kind of theeuish and cruell people, made an assault vpon them with 18. boates of theirs, each of them being armed, some with swords, some with speares, and some others with bowes and arrowes, and the whole number of them they discouered to bee about 300. men.
p.s: Narrative written by 'P. I.' from the report of Lionel Plumtree, in Hakluyt (ed. Morgan and Coote, 1886)
p.c: Written down secondhand from a participant; the casualty figure came from a prisoner.

p.h: Nomads of Bishbalik in felt tents
p.g: Klaproth translates the Ming dynasty's geography on the land of Bishbalik, north of the Tian Shan. It says the people had no houses, lived in felt tents, kept cattle, sheep, camels and horses, farmed little, lived on meat and milk, and spoke a Turkic dialect called Uighur. The same book notes that under the Mongols there had been a town of Bishbalik with a viceroy and military farming colonies.
p.q: Les habitans sont nomades, n'ont pas de maisons, et vivent sous des tentes de feutre. Ils s'occupent presqu'exclusivement de l'entretien des bœufs, des moutons, des chameaux et des chevaux. Ils n'ont que peu d'agriculture, et se nourrissent de la chair et du laitage de leurs troupeaux, qui leur fournissent l'habillement nécessaire. Leur langue est un dialecte du turc
p.s: Ming dynasty imperial geography, translated by Julius Klaproth
p.t: The inhabitants are nomads, have no houses, and live under felt tents. They occupy themselves almost entirely with keeping oxen, sheep, camels and horses. They have little agriculture and live on the meat and milk of their herds, which also supply the clothing they need. Their language is a dialect of Turkish
p.c: This scan is volume 2 (1826) despite its IA label; the OCR is rough.
p.tg: felt tents bishbalik nomads uighur ming

p.h: A khan raised up on a white felt
p.g: Babur tells how his Mongol grandfather Yunis Khan was made khan: a leading beg seated him and his new wife on a white felt and proclaimed him, according to the ancient Mongol rules (tore). Erskine's footnote links it to the felt on which Genghis Khan was said to have been proclaimed.
p.q: Shir Haji Beg having seated the Khan and Ais-doulet Begum on a white felt, according to the Tureh, or ancient Institutions of the Moghuls, they proclaimed him Khan.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.c: Family history from before Babur's birth.

p.h: Sheepskins, a knife and a pipe, but no guns
p.g: Holderness describes the Tatar winter outfit of felt cloak, sheepskin pelisse and lamb's-wool cap, with a knife, tobacco pouch, flint and steel. Under Russian rule they were not allowed firearms, and few still owned the bows of their forefathers; a local noble, Maksout Murza, had one made entirely of bone.
p.q: The sheep-skin pelisses and lamb's-wool caps, which are assumed by the Tatars in winter, increase not a little their savage looks … The use of fire-arms is not allowed them, and few remain possessed of the bows and arrows which were the national weapons of their forefathers. Maksout Murza has a bow which is formed entirely of bone.
p.s: Mary Holderness

p.h: Not a single house between Saratov and Astrakhan
p.g: Below Saratov Bruce entered Kalmyk country on the left bank of the Volga. He says the whole huge tract had not one house: the Kalmyks lived in tents, moved with horses, camels, cattle and sheep, grew no crops and ate meat (especially horse), fish and game, with plenty of milk and a strong clear spirit made from mare's milk.
p.q: in all which immense tract there is not so much as one single house to be seen, as they all live in tents, and remove from one place to another in quest of pasturage for their large herds of cattle, consisting of horses, camels, cows, and sheep ; they neither sow, nor reap, nor make hay for their cattle, so that they live without bread
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.tg: kalmyks tents herds mare's milk no houses

p.h: Horseflesh, honey mead and the tea trade
p.g: Kazan Tatars, Haxthausen reports, avoid pork as Muslims but prize horseflesh above all, brew mead, and control much of the tea trade. On the same page he admires Kazan leather boots embroidered with gold and silver and calls Tatar peasants excellent beekeepers.
p.q: They live principally upon animal food, avoiding pork, which is forbidden by the Koran ; horseflesh is considered by the common Tatars the choicest food. They are very fond of honey, and make good mead from it. The higher classes drink much tea ; and a large proportion of the tea-trade being in their hands, the best sorts are found among them.
p.s: August von Haxthausen (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)

p.h: Rafts towed by swimming horses
p.g: Travelling to Kaffa with a Lithuanian embassy escorted by Crimean Tatar horsemen, Contarini had to cross the broad river dividing Russia from Tartary. The Tatars built a raft of lashed timbers and branches, then swam their horses across holding their necks, with the raft tied to the horses' tails. He thought he had never been in greater danger.
p.q: the Tartars began to cut timbers, which they tied together, and covered with branches to form a raft, and our things being placed on it the Tartars entered the river holding on to their horses' necks, while our raft was attached to their tails by cords. Thus mounted, the horses were driven across the river, which we passed by the help of God.
p.s: Ambrogio Contarini (translated by S. A. Roy, 1873)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars (escort sent by the khan)
p.c: The text does not name the river; the Dnieper is the likely crossing on this route.

p.h: Baptisms at Kamul, on a promise of no church taxes
p.g: In an aside on church tithes, Marignolli recalls that at Kamul (Hami), where there were 'many Tartars and other nations', converts refused baptism until the friars swore they would never demand anything worldly from them afterwards. Once the friars promised, and even helped the poor from their own funds, crowds of men and women were baptised. He uses the story to argue against forcing tithes on new converts.
p.q: ubi primo conversi nolebant baptizari, donec juravimus, nihil temporale post baptismum extorquere ab eis, ymo de nostro indigentibus providere, quod & fecimus, sic multitudo civitatis utriusque sexus baptismum libentissime receperunt.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars and other peoples of Kamul
p.t: where at first the converts would not be baptised until we swore that we would extract nothing worldly from them after baptism, but would rather provide for the needy from our own; which we did, and so a multitude of the city, of both sexes, received baptism most willingly.
p.c: The mention of Tartars at Kamul is on the previous page (n144); conversion numbers are the missionary's own claim.

p.h: Marriage sight unseen
p.g: She explains that a Crimean Tatar groom never saw his bride before the wedding and relied on a matron go-between. The groom then bargained with the father, usually offering a cow and some sheep; the imam married the couple with little ceremony, and the groom treated his friends to pipes, coffee and sherbet outside the house.
p.q: for an inhabitant of the Taurida never sees his bride till the nuptial torch is lighted up; so that if it were not for the friendly ministry of a grave matron, or go between (the Pronuba of the Antients), who has the privilege of taking a peep at the bride, a man might marry the grandmother instead of the daughter.
p.s: Maria Guthrie (letter, translated by Matthew Guthrie, 1802)
p.c: She says herself that 'all is mystery' about women's lives; this is what she was told.

p.h: Fake embassies from 'Tartar princelings'
p.g: At Suzhou, the account explains, caravans from the west entered China as 'embassies' bringing tribute of jade and other goods every six years, with forged letters from their kings offering submission. The emperor paid their costs, so the posts were bought and sold. China received similar embassies from Cochinchina, Siam, the Ryukyus, Korea and some Tartar princelings, at huge cost to the treasury; Ricci thinks the officials knew it was a sham and kept it up to flatter the emperor.
p.q: cum tempus legationis advenit publicas Regum suorum litteras effingunt, quibus Sinarum Regi clientelare obsequium deferunt. Similes legationes e variis regnis admittunt Sinae e regnis Caucincino, Sian, Leuchieu, Coriano, & ab aliquot Tartarorum Regulis non sine incredibili aerarii publici sumptu, quibus artibus ipsi Sinae (qui fraudem minime ignorant) Regem suum ludunt
p.s: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)
p.pe: Western merchants posing as envoys; minor Tartar rulers
p.t: when the time for the embassy comes, they forge official letters from their kings offering the King of China the homage of a vassal. The Chinese admit similar embassies from various kingdoms, from Cochinchina, Siam, the Ryukyus and Korea, and from some Tartar princelings, at an incredible cost to the public treasury; by these tricks the Chinese themselves (who are well aware of the fraud) deceive their own King
p.c: A hostile outsider's reading of the tribute system.

p.h: Horse-flesh for feasts, mutton every day
p.g: Palafox says the Tartars eat and drink heartily, care more for quantity than quality, and count horse-flesh their greatest delicacy. Their daily food is mutton from their great flocks, plus venison they hunt in the mountains, and he claims they eat their meat nearly raw 'according to the custome of Barbarians'. On the page before he says they despise soft music and love only the harsh sound of the trumpet.
p.q: They account Horse-flesh their greatest dainty… But their ordinary food is Mutton, and they have great flocks of Sheep : They eat likewise all sorts of Venison,
p.s: Juan de Palafox y Mendoza (English translation, 1676)
p.c: Second-hand and coloured by the stock European image of 'barbarian' eating.

p.h: Chinggis Khan's self-portrait: one coat, one food
p.g: Bretschneider prints the Khan's letter inviting Changchun, dated 15 May 1219 and preserved in the fourteenth-century Chinese miscellany Cho keng lu. In it Chinggis sets himself against luxurious China: he lives in the 'northern wilderness', eats what his herdsmen eat and wears the same rags. Bretschneider stresses that the Khan could not write, so the polished classical Chinese was put down by a secretary, very likely Yelu Chucai.
p.q: Heaven has abandoned China owing to its haughtiness and extravagant luxury. But I, living in the northern wilderness, have not inordinate passions. I hate luxury and exercise moderation. I have only one coat and one food. I eat the same food and am dressed in the same tatters as my humble herdsmen.
p.s: Letter issued in Chinggis Khan's name (1219), written in classical Chinese by a secretary and preserved in the Cho keng lu (translated by E. Bretschneider, 1888)
p.c: A self-portrait in a formal letter meant to persuade; the frugal ruler is also a Chinese ideal, and the wording is a secretary's. The letter is not part of Li Zhichang's diary.

p.h: No images in the mosque
p.g: After visiting the Indian temple at Astrakhan, Hanway contrasts the Muslim Tatars, who abhor image worship so much that they will not carry coins stamped with a man, bird or beast into their temples. Their worship is silent prostration, with the priest calling on the lord of nature through Muhammad. He adds that the Nogais are Muslims who look like the Kalmyks 'but better favoured'.
p.q: The Tartars hold this image worship in the utmost abomination; they will not carry even money which has any impression of man, bird, beast, creeping thing, or insect, into their temples. Their devotion is in silence and prostrations,
p.s: Jonas Hanway (Historical Account, 1753)

p.h: Jumping through fire after childbirth
p.g: A Mongol or Kalmyk mother, Strahlenberg says, is purified after childbirth by jumping three times through a fire before the lama and her relatives. He adds that they wear or keep a small three-headed idol, made of clay or metal, brought from Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He collects these customs to show a sacred number three.
p.q: It is a Custom, to this Day, with the Mungals and Kalmucks, that when a Woman bears a Child, and is afterwards re-admitted into the Community of the People, she must, in the Presence of their Lama, or Priest, and her nearest Relations, jump Three Times thro' a Fire; Which they call the Purification.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.c: He does not say he saw this himself.

p.h: A Khan who spread Islam by force
p.g: Coxe gives one reason Kuchum's khanate was fragile: much of it was newly conquered, and he had alienated his 'idolatrous' (shamanist) subjects by pushing Islam on them with intolerant zeal. It is a useful reminder that 'Tartar' Siberia was religiously mixed, with Islam still spreading in the sixteenth century.
p.q: He had newly acquired a large part of his territories by conquest; and had, in a great measure, alienated the affections of his idolatrous subjects by the intolerant zeal, with which he introduced and disseminated the Mahometan religion.
p.s: William Coxe (compiling G. F. Müller)
p.pe: Siberian Tatars and their subject peoples
p.c: 'Idolatrous' is the source's word for the region's shamanist peoples.

p.h: Khan Uzbek turns Muslim, with an army counted in tens
p.g: Sanudo warns the Pope that the Sultan of Egypt, with gifts and treaties, had drawn 'the Emperor of the Tartars named Husbecho, who rules in Gazaria and other northern parts' to accept Islam. Trustworthy people told him Uzbek's cavalry was so vast that, his army being organised in tens, he could take just three of every ten and still field an almost unbelievable host.
p.q: prædictus Soldanus Imperatorem Tartarorum, nomine Husbecho, qui in Gazaria, & aliis Septentrionis partibus dominatur, immutauit taliter & attraxit, vt legem receperit perfidi Mahumeti … Nam à nonnullis dignis fide asseritur quod dictus Husbecho, habet equitum multitudinem adeò numerosam, vt subtrahendo tres de decem, cum per decuriones habeat exercitum ordinatum, ex solis ternariis in campo ponit ita militiam copiosam, quod quasi incredibile videatur.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: the said Sultan so changed and drew the Emperor of the Tartars, named Uzbek, who rules in Gazaria and other northern parts, that he received the law of the faithless Muhammad ... For it is asserted by some trustworthy people that the said Uzbek has so numerous a multitude of horsemen that, taking three out of ten, since he has his army ordered by tens, from the threes alone he puts so large a force in the field that it seems almost incredible.
p.c: Uzbek's conversion was his own and not simply the Sultan's doing; the army figure is hearsay.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: uzbek khan golden horde islam gazaria army

p.h: Kirghiz snow-treaders keep the pass open
p.g: In winter the snow in the passes west of Kashgar lay a man's height deep or more. Izzet Ullah describes Kirghiz posted along the road whose job was to trample the snow hard so caravans could cross. Even so, several horses died, including his own.
p.q: The Kirghizes tread the snow down so as to make it hard, and then the caravans pass; a certain number of Kirghizes are appointed to this duty,
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)

p.h: Wrestlers in rolled-up trousers
p.g: Invited to watch wrestling, Unkovsky sat near the ruler under awnings on tall poles. He describes bouts between the ruler's side and his son Galdan Tseren's side, with bets and judges who wrote down the results. The wrestlers came out bare but for trousers rolled above the knee, raised their arms, glared to look fearsome, and gripped each other by the trousers. A bout only counted when a man was thrown flat on both shoulders.
p.q: И тако съ обѣихъ сторонъ выходятъ борцы нагіе, токмо въ штанахъ, которыя подобраны выше гораздо колѣнъ. И не дошедъ единъ отъ другого сажени за четыре, подымутъ руки вверхъ, и искося глаза (являя себя страшливыми), потихоньку сходятся; и какъ сойдутся, и принаклонясь, схватываются за штаны
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: And so from both sides the wrestlers come out naked, only in trousers rolled up well above the knee. And when they are about four sazhens from each other they raise their arms, and, rolling their eyes (to make themselves look fearsome), slowly close in; and when they meet they bend forward and seize each other by the trousers

p.h: The veiled bride and the child who unveils her
p.g: Visiting his uncle in Samarkand at the age of five, Babur found the new bride still veiled 'according to the custom of the Turks', and was told to take the veil off. The translators' note explains the custom: a Turki bride stayed veiled for a time after marriage until a child of the family pulled the veil off and ran, which was thought to bring the child luck in marriage.
p.q: she still kept her face covered with a veil, according to the custom of the Turks. He directed me, and I took off her veil.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)
p.c: The explanation of the custom is in the translators' footnote.

p.h: The happiest peasantry possible
p.g: Webster ends his Crimean chapters defending Tatar 'laziness' against Russian complaints: the Tatar sits on his roof under his grandfather's walnut tree and wants nothing more. He honestly adds that, not speaking their language, a traveller may mistake the look of happiness for the real thing.
p.q: The Russians exclaim against the laziness of the Tartars: but wherefore should they work? They are the happiest peasantry possible without it … not understanding their language, we may mistake the appearance of happiness for its reality.
p.s: James Webster
p.c: A romantic generalisation, which Webster himself qualifies.
p.tg: character peasants russian rule walnut trees

p.h: Shamans turned Muslims
p.g: Wood reports that the Kirghiz had converted from shamanism to Islam in the early 1600s, and that his Uzbek companion claimed the old beliefs lingered. Their chiefs, called Bai, had patriarchal rather than despotic authority.
p.q: They were converted from the Shamanian superstition to Mohamedanism early in the seventeenth century. The former belief, if I may credit Abdal Ghani, is not yet thoroughly eradicated ; though in our intercourse with the people, they seemed like all proselytes to erring creeds, to be filled with the most abject reverence for their new doctrines.
p.s: John Wood
p.c: The date of conversion is Wood's statement without a source; the survival of shamanism is his guide's claim.

p.h: An Afghan court ceremony 'borrowed from the Chinese Tartars'
p.g: Conolly retells a Persian anecdote about presentation at the court of Ahmad Shah Durrani: two officers ran the visitor up to the king at a trot, shouted his name and whisked him away again. He calls the ceremony 'borrowed, apparently, from the Chinese Tartars', then admits this is only 'the Persian account'.
p.q: The Dooraunee ceremony of presentation at court is a very strange one, borrowed, apparently, from the Chinese Tartars, … the person upon whom the honour is to be conferred, being placed between two of the officers of the court, who run him up at a trot to within a certain distance of the king
p.s: Arthur Conolly (1834)
p.pe: Durrani Afghans; Chinese Tartars (Manchus) as supposed source
p.c: A secondhand Persian story; the 'Chinese Tartar' origin is Conolly's guess.
p.tg: court ceremony durrani chinese tartars anecdote

p.h: A stone for a man who lifted her veil
p.g: At Alupka, beside Count Vorontsov's new palace, Kohl saw the Tatar village with a handsome new mosque the count had built 'for his Tartars'. When one of Kohl's companions lifted a passing Tatar woman's veil, she threw a great stone at him, and Kohl says they all took the lesson.
p.q: On the top of one stands the handsome new mosque, built by Count W. for his Tartars. One of our party had the temerity to lift the corner of the veil of a Tartar woman who was passing, to get a peep at her face … for the lady took up a great stone and hurled it at him
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844)
p.c: 'Count W.' is Count Mikhail Vorontsov, governor-general of New Russia.

p.h: Conquest 'like the Spaniards in South America'
p.g: Summing up the Russian conquest of Siberia, Cochrane writes that Tartar tribes who would not readily submit 'were at once exterminated', with a cruelty like that of the Spaniards in the Americas. Only Chinese resistance on the Amur, ending in the treaty of 1689, stopped the Russians from taking Mongolia.
p.q: Those tribes of Tartars who were not readily reducible to obedience, were at once exterminated; and something like the same merciless cruelty which characterised the Spaniards in South America, was practised in Siberia.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824), translating a biographical note on a map
p.pe: Siberian Tatars and other native peoples
p.c: A sweeping judgment from a second-hand history; it is not clear whether the words are the map note's or Cochrane's own.

p.h: Shamanism that Islam and Lamaism never fully uprooted
p.g: Schott says conjuring the dark powers by magic is found among all the peoples of his Finno-Tatar family, and that neither Lamaist Buddhism nor Islam had everywhere managed to push it out. In North Asia, he writes, it stayed 'raw shamanism', while among the Finns of Finland the same magic songs grew into poetry and the Kalevala-style epics. It is a sweeping comparison from books rather than fieldwork, but it records how European scholars saw shamanism as the shared old religion under the later faiths.
p.q: finden wir zwar bei allen Völkern des finnisch-tatarischen Geschlechtes … der Lamaismus und selbst die Religion Muhammeds hat ihnen nicht allerwärts mit Erfolg entgegengewirkt … was aber in Nordasien rohes Schamanenthum blieb und noch jetzt bei den verwilderten Finnenstämmen der Polarländer keinen anderen Namen verdient, das verklärte sich bei den Suomalaiset Finnlands zu wahrer Poesie
p.s: Wilhelm Schott
p.pe: Turkic, Mongol, Tungusic and Finnic peoples (Schott's 'Finno-Tatar' family)
p.t: [such conjurations of the dark powers] we do find among all the peoples of the Finno-Tatar family … Lamaism and even the religion of Muhammad have not everywhere countered them with success … but what in North Asia remained raw shamanism, and among the degraded Finnish tribes of the polar lands still deserves no other name, was transfigured among the Suomalaiset of Finland into true poetry
p.c: A generalisation from books, with openly condescending language ('raw', 'degraded') about Siberian and polar peoples.
p.n: OCR normalized; the two dashes around the middle clause in the original are shown as ….

p.h: Kalmyks and Nogais: no fixed homes, and horsemeat softened under the saddle
p.g: At Saratov Struys first met the Kalmyks, whom he calls the ugliest of men. Kalmyks and Nogais, he says, have no fixed dwellings and move camp as the grazing allows; they prefer horsemeat and eat it after softening it under the saddle. The saddle-meat story is an old European stereotype about steppe riders. On the same page he wrongly calls the Kalmyks Muslims; they were Buddhists.
p.q: Ils n'ont point de demeures fixes … mais de toutes les viandes, celle de cheval est plus à leur goût. Tout l'aprêt qu'ils y font, est de la mettre sous la selle, où étant un peu amollie par la chaleur du cheval, ils l'en retirent, & en font leurs meilleurs repas.
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: They have no fixed dwellings … but of all meats, horse is most to their taste. All the preparation they give it is to put it under the saddle, where, being a little softened by the horse's warmth, they take it out and make their best meals of it.
p.c: The saddle-meat tale is repeated from much older writers, and the page is openly hostile.

p.h: The 'dog-using' and 'deer-using' tribes of the Amur
p.g: The gazetteer lists the northeastern peoples who brought tribute to the Qing post at Ningguta, measuring each by distance: the Fiyaka seven or eight hundred li beyond the three-river confluence, the Kiler three thousand li away on the sea coast, the Kuyala facing Korea across the Tumen. Beyond the 'dog-using' tribes lay a 'deer-using' (reindeer) tribe. These are the peoples European maps grouped in 'Eastern Tartary'.
p.q: 又東北行七八百里曰費雅喀自寕古塔東北行三千里曰奇勒爾東濵大海…庫雅喇其地在圖們江北岸與朝鮮之慶逺相對…而使鹿部又在使犬諸部之外
p.s: Agui, Liu Jinzhi and the Qianlong commission, Imperially Commissioned Gazetteer of Shengjing (1784 recension; Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pe: Fiyaka (Nivkh), Kiler, Kuyala and other tribute peoples
p.t: Another seven or eight hundred li to the northeast are the Fiyaka. Three thousand li northeast of Ningguta are the Kiler, who border the great sea on the east... The Kuyala: their land lies on the north bank of the Tumen river, opposite Kyongwon in Korea... And the deer-using tribe lies beyond the dog-using tribes.
p.tg: tribute peoples fiyaka reindeer dogs amur

p.h: Tatar orchards that look as if nature planted them
p.g: Hablizl was struck by the Tatar gardens in the valleys, with fruit trees mixed among shade trees round the fences. He saw almost no sign of labour in them, so that they looked planted by nature alone, and the Tatars seldom grafted or pruned their trees, yet they got the best fruit; the vines grew huge, crawling on the ground or up the trees. His tone is that of a Russian official who thought the land could be 'improved'.
p.q: … so bemerkt man überall äußerst wenig Spuren von angewandter Mühe und Arbeit. Eben deswegen hat es auch das Ansehen, als ob sie von der Natur allein angelegt worden wären. Ungeachtet der fast gänzlich mangelnden Aufsicht, gerathen die meisten Früchte vorzüglich gut. Selten pfropfen die Tataren ihre Bäume, oder bemühen sich, wie es sonst gewöhnlich ist, sie zu reinigen und dennoch erhalten sie von ihnen die besten Früchte.
p.s: Karl Ludwig Hablizl (German translation, 1789)
p.t: … one sees everywhere very few traces of effort and labour applied. For that very reason they look as though they had been laid out by nature alone. Despite the almost complete lack of care, most fruits turn out exceptionally well. The Tatars seldom graft their trees, or take the trouble, as is usual elsewhere, to prune them, and yet they get the best fruit from them.
p.c: An outsider's judgement; what looked like neglect may have been a different way of gardening.

p.h: A seal, not a signature
p.g: In a footnote to a pass issued by the Tibetan Panchen Lama that he found among the Kalmyks, stamped with a red seal, Pallas explains that the Mongol and Tatar peoples of Asia confirm letters and documents not by signing their names but by printing the mark of their seal or signet ring (tamga) in colour beneath them; without it, even a signed name is not considered valid.
p.q: Die Mongolischen sowohl, als tatarischen Völker Asiens pflegen ihre Briefe und Handschriften nicht mit Unterschrift des Namens, sondern durch das mit Farbe darunter abgedrukte Zeichen ihres Signets oder Petschierrings (Tamga) zu bekräftigen, ohne welches selbst die Namensunterschrift nicht für gültig gehalten wird.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Sammlungen historischer Nachrichten über die mongolischen Völkerschaften, part 2, 1801) (footnote)
p.pe: Mongol and Tatar peoples of Asia
p.t: The Mongol as well as the Tatar peoples of Asia are accustomed to confirm their letters and manuscripts not by signing their name, but by the mark of their signet or seal ring (tamga) printed underneath in colour, without which even a signature is not considered valid.

p.h: Merchants and 'the caravan from Cathay'
p.g: In the chapter on merchants the poet advises the prince to welcome them: they travel from east to west, bring the finest clothes and 'wonders', and without them nobody could dress well in winter or see strings of pearls. When 'the caravan of Cathay' (China) sets out, thousands of gifts follow. It places the Turkic court of Kashgar on the great trade road between China and the west.
p.q: 7 Gäbe es keinen Kaufmann, der die Welt durchzieht, Wie könntest du dich kleiden in der Mitte des rauhen Winters? 8 Wenn Chatai's Karavane dahinzieht, so ist es eine Karavane, Von wo tausendfache Spenden kommen sollen.
p.s: Yusuf Khass Hajib, Kutadgu Bilig (1069 to 1070), in Vambery's German translation (1870)
p.pe: Qarakhanid Turks and Silk Road merchants
p.t: 7 If there were no merchant who travels the world, how could you clothe yourself in the middle of harsh winter? 8 When Cathay's caravan sets out, it is a caravan from which thousandfold gifts will come.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
p.tg: trade caravan cathay merchants silk road

p.h: The Eight Banners and the ring hunt
p.g: Martini gives an early European description of the Eight Banners: white (the imperial banner), red, black and yellow, and four more made by mixing colours. Every soldier knows his colour and where in the city his arms and horse are kept, so the whole army is ready in half an hour at a horn call. On the next pages he adds that they carry no baggage, eat meat half cooked or their own horses and camels, and hunt by encircling a whole mountain.
p.q: under these eight colours are comprehended all the Forces of the Kingdom of China, whether they be Natives or Tartars ; the first of which is White, called the Imperial Banner ; the second is Red, the third is Black, the fourth is Yellow;… so as every Souldier knows his own colours, and to what part of the City to repair, where they have ever their Arms and Horses ready
p.s: Martino Martini (English translation, London 1654)
p.c: The real banner colours were yellow, white, red and blue (plain and bordered); Martini's 'black' may be a mistake.

p.h: A skin on a pole to plead with God
p.g: Bruce calls the Mari (Cheremis) of the middle Volga 'Tartars' and describes them as heathens without churches or priests. When they sacrificed a horse, cow or sheep they hung its skin on a high pole and prayed to it to intercede with God for more cattle. He adds details on naming, polygamy and dress.
p.q: when they offer a sacrifice to God, they kill a horse, cow, or sheep, and extend its skin on a high pole, which they implore to intercede for them with God, that he may increase the number of their cattle. They have a high veneration for the sun and moon … They make use of no churches, priests, or books
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)
p.c: The Mari are a Finnic people, not Tatars; this account closely matches Olearius and is probably borrowed.

p.h: Distilling brandy from mare's milk
p.g: The same people drank water, or black brick tea boiled with mare's milk and butter, and they distilled a clear spirit from mare's milk called arak. Ides records the method: boil fresh milk, sour it with old milk, stir it hourly, then distil it twice in sealed pots joined by a reed. He notes that Siberian cows gave no milk once the calf was weaned, which is why mare's milk was so important.
p.q: They also draw off a sort of Brandy from Mares-Milk, which they call Kunnen, or Arak, and is distilled in the following manner. The New-Milk is first boiled, then put into a Fat, to which is added some Stale-Milk, and this mixture is stirred every Hour … then it is fit to drink, being as clear, and strong, as Malt Spirits, and very soon intoxicates.
p.s: Evert Ysbrants Ides (English translation, 1706)

p.h: Forty brothers, one father: polygamy and a Tatar village
p.g: Michalo argues that polygamy is why the Perekop Tatars, so often slaughtered by the Lithuanians, keep springing back. He cites a troop of forty full brothers in the army of Sultan Islam Giray, all sons of one Omeldesz by wives and concubines within little more than a year, and a Tatar village on the Vaka river in Lithuania still called 'Forty Tartars', that is, forty brothers. He adds that both Tatars and Muscovites keep their women without freedom.
p.q: haec multitudo uxorum facit ut vicini nostri Tartari Precopenses toties a nobis ad internecionem caesi, rursum repullulascant. nec ita pridem in copijs Oslam Soltani fuerunt 40. fratres collectanei eius, cuiusdam Omeldesz 40. filij simul
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 7 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.pl: Crimea; a Tatar village on the Vaka river (Lithuania)
p.t: this multitude of wives is why our neighbours the Perekop Tartars, so often cut down by us to the last man, spring up again. Not long ago in the forces of Sultan Islam there were forty brothers, his comrades, forty sons at once of a certain Omeldesz

p.h: Chinese annals: felt tents, grazing, and stones for enemies killed
p.g: Thomsen quotes Chinese annals (through Stanislas Julien's translations) on the customs of the Turks, the 'Tou-kioue': they wear their hair loose, fold their robes to the left, and live in felt tents, moving wherever they find water and grass. At burials they set up stones beside the grave, one for each enemy the dead man had killed, sometimes a hundred or a thousand. Thomsen says these notices describe a time somewhat earlier than the inscriptions.
p.q: «Les Tou-kioue laissent flotter leurs cheveux, jettent à gauche le pan de leur vêtement, et habitent sous des tentes de feutre. Ils se transportent d'un lieu à un autre, suivant qu'ils y trouvent de l'eau et des herbes. Leur principale occupation est l'élève des troupeaux et la chasse.
p.s: Chinese dynastic annals (6th to 7th century) in Stanislas Julien's French translation, quoted by Vilhelm Thomsen (1896)
p.t: 'The Tujue let their hair hang loose, fold the flap of their garment to the left, and live in felt tents. They move from one place to another according to where they find water and grass. Their main occupation is raising herds and hunting.'
p.c: An outside Chinese view, translated twice before reaching this page.
p.n: Checked against the page image.
