p.h: A ten-year-old breaks a wild stallion
p.g: At Prince Tumene's, Kalmyk riders lassoed wild horses from the herd and rode them bareback, clinging to the mane, until they were caught up by other horsemen. Then a boy of about ten did the same on a huge white stallion. Adèle adds that even Kalmyk women practise the sport.
p.q: But what was our amazement when we saw a boy of ten years come forward to undertake the same exploit! They selected for him a young white stallion of great size, whose fiery bounds and desperate efforts to break his bonds, indicated a most violent temper.
p.s: Adèle Hommaire de Hell (English translation, 1847)

p.h: The Shah's falcons from beyond Astrakhan
p.g: Invited to hunt with Fath Ali Shah near Sultaniyeh, Jaubert notes that the Persians kept up falconry, an expensive taste he thinks they probably got from the Tartars. The Shah's many falcons came from the lands north-east of Astrakhan, each with its own name and trainer.
p.q: leur vient probablement des Tartares. Le Chah possède un grand nombre d'oiseaux de cette espèce, provenant des pays situés au nord-est d'Astrakhan, et qui sont dressés avec beaucoup d'art. Chaque faucon a son nom propre et un instituteur particulier.
p.s: Pierre-Amedee Jaubert
p.pe: Qajar court; falcon-rearing peoples north-east of Astrakhan
p.t: probably came to them from the Tartars. The Shah owns a great number of birds of this kind, from the countries north-east of Astrakhan, which are trained with much art. Each falcon has its own name and its own trainer.
p.c: The Tartar origin of Persian falconry is Jaubert's guess.

p.h: Sheepskin vests and a double scalp-lock
p.g: Avril lists Siberian peoples, the 'Ostiaks, Bratski, Jacuti and Tongusi', as further kinds of Tartars and guesses they are Kalmyk hordes tamed by contact with the Russians. He then describes their looks and dress: sheepskin vests tied with a cord carrying bow and quiver, heads shaved to the crown with a double lock, and a round bonnet whose coloured silk tuft marked the horde.
p.q: Their Habits are for the most part all alike, consisting of several Sheep-skins sow'd together, which they fit to their bodies in the form of Vests, and gird about their Wastes with a Cord, wherein hangs their Bow and Quiver, with which they go always arm'd. They shave their Heads to the very Crown, where they preserve a Tuft thick enough to make a double lock
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.pe: Ostyaks, Buryats, Yakuts and Tungus (called 'other Tartars')
p.c: Hearsay that lumps very different Siberian peoples together; the Kalmyk-origin theory is Avril's guess.

p.h: Bashkirs who live on honey, game and fish
p.g: Along the Belaya and Ufa rivers up to the Ural mountains, the book says, 'all live Bashkirs', and they feed on honey (from forest beekeeping), game and fish, and have no ploughland. It is a one-line ethnographic note from the frontier, about a Turkic people that western maps often put under 'Tartary'.
p.q: А отъ устья рѣки Бѣлыя-Воложки, съ верхъ и по рѣкѣ по Уфѣ, по обѣимъ сторонамъ и до Аральтовы горы и далѣе, все живутъ Башкиры, а кормля ихъ медъ, звѣрь, рыба, а пашни не имѣютъ.
p.s: Book of the Great Map (1627), ed. Yazykov (1838)
p.t: And from the mouth of the river Belaia Voloshka, upstream and along the river Ufa, on both sides as far as the Aral'tova mountain and beyond, all live Bashkirs, and their food is honey, game and fish, and they have no ploughland.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.
p.tg: bashkirs honey hunting fishing no agriculture

p.h: Unveiled women in coin-covered caps
p.g: Turkmen women did not hide from strangers or wear full veils, only a cloth over the lower face. Fraser describes their tall shako-like caps covered in gold coins, silver bells and set stones, which he thought looked more like horse trappings than jewellery.
p.q: The Toorkoman women are not shut up, or concealed like those of most Mahometan countries, nor do they even wear veils … most of them wear a lofty cap, with a broad crown resembling that sort of soldier’s cap called a shako … The front of this is covered with ornaments of silver or gold, in various shapes ; most frequently gold coins, mohrs or tomauns, strung in rows
p.s: James Baillie Fraser

p.h: The Kalmyk khan dines with Peter the Great
p.g: On the way to Derbent, Peter the Great met Ayuka, khan of the Volga Kalmyks, on a galley on the river. Bell watched the khan arrive on horseback with his sons and fifty horsemen, and the queen arrive in a covered wagon with her daughter. He describes Ayuka as a wise old man, the princess as a Kalmyk beauty in Persian brocade, and notes that the khan promised Peter five thousand horsemen on the spot.
p.q: Soon after the Ayuka-Chan was got on board the galley, the Queen arrived on the shore, in a covered wheel-machine, attended by one of the princesses her daughter, and two ladies, who were also escorted by a troop of horsemen. … The Ayuka-Chan is an old man, about seventy years of age, yet is hearty and chearful.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.tg: ayuka khan peter the great diplomacy kalmyks wagons

p.h: A horse thief spared, his horse executed and eaten
p.g: At the camps of Sultan Arungasi, Eversmann watched the punishment of a horse thief whose life the sultan spared, hoping the mercy would buy luck for his journey. The thief, blackened with charcoal and half naked, was chased twice round the tents, once with a rope in his mouth tied to a horse's tail; then his horse's throat was cut in his place and the crowd carved it up alive for supper. Eversmann then lists the sultan's four laws: death for stealing livestock, a blood price of 500 to 2000 sheep for murder, both ears cut off for stealing a hobble, and whipping for small offences.
p.q: Nachdem dieses geschehen war, wurde seinem Pferde statt seiner der Hals abgeschnitten, und jeder aus der Menge der zusehenden Kirgisen schnitt sich, da es noch zappelte, ein Stück Fleisch davon ab, um sich Abends ein leckeres Mahl daraus zu bereiten, und kein Restchen blieb vom Pferde zurück.
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.t: When this had been done, his horse's throat was cut instead of his, and each of the crowd of watching Kirghiz cut himself a piece of meat from it while it was still twitching, to make himself a tasty meal in the evening, and not a scrap of the horse was left.
p.c: Eversmann calls the ceremony silly; the laws he lists are 'as far as I know' his informants' summary.
p.tg: law punishment horses kazakhs horse meat

p.h: Shooting backwards while they flee
p.g: Hayton, who fought beside Mongol armies, describes their tactics: when they flee they do so in ordered squadrons, and pursuing them is dangerous because they shoot backwards as they ride, wounding men and horses, then wheel round on careless pursuers. Their army looks smaller than it is because they ride packed close, so a thousand Tartars look like five hundred.
p.q: Quando Tatari vertunt in fugam, fugiunt omnes simul per turmas et acies ordinatas; et valde periculosum est sequi eos, quoniam retrograde sagictas jaciunt fugiendo, et equos et homines vulnerant et occidunt. … Exercitus Tatarorum non est magne apparencie, quia omnes simul congregatim incedunt, ita quod acies mille Tatarorum quingentorum apparenciam non habet.
p.s: Hayton of Corycus, Flos historiarum terre Orientis (Latin version by Nicolas Falcon, 1307), ed. Ch. Kohler (1906)
p.t: When the Tatars turn to flight, they all flee together in ordered squadrons and lines; and it is very dangerous to follow them, because as they flee they shoot arrows backwards and wound and kill horses and men. … The Tatar army does not look large, because they all ride packed together, so that a line of a thousand Tatars does not look like five hundred.

p.h: Prayers in a Tatar mosque at Tobolsk
p.g: At Tobolsk the governor's learned son took the envoy's party to a Tatar mosque. Brand describes a plain room with large open windows and carpets, the worshippers leaving their shoes at the door and sitting cross-legged in rows, a white-robed chief priest in a turban, a loud call, kneeling, and the priest looking over his right and then his left shoulder.
p.q: daß er uns in eine tartarische Mosquee, Meschets oder Kirche führte, die ringsherum grosse Fenster hatte, welche alle offen stunden, der Boden war mit Tapeten belegt, ohne daß andere Zierrathen darin zu sehen waren, die Leute so hinein giengen, liessen vor der Thüre ihre Schuhe oder Bismacken stehen, und setzen sich ordentlich in gewissen Reyhen mit unter sich geschlagenen Füssen nieder
p.s: Adam Brand (Neu-vermehrte Beschreibung, Lübeck 1734)
p.t: that he took us into a Tartar mosque, Meschet or church, which had large windows all round, all standing open; the floor was laid with carpets, with no other ornaments to be seen; the people who went in left their shoes or boots before the door and sat down in orderly rows with their feet crossed under them

p.h: Tartar women fought like men
p.g: Among the cruelties of the occupation, Thomas reports that the Tartars' women armed themselves like men and rode boldly into battle. He adds that they treated captive women even more savagely than the men did, killing good-looking ones out of jealousy and disfiguring others to make them servants. Mongol women travelling and sometimes fighting with the army are also mentioned by Matthew Paris's informants.
p.q: Praeterea mulieres Tartarorum virili more armis accinctae in pugnam audacter ferebantur, ut viri, hae in mulieres captivas atrocius saeviebant, si quas enim venustiori vultu cernebant, ex quibus zelotypiae motum possent aliquatenus formidare, statim extracto gladio perimebant
p.s: Thomas, archdeacon of Split, Historia Salonitana, in the first edition by Ivan Lučić (Lucius), Amsterdam 1666
p.t: Moreover the women of the Tartars, girded with arms in the manner of men, charged boldly into battle like men; they raged more cruelly against captive women, for if they saw any with a more beautiful face, of whom they might in any way fear jealousy, they at once drew a sword and killed them
p.c: An atrocity report Thomas did not witness.

p.h: Tatar villagers with carpets and cushions
p.g: In the Tatar farming villages beyond Kazan, Erman found people neatly dressed, the men with shaved heads under tight caps and trimmed beards, in contrast to the wild hair of Russian peasants. Their houses always had good carpets and cushions, and the women, in loose white gowns, never helped with rough work like harnessing horses.
p.q: Men and women here are neatly clothed. The smooth-shorn pate of the former, covered with the tight-fitting cap, and the precise cut of their beards, form a striking contrast with the savage head of hair, completely in a state of nature, which is usually worn by the Russians. Their houses are never without some good carpets and cushions to cover the seats and beds.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

p.h: Chinggis Khan's terms to the Jin envoy
p.g: The envoy's own report says nothing about his audience, so Bretschneider adds the entry from the Yuan shi, the official history of the Mongol dynasty. Chinggis reminds him that he had offered peace if the Jin ruler gave up everything north of the Yellow River and took the lesser title of wang (king), but his general Muqali had since conquered those lands anyway. On the next page the Khan adds that the Jin must also hand over the cities of Kuan si that still held out, and only then may their ruler keep the south as a king.
p.q: The emperor said to him: "I formerly asked of your sovereign to cede the land north of the Yellow River, and to reign over the country south of it with the title of wang (king). On these conditions I would have suspended the war. But now Mu-hua-li … has already conquered all these countries, and you are compelled to sue for peace."
p.s: Yuan shi (official history of the Mongol Yuan dynasty), annals for 1221, translated by E. Bretschneider as an addition to the Pei shi ki
p.pe: Chinggis Khan and the Jin envoy
p.c: Not part of the envoy's report. Bretschneider notes that the Yuan shi dates the events of the western campaign a year too early.
p.tg: diplomacy war jin muqali yellow river

p.h: To Tartars, Latin Christians looked like idol-worshippers
p.g: In a chapter on how idols began, Marignolli admits an uncomfortable fact he learned abroad: Jews, Tartars and Saracens, and even some Eastern Christians, think Western Christians are the worst idolaters. Eastern Christians honour painted images but loathe the carved faces and frightening sculptures found in Latin churches, such as those on Saint Adalbert's tomb in Prague.
p.q: Judei tamen, Tartari, & Sarraceni iudicant nos pessimos ydololatras, & non solum gentiles, sed eciam Christiani quidam. Nam licet illi Christiani venerentur picturas, abhominantur tamen larvas, facies, & horrendas sculpturas, sicut sunt in Ecclesiis: patet in sepulcro sancti Adalberti in Praga.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.t: Yet Jews, Tartars and Saracens judge us the worst of idolaters, and not only the heathen but even some Christians. For although those Christians venerate paintings, they abhor masks, faces and horrible sculptures such as there are in our churches, as can be seen at the tomb of Saint Adalbert in Prague.

p.h: Woken by a Tatar bride's procession
p.g: At dawn in Bakhchysarai Jesse was woken by drums, gongs and bagpipes accompanying a Tatar bride in a curtained carriage drawn by two ponies, lit by torch-bearers. The same page gives his unimpressed verdict on the Khans' mausoleum and the palace's 'diminutive apartments'.
p.q: the concert was in honour of a Tartar bride, whose equipage, drawn by two ponies, was surrounded by curtains and torch-bearers, lighting her to the hymeneal couch, in a manner truly classical … The mausoleum of the Khans is a wretched edifice after that of the Sultans at Constantinople
p.s: Captain William Jesse
p.c: He mocks Tatar music.

p.h: A model farm run by a Tatar general
p.g: Passing through villages owned by Major General Tevkelev, a Muslim of Tatar descent whose serfs were all Tatars, Pallas praises the order and cleanliness of the grain stores, sheaves, fields and even the peasants' households as an example of good husbandry, unusual in the region. The general was away celebrating the Tatar ploughing festival, Saban.
p.q: Die drey letztern Dörfer gehören dem Generalmajor Tewkelef, welcher tatarischer Herkunft und der mahometanischen Religion zugethan ist, auch lauter Tataren zu seinen zahlreichen Unterthanen hat.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars (Muslim estate owner and peasants)
p.t: The last three villages belong to Major General Tevkelev, who is of Tatar descent and an adherent of the Muslim religion, and has nothing but Tatars among his numerous subjects.

p.h: Kalmyks swim for bread thrown from the boat
p.g: Sailing back up the Volga, de Bruyn saw Kalmyks fishing with lines along the bank, with two-humped camels around them, and threw them bread, which they swam out to fetch. Ashore, Kalmyk men and women could not stop staring at his clothes and handling them. His boat kept to the east bank to avoid the Tartars on the other side, whom he calls great thieves.
p.q: Nous vîmes plusieurs Calmuques le long du rivage pêchant à la ligne, & nous leur jettâmes dans l'eau, du pain qu'ils allèrent prendre à la nage. Il y avoit des chameaux à 2. bosses autour d'eux … nous trouvâmes plusieurs Calmuques tant hommes que femmes, qui ne pouvoient se lasser de regarder mon habillement
p.s: Cornelis de Bruyn (French translation, Voyages de Corneille Le Brun, 1718)
p.t: We saw several Kalmyks along the bank fishing with lines, and we threw bread into the water for them, which they swam out to fetch. There were two-humped camels around them … we found several Kalmyks, both men and women, who could not tire of looking at my clothes

p.h: Honest at home, raiders abroad
p.g: An enemy's surprisingly warm verdict: Chevalier calls the Tartars among the least vicious of nations, chaste, sincere and faithful, with no thieves or false witnesses among themselves. He explains their raids on Christian lands by saying they did not regard robbing 'infidels' as wrong. On the next page he says Polish nobles trusted young Tartar servants with the keys to their money and jewels.
p.q: As to their Morals, there are very few Nations to be found less vitious, for besides their continence, they are extremely sincere, and faithful, they have no Thieves or false witnesses amongst them, little injustice or violence, and live in Union and great tranquility
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)
p.c: A generalisation; on the next page Chevalier adds his own observation that Polish nobles trusted young Tartar servants with their money and jewels.

p.h: Burning the dead in an earthen pyramid
p.g: Huc describes several Mongol funerals: nomads left the dead on hilltops or in ravines for eagles and wolves, while rich families built a pyramid-shaped earth furnace around the standing body, burned it, and had the Grand Lama knead the powdered bones with meal into cakes that were stacked and placed in a small tower.
p.q: The richer Tartars sometimes burn their dead with great solemnity. A large furnace of earth is constructed in a pyramidical form. Just before it is completed, the body is placed inside, standing, surrounded with combustibles.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: Milk, dried cheese and milk brandy
p.g: A tall lama told the travellers about a cattle plague that had left the steppe people short of food. Timkovsky records their diet: meat when herds were large, otherwise milk, dried cheese (kourout) and millet, with a milk brandy drunk in summer. On the facing page he adds that they made coarse felt from sheep's wool, twisted horsehair into ropes, and had 'neither handicrafts nor manufactures'.
p.q: When they possess many cows and sheep, they subsist upon their flesh, otherwise they content themselves with milk and dried cheese (bissalak and kourout), they likewise make use of a kind of millet (shara bonda). To exhilarate their spirits they drink, though only in summer, a kind of brandy, which they extract from milk.
p.s: George Timkowski (English translation, 1827)
p.tg: food milk kurut milk brandy felt

p.h: Tver kills the Horde's envoy, and a Tatar army lays the land waste
p.g: In 1327 Prince Alexander of Tver killed many Tatars in Tver and other towns, after the mighty envoy Shevkal had come from the Horde with a large Tatar retinue. That winter a huge Tatar army took Tver, Kashin and the Torzhok district and 'laid the whole Russian land waste'. Novgorod escaped by paying the Tatar envoys 2000 in silver and sending gifts to the commanders.
p.q: князь Александръ Михаиловичь изби Татаръ много, во Тфери и по инымъ городомъ … пришелъ бо бяше посолъ силенъ изъ орды, именемь Шевкалъ, съ множествомъ Татаръ. … На ту же зиму приде рать Татарьская, множество много, и взяша Тфѣрь, и Кашинъ, и Новоторжьскую волость, и просто рещи всю землю Русьскую положиша пусту
p.s: Novgorod First Chronicle (PSRL vol. 3, 1841)
p.pe: Golden Horde envoy Shevkal (Chol Khan) and a punitive Tatar army
p.t: Prince Alexander Mikhailovich killed many Tatars in Tver and in other towns … for a mighty envoy had come from the Horde, named Shevkal, with a multitude of Tatars. … That same winter a Tatar army came, a very great multitude, and took Tver, and Kashin, and the Torzhok district, and, to put it simply, laid the whole Russian land waste
p.c: The OCR prints the year as 6855; the event belongs to 6835 (1327).
p.tg: tver uprising envoy punitive raid tribute

p.h: Hundreds of graves marked with family signs
p.g: On a high steppe field Georgi found an old burial ground of 400 to 800 graves, neither raised nor fenced, marked by upright cut sandstones. Most stones carried only the dead person's personal mark, the tamga, which people used instead of signing their name; broader stones added an Arabic prayer and the year of death. With his own mullah and those of nearby villages he had many epitaphs read.
p.q: 400 bis 800 mit Grabsteinen gezeichnete Gräber. Die Gräber selbst sind weder erhoben, noch eingefaßt. … Diese bestehen der grössesten Zahl nach aus säulenförmig gehauenen, vierseitigen oder etwas platten Sandsteinen … den mehresten ist blos da Handzeichen (Tatarisch Tamgar) dessen sich der Verstorbene statt der Unterschrift des Namens zu bedienen
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: 400 to 800 graves marked with gravestones. The graves themselves are neither raised nor enclosed. … Most of these [stones] are four-sided or somewhat flat sandstones cut like columns … on most of them only the hand-mark (Tatar tamga) is carved, which the dead person used [to use] instead of signing his name
p.c: The OCR reads 'Tamgar'; the word is the Turkic tamga, a clan or personal mark.

p.h: Under the bamboo: the Chinese cry, the Tartar is silent
p.g: Travelling south, Barrow saw beatings with the bamboo almost daily. He contrasts the two peoples: a Chinese cries out and thanks the official on his knees, while a Tartar bears it silently and then grumbles, disputing a Chinese official's right to flog him.
p.q: In travelling through the country, a day seldom escaped without our witnessing the application of the Pan-tsé, or bamboo… A Chinese suffering under this punishment cries out in the most piteous manner; a Tartar bears it in silence.
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: A generalisation from what he happened to see.

p.h: Chinese warhorses that bolt at a Tartar neigh
p.g: Describing Chinese livestock, Ricci says the Chinese do not know how to break horses and simply geld them to make them docile. Their cavalry horses are countless but so feeble that they flee at the mere neigh of a Tartar horse, which makes them nearly useless in war. It is a Jesuit's jab at Ming cavalry and a measure of the fear the steppe horsemen still inspired.
p.q: Eos Sinae domare minime norunt, castrati omnes mansuescunt, quotquot ad usus quotidianos adhibentur. Equi porro militares sunt propemodum innumerabiles, sed ii ita degeneres atque imbelles, ut ne hinnitu quidem equi Tartari sine fuga ferant
p.s: Matteo Ricci, edited and translated into Latin by Nicolas Trigault (1615)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongol horsemen), compared with the Chinese
p.t: The Chinese hardly know how to break them; all those used for everyday work are tamed by gelding. War horses are almost countless, but so degenerate and unwarlike that they cannot bear even the neigh of a Tartar horse without running away
p.c: A sweeping judgement meant to impress European readers.

p.h: Horse meat is cooked, not eaten raw
p.g: Bell corrects a common European belief that Tartars eat raw meat. On campaign the Kalmyks live on balls of dried curd dissolved in water, and when that fails they kill spare horses and roast the meat on broken arrows. Their smoked or sun-dried horse meat, he says, cannot fairly be called raw, and he tasted it himself.
p.q: They broil or roast the flesh before the fire, on pieces of broken arrows, and never eat it raw, as is commonly believed, unless compelled by necessity. They have indeed large thick pieces of horse-flesh, smoked or dried in the sun, which they eat; but this cannot properly be called raw.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)

p.h: A frontier chief who refused 150 rupees
p.g: At Peenoo in Spiti, Gerard asked the headman (styled Lafa) for leave to return by the Taree pass. The man sent back his 150 rupees and said the travellers were welcome to goats, sheep and blankets, but not to that road, though he would not fight them. Gerard admired his firmness and goes on to say that the Tartars of the Chinese frontier were as strict about strangers as officials at Peking; he had been turned back at four different points the year before.
p.q: The Chinese Tartars, on this remote frontier of their vast empire, are just as vigilant respecting the non-admission of strangers as their countrymen at Pekin : no sum of money, however great, will bribe them to infringe the orders of their superiors.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (ed. George Lloyd, 1841)
p.pe: Tibetans of Spiti; officials of Chinese-ruled Tibet

p.h: The emperor: 'We Manchus have our own rites'
p.g: Parrenin translates the Yongzheng emperor's words to his ministers about a Manchu prince who had become Christian: every nation honours Heaven in its own way; the Manchu rite is the Tiaochin, when all burn incense and paper on New Year's day; Mongols, Chinese, Muscovites and Europeans each have their own. The prince, as a Manchu, should follow the Manchu rite. A footnote says the Tiaochin had no fixed form and each family did it its own way.
p.q: Le rite des Tartares Mantcheoux est le Tiaochin, il n'y a personne qui le premier jour de l'an ne brûle des odeurs & du papier, & cela pour honorer le Ciel. Nous autres Mantcheoux, nous avons nos rites particuliers; les Mongous, les Chinois, les Moscovites, les Européens, &c. ont aussi chacun le Tien qui lui est propre.
p.s: The Yongzheng emperor, as translated by Dominique Parrenin (letter of 26 September 1727)
p.pe: Manchus; the Yongzheng emperor and a Christian Manchu prince
p.t: The rite of the Manchu Tartars is the Tiaochin: there is no one who does not burn incense and paper on the first day of the year, and that is to honour Heaven. We Manchus have our own particular rites; the Mongols, the Chinese, the Muscovites, the Europeans and so on also each have the Tien [Heaven] proper to them.
p.c: Parrenin's translation of an edict hostile to Christianity; 'Tiaochin' is his transcription of a Manchu household rite.
p.tg: religion shamanism heaven manchus new year

p.h: Marriage as a contract of sale
p.g: Huc says Mongol marriages were arranged by parents through go-betweens, and that the bride's family was paid in horses, oxen, sheep, cloth, butter, brandy and flour. The Mongols themselves spoke of 'buying' and 'selling' a daughter. He goes on to describe a mock fight at the bride's door, a gallop to the new tent, polygamy and easy divorce.
p.q: The thing is indeed very clearly expressed in their language; they say, "I have bought for my son the daughter of so and so." "We have sold our daughter to such and such a family." The marriage contract is thus simply a contract of sale.
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: Sledges from post to post, and Kyrgyz dog teams
p.g: West of Bolad, Chang De found that coins were of gold, silver and copper with inscriptions but no square hole, and that in the land he calls Ma'a horses pulled sledges from one post station to the next, carrying heavy loads at speed. He adds, as a report, that the Kyrgyz used dogs in place of horses. Bretschneider doubted there were sledges on this route but noted that Marco Polo also mentions dog sledges in Siberia.
p.q: 至麻阿中以馬撁拖床逓鋪負重而行疾或曰乞里乞四易馬以犬
p.s: Liu Yu, Record of an Embassy to the West, from Chang De's report (Qiujian ji juan 94 = Yutang jiahua juan 2; Sibu congkan text, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.pl: Between Bolad and the Chu valley, Central Asia (Ma'a)
p.pe: Peoples of the Chagatai realm; Kyrgyz (Qirqis)
p.t: On coming into Ma'a, they use horses to pull sledges from post station to post station, carrying heavy loads and going fast. Some say that the Qiliqisi (Kyrgyz) use dogs in place of horses.
p.c: The dog-sledge detail is introduced with 'some say'.

p.h: 'Tartar cookery' on the road to Ladakh
p.g: Moorcroft saw his Lahouli porters cook a sheep that had died in the night: skinned, cut up and boiled whole in a big cauldron with all the innards, together with cakes of flour mixed with the blood. He calls it 'Tartar cookery' and admits he did not care to join in.
p.q: We had an opportunity here of witnessing Tartar cookery on a more sumptuous scale than usual, but it was not of a character to invite a participation in the meal. A sheep belonging to some of the carriers having died in the night, the carcase was skinned and cut up, and boiled in a large cauldron, together with all the viscera
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)

p.h: A sacrifice thrown against a hide on a post
p.g: On holy days the Cheremis tie the freshly flayed hide of a cow, sheep or horse to a post, roast the meat, and throw a dish of it and a cup of mead against the hide while murmuring prayers. The page adds that they revere the sun, fire and water above all visible things.
p.q: Ils ont pour cela des jours consacrés, ausquels ils commencent la cérémonie par attacher à un poteau, une peau de vache, de mouton ou de cheval écorché exprès: ils en mettent la chair sur la braise; & quand elle est rôtie, ils la coupent par petits morceaux, dont ayant rempli un plat, ils le prennent d'une main & une tasse d'hidromel de l'autre, puis jettent le tout contre la peau
p.s: Jan Struys (French translation by Glanius, Amsterdam 1681)
p.t: For this they have holy days, on which they begin the ceremony by tying to a post the hide of a cow, sheep or horse flayed for the purpose; they put the meat on the coals, and when it is roasted they cut it into small pieces, fill a dish with them, take it in one hand and a cup of mead in the other, then throw the whole against the hide
p.c: Very close to Olearius's description of the Cheremis, so probably copied.

p.h: Dice worn on every Tartar belt
p.g: Turner says that no journey, marriage or naming was done in Tibet without first seeking an omen, often from a monk skilled in divination. For small decisions people simply threw dice, which is why a pair of dice hangs from a Tartar belt. He cheerfully admits he travelled only when his own monk-diviner said so.
p.q: in trivial affairs, the mind is often governed by a casual cast of the die; and hence, dice are almost always found to constitute an appendage to a Tartar dress.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)

p.h: Why the Tartars could never hold Syria: summer heat and no grass
p.g: Arguing against landing a crusade in Armenia, Sanudo notes that the Tartars had often overrun almost all of Syria but always had to give it up and let the Sultan retake it. They could not cross the desert into Egypt, and could not stay through the summer because of the great heat and the lack of pasture for their horses and herds. It shows how nomad armies were tied to grass.
p.q: Et considerandum est quod multoties Tartari cucurrerunt per terram, & cœperunt quasi omnes contratas de Semo, & de Syria: sed quia non potuerunt transire desertum per quod transitur in Ægyptum … Et si dici vellet quod Tartari compulsi fuerunt relinquere acquisita, hoc fuit, quia non potuerunt in æstate commorari propter intensionem caloris, & propter defectum herbatici, quod non habuerunt pro suis equis pascēdis & gregibus
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: And it should be considered that many times the Tartars overran the land and took almost all the districts of Sham and Syria: but because they could not cross the desert by which one passes into Egypt ... And if one wished to say that the Tartars were forced to give up what they had taken, this was because they could not stay in summer on account of the intense heat, and on account of the lack of grazing, which they did not have for pasturing their horses and herds
p.c: A strategic argument, but it matches what modern historians say about Mongol logistics in Syria.

p.h: An emperor buried in his tent with a mare and foal
p.g: When a Tartar emperor dies he is seated in his tent with a table of meat and a cup of mare's milk, a mare with her foal and a saddled horse, then buried in a great pit, tent and all, so he will have a house, horses and milk in the next world. Mandeville adds that graves were sometimes hidden under replaced turf. The details match Carpini's report, which Mandeville used.
p.q: And when the emperor dieth, men set him in a chair in midst the place of his tent. And men set a table before him clean, covered with a cloth, and thereupon flesh and diverse viands and a cup full of mare's milk. And men put a mare beside him with her foal, and an horse saddled and bridled.
p.s: 'Sir John Mandeville' (Cotton manuscript, modern spelling ed. A. W. Pollard, 1900)
p.c: Borrowed from Carpini's eyewitness-based account (compare W043, Rockhill's note at p. 81).
p.tg: burial tent mare's milk horses afterlife

p.h: Muslims without mosques or mullahs
p.g: Levshin describes Kazakh Islam as loose: they count themselves Sunnis alongside Turks, Tatars, Bukharans and Khivans and practise polygamy, but do not keep the fasts or ablutions, find praying five times a day too hard, and have no mosques and no mullahs chosen from among themselves. Sometimes elders read prayers with others kneeling around them.
p.q: Постовъ и омовенія, весьма благоразумнаго постановленія Магометова, Киргизы не соблюдаютъ; молиться по пяти разъ на день, находятъ они для себя труднымъ; мечетей и избранныхъ изъ среди себя муллъ не имѣютъ. Иногда молитвы читаются стариками въ присутствіи многихъ стоящихъ около нихъ на колѣнямъ
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: Fasts and ablution, a very sensible institution of Muhammad, the Kirghiz do not observe; they find praying five times a day hard for themselves; they have no mosques and no mullahs chosen from among themselves. Sometimes prayers are read by old men in the presence of many people kneeling around them
p.c: An outsider's judgment of religious practice; Kazakh Islam had its own shrines and holy men that Levshin mentions elsewhere.

p.h: Tibetans with 'quite the Tartar face'
p.g: This is one of the few things Stewart saw himself. The Tibetan envoys in Calcutta struck him as fairer and ruddier than their neighbours, with 'the Tartar face'. He goes on to describe coarse home-woven woollens, Siberian furs for the rich, a Bhutanese envoy in conical hat and silk tunic, and a diet of milk, cheese, butter and barley.
p.q: The Thibetians are of a smaller size than their southern neighbours, and of a less robust make. Their complexions are also fairer, and many of them have even a ruddiness in their countenances unknown in the other climates of the east. Those whom I saw at Calcutta appeared to have quite the Tartar face.
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.c: 'Tartar face' is a stock eighteenth-century physical label, not an ethnic finding.

p.h: No locks on their wagons, and living on mare's milk
p.g: In the same chapter Sanudo, following Carpini, praises Tartar honesty and endurance: there are no robbers or thieves of anything valuable among them, so the tents and carts where they keep their treasure are never locked; they welcome anyone who comes while they eat, can go a day or two without food and still sing and play, and when heading for lands short of food they take mares and cows along and live on the milk.
p.q: Prædones vel fures notabilium rerum, inter eos non sunt: ideoq; stationes & currus eorum, vbi thesauros conseruant, seris aut vectibus non firmant. Honorant se mutuò, & sunt ad inuicem familiares; omnem accedentem, dum comedunt, ad conuiuiū recipiunt … & quando ad terram pergunt, vbi putant adesse victualiū inopiam, equas, vaccas & alia animalia secū portant; & de lacte viuunt.
p.s: Marino Sanudo Torsello (Liber secretorum fidelium crucis, c. 1321; ed. Bongars, Hanau 1611)
p.t: Robbers or thieves of valuable things are not found among them: so their dwellings and carts, where they keep their treasures, they do not secure with locks or bars. They honour one another and are friendly among themselves; everyone who approaches while they are eating they receive at the meal ... and when they go to a land where they think there is a shortage of food, they take mares, cows and other animals with them, and live on the milk.
p.c: Copied from Carpini, who also stressed their arrogance and cruelty to outsiders.

p.h: A father's duty: school and an early marriage
p.g: From what Tatars told him, Lepekhin picked out two rules he thought did them credit and could serve as an example to many fathers. A Tatar father who did not send his son to school, to learn reading, writing and religion, was held to commit an unforgivable sin, and it was an equally serious fault to leave one's children long unmarried out of stubbornness or greed.
p.q: Aus ihren Erzählungen habe ich zweyerley bemerkt, das ich nicht verschweigen kann, … den Tatarn zum Ruhm gereicht, sondern auch vielen Vätern zum Exempel dienet. … wird es für eine unverzeihliche Sünde angerechnet, wenn er … nicht in die Schule thut, sowohl um lesen und schreiben zu lernen, … der Religion unterrichtet zu werden.
p.s: Ivan Lepekhin (German translation, 1774)
p.t: From their accounts I have noted two things that I cannot pass over in silence, [which not only] redound to the credit of the Tatars but also serve as an example to many fathers. … it is counted an unforgivable sin if he does not put [his son] into school, both to learn to read and write and [to be] instructed in religion.
p.c: A few words are lost at the left edge of the scan; the gaps are marked.

p.h: Sour milk for the poor, meat for princes, brick tea for all
p.g: In summer the Kalmyks lived almost entirely on sour milk: mare's milk (tschigan) for the rich, cow's milk for the poor. Only the prince and great men ate meat, because the herds were their whole wealth. Their tea came from China by way of Siberia as hard cakes of coarse leaves and stalks, boiled with butter or sheep's-tail fat and salt.
p.q: None but the Prince, and the great men, had flesh in their kettles, for the whole wealth of the nation consists in their flocks and herds, and they are forced to use them sparingly. In winter, when they are short of milk, they buy meal from the Russians who inhabit the shores of the Volga
p.s: Heinrich August Zwick (English edition, 1831)

p.h: They seem to rain arrows rather than shoot them
p.g: Julian's report on how the Tartars fight: they shoot farther than other nations, and in the first clash 'do not seem to shoot but to rain arrows', while swords and lances are said to be less suited to them. Their army is organised so that one Tartar commands ten men and a centurion commands a hundred, so that spies cannot hide among them.
p.q: dicitur, quod longius jaciunt, quam alie consueverint naciones. In prima congressione belli, ut dicitur, non sagittant, sed quasi pluere sagittas videntur.
p.s: Friar Julian of Hungary, O.P., report to the bishop of Perugia (c. 1238), in the text printed by Hormayr (1842)
p.t: it is said that they shoot farther than other nations are accustomed to. In the first clash of battle, it is said, they do not shoot, but seem as it were to rain arrows.

p.h: A 'Tartar custom': sharing out a dead man's goods
p.g: After Goes died at Suzhou, the Muslim merchants of the caravan seized his goods, destroyed his diary (which recorded their debts) and bound his companion Isaac, threatening to kill him unless he invoked Muhammad. The account explains that among these merchants a 'Tartarea' custom had taken hold: the goods of anyone who died on the road were divided among all. Three centuries earlier Pegolotti (W116) warned that the lord of the land seized a dead merchant's goods on the Tartar road.
p.q: Tartarea plane consuetudine inter Negotiatores illos invaluit, ut morientium in itinere Negotiatorum bona inter omnes dividantur, hac ex causa Benedicti Socium Isaac vinxerunt, mortem minati, nisi Mahometem inclamasset.
p.s: Nicolas Trigault, from Matteo Ricci's commentaries (1615)
p.t: Among those merchants a thoroughly Tartar custom has taken hold, that the goods of merchants who die on the road are divided among them all; for this reason they bound Benedict's companion Isaac and threatened him with death unless he called on Muhammad.
p.c: 'Tartarea' can mean 'Tartar' or 'hellish' in Latin, and here probably carries both. The story comes from the Jesuit side of a dispute.

p.h: Milk, cheese, meat and a steppe spirit
p.g: The Mongols, Verbiest says, grew no crops and lived on milk, cheese and meat, with a distilled drink he compares to European aqua vitae (almost certainly milk spirit), which they drank at feasts. He then turns contemptuous, likening them to the herds they tended.
p.q: They pass their Life either in Hunting, or doing nothing. And as they neither Sow nor cultivate the Earth, so they make no Harvest. They Live upon Milk, Cheese, and Flesh, and have a sort of Wine, not much unlike our Aqua-vitae ; with which they make their Feasts, and are often Drunk.
p.s: Ferdinand Verbiest (English translation, 1686)
p.c: The food is observed; the judgement that they do nothing but eat and drink is Verbiest's prejudice.

p.h: Kazakh nomads who irrigate millet fields
p.g: On the way to the Chinese post, Rose passed several auls (travelling camps) of Kazakhs of the Great Horde and saw fields beside them. He notes that the millet grew well because the Kazakhs were skilled at irrigation, cutting little ditches to bring mountain water to the fields, and heard that they also grew wheat. A useful corrective to the idea of purely herding nomads.
p.q: Wir kamen bei mehreren ihrer Aule vorbei, wie man ihre zusammen herumziehenden Gemeinden nennt, und fanden in der Nähe derselben auch den Boden stellenweise bebaut. Meistentheils sahen wir Hirse (Holcus Sorgum) gezogen, die überall recht gut stand, weil die Kirgisen den Acker sehr geschickt zu bewässern verstehen, und ihn überall mit kleinen Gräben durchschneiden, durch welche das Wasser von den Bergen dem Acker zugeführt wird.
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.pl: Irtysh valley near the Chinese border, East Kazakhstan
p.t: We passed several of their auls, as their communities that travel about together are called, and near them also found the ground cultivated in places. Mostly we saw millet (Holcus sorghum) grown, which stood very well everywhere because the Kirghiz know how to irrigate the field very skilfully, cutting it through everywhere with small ditches by which water from the mountains is led to the field.

p.h: Arrows like locusts at the river Sajó
p.g: At the battle by the river Sajó (Mohi), the Tartars crossed at night by a ford, surrounded the royal camp at dawn and shot into it. Roger says the arrows were so thick they almost shaded the fighters and flew through the air like swarms of locusts, so that the king could not even draw up his lines. He was not in the battle himself and writes from survivors' reports.
p.q: Tanta enim erat crebrosa emissio sagittarum, quod fere umbram pugnantibus faciebant; et sagittae sicut locustae et bruchus congregatim vadunt, per aera volabant. Et sic sagittarum ictus minime sufferre valentes, infra circulum exercitus retro ibant. Rex vero acies non poterat ordinare
p.s: Master Roger (Rogerius), Carmen miserabile, in the 1885 Budapest edition (Chronica minora)
p.t: For so dense was the shooting of arrows that it almost made shade for the fighters; and the arrows flew through the air as locusts and grasshoppers go in swarms. And so, unable to bear the strikes of the arrows, they fell back inside the ring of the army. The king could not draw up his battle lines

p.h: Robes 'in the Tartar fashion'
p.g: Retelling the old legend of Queen Semiramis, who disguised herself as her son, Marignolli explains her disguise with clothing he had seen on his travels: robes 'in the Tartar fashion', wrapped over across the chest, with long sleeves, long skirts covering the feet and trousers for riding. The legend is classical; the comparison to Tartar dress is his own.
p.q: ipsa invenit sibi vestes thartarico modo formatas, ante pectus replicatas, ne mamille apparerent, longas manicas, ne mulieris manus viderentur, longas vestes, ad cooperiendum pedes, bracas, quando equum ascendebat, & precepit nomine filii, quod omnes tali veste uterentur
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongols), as a model for a dress style
p.t: she devised for herself clothes made in the Tartar fashion, folded over across the chest so that her breasts would not show, with long sleeves so that a woman's hands would not be seen, long robes to cover the feet, and trousers for when she mounted a horse; and she ordered in her son's name that everyone should wear such clothing
p.c: A legend about ancient Assyria; only the description of the 'Tartar fashion' reflects what he saw.

p.h: Christians backed the Tartars and lost
p.g: Semedo explains why Jesuits found no trace of the Christians Marco Polo described. When the Tartar ruled China there were many Christians with fine churches, favoured by him. When Hongwu fought to recover the kingdom, the Muslims sided with the Chinese and kept their liberties and mosques, while the Christians sided with the Tartar and went down with him: some died, some converted, some hid.
p.q: Quando el Tartaro dominò la China, avia en ella muchos Christianos, con Iglesias bien suntuosas, que se hallavan favorecidos dèl, como parece de las Relaciones del Veneto. … Los Christianos tomando la voz del Tartaro, i quedando èl perdido en aquella accion, precisamente quedaron tambien perdidos en su estado
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.pe: Tartars (Mongol Yuan rulers); Christians and Muslims in China
p.t: When the Tartar ruled China there were many Christians in it, with quite sumptuous churches, who found themselves favoured by him, as appears from the accounts of the Venetian [Marco Polo]. … The Christians, taking the side of the Tartar, and he being lost in that action, necessarily were also lost in their standing
p.c: Semedo's own reconstruction, built on Marco Polo and Jesuit reasoning.

p.h: Pipes, Chinese tobacco and watermelon with Kazan's Tatar governor
p.g: On arriving at Kazan Chappe was received by the governor, a Tatar prince. They sat round a table covered with a fine carpet; four long pipes and a porcelain jar of Chinese tobacco were set out, then local liqueurs, preserves, fruit and a watermelon so delicious that Chappe ate nothing else and took home seeds, which failed to grow in France.
p.q: J'arrivai à Cazan le premier Octobre. Un Prince Tartare en étoit le Gouverneur … nous nous assimes autour d'une table couverte d'un beau tapis : on y plaça quatre grandes pipes & un vase de porcelaine rempli de tabac de la Chine : je fumai quelques instants. On servit aussi-tôt des liqueurs du pays; des confitures, avec des fruits & un melon d'eau
p.s: Jean Chappe d'Auteroche
p.pe: a Tatar prince serving as governor of Kazan
p.t: I arrived at Kazan on the first of October. A Tartar prince was its governor … we sat down round a table covered with a fine carpet: four large pipes were placed on it and a porcelain jar full of Chinese tobacco; I smoked for a few moments. Then local liqueurs were served, preserves with fruit, and a watermelon

p.h: What the Chinese fought to keep at the Tartar conquest
p.g: Ellis notes that the executioners' conical caps kept an ancient shape that the Chinese had been anxious to preserve when the Manchus conquered China, along with the sanctity of their ancestors' tombs. It hints at what the Chinese cared most to keep under their new rulers.
p.q: These, I afterwards learnt, were the public executioners, and that the shape of their caps was one of ancient form, which the Chinese, at the Tartar conquest, were most anxious to retain. The sanctity of the tombs of their ancestors was another and more reasonable object of their anxiety.
p.s: Henry Ellis (footnote)

p.h: Nogai horses for sale below Simonov
p.g: Nogai envoys arrived with letters from their mirzas asking for friendship. The grand prince lodged them at the 'Nogai Court' in Moscow and let them sell their horses on the meadow below the Simonov monastery. That year the horses were cheap: early snow had left no grazing, and many barely arrived alive or died. Steppe horse herds for Moscow's cavalry were the Nogais' great export.
p.q: И князь великій пожаловалъ ихъ, дружбу свою хочетъ къ нимъ дръжати, и велѣлъ ихъ поставити на Нагайскомъ дворѣ, а съ коньми торговати подъ Симановымъ на лугу. И быша лошади дешевы, едва и живы пришли, а иныхъ много помроша, понеже снѣгъ палъ рано, безъкорміа ради.
p.s: Nikon Chronicle, PSRL vol. 13, part 1 (1904)
p.pe: Nogai envoys and horse traders of Koshum-mirza
p.t: And the grand prince favoured them, and wishes to keep his friendship with them, and ordered them lodged at the Nogai Court, and to trade their horses on the meadow below Simonov. And the horses were cheap, they barely arrived alive, and many others died, because snow fell early, for lack of fodder.

p.h: Oaths at a saint's tomb and fortune-telling sticks
p.g: The Yomut Turkmens settled disputes by swearing an oath over a saint's tomb, believing a perjurer could only escape damnation by dying on the spot. Muraviev also describes Khivan fortune-tellers who read letters from a book, or threw sticks onto a circle of other sticks each standing for a letter.
p.q: The Yomud Turcomans adore a Saint over whose tomb they settle their differences by an oath. A false oath under those circumstances is unknown, for it is firmly believed that whoever forswears himself over the tomb can only save himself from eternal punishment by dying on the spot.
p.s: Nikolai Muraviev (translated by W. S. A. Lockhart, 1871)

p.h: Muslim Tatars in the streets of Vilnius
p.g: In a polemical letter to King Stephen Bathory, Possevino points to Vilnius, capital of Lithuania, where the king could see on one side 'faithless Tartars' and schismatic Ruthenians and heretics of many kinds, and on the other many Catholics. The Tartars are 'faithless' because they follow Muhammad. It is a glimpse of the settled Muslim Tatar community of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
p.q: Venisti non ita pridem ad hanc ciuitatem Lituaniæ caput. Hic vides ex altera parte perfidos Tartaros & schismaticos Ruthenos, ac varia hæreticorum genera, ipsos autem ex altera parte Catholicos plurimos. Et Tartari quidem, quoniam Mahometem sectantur, Rutheni autem quoniam cum schismate multos errores hauserunt
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J., letter to the King of Poland (Moscovia et alia opera, Cologne 1587)
p.t: You came not long ago to this city, the capital of Lithuania. Here you see on one side faithless Tartars and schismatic Ruthenians, and various kinds of heretics, and on the other side very many Catholics. And the Tartars indeed because they follow Muhammad, the Ruthenians because with their schism they have drunk in many errors
p.c: Religious polemic; it tells us Tatars were a visible Muslim group in Vilnius, not how they lived.

p.h: Raids that emptied the countryside
p.g: Explaining why Muscovy seemed half empty, Possevino lists plague, wars and the constant Tartar raids, including the burning of the capital twelve years earlier. Abandoned ploughland and young forest showed where people had once lived, while the north stayed well peopled because the Tartars never raided there. He checked this with Italian and Spanish captives freed through him who had walked across the country.
p.q: Tartarorumq; continentes excursiones, ipsaq; ab ijsdem ante duodecim annos combusta Regia … At verò dedolati agri, & recentes Syluæ, quæ passim succreuerunt, indicia sunt frequentiorum anteà incolarum: licèt quæ regiones supra Moscuam versùs Septentrionem vergunt, eæ admodùm frequentes incolas habeant, quòd excursiones illuc Tartari non fecerint, & salubriore cœlo fruantur
p.s: Antonio Possevino, S.J. (Moscovia, Vilnius 1586)
p.t: ... and the continual raids of the Tartars, and the capital itself burned by them twelve years ago ... But the abandoned fields, and the young woods that have grown up everywhere, are signs of formerly more numerous inhabitants: although the regions that lie north of Moscow have a fairly dense population, because the Tartars have not raided there, and they enjoy a healthier climate.
p.c: Part observation, part report from freed Italian and Spanish captives; war with Poland and famine also emptied the land.

p.h: Turkmen elders who could advise but not punish
p.g: Wolff describes his Turkmen guides as truly 'masterless': their greybeards (aqsaqals) could give advice and lead raids, but had no power to punish anyone.
p.q: The Turkomauns my guides were, in the strictest sense of the word, masterless : for their Aga Sakals, ' lords with the beard,' have only a right to give advice, and to conduct them on their plundering expeditions, but they have no power to punish.
p.s: Joseph Wolff

p.h: Astrakhan's Tatars: the town's craftsmen
p.g: Rose calls the Astrakhan Tatars the descendants of the city's and the region's former inhabitants, still numerous, and like the Kazan Tatars. As in Kazan they were the real manufacturers of the town, especially dyers, tanners and soap-boilers, though the famous madder-dye works he visited was run by an Armenian.
p.q: Was endlich die Tataren betrifft, so sind sie die Abkömmlinge der ehemaligen Bewohner der Stadt und des Landes und auch jetzt noch zahlreich. Sie sind den Tataren von Kasan ähnlich, und auch in Astrachan wie dort, die eigentlichen Fabrikanten, besonders Färber, Gerber und Seifensieder.
p.s: Gustav Rose
p.t: Finally, as for the Tatars, they are the descendants of the former inhabitants of the city and the land and are still numerous. They are like the Tatars of Kazan, and in Astrakhan as there they are the real manufacturers, especially dyers, tanners and soap-boilers.
p.c: Damaged OCR on this page; several words were restored.

p.h: 'No Tartar has more than one wife'
p.g: Sheltering from rain with a Tatar named Ali Mustapha Oglu, Kohl asked a guest how many wives he had. The answer was firm: one, as for every decent Tatar. The same man then told Kohl about his village's lawsuit against a Russian landowner who had turned a grant of 700 acres into 20,000 by enclosing Tatar woods and meadows.
p.q: We inquired of him how many wives he had, and his answer was, “Of course only one! No Tartar has more than one wife, except such as are rascals;” so that it appears Mahomet's indulgent permission to have four is made but little use of.
p.s: J. G. Kohl (English abridged translation, 1844), quoting a Tatar villager

p.h: Portuguese cannon against the Tartars, 1621
p.g: In 1621 the city of Macau sent the emperor three large cannon with gunners. One burst at a demonstration in Beijing, killing three or four men, but the guns were still sent to the Tartar frontier. The Tartars, not knowing the new weapon, came too close, were hit by a shower of iron fragments, and fled; afterwards they were more careful.
p.q: Todavia embiaronse a la frontera de los Tartaros, que no sabiendo de la nueva arma, i llegandose màs de lo que les convenia, provaron un rocîo de troços de hierro, de que cayeron muchos, i todos fueron huyendo. Despues se acautelaron.
p.s: Álvaro Semedo, S.J. (Spanish edition by Manuel de Faria e Sousa, Madrid 1642)
p.t: Nevertheless they were sent to the frontier of the Tartars, who, not knowing of the new weapon and coming nearer than was good for them, tasted a shower of pieces of iron, from which many fell, and all fled. Afterwards they became cautious.

p.h: Felt idols on the doors of their wagons
p.g: Fletcher says that, unlike Turks, Tartars keep silk or cloth human figures fastened to the doors of their 'walking houses' as house guardians, made by religious women, and bow to a huge image of their khan when the army marches. He also calls them much given to witchcraft and omens.
p.q: Herein they differ from the Turkish religion, for that they have certeine idole puppets, made of silke or like stuffe, of the fashion of a man, which they fasten to the doore of their walking houses, to be as Janusses or keepers of their house. And these idols are made not by all, but by certeine religious women
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)
p.c: This closely follows 13th-century friars' descriptions of pagan Mongols; the Muslim Crimean Tatars of 1590 are unlikely to have kept such idols.

p.h: Sell your wife, never your dog
p.g: Wood notes a twist in Uzbek manners: asking a man to sell his wife was no offence, but asking to buy his dog was an insult, and 'dog-seller' was about the worst name one Uzbek could call another. He goes on to praise Uzbek women as fine housekeepers.
p.q: To ask an Uzbek to sell his wife would be no affront, but to ask him to sell his dog would be an unpardonable insult, "Suggee ferosh," or dog-seller, being about the most offensive epithet that one Uzbek can apply to another.
p.s: John Wood

p.h: A radish harvest in a land too cold to farm
p.g: Rashid notes that no crops grew around Karakorum because of the fierce cold, and that farming there only began in Ogedei's reign. When a man managed to raise a few radishes and brought them to the khan, Ogedei had them counted and paid him one silver ingot for each. The story shows a steppe capital fed from outside, where a home-grown vegetable was a marvel.
p.q: دیکر چون در حدود قرا قوروم از افراط سرما زراعت نمی باشد در عهد دولت قاآن آغاز آن کردند شخصی ترب کاشت و چندی حاصل آمد آنرا به بندکی قاآن آورد فرمود تا آنرا برکها بشمارند صد عدد بر آمد فرمود تا اورا صد بالش دادند
p.s: Rashid al-Din (Persian text ed. E. Blochet, 1911)
p.t: Another: since there is no farming around Qara Qorum because of the extreme cold, they made a start at it in the reign of the Qa'an. A man sowed radishes and a few came up. He brought them to the Qa'an, who ordered them to be counted, leaves and all; they came to a hundred, and he ordered that the man be given a hundred balish.
p.c: Another generosity anecdote from the Juvaini tradition.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this Persian text is garbled).

p.h: 'You are both right': a Sunni and a Shia before the judge
p.g: Poussett told Weber that a Persian and a Muslim Tatar at Astrakhan had quarrelled over religion and taken their complaint to the Russian commandant. When he learned that the Tatar had called the prophet Ali, and the Persian the prophet Muhammad, a cheat and a vagabond, the commandant shrugged and ruled that he could punish neither, since both were right. Poussett also praised the Astrakhan Tatars' orderly life and hospitality.
p.q: daß der Tartar den Prophet Aly, und hinwiederum der Persianer den Propheten Mahomet, vor einen Betrüger und Landstreicher gescholten, so ziehet der Commendant die Schulter, und spricht das Urthel: Ihr Herren, ich kan weder einen noch den andern von euch strafen, denn ihr habt alle beyde recht.
p.s: Friedrich Christian Weber (Das veränderte Russland), reporting Poussett of Astrakhan
p.pe: Muslim Tatars and Persians at Astrakhan
p.t: that the Tartar had abused the prophet Ali, and the Persian in turn the prophet Muhammad, as a cheat and vagabond, the commandant shrugs his shoulders and pronounces judgement: Gentlemen, I can punish neither the one nor the other of you, for you are both right.
p.c: Cited from the 1744 reissue, which reprints the 1721 text page for page with clearer OCR. Two words ('Persianer', 'Betrüger') are damaged in this copy and read from the 1721 edition (T0707 n187).

p.h: Sheepskins, bows and whips no European could copy
p.g: The Tartars living out on the steppe wore sheepskins and sheepskin caps and carried a scimitar, bow and about twenty arrows, all homemade from horse parts. Chevalier admires their plaited whips, which he says French and German saddlers could not imitate, and notes they were beginning to use firearms.
p.q: The Tartars who live abroad, are habited in Sheep-skins with a Cap of the same Stuffe; their Arms are ordinarily a Cimeter, a Bow and a Quiver, with about twenty Arrows … of which also they make their Whips so neatly, by a particular Art which they have, that our Sadlers in France and Germany have not yet been able to imitate them
p.s: Pierre Chevalier (translated by Edward Brown, 1672)

p.h: Horse-flesh: better than the tenderest beef
p.g: Many poorer Yakuts had been baptised, Sarychev says, perhaps to escape the poll-tax for a few years. The rich stayed pagan because Orthodox fasts would forbid their many wives and their food: meat, butter, milk and above all horse-flesh, their greatest delicacy. In summer they made kumis from mare's milk 'after the manner of the Tartars'.
p.q: The rich are not disposed to renounce a plurality of wives, nor the use of meat, butter, milk, and above all, horse-flesh, during the fasts … The latter is the greatest delicacy they can possibly conceive; and they often tell the Russians, that if they were once to make a proper meal from the flesh of a horse, they would in future prefer it to the tenderest beef.
p.s: Gavriil Sarychev (English translation, 1806)

p.h: The Uzbek turning charge
p.g: Describing how he lost the battle, Babur explains the Uzbek method: they always tried to turn the enemy's flank (the tulghama), and charged front and rear together, shooting arrows at full gallop, chiefs and common men mixed together, retreating just as fast if driven back. Babur escaped by swimming his armoured horse across the Kohik river.
p.q: In battle, the great reliance of the Uzbeks is on the Tulghmeh (or turning the enemy's flank). They never engage without using the Tulghmeh. Another of their practices is to advance and charge in front and rear, discharging their arrows at full gallop, pell-mell, chiefs and common soldiers, and, if repulsed, they in like manner retire full gallop.
p.s: Babur (translated by John Leyden and William Erskine, 1826)

p.h: Turkmen tents half-buried in snow
p.g: On the desert road to Bukhara the caravan passed Turkmen tents. Mohan Lal notes that they had large herds, lived on meat, curds and bread, fed their horses on meat and gave them salt water, and spent the winter in tents half-buried in snow. He adds bluntly that plundering caravans was their real trade and that they held many Persian (Qizilbash) slaves.
p.q: There we observed a few tents of Turkmans; they possess large herds of cattle, and live upon meat, curd, and bread. They feed their horses generally with flesh, and give them salt-water to drink. They do not much mind the cold of the winter, which they pass in tents, half-buried under the snow. Plundering the caravans is the proper occupation of these Turkmans.
p.s: Mohan Lal (1846 edition)
p.c: He saw the tents; the details of winter life and horse-feeding are probably what he was told.

p.h: Four hundred ungreased wheels
p.g: At the entrance to the Crimea Webster met a Tatar caravan of about a hundred wagons, drawn by oxen and camels, whose ungreased wheels made an 'excruciating' noise. The Tatars in their black lambskin caps, the camels and the bustards on the plain struck him as a novel eastern scene.
p.q: These people never grease the wheels. The creaking of one is sufficiently offensive; but the noise of four hundred was absolutely excruciating. The Tartars, too, were singing, which, with them, is another term for howling … The Tartars, in their black lamb-skin caps and eastern dresses, the camels grazing on each side of the road
p.s: James Webster
p.c: Mocking tone about Tatar song.
p.n: OCR normalized; a dash in the original replaced by a comma.

p.h: Left behind with a sheep and a jar of water
p.g: Bruce says the Kalmyks feared smallpox like the plague. When someone caught it they struck camp and fled, leaving the sick person in their worst kibitka with a killed sheep, water and firewood; few survived. On the same page he describes being served roast and boiled suckling foal by Prince Dasan, and calls it delicious.
p.q: The small-pox is as much dreaded among the Kalmucks as the pestilence amongst us : when any of them are seized with it, they immediately break up their camp and fly, leaving the sick person in one of their worst kibbets with a killed sheep, part of which is roasted and part raw, and a jar of water and some wood for fire
p.s: Peter Henry Bruce (published 1782)

p.h: Chinese funeral figures as a relic of Scythian burials
p.g: Barrow says the Chinese once buried slaves and concubines with rulers, now replaced by tinfoil figures and statues on graves. He guesses this descends from a Scythian or Tartar custom that Herodotus described, in which horses, slaves and concubines were killed and set around a king's tomb.
p.q: Formerly it was the custom to bury slaves with emperors and princes and sometimes also their concubines alive… this seems to be the remains of a Scythian or Tartar custom, which, according to Herodotus, was commonly observed at the funerals of their sovereigns, when their horses, their slaves, and their concubines were impaled alive and placed in order round the tyrant's tomb.
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: The Tartar link is Barrow's guess from Herodotus.

p.h: Seven wolves chasing two horses: the end of the world in the stars
p.g: In a chapter on Kazakh knowledge of the sky, Levshin says herdsmen navigated the trackless steppe by the stars and told time by them 'as a European looks at his pocket watch'. They saw the Great Bear as seven wolves chasing two horses, a white and a grey gelding; when the wolves catch and eat the horses, the world will end.
p.q: Не раздѣляя звѣздъ, составляющихъ Большую медвѣдицу … Киргизы говорятъ, что онѣ состоятъ изъ 7 волковъ, которые гонятся за бѣгущими отъ нихъ двумя лошадьми, Акъ-бузатъ (бѣлый меринъ) и Кукъ-бузатъ (сѣрый меринъ), и что, когда первые, догнавъ сихъ послѣднихъ, съѣдятъ ихъ, то сдѣлается преставленіе свѣта.
p.s: Aleksei Levshin (1832)
p.t: Not separating the stars that make up the Great Bear … the Kirghiz say that they consist of 7 wolves chasing two horses fleeing from them, Ak-buzat (the white gelding) and Kuk-buzat (the grey gelding), and that when the former catch the latter and eat them, the end of the world will come.
p.tg: stars great bear folklore end of the world navigation

p.h: Turks and Kipchaks versus the Kirghiz
p.g: Near Andijan, Izzet Ullah passes the spring and summer pastures of the Turks and Kipchaks, some 10,000 to 12,000 families, whom he admires as prosperous, well dressed and soldierly. He is scornful of the poorer Kirghiz. A page earlier he notes 'many Tartar stations' where herds of horses graze, and just after this he meets Kalmaks who 'are Musalmans', a surprise since most Kalmyks were Buddhist.
p.q: the adjacent country is divided into the pasture grounds of the Turks and Kapchaks… These two tribes amount here to 10,000 or 12,000 families: they are a strong good-looking people, apparently in a prosperous condition, well dressed, and of military bearing, and present a striking contrast to the Kirghizes, who are a mean-looking race, ill-fed, housed, and clothed,
p.s: Mir Izzet Ullah (translated by H. H. Wilson)
p.pe: Turks, Kapchaks (Kipchaks), Kirghiz and Muslim Kalmaks
p.c: His judgement of the Kirghiz is a townsman's prejudice.

p.h: Execution called 'sleep', and a blank space for the lord's name
p.g: Two sharp details of Mongol court manners. When writing to a superior, a Tartar leaves a gap where the lord's name belongs and writes the name out in the margin. When a man is condemned, the lord says 'cut him and make him sleep', because they do not call death death, and the condemned simply holds out his arms to be bound.
p.q: Cum scribunt suis maioribus, tantam reuerenciam habent et seruant, quod non scribant nomen sui maioris in suo loco, sed dimittunt spacium vacuum et postea scribunt nomen de foris in margine in alio loco.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1873)
p.t: When they write to their superiors they keep such reverence that they do not write their superior's name in its place, but leave an empty space and afterwards write the name outside, in the margin, in another place.

p.h: Three hundred Tartars drowned in a forced baptism
p.g: Fletcher reports that Russians offered captured Tartars their lives if they accepted baptism, but few agreed. The year after the 1571 fire, a captured Tartar noble and 300 of his men refused, and were 'baptized' by being knocked on the head and thrust into the river.
p.q: The yere after Mosko was fired by the Chrim Tartar, there was taken a Dwoymorsey, one of the chiefe in that exploit, with 300 Tartars more : who had all their lives offered them, if they would be baptized after the Russe manner. Which they refused all to doo … they were all baptized after a violent manner, being thrust downe with a knock on the head into the water.
p.s: Giles Fletcher (1591; ed. E. A. Bond, 1856)

p.h: 'Where would the rabble Tatars learn the sword?'
p.g: Ibn Arabshah gives the Ottoman sultan Bayezid a furious reply to Timur's letter. Bayezid scorns the idea that he is like 'the Tatars of the Dasht' and says Toqtamish's army was mostly treacherous: the rabble Tatars, he says, have no skill with the sharp sword and nothing but volleys of arrows, unlike the lions of Rum.
p.q: واما توقتاميش خان فان غالب عسكره خان ومن اين للتتار الطغام الضرب بالبتار الحسام وما لهم سوى رشق السهام بخلاف ضراغم الاروام
p.s: Ahmad ibn Arabshah, putting words in the mouth of the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I
p.pe: Tatars of the Golden Horde (Toqtamish's army), as seen by the Ottomans
p.t: As for Toqtamish Khan, most of his army betrayed him; and where would the rabble Tatars get striking with the keen, cutting sword? They have nothing but the showering of arrows, unlike the lions of Rum.
p.c: A speech composed by Ibn Arabshah for Bayezid, not a record of real words; useful for how the name Tatar was used as an insult.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled); vowel marks and the asterisk dividers of the rhymed prose omitted.

p.h: Horse races before a Tatar wedding
p.g: Gmelin and Müller drove out to a Tatar wedding at Sabanaka near Tobolsk. Before any wedding, he was told, riders race their horses to the bride's house for prizes put up by both families; this time they included red damask, a fox pelt, cotton cloths brought from the Kalmyk lands and a red horsehide. A few pages on, the akhun (Muslim cleric) told the groom his chief duty: not to take another wife without the consent of the one he was marrying.
p.q: Es ist dieses eine alte hergebrachte Gewohnheit bey allen Tatarischen Hochzeiten, daß viele Pferde, ehe die Hochzeit angehet, vorher dieses Schauspiel machen müssen. Und damit es allezeit Reuter und auch Leute, die die Pferde dazu lehnen, geben möge, so sind sowohl von Seiten des Bräutigams, als der Braut verschiedene Preise ausgesetzt
p.s: Johann Georg Gmelin (German original, Göttingen, 1751)
p.t: It is an old custom at all Tatar weddings that many horses must first put on this show before the wedding begins. And so that there may always be riders, and people to lend horses for it, various prizes are put up both by the bridegroom's side and by the bride's

p.h: Two horses each, and the Volga swum
p.g: After a Kalmyk raid on the Karakalpaks, Cook describes how Kalmyks went to war: bow, quiver and scimitar, at least two horses per man, herds grazing as they marched. He says he had seen thousands cross the Volga by swimming their animals, and that lame or dead horses were cut up and shared as food.
p.q: The Kalmucks in time of war are armed with a bow and a quiver full of arrows of different shapes, and a large scymitar. Every man has at least two horses … They need neither bridges nor boats to cross rivers, for I have seen thousands cross the Volga by swimming their cattle over
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.tg: war horses archery river crossing kalmyks

p.h: Brick tea, 'the grand luxury of the Tartars'
p.g: Huc explains 'Tartar tea': coarse tea leaves pressed into bricks, broken off, boiled until red, salted and mixed with milk. He says the Tartars (with the Russians) were its only consumers. Elsewhere he notes that at Urga bricks of tea served as money.
p.q: the coarser leaves, with which are mixed up the smaller tendrils, are pressed together in a mould, in the form and of the size of the ordinary house brick. Thus prepared, it becomes an article of considerable commerce, under the designation of Tartar-tea, the Tartars being its exclusive consumers, with the exception of the Russians
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: A 'mosque' of whirling, groaning devotees
p.g: Craven watched men going round in a circle in a mosque, groaning and flinging their heads to the ground until they fell senseless and were dragged into side recesses; one had lain there forty hours without food. She calls it 'mummery' and was disgusted. She also notes the tall, narrow minarets and the town's trade in coloured Morocco leather.
p.q: I went to a Mosque, where several pious Mussulmen were going round in a circle in the midst of the building, groaning and flinging their heads almost to the ground and them up again, a constant motion which with the moving round one way soon put them into a kind of torture
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.pe: Crimean Tatar Muslims (a Sufi dervish circle)
p.c: She did not understand what she saw and says so with open contempt; this was a dervish ritual (dhikr), not ordinary mosque worship.

p.h: Choosing exile rather than an oath to the Tsaritsa
p.g: Craven's host, the Russian governor, was said to have reconciled the Tatars to their new ruler by gentleness and firmness. She adds, 'to their honour', that those who could not bear to swear allegiance did not stay but left for the Caucasus, and had since repented. A rare note, from the Russian side, of the emigration that followed annexation.
p.q: I am told he has conciliated the Tartars to their change of sovereign very much by his gentleness and firmness … To their honour, I find none would stay who could not bear the idea, of taking the oaths of allegiance
p.s: Elizabeth Craven (letters published London, 1789)
p.pe: Crimean Tatars after the Russian annexation of 1783
p.c: Told her by Russian officials; she hears nothing from the emigrants themselves.

p.h: A Nogai murza's fresh grave of cut stone
p.g: Opposite the mouth of the Tashla, Güldenstädt found the new grave of a Yedisan Nogai murza buried the previous winter. Blocks of shell conglomerate, dug from the grave pit itself and squared, had been laid loose in a man-sized rectangle about three feet high. A second grave like it lay further on. It shows a living steppe people marking graves with cut stone, and on the same page he suggests the same rock could supply building blocks for the planned Russian colonies.
p.q: im vorigen Winter hier begrabenen Jedissanischen Mursa. Zu Quadersteinen gehauene Muschel-Conglomerate, die aus der Grube des Begräbnisses selbst genommen, waren in einen länglichten, der Menschengröße proportionirten Vierek, an 3 Fuß übereinander, loß gelegt.
p.s: Johann Anton Güldenstädt (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1791)
p.t: [the grave] of a Yedisan murza buried here last winter. Shell conglomerates cut into square blocks, taken from the pit of the grave itself, had been laid loose one on another, about 3 feet high, in an oblong rectangle proportioned to a man's size.

p.h: 'Kam', the Tatar word for a shaman since Rubruck's day
p.g: Comparing medieval reports with what he saw in Siberia, Fischer notes that the soothsayers Carpini and Rubruck described among the Mongols, who beat drums and went out of themselves, can still be seen among the Yakut shamans. In a footnote he adds that Rubruck's word 'Cham' for such a seer is still used by the Tatars of the Kacha, the Teleuts, and the Chulym and Baraba Tatars for their sorcerer-priests.
p.q: Rubruquis sagt Chap. 19, das wort Cham bedeute einen weißager, und alle leute von dieser sorte werden unter den Mogols Cham genannt… Dieser name ist noch heutiges tages gebräuchlich bei den Tataren am Katscha-fluß, bei den Teleuten, Tschulümern und Barabinen, und wird ihren zauberpriestern gegeben.
p.s: Johann Eberhard Fischer (Sibirische Geschichte, introduction, 1768) (footnote)
p.pe: Kacha Tatars, Teleuts, Chulym and Baraba Tatars; medieval Mongols
p.t: Rubruck says, chapter 19, that the word Cham means a soothsayer, and that all people of this sort are called Cham among the Mongols… This name is still in use today among the Tatars on the Kacha river, among the Teleuts, the Chulym people and the Baraba people, and is given to their sorcerer-priests.

p.h: Brothers sharing one wife
p.g: Explaining his population figures, Gerard notes that polyandry (several husbands for one wife) was common in Kinnaur and in 'Chinese Tartary'. His footnote adds that so many people became celibate monks and nuns that in some villages they were almost half the population.
p.q: Polyandry also exists in Chinese Tartary and in the hilly tracts towards the plains. Besides this drawback on the increase of the population, there is another peculiar to Chinese Tartary and the adjoining countries ; that is, celibacy, which is professed by numbers of the inhabitants : and in some villages the monks and nuns form almost half the population.
p.s: Alexander Gerard (footnote; ed. George Lloyd, 1841)

p.h: An oath sworn on one's marriage
p.g: Pallas, who lived in the Crimea, says the Muslim clergy quietly taught that an oath on the Koran did not bind towards an infidel. The Russian governor therefore introduced the 'Dallak' oath, by which a man who swore falsely renounced his wife, so that 'a Tartar, who has any conjugal affection, will not easily forswear himself'. Pallas adds that even this was sometimes broken.
p.q: But a more solemn form of swearing, termed Dallak, is at present, on important occasions, adopted even in Turkey, by which the person taking such oath binds himself, in case of perjury, to renounce his wife; so that a Tartar, who has any conjugal affection, will not easily forswear himself,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.c: Pallas writes as a Russian official's friend and is openly suspicious of the Tatar clergy.

p.h: A Tartar archer hits a palm-sized mark three times
p.g: While the embassy camped ashore, the Tartar escort put on a display of arms. One bowman shot three arrows in a row through a target no bigger than a hand at thirty-five paces and was paid a small coin. A small eyewitness scene that matches the Manchus' fame as archers.
p.q: The Tartars in the mean time, to show some pastime, exercised their Arms before the Tent of the Embassadours, which was performed by them with much dexterity. Amongst the rest, there was one with a Bow and Arrow, who was so rare a Marks-man, that he shot thrice together through the white, no broader then the Palm of a Hand, at the distance of thirty five Paces
p.s: Johan Nieuhof (English translation by John Ogilby, 1669)
p.pl: Guangdong, on the river north of Canton

p.h: A woman shaman of the Baraba steppe
p.g: The ambassador made a point of testing the shamans he met. In the Baraba the party visited a famous female shaman who ignored them until she had smoked, drunk brandy and received presents. She then brought out her spirit image and a ringed drum and sang with her neighbours. Bell judged her answers as ambiguous as any oracle's, and noted she was young and very handsome.
p.q: First, she brought the shaytan; which is nothing but a piece of wood, wherein is cut something resembling a human head, adorned with many silk and woolen rags, of various colours; then, a small drum, about a foot diameter, to which were fixed many brass and iron rings, and hung round also with rags.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.pl: Baraba steppe (between Tara and the Ob)
p.pe: Barabintsy, 'a mixture of different Tartar tribes'
p.c: Bell's tone is openly dismissive; he treats all shamans as frauds.

p.h: Kachin weddings and the bride who must lie flat
