p.g: Pallas reports that the Kachin Tatars, rich herders who had not taken up farming or Christianity, keep one wife, court for years, and hold two weddings. The groom's father must set up a new yurt for the couple, while the bride's father supplies the household goods. After the betrothal the father-in-law never sees his son's wife again, and if they meet she must throw herself flat on the ground until he has passed.
p.q: Die erste Hochzeit wird beym Brautvater, die andre beym Bräutigam gefeyert, wo des Bräutigams-Vater dem jungen Paar eine neue Jurte aufstellen muß… Ausser bey der ersten Freywerberey sieht der Schwiegervater seines Sohns Frau niemals wieder, geht nie in die Jurte des Sohns und geschieht es ja, daß er seiner Schwiegertochter begegnet, so will die Gewohnheit, daß sich diese platt auf die Erde niederwirft
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: The first wedding is held at the bride's father's, the second at the groom's, where the groom's father must set up a new yurt for the young couple… Except at the first wooing the father-in-law never sees his son's wife again, never goes into the son's yurt, and if he does meet his daughter-in-law, custom requires that she throw herself flat on the ground.

p.h: Dervishes 'snorting' in the Khans' mosque
p.g: For a few rubles, Webster's party had thirteen men, five of them dervishes, perform their ritual (a zikr) in the Khans' mosque. He describes the rhythmic bowing and rasping breath in comic, hostile terms, yet on the next page concedes the rite was 'civilization' next to the flagellations he had seen in Rome.
p.q: They first snorted with great fury, then bellowed as furiously; the bellow consisting of three notes, like that of a calf, or a bull. Each time they bent forward with a violent motion. The rite altogether is absolutely terrific, and must be most fatiguing.
p.s: James Webster
p.c: A paid performance for tourists, described with open ridicule.

p.h: Turkmens pray without mosques
p.g: On his first journey Wolff noted that the Turkmens had no mosques, praying alone in the open or in their tents and gathering twice a year in the desert for common prayer. He also records a claim by the Jews of Turkestan that the Turkmens descend from the biblical Togarmah.
p.q: All the Jews of Turkistaun assert that the Turkomauns are the descendants of Togarmah, one of the sons of Gomer, mentioned in Genesis x. 3. The Turkomauns have no mosque; they pray apart from each other, either in the field or the tent. Twice in the year they assemble in the desert, and prefer their prayer.
p.s: Joseph Wolff
p.c: The biblical ancestry is a Jewish tradition Wolff repeats.

p.h: Prisoners tied beneath the horses' bellies
p.g: In revenge for a Kalmyk raid, some 15,000 Karakalpaks crossed the frozen Volga, killed Kalmyk old and young and carried off the youths. Cornered by a Russian force, they broke through and fled, leaving about three hundred Kalmyk prisoners bound to horses by their feet. The Kalmyks then rode off with thousands of the Russians' own horses and camels.
p.q: they, being about fifteen thousand, made a very sudden unexpected attack upon the Russians, and actually, bravely broke through them, got over the ice, and fled to the desart, leaving about three hundred Kalmuck prisoners fixed to their horses, by tying their feet with cords to one another under the horses bellies.
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.pe: Karakalpaks, Kalmyks, Russian Cossacks and Tatars
p.c: Cook was at Astrakhan but not with the troops; numbers are reported.

p.h: A hundred thousand Kalmyks every winter
p.g: At Astrakhan Avril learned that the Kalmyks, though at peace with the Nogais, came every winter into the milder plains between Astrakhan and the Caspian to feed their herds, which were all their wealth. The Russians could not stop these visits of over 100,000 people, and paid yearly presents to prevent raids, which the Kalmyks came to treat as a duty owed.
p.q: Which Annual Visits of above a hunder'd thousand men at a time, though they Be no way pleasing to the Muscovites, however they are forc'd to suffer 'em, and not only so, but to humble themselves to that degree, as to make 'em Presents duely every year, to hinder their Incursions
p.s: Philippe Avril (English translation, 1693)
p.c: The number is a report, not a count.
p.tg: kalmyks tribute herds winter pasture russia

p.h: Tartar women with unbound feet
p.g: Crossing Beijing, the embassy noticed that most women in the watching crowds were said to be of Tartar race. Unlike Chinese women their feet were not bound, and they wore broad-toed shoes with thick soles. On the next page Staunton adds that some Tartar ladies rode on horseback astride, like men.
p.q: Among the spectators of the novel sight, some women were observed. The greatest number were said to be natives of Tartary, or of a Tartar race. Their feet were not cramped, like those of the Chinese; and their shoes with broad toes, and soles above an inch in thickness, were as clumsy as those of the original Chinese ladies were diminutive.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton

p.h: Nine months without hearing of a single lawsuit
p.g: Justice follows Muslim law: cadis judge in the towns, beys in the villages, and the khan with his council decides capital and property cases. Even the poorest Tatar or foreigner can put his case to the khan in person without lawyers or delays. Broniewski says that in more than nine months there he never heard of a criminal or civil case or a feud among them.
p.q: Extremæ enim conditionis Tartari vel peregrini homines coram Iudicibus & Chano ipso, à quo semper audiuntur, & celeriter expediuntur, iniurias suas ipsi per se liberè admodum exponunt … Mensibus amplius nouem ibi ego mansi, nec audiui prorsus aliquem actum criminalem, nec ciuilem inter eos contigisse, nec inimicitiarum causa compositionem aliquam obtigisse.
p.s: Marcin Broniewski (Martin Broniovius), Tartariae descriptio (written 1579), printed in the 1595 Cologne edition of Possevino's Moscovia
p.t: For Tartars of the lowest condition, or foreigners, set out their wrongs quite freely by themselves before the judges and the khan himself, by whom they are always heard and quickly dispatched ... I stayed there more than nine months, and never heard that any criminal or civil action had taken place among them, nor any settlement made on account of feuds.
p.c: An envoy kept under escort saw little of daily disputes; the praise also serves as a rebuke to his own society.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR garbled); long s normalized.

p.h: A leather bag of kumiss from the khan
p.g: The khan's welcome gift was practical steppe hospitality: sheep, a horse and a skin of kimiz (kumiss), fermented mare's milk, which Ibn Battuta notes was highly valued as a drink. He also explains that each of the khan's wives had her own household, and that a visitor was expected to call on every one of them.
p.q: Upon this day I was presented to the Sultan, who received me very graciously, and afterwards sent me some sheep and a horse, with a leathern bag of kimiz, which is the milk of a mare ; and very much valued among them as a beverage.
p.s: Ibn Battuta (translated by Samuel Lee, 1829)

p.h: Kalmyk women pitch the tent and saddle the horse
p.g: Pallas describes the inside of the tent, with its iron tripod over the fire and cast-iron pans bought from Russian ironworks, then the division of labour. Men only make and mend the tents; women milk, dress hides, sew, strike and raise the tent, and even saddle the husband's horse.
p.q: Die häusliche Arbeit liegt bloß dem weiblichen Geschlecht ob. Die Männer bemühen sich in nichts, als in Ausbesserung und Verfertigung der Hütten… Das Weibsvolk muß die Hütte abnehmen, alle Sachen aufpacken, und auch die Hütte wieder aufstellen. Sogar muß das Weib dem Manne das Pferd satteln und vor die Hütte führen, wenn er verreisen will.
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (Reise, first edition, St Petersburg 1771-1776)
p.t: Housework falls on the female sex alone. The men busy themselves with nothing but mending and making the huts… The women must take down the hut, pack up everything and put the hut up again. The wife must even saddle her husband's horse and lead it to the hut when he wants to ride out.

p.h: Verbal courts and savage punishments
p.g: In his closing description of the Dzungar state Unkovsky says the ruler took no great decision without his council of zaisangs, and that the court (zargo) of ten or more zaisangs judged cases orally, not in writing. Capital sentences were carried out by flogging to death or by tying limbs to horses' tails, though he adds that such executions were rare.
p.q: Суды рѣшатъ не письменно, но на словахъ. Ежели за важныя дѣла кого на смерть осудятъ: иныхъ, поставя на колѣнки, плетьми до смерти убиваютъ; иныхъ же, привязавъ къ лошадинымъ хвостамъ руки и ноги, и тако оныя лошади на бѣгу тѣмъ людямъ руки и ноги отрываютъ. Однакожъ, рѣдко у нихъ оныя казни случаются.
p.s: Ivan Unkovsky (ed. N. I. Veselovsky, 1887)
p.t: They decide cases not in writing but orally. If they condemn someone to death for serious matters, some they kneel down and flog to death with whips; others they tie by the hands and feet to horses' tails, and the horses, running, tear off those people's arms and legs. However, such executions happen rarely among them.
p.c: Part of a general summary built from inquiry, not an execution he witnessed.

p.h: A quarter of an hour to eat hundreds of roast oxen
p.g: Describing the khan's duty to join Ottoman wars with 100,000 men, Zuev reports how the Tatar army was welcomed on reaching the Turkish camp: hundreds of roasted oxen and two or three thousand sheep on spits were laid out in rows on the open field with heaps of bread, and at a cannon shot the Tatars fell on the food and ate it all within a quarter of an hour. He adds that they carried no provisions, lived on plunder in enemy country, and were cruel foes, a judgement coloured by long wars.
p.q: es wurden den Tag nach der Ankunft des Heers einige hundert gebratene Ochsen, und zwey bis dreytausend Schaafe, auf Spießen, in verschiednen Reihen, auf freyem Felde ausgestellet, und zwischen selbigen große Haufen Brod aufgeworfen; sobald alles fertig war, ward durch einen Kanonenschuß das Signal gegeben, worauf die Tatarn auf die Speisen zufielen, und selbige in solcher Geschwindigkeit verzehrten, daß in einer Viertelstunde nichts mehr übrig war.
p.s: Vasily Zuev (Sujef), 'Nachrichten von der Krim', in Neue Nordische Beyträge vol. 4 (1783), edited by P. S. Pallas
p.t: the day after the army arrived, several hundred roasted oxen and two to three thousand sheep on spits were set out in several rows on the open field, with great heaps of bread thrown up between them; as soon as all was ready, the signal was given by a cannon shot, whereupon the Tatars fell upon the food and devoured it so quickly that within a quarter of an hour nothing was left.
p.c: Hearsay about earlier campaigns, written in the year Russia annexed the Crimea; the remarks on Tatar cruelty reflect Russian hostility.

p.h: Islam arrives, idols linger
p.g: Barbaro says Islam had taken hold among the Tartars only about a hundred years before he wrote, in the time of the warlord Edigu. Before that, some were Muslims but each believed what he liked, and some worshipped idols of wood and rags carried on their carts. On another page a Tatar tells him there are still plenty of secret idolaters.
p.q: The faith of Macomett beganne to take place amonge the Tartariens about an C yeres past. In dede some of them were Macomettanes before, but everie man was at his libertie to believe what hym best liked ; so that some worshipped ymags of woode, and of ragges
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro (Tudor translation by William Thomas, c. 1550)
p.c: Historians usually date the Golden Horde's official conversion to Khan Uzbek (1313); Barbaro's timeline reflects what he was told.

p.h: Horse fairs on the Great Wall
p.g: After Altan Khan made peace in 1571, the Ming set rules for border markets: the Mongols would bring gold, silver, cattle, horses, hides and horsetail, and Chinese merchants satin, silk, cloth and iron cooking pots. Each market ran for a month, with three hundred Mongols camped outside the wall and five hundred Chinese troops guarding the marketplace. Iron pots were a key trade good because the Mongols could not easily make them.
p.q: 一立互市其規如𢎞治初北部三貢例蕃以金銀牛馬皮張馬尾等物啇販以縀紬布匹釡鍋等物開市日来者以三百人駐邉外我兵五百駐市場期盡一月
p.s: Zhang Tingyu and the Qing history office, History of the Ming (Siku quanshu Wenyuange copy, Kanseki Repository transcription)
p.t: One: establish border markets, on the model of the northern tribes' three tributes at the start of Hongzhi. The fan (Mongols) bring gold, silver, cattle, horses, hides, horse tails and such; the merchants bring satin, silk, cloth and iron pots and cauldrons. On market days three hundred of those who come are to camp outside the wall, and five hundred of our soldiers are to be stationed at the marketplace; the market lasts a full month.
p.c: A summary of the governor Wang Chonggu's proposals as quoted in the history.
p.tg: trade horse markets iron pots great wall altan khan

p.h: Karachay marriage and the 'price of blood'
p.g: Klaproth describes the Karachay as usually monogamous and unusually kind to their wives. As among other Tartars, the bride's parents receive a kalym (bride price), here called 'the price of blood'; a rich groom sends the bride a full outfit and she is brought to him at night, followed by three days of feasting and dancing.
p.q: In general they take only one wife… so that here, as among the Europeans, the wife is the companion, and not the menial servant, of the husband… Among them, as among the other Tartars, the parents, on the marriage of a daughter, receive a kalim, which is here termed the price of blood.
p.s: Julius Klaproth (English translation, 1814)
p.c: Klaproth's Karachay material came mainly from one Armenian informant.

p.h: Evening prayer at the Kaban Lake mosque
p.g: Erman was allowed into the great mosque of the Tatar quarter by Lake Kaban for evening prayer. In the entrance hall stood old gravestones dug up nearby, before which worshippers prayed in silence. Inside the plain round hall, men in white sat 'as motionless as statues' while the imam chanted the Koran; then the visitors were politely asked to leave. Erman was deeply moved by the simplicity and piety.
p.q: We entered first into a wide quadrangular hall: along the walls are placed rows of tall grave-stones, dug up in the vicinity, and set up here to perpetuate the memory of some saintly characters. The Tatars, as they came in, stood for a little time in silent prayer before these stones.
p.s: Adolph Erman (translated by W. D. Cooley, 1848)

p.h: Mongol chiefs made Knights of Malta
p.g: Near Irkutsk, Holman heard of a settlement of 'Mongul Tartars' at Tunka near the Chinese frontier, whose chiefs had been made Knights of Malta by Emperor Paul (Paul was Grand Master of the Order from 1798 to 1801). Holman doubts they could have understood the honour beyond the star and ribbon.
p.q: The Emperor Paul made some of the chiefs of these Mongul Tartars Knights of Malta! It must be difficult to conceive how these people would contemplate the nature or duties of such a creation, or appreciate the honour conferred upon them
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.c: Reported to Holman, not seen; his dismissive comment is his own. Holman puts 'Toonga' about sixty miles from Irkutsk; the identification with Tunka is ours.
p.tg: buryats knights of malta emperor paul honours

p.h: The Tatars' mocking war cry: 'John, you sleep, I tie you up'
p.g: Michalo complains that Lithuanian soldiers idle in taverns while Muscovite and Tatar frontier troops stand watch in turns, and that the Tatars mock Lithuanian carelessness with a well-known jibe: 'John, you sleep; I am binding you.' He adds that Lithuania even pays yearly gifts to the Perekop khan.
p.q: taxant hanc nostram supinam securitatem, hostes nostri Tartari, usitato suo scommate, cum nos post comessationes somno sepultos, his secum verbis invadunt: Iohannes tu dormis, ego te vinciens
p.s: Michalo the Lithuanian, De moribus Tartarorum, Lituanorum et Moschorum, fragment 8 (c. 1550; Basel, 1615)
p.t: our enemies the Tartars mock this lazy carelessness of ours with their usual jibe, falling upon us when we lie buried in sleep after our feasting, with these words: 'John, you sleep; I, tying you up...'
p.c: The jibe ends on the next page (n36, p. 30) with 'laboro' ('I am at work tying you up'); the quote stops at the page break.

p.h: Women strike the yurts and saddle the horses
p.g: Meyer lists the division of labour in a Kazakh camp. Women took down and put up the yurts, gathered fuel, milked, cooked, wove and sewed, and even saddled their husbands' horses. Men watched the herds, carved wooden goods (including the lattice frames of the yurts, as the same page says), worked as smiths and went raiding. Grain was grown only by slaves.
p.q: Die meisten Arbeiten werden von den Weibern verrichtet. Sie müssen die Jurten abbrechen und wieder aufbauen, Holz und Feuermaterial zusammensuchen, das Vieh melken, die Speisen und Getränke zubereiten, Zeuge weben, Kleider und Stiefeln nähen; ja sie müssen auch die Pferde satteln und dem Manne vorführen. Die Männer dagegen beschäftigen sich fast nur mit Bewachung der Heerden, mit Schnitzen der Holzwaaren, mit Schmieden u. s. w. und mit Räubereien.
p.s: Carl Anton Meyer (diary printed in Ledebour's Reise, part 2, 1830)
p.t: Most of the work is done by the women. They must take down and put up the yurts again, gather wood and fuel, milk the cattle, prepare food and drink, weave cloth, sew clothes and boots; indeed they must also saddle the horses and lead them to their husbands. The men, by contrast, busy themselves almost only with guarding the herds, carving wooden goods, smithing and so on, and with robbery.
p.c: A general sketch from a short stay plus informants; 'robbery' reflects the frontier Russian view of Kazakh raiding.

p.h: Kazan's Tatars: clean, honest, better farmers
p.g: Sauer found Kazan a well-built trading city of Russians, Tatars and Armenians, and at the governor's dinner on 6 January 1786 the Muslim chief priest sat at table with the Orthodox bishop and a Lutheran pastor. Riding east from the city, he praises the Tatar villagers: Muslims, clean, honest and hard-working, whose land yielded nearly twice what Russian farmers got from the same ground.
p.q: The Tartars are Mahometans, and very clean in their persons and habitations. The women are, in general, very handsome, and dress extremely neat. They are industrious, honest, and peaceable; and, under their management, a piece of ground of a given extent will produce nearly twice as much as the Russians obtain from an equal quantity. All the villages are built in vallies on the borders of rivers
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)

p.h: Tartar soldiers paid double
p.g: From a Chinese officer's figures Staunton reports that much of the cavalry was Tartar, that Tartars held the posts of trust, and that a Tartar horseman drew seven ounces of silver and twenty measures of rice a month, against three and three-tenths ounces and fifteen measures for a Chinese horseman.
p.q: Of the troops, especially cavalry, a vast number are Tartars, who have a higher pay than their Chinese fellow soldiers. The principal officers of confidence in the army are Tartars also. … A Tartar horseman, seven similar ounces of silver, and twenty measures of rice for the same period.
p.s: George Leonard Staunton
p.c: Figures supplied by the mandarin Van-ta-Zhin, whom Staunton thinks candid but not always careful.

p.h: The first kumiss of spring, and a cup that fell
p.g: Mirza Haidar's father told him of a spring feast held, by old Moghul custom, when the new kumiss (fermented mare's milk) came in. Just as the amir offered the khan a cup, news came of an envoy from Timur demanding tribute, and the cup fell from the khan's hands. The amir consoled him with verses about not grieving over tomorrow.
p.q: I have frequently heard my father (upon whom rest the mercy of God) relate that in the beginning of the spring the new kimiz had come in, and on that day, according to an ancient Moghul custom, a great feast had been prepared.
p.s: Mirza Haidar Dughlat (translated by E. Denison Ross, 1895)

p.h: Mare's-milk brandy thrown on the fire
p.g: Strahlenberg confirms, from questioning Yakuts himself, Isbrand Ides's report that at a set time of year they sprinkle a brandy distilled from mare's milk into a great fire, towards the east, as an offering to heaven. On the same page he says Yakuts wore their hair long, unlike their neighbours, and until recently buried a faithful servant alive with a dead master, a custom the Russians had forbidden.
p.q: …That, at a certain Time of the Year, they make a great Fire, into which they sprinkle a Sort of Brandy distill'd from Mare's Milk, towards the East, and thereby make an Offering to Heaven. I took an Opportunity of enquiring into the Truth of this Relation, of several of the Jakutians themselves, who all confirmed it.
p.s: Philipp Johann von Strahlenberg (English translation, 1738)
p.pe: Yakuts, a Turkic people he counts among the Tartars
p.tg: yakuts mare's milk offerings fire burial

p.h: Circassian 'fault-fines' paid in goods and slaves
p.g: During the khan's war with the Kabardians, the main text says the Circassians in the khan's own army secretly told the Kabardians to attack the Tatars by night and promised to change sides. A footnote explains a custom of the khanate's relations with the Circassians: when they committed an offence, they paid the khan a fine called 'ayiplik' in goods, slave girls and slaves. It shows tribute, law and the slave trade in the khanate's frontier politics.
p.q: چرکسلر بر قباحت ایشله دکلری زمان ( عیبلق ) نامیله خانلره قباحتلرینه کوره اموال ، جواری و کوله لر تقدیم ایدرلردی .
p.s: Editorial footnote in the Istanbul 1911 print of Halim Giray's Gulbun-i Hanan
p.t: When the Circassians committed an offence, they used to present to the khans, under the name 'ayiplik' (fault-fine), goods, slave girls and slaves according to their offence.
p.c: An explanatory footnote in the 1911 print; the custom is described in general terms without a date.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this print is garbled).

p.h: A priest flogs his Tartar guides
p.g: In a footnote Sauer tells why he calls the expedition's priest 'more than savage'. On the road to Okhotsk the priest lost some food, assumed his two Tartar guides had stolen it, and had them tied to trees and flogged so badly that one died. Runaway exiles turned out to be the thieves. The priest said no harm was done because the guides were not Christians.
p.q: On a mere supposition that his two Tartar guides had taken it, he tied each of them up by an arm to a tree, and had them flogged to such a degree, that one of them died, and the other never recovered the use of his arm: it was afterwards known, that some runaway exiles hid in the woods were the thieves.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802), footnote
p.pe: 'Tartar' guides (on this road, most likely Yakuts)
p.c: Sauer was not present; he tells it to show the priest's character. The same priest burned the Aleuts' carved masks, as Sauer reports on this page.

p.h: A Chinese picture of the far north-west: white nights and blue-eyed horsemen
p.g: The Chinese annal describing the Mongol attack on the 'tribes of the state of Kincha' (Kipchak) says the land lay 30,000 li from China, that its summer nights were so short the sun barely set before rising, that it bred fine horses, and that its people were brave, with blue eyes and reddish hair. Bichurin notes on the facing page that this is the Mongol invasion of Russia in 1237.
p.q: Лѣтомъ ночи бываютъ чрезвычайно коротки. Солнце едва закатится, и тотчасъ всходитъ. Сія страна производитъ отмѣнныхъ лошадей … Мужественны и храбры … Глаза имѣютъ синіе (голубые), волосы рыжеватые.
p.s: Tongjian gangmu (Chinese annal), translated by Iakinf Bichurin, 1829
p.pe: Kipchaks (Polovtsy) and neighbours, as described in Chinese annals
p.t: In summer the nights are extremely short. The sun barely sets and at once rises again. This country produces excellent horses … They are courageous and brave … Their eyes are blue, their hair reddish.
p.c: Second-hand Chinese geography of a land its compilers never saw; parts of the OCR on this page are illegible and were left out.
p.n: The scan's machine-read text is too damaged to confirm this quote automatically. Check it against the page.
p.tg: kipchaks white nights blue eyes rus western campaign

p.h: Kangxi kills a bear with a half-pike
p.g: Davis says the emperors Kangxi and Qianlong kept up 'the hardy and warlike habits of the Manchows' with great ring hunts north of the Wall, led by a small army with falconers. He quotes Gerbillon: Kangxi shot a bear with an arrow from across a valley, then dismounted and finished it with a half-pike 'used by the Manchows against tigers'. Davis contrasts this with the later emperors who kept cancelling the hunt.
p.q: The Emperor, upon this, alighting from his horse took a half-pike, used by the Manchows against tigers, and, accompanied by four of the ablest hunters armed in the same way, he approached the bear and killed him outright with a stab of his half-pike.
p.s: Jean-François Gerbillon, quoted by John Francis Davis
p.pe: Manchu emperors and their hunting army
p.c: A quotation from Gerbillon's journal, not Davis's own observation.
p.tg: hunting kangxi bear ring hunt manchus

p.h: Guests seized by the reins
p.g: Turkmen hospitality, Fraser was told, was so insistent that people ran out of the first tent a stranger reached, grabbed his horse and made him their guest; going on to another tent was an insult. In a footnote he warns that his informant made the tribes sound more trustworthy than they were.
p.q: When any stranger (who is not an acknowledged enemy) enters a camp, he is saluted at the first tent he approaches by its inhabitants, who run out, seize his reins, and insist on his alighting, and becoming their guest; even should the tent contain but a single
p.s: James Baillie Fraser, quoting informants
p.c: Fraser says this part came almost word for word from informants and may overstate Turkmen trustworthiness.

p.h: Frozen half-moon dumplings for winter journeys
p.g: Part 2 of Weber's work prints an account 'Of Tartarian Bukhara' by an author who says he had been in Little Bukhara himself. He notes that the men's dress differs little from the Tartar, that they eat with their fingers and wooden spoons, drink tea with milk, salt and butter, and fill half-moon-shaped pastries with chopped meat, which they freeze and carry in a sack on long winter journeys to boil into soup.
p.q: Sie füllen mit denselben eine Art Pasteten, die wie ein halber Mond gestaltet sind. Auf weiten Reisen, insonderheit in Winter, nehmen sie einen guten Vorraht von diesen Pasteten mit, und tragen sie bey sich in einem Sakke. Wenn nun diese Speise vorher an der Luft rechtschaffen durchgefroren ist, so wird sie in einem siedenden Wasser gekocht, und eine ziemlich gute Suppe davon gemacht.
p.s: Anonymous account 'Von der Tartarischen Bucharey' in Weber, part 2 (1739)
p.pe: Bukharans of Little Bukhara (Turkic Muslims of the Tarim oases, then under Zunghar rule)
p.t: They fill a kind of pastry, shaped like a half moon, with it. On long journeys, especially in winter, they take a good supply of these pastries with them and carry them in a sack. When this food has first frozen thoroughly in the air, it is cooked in boiling water, and a fairly good soup is made of it.
p.c: The author is not named; he says he had visited Little Bukhara.

p.h: Coffee-houses, hawking and a singer with a guitar
p.g: Noble Tatars love hawking and hare-hunting; in town, men spend whole days cross-legged in coffee-houses, smoking and talking. Sometimes a singer recites stories or verses to a guitar-like instrument while the listeners nod in approval. Reuilly finds Tatar song 'grave, harsh, and discordant' and describes a dance of shaking limbs with the feet barely leaving the ground.
p.q: Hawking and hunting the hare, form the greatest delight of the noble Tartars. In the towns their amusements are reduced to meeting in the coffee-houses… Sometimes a singer recites a story or chaunts verses, accompanying himself with a bad instrument, in the shape of a guitar; the assembly listens with the greatest attention, and expresses the pleasure it receives by slight motions of the head.
p.s: Jean Reuilly (English translation, 1807)

p.h: Thirty thousand Christian Alans at the Khan's court
p.g: Among the Khan's great men, Marignolli counts more than thirty thousand Alans, a people from the Caucasus whom the Mongols had taken into their service, who were Christians 'in fact or in name' and called themselves the Pope's slaves. He also explains that the peoples of the East called all Western Europeans 'Franks'. The passage shows how mixed in religion and origin the Tartar empire's elite was.
p.q: Summi eciam principes … Imperii tocius, plus quam triginta millia, qui vocantur Alani, … sunt Christiani, re vel nomine, & dicunt se Sclavos Pape, parati mori pro franquis, sic enim vocant nos, non a francia, sed a franquia.
p.s: Giovanni de' Marignolli (Latin text ed. Gelasius Dobner, 1768)
p.t: The highest princes of the whole empire, more than thirty thousand, who are called Alans … are Christians, in fact or in name, and they call themselves the Pope's slaves, ready to die for the Franks; for so they call us, not from France but from 'Franquia'.
p.c: The number is Marignolli's estimate, and he is keen to show the East as friendly to the Pope.

p.h: Sheep sacrificed to a 'volcano' in Lake Alakol
p.g: At Orenburg in 1829 Humboldt copied a caravan report from the papers of General Gens. It described a high mountain rising like an island in Lake Alakol that had once spewed fire and still caused storms that troubled caravans, so travellers sacrificed sheep to it as they passed. Humboldt believed the report came from a Tatar informant.
p.q: nous vîmes une très-haute montagne qui a autrefois vomi du feu. Présentement encore, ce mont qui s'élève dans le lac comme une petite île, occasionne des tempêtes violentes qui incommodent les caravanes : c'est pourquoi on sacrifie en passant quelques moutons à cet ancien volcan.
p.s: an anonymous caravan itinerary (Semipalatinsk to Yarkand) from General Gens's papers, quoted by Alexander von Humboldt
p.pe: caravan travellers between Semipalatinsk and Yarkand (Tatar informants)
p.t: we saw a very high mountain that once spewed fire. Even now this mountain, which rises in the lake like a small island, causes violent storms that trouble the caravans: that is why, in passing, people sacrifice a few sheep to this old volcano.
p.c: A later informant, the mullah Sayfulla, knew nothing of a fire mountain or of sacrifices to it, and said the offerings were made at a hot spring instead; Humboldt prints both versions.

p.h: A pole on a mound where a Turkmen died
p.g: Fraser records that when a Turkmen died, the body was washed on the spot and a small mound with a tree or pole was raised there, while the body itself was buried further out on the plain. He saw the plain dotted with these markers.
p.q: When one of these Toorkomans dies, they wash the body on the spot where he breathed his last, or as near it as possible; and on that spot they raise a little mound, by digging a circular trench, two or three feet wide, throwing the earth up in the centre; and in this mound they plant a tree, or pole, to mark the place.
p.s: James Baillie Fraser

p.h: Kublai Khan imports astronomers from Balkh and Samarkand
p.g: Barrow credits the Mongol emperor Kublai with welcoming learned men, especially Muslims, surveying the empire, reforming the calendar, bringing astronomical instruments from Balkh and Samarkand, and repairing the canal. He adds that after the Mongols were expelled the Chinese could not keep a correct almanac.
p.q: He caused a regular survey to be taken of the whole empire. He adjusted their chronology, and corrected the errors of their astronomical observations; he imported various mathematical and astronomical instruments from Balk and Samarcand; such as were then in use among the Chinese being of a rude construction
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: Compiled from Chinese annals and missionary writings.

p.h: Fines counted in nines of cattle
p.g: Bergmann translates the old Kalmyk law code, the 'Ssadschin Bitschik' (the Mongol-Oirat code). Penalties are counted in head of livestock, usually in multiples of nine: whoever forgets himself towards father, mother or teacher pays three nines, two nines or one nine; a daughter-in-law who wrongs her parents-in-law pays three nines and, if she struck them, is flogged. Thieves lose cattle and are flogged and branded, and anyone who turns to sorcerers must give his best horse to the informer.
p.q: Nach dem Ssadschist Bitschick zahlt derjenige, welcher sich gegen Vater, Mutter, Lehrer vergißt, nach Beschaffenheit des Vergehens, 3 mal 9, 2 mal 9, oder bloß 9 Stück Vieh. … Diebe sollen durch Verlust an Vieh, durch Geißelhiebe und Brandmal bestraft werden. Wer zu Zauberern und Zauberinnen seine Zuflucht nimmt, soll sein bestes Pferd dem Angeber hingeben.
p.s: Benjamin Bergmann, summarising the Kalmyk law code
p.w: Law code of the 17th century, translated 1802 to 1803
p.t: According to the Tsaadzhin Bichig, whoever forgets himself towards father, mother or teacher pays, according to the nature of the offence, 3 times 9, 2 times 9, or just 9 head of cattle. … Thieves shall be punished by loss of cattle, by lashes and by branding. Whoever takes refuge with sorcerers or sorceresses shall give his best horse to the informer.
p.c: Bergmann's summary of the Oirat code of 1640, not a full translation. He notes it had lost much of its force and that the Russian Kalmyks, too poor to pay the fines in cattle, used it more as a yardstick than a rule.

p.h: The Tatars' lament: no more tribute, and their camels and sugar carried off
p.g: The poet gives the defeated Tatars a lament as they flee toward the sea: they will never again see their land or children, never again raid Rus or collect the 'vykhod', the tribute Russian princes paid the Horde. The Russians have plundered their armour, horses, oxen, camels, wine, sugar and treasures. The list shows what a Horde army carried with it: herds, camels and luxury goods from trade.
p.q: Уже намъ, братіе, въ земли своей не бывать и дѣтей своихъ не видать, а въ Русь ратью намъ не хаживать, и выхода намъ у Рускихъ людей не прашивать. … уже бо Рускіе сынове разграбиша Татарскія узорочья, и доспѣхи, и кони, и волы, и верблуды, и вино, и сахаръ, и дорогое узорочіе.
p.s: Zadonshchina (Kirillo-Belozersk text), ed. I. I. Sreznevsky, 1858
p.pe: Golden Horde Tatars (as imagined by the Russian poet)
p.t: Now, brothers, we shall not be in our own land nor see our children, nor march in war on Rus, nor ask tribute of the Russian people. … for the sons of Rus have plundered the Tatar treasures, and armour, and horses, and oxen, and camels, and wine, and sugar, and costly finery.
p.c: A speech invented by the poet for the enemy; the 'vykhod' was in fact paid to the Horde again after 1382.

p.h: Where the Chuvash smear fat on the shrine
p.g: Captain Woodroofe's journal calls the Chuvash 'the poorest and most wretched of all mortals', tributary to Russia and heavily taxed. He could not learn their beliefs, but saw that they stick part of their food over doors and windows, and that when they kill an animal the priest eats some of the fat, greases himself and smears their place of worship with it. He adds that the neighbouring Tartars eat horse meat.
p.q: We could not discover what notions the chuvashins have of religion, but observed when they dress victuals, they stick part of it over their doors and windows; and when they kill an animal, … their priest takes out the fat, and after eating some of it and greasing himself, he smears over their place of worship,
p.s: Captain Thomas Woodroofe, his 1740 journal as printed by Jonas Hanway (1753)
p.pl: Middle Volga, between Moscow and Kazan

p.h: Muslim Tartars with stone crosses and Christian feast days
p.g: Cook says all the Tartars from Astrakhan to Derbent were Sunni Muslims, but he suspected many had once been Christians. They held yearly gatherings they could not explain, which he says fell on Greek Orthodox feast days, and he was told there were many stone crosses in the hills where they still met.
p.q: The Tartars from the borders of Astrachan to Derbent, are all Mahometans, of the sect of the Turks; but some things make me believe, that a majority of them had formerly professed the Christian religion. They have meetings at certain times of the year, where they divert themselves, without being able to account for the cause, any other way than that their ancestors did so before them
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.pe: 'Tartars' between Astrakhan and Derbent (Kumyks and Dagestani peoples)
p.c: Cook's inference; the crosses are reported, not seen.

p.h: Kazakhs bury their dead beside old 'Tatar' tombs
p.g: Eversmann accepts that the Kazakhs really had opened the old graves, not for treasure but to learn whether Muslims of old times lay there. Such places were holy to them, and they now buried their own dead only there, so that wherever a 'Tatar tomb' stands, Kazakh graves cluster around it. It shows how a later people claimed older monuments as part of its own sacred landscape.
p.q: Dass die Kirgisen die Gräber wirklich aufgegraben haben, ist wohl zu glauben, nicht etwa um Schätze zu suchen, sondern um zu wissen ob dort Muhamedaner aus alten Zeiten begraben lägen, denn solche Stellen sind ihnen heilig und nur dort begraben sie jetzt ihre Todten: überall wo man ein tatarisches Grabmahl findet, sieht man auch rund umher Kirgisische Gräber.
p.s: Eduard Eversmann
p.pl: Kuvandzhur stream, Kazakh steppe north of the Aral Sea
p.t: That the Kirghiz really dug up the graves is easy to believe, not in order to look for treasure, but to learn whether Muslims of old times lay buried there, for such places are holy to them and only there do they now bury their dead: wherever one finds a Tatar tomb, one also sees Kirghiz graves all around it.
p.tg: burial sacred sites islam kazakhs tombs

p.h: Why the Tartars became Muslims
p.g: Riccoldo explains the Ilkhanate's conversion to Islam from a missionary's frustrated point of view: the Tartars had neither law nor prophet, found Islam an easy law, and Muslims gave them rich gifts to convert, so that now 'for the most part' they have become Saracens. He adds that many still like Christians but find Christianity too hard and are offered no presents.
p.q: acceperunt legem, et facti sunt Sarraceni, maxime quia ipsi Tartari nec legem nec prophetam habebant. Vnde modo pro magna parte Tartari facti sunt Sarraceni. Nam et Sarraceni eos emunt et dant eis maxima dona, vt ipsi efficiantur Sarraceni.
p.s: Riccoldo of Monte Croce, Liber peregrinationis, ed. J. C. M. Laurent (Leipzig, 1864)
p.t: they took up the law and became Saracens, above all because the Tartars had neither law nor prophet. So now for the greater part the Tartars have become Saracens. For the Saracens buy them and give them very great gifts so that they will become Saracens.
p.c: A partisan explanation; the Ilkhan Ghazan converted in 1295, within Riccoldo's stay.

p.h: Tartar pilgrims from Russia, and letters from the Czar
p.g: According to Bogle, the Panchen Lama knew of only one European empire, Russia, because many of its Tartar subjects came to Tibet and the Czar had sent him letters and presents. The Lama admired Russia but could not believe it was a match for China ('Cathay').
p.q: Many of the Tartar subjects of Russia come to Thibet; and the Czar has even, at various times, sent letters and presents to the Lama.
p.s: John Stewart, relaying George Bogle
p.pe: Buddhist Tartar subjects of Russia (Kalmyks, Buryats and others)
p.c: Second hand, from Bogle's conversations with the Lama.

p.h: The Manchu script, 'more like the Greek'
p.g: Barrow describes the Manchu 'Tartar' language as alphabetic (or syllabic), inflected like European tongues, rich in B and R sounds, written in vertical columns from the left, and 'full, sonorous'. He predicted it would replace Chinese at court within a century.
p.q: the Man-tchoo Tartar character, which, if the present family continue on the throne for a century longer, will, in all probability, supplant the Chinese, or will at least become the court language. In the enunciation it is full, sonorous, and far from being disagreeable, more like the Greek than any of the oriental languages
p.s: John Barrow
p.c: His prediction proved wrong: Manchu declined and Chinese prevailed at the Qing court.

p.h: Dung fuel, millet and a whole sheep at one sitting
p.g: Crossing treeless plains, de Tott explains that the Nogais burn cakes of dung kneaded with sandy earth. He reports (as hearsay) that they had uprooted the old forests so no enemy could surprise them. Their everyday diet is millet and mare's milk, yet a Nogai could eat a whole sheep for a wager.
p.q: each family carefully collects the dung of the cattle, which they knead with a sort of sandy earth, and produce a turf which unfortunately smokes the Tartars more than it warms them. No people live more soberly. Millet and mares milk are their usual diet… A Noguais might lay a wager that he eat a whole sheep, and win his wager, without having an indigestion.
p.s: Baron de Tott (English translation, 1785)
p.c: The claim that the Nogais tore up the forests is something he was 'assured' of, not something he saw.

p.h: The Tatars' mare's-milk beer
p.g: Della Penna compares Tibetan barley brandy with 'the beer which the Tatars make from the milk of mares', which he says looks and tastes like water but is surprisingly strong. It is a passing but clear reference to Mongol distilled milk spirit (arkhi) or kumiss.
p.q: a kind of brandy (mixed with the beer referred to), which does not differ greatly from the beer which the Tatars make from the milk of mares, and which is like water in appearance and taste, but is of considerable strength.
p.s: Francesco Orazio della Penna, Capuchin missionary (English version in Markham's appendix, from Klaproth's edition)

p.h: 'Come and eat!': the Tatars poison Chinggis Khan's father
p.g: Riding home after betrothing his young son Temüjin, Yesügei passed a Tatar camp holding a feast. The Tatars called out that food was ready and invited him to eat; remembering an old grudge, they mixed poison into his food, and he died soon after reaching friends. The story turns on the steppe duty of hospitality, and it explains the lasting feud between Chinggis Khan's family and the Tatar tribe. Schmidt notes that he knew of no other source for the poisoning; the Secret History of the Mongols, published only later, tells the same story.
p.q: Unterwegs kam er in die Nähe eines Lagers der Tatar, woselbst ein Fest gefeiert wurde. Diese riefen ihm zu: «Es sind fertige Speisen da: komm und iss!» Jessugei folgte der Einladung, lenkte zu ihnen hin und stieg ab. Die Tatar, des alten Grolls gedenkend, mischten Gift unter die dem Jessugei dargereichte Speise
p.s: Sagang Sechen (1662); German translation by I. J. Schmidt (1829)
p.pe: Tatar tribe; Yesügei Baghatur, father of Temüjin (Chinggis Khan)
p.t: On the way he came near a camp of the Tatar, where a feast was being held. They called out to him: 'There is food ready: come and eat!' Yesügei accepted the invitation, turned towards them and dismounted. The Tatar, remembering the old grudge, mixed poison into the food handed to Yesügei
p.c: Told more than four centuries after the event, from Mongol tradition.
p.tg: tatar tribe hospitality poison feud yesugei

p.h: A priest who burned the idols
p.g: Wrangel reports that the Kolyma Yakuts were now all baptised. A priest named Slezzow, twenty years earlier, had destroyed every idol and pagan altar he found, by fire or water. Yet shamans still had followers and were consulted, even by Russians, to find stray animals or thieves. A footnote adds that newborn girls had once often been left in baskets hung in trees.
p.q: The Jakuti are now all baptized. A priest from Sredne Kolymsk visits these settlements every year. An ecclesiastic named Slezzow, who lived here twenty years ago, showed undaunted and unwearied zeal in the abolition of Schamanism. Wherever he discovered idols or heathen altars, they were destroyed by fire or by water, and none such are now to be met with.
p.s: Ferdinand von Wrangel (English translation by Mrs Sabine, 1840)
p.c: Wrangel approves of the conversion; the destruction he describes means few Yakut sacred objects survived to be seen.

p.h: The Tartar now fears China and pays a kind of vassalage
p.g: Discussing China's military system, Mendoza says the Chinese had fought continual wars with the Tartars for many years, 'although today the Tartar fears him so much that he thinks it good to be his friend, and acknowledges a kind of vassalage'. Even so, every city was guarded day and night as if the enemy were at the gate. This reflects the 1571 peace in which Altan Khan accepted a Ming title and tribute trade.
p.q: aunque el dia de oy le tiene el Tartaro tanto temor que tiene por bien de ser su amigo, y le reconosce vna manera de vasallaje. Y con estar al presente y de algunos tiempos a esta parte sin ocasion de guerra que sea de momento, tiene el mesmo cuidado en la preuençion que si tuuiera muchos y muy grandes enemigos
p.s: Juan González de Mendoza (Historia del gran Reyno de la China, Rome 1585)
p.t: although today the Tartar fears him so much that he thinks it good to be his friend, and acknowledges to him a kind of vassalage. And though at present and for some time past there has been no occasion for war of any importance, he takes the same care in preparation as if he had many very great enemies
p.c: Compiled from Chinese and missionary sources; the framing flatters the Chinese emperor.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: tribute vassalage altan khan ming frontier

p.h: Kumiss dried in bags under a horse's belly
p.g: Served soured milk (dhy) by the Lama of Phari, Turner compares it with the kumiss of the Tartars, made from mare's milk in the same way. He adds a hearsay detail: it is sometimes dried into chalk-like lumps, and the drying is done by hanging it in cloth bags under the horses' bellies.
p.q: The Kummuz of the Tartars is mare's milk, prepared by the same process: this is sometimes dried in masses till it resembles chalk; and is used to give a relish to the water which they drink, by solution with it. I have been told, that the operation of drying it, is sometimes performed by tying the Dhy tight in bags of cloth, and suspending it under their horses' bellies.
p.s: Samuel Turner (1800)
p.c: The drying detail is hearsay ('I have been told').

p.h: 'Fish-skin coats' and 'louse-eaters'
p.g: Walking in Peking, Bell records the insults exchanged between Chinese and Manchus. The Chinese call a Tartar 'fish-skin coat' because the Manchus of the Amur live by fishing and wear fish-skin coats in summer. It is a small but telling glimpse of how the ruling 'Tartars' of China were still seen as northern forest people.
p.q: When a Chinese and Tartar are angry at one another, the Tartar, in reproach, calls the Chinese louse-eater; and the latter, in return, calls the other fish-skin coat; because the Mantzur Tartars, who live near the river Amoor, subsist by fishing, and, in summer, wear coats made of the skins of fishes.
p.s: John Bell (Travels, 1763)
p.tg: manchus insults fish skin dress amur

p.h: Licking fingers and wiping hands on their shoes
p.g: After describing how Persians eat sitting on the ground, several from one dish, Jordanus says they lick their fingers instead of using a napkin and wipe the leftover grease on their shoes. The Tartars, western and eastern, do exactly the same, he adds; only the Indians eat cleanly, though also with their hands. A fastidious European's table report.
p.q: ligant digitos cum linguâ et labris, et mundant loco manutegnii, et posteà, si adhuc superest de pinguedine in manibus, mundant eas super calceos suos; et sic faciunt, per omnia, Tartari occidentales atque orientales, Indis exceptis, qui soli comedunt, licèt cum manibus, satis mundè.
p.s: Jordanus Catalani of Séverac, O.P. (Latin text, ed. Coquebert de Montbret, Recueil de voyages IV, Paris 1839)
p.pe: Persians and Tartars, western and eastern
p.t: they lick their fingers with tongue and lips and clean them instead of with a napkin, and afterwards, if any grease is still left on their hands, they wipe them on their shoes; and so do the western and eastern Tartars in everything, except the Indians, who alone eat quite cleanly, though with their hands.
p.c: 'ligant' is the printed spelling (for lingunt, 'lick').
p.n: OCR normalized against the page image.
p.tg: table manners eating hands persia prejudice

p.h: Shamans no better than an English conjurer
p.g: Sauer explains that shamans could be men or, more rarely, women, trained by an old master in lonely woods. He heard wonderful stories of their power even from Russians, but after watching them many times he was not impressed. He then describes a healing ritual in detail, with a horsehair switch, a sacrificed mare or cow, and a drum.
p.q: I have heard most wonderful relations of their power, even from the Russians; but, notwithstanding I have seen their enchantments or incantations many times, I never could discover any of their feats equal to that of a common conjurer in England.
p.s: Martin Sauer (1802)
p.c: Sauer's judgment reflects his Enlightenment scepticism.

p.h: 'Like wind and water': Katib Celebi on the Tatar character
p.g: Continuing from the European source, Katib Celebi describes the Tatars as steel-natured among mankind, restless as wind and water, with the strength of Ahriman and the might of demons. They roam the deserts like the wind; they neither eat bread nor build houses, their horses need neither shoes nor nails, and they cross rivers by swimming. It is the classic European literary picture of the steppe nomad, translated into Ottoman.
p.q: واوصاف تاتار بوقوم بنی نوع انسان میانه‌ده پولاد نهادلر وآب وباد کبی طبیعتلری حرکته معتاد اهرمن قوت ودیو زورلو ... ایل کبی یلرلر نه کندولر یورولور نه اتلری درلر بندکلری آته نه نعل حاجت نه میخ
p.s: Katib Celebi, Cihannuma (Muteferrika print, Istanbul 1732)
p.t: Qualities of the Tatars: this people are of steel nature among mankind, and like water and wind their nature is used to motion; they have the strength of Ahriman and the power of demons … they run like the wind; neither do they tire nor do their horses; the horses they ride need neither shoe nor nail.
p.c: A stereotype copied from European books, not observation; a few words at the line breaks are uncertain in the print.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR of this facsimile is garbled).

p.h: Kalmak Tatars moved to Ili as horse breeders
p.g: From merchants' reports Moorcroft learned that many 'Kalmak Tatars' had once lived around Khotan but had been deported by the Chinese to the Ili valley, where some 200,000 families bred cattle, camels and horses and paid one head in a hundred as tax. They brought ten to twenty thousand geldings a year to Ili for sale.
p.q: A considerable portion of the population of Khoten consisted formerly of Kalmak Tatars, but it is said that when the Chinese subjugated the province, they deported the Kalmaks to the cities which collectively constitute the modern city of Ila, on the river of the same name, and to the adjacent districts.
p.s: William Moorcroft (edited by H. H. Wilson, 1841)
p.c: Secondhand information; the population figure is a trader's estimate.

p.h: Painted wagons for the women
p.g: Pallas notes that each wealthy Tartar family on the lower Volga keeps two tents, one for guests and one for the women, and one or more covered two-wheeled chariots painted in various colours, with a chest of best clothes on the front. The women ride in them on migrations, drawn by oxen, while carts called araba carry the tents and chests.
p.q: …each wealthy Tartar family commonly has two tents, one for the reception of their visitors, and the other appropriated to their females. … they usually have one or more covered two-wheeled chariots for their wives and daughters. These chariots are painted of various colours; and on the fore-part there is commonly placed a chest covered with ornamental tapestry,
p.s: Peter Simon Pallas (English translation, 1812 edition)
p.pe: Kundure Tartars (a Nogai remnant) and Kirghiz

p.h: Berke, first Muslim khan of the Golden Horde
p.g: Batu's brother and successor Berke ('Burga'), Abu'l Ghazi says, met merchants from Bukhara on the road, was won over by their explanations of Islam, adopted it on the spot, and on his return ordered his subjects to follow. It is an early step in the Horde's move to Islam, the religion of the later Volga and Crimean Tatars.
p.q: he met upon the Road with several Merchants of Great Bucharia and falling into discourse with some of them, particularly upon the Articles of the Mahometan Faith, he was so pierced with the Explanations which these Men gave him of it, that he resolv'd off-hand to embrace that Religion
p.s: Abu'l Ghazi Bahadur Khan (English translation, 1730)
p.c: A simplified story told four centuries later. The page ends 'but he died before...', so check the next page for how far the conversion got.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image (corpus OCR for this volume is unreadable); long s normalized.

p.h: Women do all the work, men ride
p.g: Huc is blunt about the division of labour: Mongol women milk the cows, make butter and cheese, fetch water, gather and dry dung fuel, make clothes, tan skins and full cloth. The men's work is herding on horseback, which Huc calls more amusement than labour. The page opens with the Chinese nickname Tsao-Ta-Dze, 'Stinking Tartars'.
p.q: Among the Tartars, household and family cares rest entirely upon the woman; it is she who milks the cows, and prepares the butter, cheese, &c.; who goes, no matter how far, to draw water; who collects the argol fuel, dries it, and piles it around the tent. The making of clothes, the tanning of skins, the fulling of cloth, all appertains to her
p.s: Évariste Huc (translated by William Hazlitt, 1852)

p.h: The Lord's Prayer in Tartar
p.g: Schiltberger ends his book with the Lord's Prayer written phonetically in Armenian and in 'Tartar', a rare early European sample of a Turkic language as a captive heard it. It begins 'Atha wysum' ('our father').
p.q: This is the Tartar Pater Noster. Atha wysum chy chockta sen algusch ludur senung adung kel suii senung hauluchig belsun
p.s: Johann Schiltberger (translated by J. Buchan Telfer, 1879)
p.t: Roughly: 'Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name, thy kingdom come...' in a Turkic language.
p.c: The phonetic spelling is his German ear's rendering; the translation given here is a rough gloss of the opening only.

p.h: Tatar, the French of the East
p.g: Haxthausen was impressed that nearly all Kazan Tatars could read and write, that their village schools were run by mullahs, and that students went to Orenburg and Bukhara. In a footnote he claims their Turkic language worked as a common tongue from Persia to China and even Tunis.
p.q: The Tatar language occupies the same place in the East as the French in the West. Eastwards from Persia to China, westwards throughout all the Turkish countries, and even in Tunis, any one can make himself understood by means of it.
p.s: August von Haxthausen, footnote (translated by Robert Farie, 1856)
p.pe: Kazan Tatars and Turkic speakers generally
p.c: An enthusiastic generalisation: related Turkic languages were widely understood, but not one single 'Tatar' language everywhere he names.

p.h: Mourning in white: Tartar and Chinese customs compared
p.g: The general description sets Tartar mourning beside Chinese. Tartar mourners wear a long white robe down to the feet, girded with a rope, and their oldest boots, and they leave hair and beard unshaven for the whole mourning period. The next page adds that Tartar women change their usual black clothing to white.
p.q: Al de Tarters, zoo wel die van den huize, als bloed-vrienden trekken in den rou tijd een lange rok van wit laken aen, die hen tot op de voeten hangt, en met een tou of wronge van een selfste stoffe toegegort is … 't Hair van de baert noch hooft word hen in al dien tijd niet geschooren.
p.s: Olfert Dapper, compiled general description of China
p.t: All the Tartars, those of the household as well as blood relations, put on during mourning a long robe of white cloth hanging down to their feet, girded with a rope or twist of the same stuff … The hair of the beard and of the head is not shaved in all that time.
p.c: Compiled from earlier Jesuit writers, not observed by Dapper.

p.h: Two million Muslims 'from Great Tartary'
p.g: In Nanjing Careri notes that not all inhabitants are Chinese: there are many 'Moors come from Great Tartary', two million across China according to Father Grimaldi, who marry their daughters only within their own sect and so multiply 'like locusts'. The royal palace sits in a citadel held by a Tartar (Manchu) garrison that let no one in.
p.q: Gli abitanti, che sono in Nankin, non son tutti Cinesi, ma vi sono ancor molti Mori venuti dalla G. Tartaria (accertandomi il Padre Filippo Grimaldi, ch'in tutta la Cina ve ne siano due milioni), i quali han per politica di non casar le loro figlie, sol che nella propria Setta
p.s: Giovanni Francesco Gemelli Careri (Giro del Mondo, part IV, Naples 1700)
p.pe: Chinese Muslims (Hui) 'come from Great Tartary'; Manchu garrison
p.t: The inhabitants of Nanking are not all Chinese: there are also many Moors who came from Great Tartary (Father Filippo Grimaldi assuring me that in all China there are two million of them), whose policy is not to marry their daughters except within their own sect
p.c: The figure is Grimaldi's estimate; 'from Great Tartary' reflects the belief that China's Muslims came from Central Asia.
p.n: Transcribed from the page image; long s normalized.
p.tg: muslims hui nanjing great tartary garrison

p.h: Raw rhubarb stalks that grip the throat
p.g: In an appendix on rhubarb, Coxe (credited to Pallas) says the Tartars ate the leaf stalks of wild rhubarb raw, and that outsiders who tried them got a spasm of the throat at every meal until they grew used to it. A small, odd detail of steppe diet.
p.q: The stalks of the leaves are eaten raw by the Tartars: they produce upon most persons, who are unaccustomed to them, a kind of spasmodic contraction of the throat, which goes off in a few hours; it returns however at every meal, until they become habituated to this kind of diet.
p.s: William Coxe (from information supplied by P. S. Pallas)
p.pe: 'Tartars' of the Baikal region (probably Buryats or Mongols)
p.c: Which people Coxe means by 'Tartars' here is not stated.

p.h: Stuffed pumpkins: Tatar dolma
p.g: In his list of garden plants, Hablizl notes that long pumpkins grew in all the gardens and that the Tatars cooked them in many ways, most often stuffing them with meat to make the dish called dolma.
p.q: Die Tataren bereiten sie auf verschiedene Art zu Speisen, und essen sie häufig. Meistentheils füllen sie solche mit Fleisch, und verfertigen daraus das Gericht, welches man Dolma …
p.s: Karl Ludwig Hablizl (German translation, 1789)
p.t: The Tatars prepare them in various ways as food and eat them often. Mostly they stuff them with meat and make from them the dish called dolma.

p.h: Dressed 'a la Tatare' for a winter ride
p.g: Crossing eastern Turkey in deep winter, with the thermometer at 15 degrees below zero, Vigne kept warm by dressing in Tatar style: five pairs of stockings under big travelling boots. In the Ottoman lands 'Tatar' dress meant the outfit of the government couriers, which European travellers often copied (see Clarke, W032).
p.q: On the plain of Erzeroum, the thermometer, on a morning in the middle of February, fell to 15° below zero ; but I was clothed a la Tatare, with five pairs of stockings and large travelling boots drawn over them, so that I felt perfectly warm
p.s: Godfrey Thomas Vigne (1842)
p.c: Vigne does not describe the costume further; the link to the courier dress is an explanation, not his words.

p.h: Tartars and Samoyeds who keep cattle and boats
p.g: On the route down the Tura below Verkhoturye, Massa notes that the country is now inhabited by Tartars and Samoyeds who live by keeping cattle and also have boats. On the page before he mentions 'wild Tartars and Samoyeds' in the Ural forests who hunt costly furs for the Muscovites.
p.q: This place is now inhabited by Tartars and Samoyeds, who keep cattle as a means of subsistence, and have boats besides.
p.s: Isaac Massa's description of Siberia, as printed by Hessel Gerritsz in 1612 (English translation by F. J. Millard in the 1878 facsimile edition)

p.h: War booty that looked 'perfectly Tartar'
p.g: After British troops took a place held by the Bhutanese during the Cooch Behar war, the spoils sent to Calcutta included religious images in clay, gold, silver and enamel. To Stewart they looked exactly like the 'Tartar' art he knew from travellers' drawings. 'Tartar' here is a style label for Tibetan Buddhist art.
p.q: Images in clay, in gold, in silver, and in enamel, were sent down to Calcutta; all which appeared perfectly Tartar, as we have them represented in the relations and drawings of travellers; and there were besides several pieces of Chinese paintings and manufactures.
p.s: John Stewart (Philosophical Transactions, 1777)
p.tg: images buddhist art war booty bhutan

p.h: Rumour: Tatars stir the pot with a candle
p.g: Holman's Tatar servant often offered to cook for him, especially fish, but Holman refused because he had heard that Tatars stirred their cooking with a candle 'to give it gout' (flavour). He had also blamed the man's illness on the 'disgusting trash' Tatars liked to eat. The passage shows the kind of gossip about Tatars that travellers passed on without checking.
p.q: The Tartar often wanted to prepare dinner for me, particularly when fish was to be met with, but having heard that his countrymen were in the habit of stirring up their cookery with a candle in order to give it gout, I could not reconcile myself to take advantage of his culinary talents.
p.s: James Holman (1825)
p.c: Pure hearsay and prejudice; Holman never tested it. (Tallow candles were sometimes eaten as fat in Siberia, which may lie behind the rumour.)

p.h: Tartar gunpowder from Altai saltpetre
p.g: In his notes on the earthquake, Weymarn says the Altai near the Katun river is full of saltpetre that forms like cement in the rock clefts, and that the local Tartars and Kalmyks make strong gunpowder from it by a quick, simple method. It is a small but concrete detail about frontier peoples' technology.
p.q: is all full of a kind of Saltpetre, which is found in form of a cement, in great plenty, in the clefts and between the beds of rock ; with this the Tartars and Kalmucks make very strong and good Gunpowder, by an industrious, simple and expeditious method.
p.s: W. W. Weymarn (translated from the French, 1763)
p.pe: Tartars and Kalmucks of the Altai frontier
p.c: Weymarn does not say he watched the powder being made.

p.h: A hundred thousand tents on the Mughan plain
p.g: Crossing the plains near the Aras River, Cook was told that the kings of Persia bred their best horses there, and that the plains had held more than 100,000 tents of roving people 'as the Kalmucks do in Astrachan' when Nadir Shah took the throne. He passed a few of the last groups being moved to Khorasan on Nadir's orders.
p.q: these plains were formerly inhabited by roving people living in tents, as the Kalmucks do in Astrachan ; and that upwards of a hundred thousand tents were in these happy plains when Kouli Khan mounted the throne of Persia.
p.s: John Cook (published 1770)
p.pe: Nomadic tent-dwellers of Persia (compared to Kalmyks)
p.c: Reported figure.
p.tg: tents nomads mughan nadir shah deportation

p.h: Baltracan, the plant that fed travellers
p.g: In a letter to the Bishop of Padua, Barbaro describes 'Baltracan', a wild plant the Tartars depended on when crossing the steppe. When it sprouted, merchants set out saying 'Let us go, for the Baltracan has grown', and no one chased a runaway slave because he could live on it. He says he ate it himself and later found it in Albania and near Padua.
p.q: The Tartars have a plant in their country which they call Baltracan, the want of which would cause them great suffering, and prevent them from going from place to place, especially across those great deserts and solitudes, where they find nothing to eat except this plant, which supports them and gives them vigour.
p.s: Giosafat Barbaro, letter of 1491 (translated 1873)
p.c: The plant's modern identity is not given in the text.

p.h: Bashkirs who lived on soured mare's milk
p.g: On the steppe near the Yuryuzan, Georgi met Bashkirs with small herds, some with fewer than 50 horses, who lived only on soured mare's milk and were plump and cheerful. The Meshcheryak Tatars nearby did not migrate, farmed very little and in summer also lived on kumys like the Bashkirs.
p.q: Die Baschkiren hatten kleine Heerden und mancher unter 50 Pferden; doch lebten sie blos von gesäuerter Pferdemilch und waren feist und munter.
p.s: Johann Gottlieb Georgi
p.t: The Bashkirs had small herds, some fewer than 50 horses; yet they lived only on soured mare's milk and were plump and lively.

p.h: Hajj pilgrims on a Black Sea steamer
p.g: On the steamer to Odessa's quarantine, Jesse shared the deck with forty passengers including Tatars returning from the pilgrimage to Mecca. He sneers at their lack of washing but notes that they prostrated themselves constantly towards the Kaaba.
p.q: The Tartars were returning from a pilgrimage which they had made to Mecca; and though Mohammedans, did any thing but observe the ablutions recommended by their religion; but they unceasingly prostrated themselves in the direction of the Caaba.
p.s: Captain William Jesse
p.c: Openly contemptuous; the conditions were those of a crowded quarantine deck.

p.h: Alaskan arrows like those of the Tungus and Tatars
p.g: On Kayak Island Steller uncovered a covered storage pit full of smoked fish, sweet grass, bark and seaweed cord. Among the goods were arrows much bigger than Kamchatka ones, which he says came close to the arrows of the Tungus and Tatars and were so smooth and black that the owners must have had iron knives. It is a small sign of how Siberian travellers used Tatar gear as their measuring stick.
p.q: Unter diesen fand ich auch einige Pfeile, so an Größe die Kamtschatkischen weit übertrafen und denen Pfeilen der Tungusen und Tataren nahe kamen, sehr glatt geschabet und schwarz angestrichen, daß man allerdings eiserne Instrumente und Messer bey ihnen vermuthen sollte.
p.s: Georg Wilhelm Steller (ed. P. S. Pallas, 1793)
p.pe: Tatars and Tungus (as a comparison); Alaskan coast people
p.t: Among these I also found some arrows which in size far exceeded those of Kamchatka and came close to the arrows of the Tungus and Tatars, very smoothly scraped and painted black, so that one would certainly suppose they had iron tools and knives.

p.h: Tartary: herds on the hills, few houses
p.g: From the Wall it was four days' hard travel through hills and valleys to Jehol. Holmes found the country fertile and good pasture for immense herds of sheep and cattle, but thinly peopled, with only scattered houses in the valleys and no place of note until Jehol.
p.q: The country appeared fertile, though so rugged, and afforded good pasturage for immense herds of sheep and bullocks. It was but thinly peopled; here and there a few scattered houses in
p.s: Samuel Holmes (diary printed 1798)
p.c: The sentence continues on the next page ('the vallies, but no place of note till we entered Gehor').

p.h: Plundered by the Kaitaks, 'a Tartar tribe'
p.g: After a storm wrecks one of their boats on the Caspian shore, Nikitin's party is seized and robbed by the Kaitaks near Tarki. The Shah of Shirvan then negotiates with the Kaitak prince, his brother-in-law, for their release. The footnote labels the Kaitaks a Tartar tribe of Daghestan, an example of how widely the label was stretched.
p.q: A storm having arisen at sea, the smaller boat was wrecked on shore. Then came the Kaitaks and made the whole party prisoners, and we came to Derbend
p.s: Afanasy Nikitin (translated by Count Wielhorski, 1857); tribe identified in editorial footnote
p.pe: Kaitaks (called a Tartar tribe by the editor)
p.c: The Kaitaks of Daghestan were a Caucasian people; 'Tartar tribe' is the 1857 note's label, not Nikitin's.

p.h: Mongol middlemen in the smuggling trade
p.g: In a footnote on the Russian crown's monopoly of the Beijing caravans, Lesseps says private merchants soon slipped free of it by trading secretly with China through Mongol Tartars, who charged them dearly for their services.
p.q: Les particuliers ne tardèrent pas à se dégager des entraves tyranniques du monopole impérial; ils parvinrent à entretenir des relations secrètes en Chine par la voie des Tartares Mongols; qui leur vendirent cher leur entremise.
p.s: Jean-Baptiste Barthelemy de Lesseps (footnote)
p.t: Private traders soon freed themselves from the tyrannical shackles of the imperial monopoly; they managed to keep up secret dealings with China through the Mongol Tartars, who sold them their services dearly.

p.h: Are Tartars really great horsemen?
p.g: Told that the emperor loves hunting and excels with the bow, Ellis adds a footnote: the missionaries praise Tartars as superb horsemen, but judging by the horses he saw, he doubts they could manage fast manoeuvres.
p.q: The account of the Missionaries represent the Tartars as excellent horsemen, and that the arts of the manege are various, and much attended to. I had no opportunity of verifying the truth of this description; from the appearance of the horses I should doubt their being equal to rapid manoeuvre.
p.s: Henry Ellis (footnote)
p.c: Ellis admits he could not check the missionaries' claim.

p.h: Iron for the Mongols, copper knives for the Tatars
p.g: Steller reasons that the Itelmens must have left the mainland very long ago because they knew no metals at all, whereas the Mongols had used iron for weapons and household goods, and the Tatars copper for knives and daggers, for more than 2000 years. The statement shows how he pictured the steppe peoples as ancient metal-workers.
p.q: der Gebrauch und die Materie des Eisens unbekannt ist, wie auch der übrigen Metalle, ohnerachtet denen Mungalen der Gebrauch des Eisens zu Gewähr und Haußgeräthen, so wie denen Tataren der Gebrauch des Kupfers zu Messern und Dolchen, schon mehr als vor 2000 Jahren bekannt ist
p.s: Georg Wilhelm Steller (ed. J. B. Scherer, 1774)
p.pe: Mongols and Tatars (as Steller imagines their ancient past)
p.t: the use and substance of iron is unknown [to the Itelmens], as are other metals, although the use of iron for weapons and household goods has been known to the Mongols, and the use of copper for knives and daggers to the Tatars, for more than 2000 years
p.c: An unsupported general claim; Steller gives no source for the 2000 years.

p.h: Princes of Tartar origin
p.g: Among his hosts in Kazan were Prince Davydov, head of the post, and Prince Tenishev, an army general; Cochrane notes that both princes were 'of Tartar origin'. He then explains that Russian titles of Tatar or foreign origin did not by themselves give noble rank. The passage is a reminder that many Russian noble families traced their roots to Tatar ancestors.
p.q: Both the princes are of Tartar origin, though their character and conduct would do honour to the proudest rank of polished society.
p.s: John Dundas Cochrane (1824)
p.c: The 'though' reflects Cochrane's prejudice.
